fix(env-check): atomic .env rewrite falls back to in-place on Docker (#1394)

Reported by @aravindgandavadi on a Docker deployment via
install-docker-multi-custom-ssl.sh:

  [OpenAlgo Fernet salt] Could not write FERNET_SALT to .env
  ([Errno 13] Permission denied: '/app/utils/../.env.tmp').

The migration is using the standard tmp-file-then-rename atomic-write
pattern. Two compounding issues kill it inside the container:

1. /app is root-owned (mode 755). The Dockerfile does
   `COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . .` which chowns the *contents* of /app,
   but /app itself was created by `WORKDIR /app` and stays root-owned.
   appuser can read/execute /app but cannot create new files in it
   (EACCES on the .env.tmp open).

2. .env is a single-file bind mount (`./.env:/app/.env` in the generated
   docker-compose.yaml). Even with /app writable, .env lives on the host
   filesystem while .env.tmp lives in the container's overlay FS.
   rename(2) refuses to span those mount points and returns EXDEV/EBUSY,
   so the atomic pattern fundamentally cannot work for any Docker user
   regardless of permissions.

Fix in two layers:

* utils/env_check.py: _atomic_replace_text now detects EACCES, EPERM,
  EXDEV, EBUSY (POSIX) and falls back to an in-place rewrite — open the
  destination directly, truncate, write, fsync. Not crash-atomic in the
  strictest sense (a kill -9 mid-write could corrupt .env), but
  acceptable for a config file written once at startup, and the only
  viable path for Docker bind-mounted single files. _atomic_rewrite_dotenv
  now delegates the file-write step to _atomic_replace_text so both
  helpers share the same fallback policy.

* Dockerfile: chown /app itself (not just its contents) to appuser so
  fresh installs avoid EACCES entirely. The Python fallback still
  protects against the bind-mount EXDEV case which Dockerfile changes
  cannot fix.

Existing affected deployments recover via:
  cd <instance-dir>
  git pull
  docker compose down && docker compose up -d --build

The first boot under the new code falls into the in-place-rewrite path
(EACCES on /app/.env.tmp → fallback writes .env directly → DB migration
proceeds normally, FERNET_SALT lands adjacent to API_KEY_PEPPER as
designed). DB rows haven't been touched since the migration aborted
before any DB pass on the previous boot, so no data loss.

Verified with synthetic fixtures covering each error case:

  Test 1 PASS: normal atomic-rename path works
  Test 2 PASS: EACCES on parent dir → in-place rewrite fallback works
  Test 3 PASS: tmp file cleaned up after successful rename
  Test 4 PASS: EXDEV (Docker bind-mount) → in-place rewrite fallback works

Plus end-to-end on the live .env:
  Migration banner: False  (idempotent fast-path skip — already provisioned)
  DB readable: True        (existing FERNET_SALT preserved, decrypt OK)

fix(env-check): degrade gracefully when .env is unwritable + pin Docker UID 1000 (#1394)

@aravindgandavadi reported the previous fix (a1455ff1) didn't help his
deployment — even with the EACCES/EXDEV/EBUSY fallback to in-place
rewrite, his container still crashes with:

  [OpenAlgo Fernet salt] Could not write FERNET_SALT to .env
  ([Errno 13] Permission denied: '/app/utils/../.env').

Note the path: not '/app/.env.tmp' (which the previous fix handled) but
'/app/.env' itself — the bind-mounted host file is unwritable from the
running appuser. That happens when:

* The Dockerfile's `useradd --create-home appuser` lets the system pick
  a UID. On most base images this lands on 1000, but ARM64 builds with
  pre-existing system users at low UIDs can land elsewhere. The install
  scripts chown the host's .env to UID 1000:1000 mode 600, so a UID
  mismatch silently locks appuser out of writes through the bind mount.

* The host's .env happened to get chowned to root or another user
  (sysadmin running install.sh as the wrong user, restored backup, etc).

Two changes:

1. **Make the migration non-fatal.** Three .env-write paths in
   _ensure_fernet_salt previously called sys.exit(1) on OSError. They
   now log a warning via _warn_fernet_write_failed and return. auth_db's
   _resolve_fernet_salt already falls back to b"openalgo_static_salt"
   when FERNET_SALT is missing or invalid, so the app boots and runs
   normally with the legacy security posture. The per-install salt
   rotation is *deferred* until the operator fixes permissions — but
   service is preserved.

   This is a deliberate trade-off: the static-salt vulnerability is real
   but not exploitable from a clean network position. Bricking the app
   to force the fix is worse than running with deferred security.

2. **Pin appuser UID/GID to 1000 in the Dockerfile.** Adds an explicit
   `groupadd --gid 1000 appuser && useradd --create-home --uid 1000 ...`
   so fresh container builds always have UID 1000, matching the install
   scripts' `chown 1000:1000 .env` on the host. Existing installs need
   `docker compose down && docker compose up -d --build` to pick up the
   new image.

Existing affected deployments recover with `git pull && docker compose
up -d --build`. The first boot under this code:

  - falls into Case D (no FERNET_SALT line in .env)
  - tries _atomic_replace_text which now hits in-place rewrite fallback
  - in-place rewrite fails with EACCES → _warn_fernet_write_failed runs,
    function returns
  - auth_db sees FERNET_SALT unset → uses legacy static salt
  - app boots normally, all stored credentials remain decryptable
  - one-time warning in stderr explains the deferred rotation and
    common Docker fixes (UID mismatch, host .env permissions)

Once the operator fixes the host-side .env permission, a restart picks
up the migration cleanly.

Verified non-fatal path with an unwritable directory + readonly file
fixture — function returns without sys.exit, FERNET_SALT stays unset,
auth_db falls back to legacy static salt, DB decryption continues.

   owned) is obsolete — every install script now does
   `chown 1000:1000 .env && chmod 600`, and the Dockerfile pins appuser
   to UID 1000, so 600 is owner-readable inside the container without
   needing world-read. Expected mode is now 0o600 on every platform.

   un-migrated because it was encrypted under a salt that was already
   lost — see #1394's user log), every WebSocket reconnect attempt fired
   the same error, spamming hundreds of identical entries into
   errors.jsonl. Now the function fingerprints the failing ciphertext

   WS even though new credentials were correctly written to the DB.
   Production runs gunicorn -w 1 (single worker per CLAUDE.md), so the
   registry lives in the very same process as upsert_auth — a direct
   in-process call is correct and minimal. The existing ZeroMQ
   publish_all_cache_invalidation publish stays for hypothetical
   multi-process futures.

4. blueprints/admin.py adds _secret_strength_status() which surfaces
   per-secret randomization status:
     APP_KEY randomized       → not in COMPROMISED_APP_KEYS
     API_KEY_PEPPER randomized → not in COMPROMISED_PEPPERS

   Rendered in the markdown system report and the React Diagnostics
   page (with destructive-variant badge when False) so operators can
   see at a glance whether they skipped install.sh and copied
   .sample.env directly. Requested by @aravindgandavadi in #1394.

psutil.wait_procs internally calls select.poll(), which eventlet's
monkey-patched select module does not expose on Linux. Under the

* fix(paytm/ws): close file-descriptor leaks in streaming layer

Eliminates a set of FD-leak paths in the Paytm WebSocket integration
that could orphan sockets or pin reconnect threads under load.

PaytmWebSocket (broker/paytm/streaming/paytm_websocket.py)
- Move `wsapp`, `subscriptions`, `RESUBSCRIBE_FLAG` from class-level to
  instance state. The previous class-level dicts were shared across all
  PaytmWebSocket instances and replayed one user's subscriptions onto
  another's socket on reconnect.
- Remove the recursive `close_connection() + connect()` retry from
  `_on_error`. It ran inside `run_forever()` on the WS thread and
  re-entered a second `run_forever()` while the old WebSocketApp's
  socket was still being torn down. Reconnect is now owned solely by
  the adapter.
- Drop the now-dead `max_retry_attempt` / `retry_delay` /
  `retry_multiplier` / `current_retry_attempt` fields (and constructor
  params) — nothing references them anymore.
- Add `ping_timeout=10` to `run_forever()` so half-open sockets (server
  silently drops TCP) are torn down instead of pinning an FD forever.
- Switch SSL to `ssl.CERT_REQUIRED`. Paytm's WSS endpoint serves a
  valid DigiCert / GeoTrust wildcard cert; there's no Paytm-specific
  reason to skip verification.
- Wrap `wsapp.close()` in try/except and null `self.wsapp` in finally
  so a close-time exception doesn't skip the rest of the shutdown
  sequence and stale references can't `send()` on a closed socket.

PaytmWebSocketAdapter (broker/paytm/streaming/paytm_adapter.py)
- Funnel both `connect()` and `_on_close`-driven reconnects through a
  single `_start_reconnect()` gated by a `_reconnecting` flag, so at
  most one `_connect_with_retry` thread runs at a time. Previously two
  reconnect paths could race and orphan WebSocketApp sockets.
- Rewrite `_connect_with_retry` as the sole owner of the
  `ws_client.connect()` lifecycle. On each return, treats long-lived
  connections (>=30s) as a recovery (reset backoff) and short ones as
  a failed attempt (exponential backoff). `_on_close` no longer spawns
  parallel reconnect threads.
- Make the retry-backoff sleep interruptible via `_shutdown_event`, so
  `disconnect()` doesn't have to wait out a 60s nap before the thread
  exits.
- `disconnect()` now joins the reconnect thread (10s timeout) before
  releasing ZMQ, and is idempotent via `_disconnected` so atexit can't
  double-call `cleanup_zmq()`.
- Register `atexit.register(self.disconnect)` in `initialize()` (once,
  guarded by `_atexit_registered`) so ZMQ + WS cleanup runs even on
  unhandled-exception or `sys.exit()` paths.
- Extract `_teardown_ws_client()` helper. Re-`initialize()` calls (e.g.
  account switch) now tear down the previous `ws_client` before
  replacing it, instead of leaking its WebSocketApp and reconnect
  thread for the duration of the old ping_timeout window.

* fix(iiflcapital/ws): close file-descriptor leaks across reconnect cycles

Audit of the new IIFL streaming layer surfaced four FD/handle leaks that
compound across reconnects. Verified via mock-broker regression — 9
scenarios x up to 50 cycles each, per-cycle delta is 0 handles / 0 threads.

* connect() partial-failure leak: any exception after wrap_socket() — a
  failed _send_connect(), a CONNACK read timeout, or a malformed CONNACK —
  left the TLS socket open. Caller would just retry and create a new one.
  Now the post-wrap setup is wrapped in try/BaseException that closes the
  FD before re-raising.

* Broker-FIN leak: when the broker closes the connection mid-session, the
  reader loop exits cleanly via MqttError but never closes self._sock —
  the FD sat in CLOSE_WAIT until garbage collection (one FD per reconnect).
  Reader's finally now closes the socket and also sets _stop_event so the
  keepalive thread wakes immediately instead of blocking another
  keepalive/2 seconds. Without the event wake, the keepalive thread plus
  its kernel handles leaked for up to 10s after each disconnect.

* Reconnect race: _reconnect_loop only checked running / _stop_event
  before the backoff sleep, not after. stop() called between the wait and
  the connect call would still open a new socket. Now re-checks state
  after the sleep wakes.

* Adapter re-init: initialize() called twice without an intervening
  disconnect() (issue #765 force-reinit pattern) replaced ws_client
  silently. The previous client's reader and keepalive threads were kept
  alive by their captured `self` reference, so neither the threads nor
  their TLS socket were ever reclaimed. initialize() now stops and nulls
  any existing ws_client before creating the new one.

* fix(websocket): self-heal pool on stale auth-token failure (#1419)

When a broker adapter returns or raises an auth error (401/403/token

* fix(websocket): spawn WS proxy as subprocess under gunicorn+eventlet (#1421)

In-process WS+Flask under eventlet shares one process with the eventlet
hub, so monkey-patched stdlib semaphores touched from both the hub and
the WS asyncio thread (logging RLock, socket.io lock, broker adapter
threading.Lock) trigger "greenlet.error: Cannot switch to a different
thread" and silently corrupt WS state.

Detect eventlet at runtime via is_monkey_patched("socket"). When active,
spawn `python -m websocket_proxy.server` as a child process with no
monkey-patching, so all locks are real OS primitives. Atexit handler
SIGTERMs with SIGKILL fallback; child stays in the gunicorn cgroup so
systemd reaps it on hard crash. Dev-server path (no eventlet) unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(websocket): preserve subscriptions across auth-recovery rebuild

_attempt_auth_recovery() calls initialize(force=True) which clears
subscription_map, so the prior recovery flow restored only the one
symbol that triggered it and silently dropped every other previously
subscribed feed. Snapshot the (symbol, exchange, mode) keys under lock
before the rebuild and re-issue each via _subscribe_inner() after the
reconnect succeeds.

depth_level isn't tracked in subscription_map, so mode=3 restores use
the default depth (5) — flagged in the comment.

subscribe() retry path retained the cached FyersAdapter (with its stale
access_token) instead of rebuilding it. Combined, the ConnectionPool
self-heal had nothing to match on and couldn't refresh the token.

fix(auth): revoke broker token at daily session rollover to fix dead WS next morning (#1419)

The 3 AM IST session auto-expiry preserved the DB broker token
(revoke_db_tokens=False, from 5ee939ff8 "decouple web session expiry from
API token revocation"). But Indian broker tokens are invalidated broker-side
at the daily rollover, so the preserved token is dead. On the next manual
login, _try_resume_broker_session saw a present, non-revoked token, passed a
narrow REST funds check, and skipped broker OAuth — rebuilding the WebSocket
adapter with the dead token. Result: persistent 403 "Authentication failed"
on the feed until a container restart forced a real re-auth.

Manual logout already revokes the DB token (is_revoked=True), which is why the
issue only bit users who closed the browser instead of logging out. This makes

fix(broker/ws): read fresh token on (re)connect + self-heal Zerodha auth failures (#1419)

Two gaps remained after 340010ca/3f167e23a, both surfacing only under Docker,
where the WS proxy runs as a SEPARATE process with its own auth cache (synced
only by a best-effort ZMQ broadcast). A cached token read in that process can
hand back yesterday's dead token after the ~3 AM rollover.

Part 1 — bypass the cache on every (re)connect token read (32 sites, 28
adapters). All get_auth_token() reads in streaming adapters/clients build or
rebuild a broker WS connection, so they now pass bypass_cache=True and read the
current token straight from the DB. This includes reconnect-path reads that
340010ca missed — notably Kotak's _recreate_ws_client (kotak_adapter.py:729),
which re-read the STALE cached token on every reconnect and so looped forever
after the rollover (never picking up the post-login token; reported on #1419).
Same gap fixed in shoonya/samco/angel reconnect reads.

Part 2 — Zerodha self-heals on auth failure instead of dying on the first 403.
Previously _mark_fatal_error stopped the client immediately, so the reconnect
loop broke BEFORE reaching _refresh_access_token() — the bypass_cache refresh
340010ca added was dead code for the exact failure (403) that occurs. Now the
loop re-reads a fresh token from the DB and retries up to 3 times, giving up
only if a genuinely fresh token still fails or the DB token is unchanged (so we
never hammer a known-bad token). This mirrors what Upstox already does (no auth
short-circuit), which is why Upstox recovered and Zerodha did not.

bypass_cache reads once per (re)connection — negligible cost, strictly more
correct. Crypto/24-7 brokers (deltaexchange) included for consistency; harmless
since they have no daily rollover.

fix(broker/ws): feed data-stall watchdog from ping/pong so it stops false-firing (#1419)

The data-stall watchdog force-reconnects when no data arrives for DATA_TIMEOUT
(90s). That clock was advanced only by inbound market data, so on brokers that
send no application heartbeat the clock froze whenever the market was quiet or
closed — tripping a needless reconnect loop every 90s (and, after the
per-reconnect token/URL refresh, re-hitting the authorize endpoint each cycle).
Zerodha never showed this because Kite sends a 1-byte heartbeat that keeps its
identical watchdog satisfied.

Feed the liveness clock from the WebSocket protocol pong (and server ping),
mirroring Kite's heartbeat — the watchdog now fires only when the socket is
genuinely dead (no data AND no pong), with no market-hours/clock logic:

- upstox: add on_ping/on_pong stamping _last_message_time at both connect sites.
- fyers HSM: enable ping_interval/ping_timeout on run_forever (it had NO
  keepalive at all) and add on_ping/on_pong stamping _last_message_time.

perf(db): enable WAL + synchronous=NORMAL for all SQLite connections

All six databases ran in default rollback-journal mode: every commit a
full fsync, and writers block readers — the root cause of the
database-is-locked errors documented in CLAUDE.md troubleshooting.

A process-wide SQLAlchemy Engine connect listener in database/__init__.py
now applies PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL and synchronous=NORMAL to every
SQLite connection, regardless of which module created the engine (the
package __init__ runs before any database.<module> import, so no engine
escapes it). Non-SQLite backends (PostgreSQL, DuckDB) are untouched.
Pragma failures are swallowed so a locked first-time conversion can
never break a connection.

Validated: openalgo.db, latency.db, logs.db, sandbox.db and health.db
all report journal=wal synchronous=NORMAL through their live engines.

fix(socket): share one Socket.IO connection per tab (fixes multi-tab hang)

Root cause (architectural): the dev server runs Flask-SocketIO with
async_mode="threading", so the frontend forces long-polling
(transports:['polling'], upgrade:false). Each Socket.IO client then holds a
persistent HTTP connection, and the browser's ~6-connections-per-host limit is
shared across ALL tabs of a profile. Every useOrderEventRefresh opened its OWN
connection (on top of the global SocketProvider one), so 2 sockets/tab × multiple
tabs exhausted the pool — navigation/data requests queued and the app hung
(the "second session hangs / same tab hangs" report).

exposed by SocketProvider/useSocket (it only attaches/detaches its event listeners
and never disconnects the shared socket). One Socket.IO connection per tab instead
of N — multiple tabs no longer exhaust the browser connection pool.

fix(whatsapp): marshal wars callbacks off the eventlet hub to prevent freezes (#1515)

wars fires its callbacks (on_message/on_disconnect, and on_qr/on_pair_code
during pairing) from its own native tokio OS threads, never from a greenlet.
Under gunicorn's eventlet worker, performing any eventlet-monkey-patched
operation from those threads (SocketIO emit, the DB session, a green
Event/Queue wait) poisons the single eventlet hub with
"greenlet.error: Cannot switch to a different thread" and hangs the whole
worker (#1479).

Fix: the callbacks now only append raw primitives to a thread-safe deque
(atomic under the GIL, no green primitive). The bot-loop greenlet drains the
deque and performs all green work on the hub. Pairing polls is_connected()
on its own greenlet (time.sleep yields under eventlet) and drains the
QR/pair-code events there, instead of emitting from the tokio callback thread.

fix(definedge): anchor intraday history end-time to IST to stop data lag on non-IST hosts

Definedge's /sds/history endpoint ignores the 'to' boundary and returns all
candles up to the latest available, so get_history() clips client-side with
df[timestamp] <= to_date. For end_date == today, to_date was pd.Timestamp.now()
(server-local wall-clock) compared against naive-IST candle timestamps.

On a UTC/non-IST deployment now() is ~5.5h behind IST, so the clip silently
dropped the most recent ~5.5h of candles (e.g. intraday data stopping at ~09:30
when it is really 15:00 IST). On an IST host it happened to work, masking the bug.

Fix: anchor 'now' to IST wall-clock via pd.Timestamp.now(tz='Asia/Kolkata').tz_localize(None)
so the clip is correct regardless of host timezone. Broker-only change.

fix(tradesmart): throttle data API to 120/min cap with retry on rate-limit

TradeSmart (Noren) caps data APIs at 120 requests/min per user, but the
shared limiter ran at 0.12s/req (~500/min), so a burst of quotes — e.g. a
90+ symbol option chain or the OI tracker fetching futures + chain — tripped
"Order Recieved N in a current minute exceeds Limit 120 for user" and failed.

Match the Flattrade reference: raise TRADESMART_MIN_REQUEST_INTERVAL to 0.55s
(~109/min) so the single module-global gate keeps the whole app — quotes,
option chain, OI tracker, scalping, history — under the ceiling, and add
_is_rate_limit_error + exponential-backoff retry (3 attempts) in
_get_api_response so a transient overflow degrades to slower-but-successful
instead of erroring out. Genuine errors and the "no data" empty-result path
are unaffected.

fix(websocket): make ZMQ bus fan-in (SUB binds, PUBs connect) so ticks flow under gunicorn+eventlet

Under gunicorn+eventlet the WS proxy runs out-of-process (a subprocess on
bare-metal install.sh, a separate `python -m websocket_proxy.server` on Docker
start.sh) while the cache-invalidation publisher runs in the gunicorn process.
Both created a SharedZmqPublisher that BOUND ZMQ_PORT (5555). Being a
per-process singleton, the two binders raced: the gunicorn process won 5555 on
login, the WS process's market-data publisher fell back to 5556 via the bind
port-scan, while the proxy SUB stayed fixed on 5555. Result: auth + subscribe
succeeded but no market_data ticks were ever delivered. It worked on the
single-process dev server (one binder) and broke only on eventlet servers, which
made it hard to spot. The break is in shared ZMQ plumbing, so it is broker-agnostic.

Flip the topology to fan-in: the proxy SUB is the sole binder and every publisher
CONNECTs to it (many PUB connects to one SUB bind is valid ZMQ). Remove the
port-scan / 5556 fallback and the runtime os.environ["ZMQ_PORT"] mutation, so
ZMQ_PORT is fixed by config and never drifts (5555 single-instance, 5555+i-1 per
instance under install-multi.sh). Add the missing ZMQ_PORT default on the SUB bind.

Applies to all deployment modes: dev thread, install.sh subprocess, Docker
start.sh, and install-multi.sh. Documented the invariant in CLAUDE.md so it is
not reintroduced.

Verified with a fan-in smoke test: PUB-connect -> SUB-bind delivers data on the
configured port; connect()/cleanup() are idempotent.

fix(auth): don't tear down shared broker WS feed on multi-session login (#1591)

A second device/browser logging in resumes the existing broker session and
re-persists the SAME token via upsert_auth(). upsert_auth() unconditionally
published a ZMQ CACHE_INVALIDATE_ALL (the out-of-process proxy disconnects the
broker adapter + pool) and called cleanup_pools_for_user() in-process — tearing
down the single shared broker WebSocket feed that the already-connected first
device was using. Symptoms: Shoonya ticks stop until a page refresh; Flattrade's
single-active-session Noren backend drops the token ("broker session expired").

That teardown is only correct for a genuine token change (real login, daily ~3 AM
rollover, logout/revoke — the #1394/#765/#851 fix). Gate it: compare the new
token/feed-token/broker/revoke flag against the stored row (decrypted plaintext —
Fernet ciphertext is non-deterministic), and on an unchanged session clear the
cheap in-process caches and return early, leaving the live feed up. Multiple
devices share one server-side feed by design, so both now stream simultaneously.

- database/auth_db.py: token-change detection gates ZMQ publish + pool cleanup
- test/test_auth_upsert_multisession.py: 5 regression cases
- CLAUDE.md: document the shared-feed multi-session invariant

fix(auth): don't let a stale cookie revoke another device's fresh token at rollover (#1591 audit #1)

The daily ~3 AM IST expiry path (app.py before_request / check_session_validity
-> revoke_user_tokens(revoke_db_tokens=True)) revoked the single shared broker
token based only on the CURRENT cookie's login_time. In a multi-device setup,
a device left idle overnight would, on its first request after the rollover,
blindly revoke a token that ANOTHER device had already re-established that
morning — kicking the fresh device and collaterally killing API-key/webhook
access (is_revoked invalidates get_auth_token_broker).

for a session that authenticated at/after today's rollover boundary. If one
exists, the shared token is fresh, not stale — suppress the global revoke + ZMQ
cache-invalidation (which would also tear down the fresh device's WebSocket feed)
+ clear_user_sessions + force_logout, and instead drop only this stale device's
own session row. The normal rollover (all sessions stale) still revokes and
force-logs-out as before, preserving the #1419 fix.

fix(latency): stop dict-typed error crashing the latency logger

A failed data/order API request (e.g. /history called without apikey)
returns marshmallow validation errors as a dict in the response
"message". track_latency forwards that message to
OrderLatency.log_latency as `error`, but the error column is a String,
so SQLite raises "Error binding parameter 14: type 'dict' is not
supported" and the latency row is lost.

at the storage boundary in log_latency, so the one fix covers all
latency-tracked endpoints. The request itself still returns HTTP 400
with the field errors; only the async latency record changes.

Arrow's ds.arrow.trade server tracks client liveness via an application-level

- drop ping_interval/ping_timeout from run_forever

fix(fyers): return empty funds on error instead of fabricated zeros

broker/fyers/api/funds.py's get_margin_data() returned a fabricated
zero-balance dict (availablecash "0.00", collateral "0.00", …) on every
error path — including HTTP 401 for an expired/invalid daily token. That
makes an expired session look like a live, zero-balance account: callers
that treat a funds success as "session live" are misled, and an expired
token is reported as healthy.

Return {} (empty) on error instead of fabricated zeros. A genuinely empty
account still returns real zeros via the normal success path, so this only
changes the ERROR path. The one exception preserved is a transient 429
rate-limit, where serving genuinely-cached real data (with backoff) stays
correct.

This pairs with #1597 (treat empty broker funds as an error, not success):
returning {} lets funds_service surface the invalid/expired session instead
of masking it as a zero-balance success.

fix(orders): warm ZMQ publisher at boot — first order event was dropped under gunicorn

Under gunicorn+eventlet the market-data adapters run in the websocket_proxy
subprocess, so the Flask process' SharedZmqPublisher connected lazily on the
FIRST order event — and a fresh ZMQ PUB drops messages sent before the
PUB<->SUB handshake settles (slow-joiner), silently losing that event. The
dev server never hit this because in-process market-data adapters warm the
same singleton at startup.

Fix: connect the publisher in the order-update boot thread, plus a one-time
250ms settle on any cold-connect in the relay subscriber. Verified on a
fresh gunicorn+eventlet instance: the very first order event now reaches
subscribe_orders clients through the out-of-process proxy.

fix: surface pepper mismatch and add DB recovery tooling (#1660)

Issue #1660 reported two unrelated symptoms: a "no such table: auth"
traceback on first run, and "Invalid credentials" on an account that was
just created, with no working password recovery.

Startup race (the traceback):
start_order_update_adapters_on_boot() ran from create_app() and queried
the auth table immediately, while table creation happens on a different
background thread started later in setup_environment(). On a fresh
install the scan won the race and logged a traceback that looks fatal
but is not. app.db_ready now lives on the app from create_app() so the
boot scan can wait on it; setup_environment() reuses it. The ZMQ
publisher still warms immediately - only the auth query waits. The scan
also drops its scoped session explicitly, since no Flask teardown fires
for a plain daemon thread.

Login failure (the real problem):
Argon2 hashes are salted with API_KEY_PEPPER, so any change to it after
account creation makes every password fail with a bare "Invalid
credentials". _generate_keys_on_first_run documents a "warn re PEPPER"
branch for the populated-DB case that was never implemented, so an
install left on the public sample pepper said nothing at all. That
branch now warns on every startup, covering both consequences: stored
broker tokens are encrypted under a published value, and login is
already broken if the account predates the change.

The version-mismatch prompt is where users are actively told to edit
.env, so it now names API_KEY_PEPPER, FERNET_SALT and APP_KEY as values
that must be carried over verbatim rather than copied from .sample.env.

New tooling:
- upgrade/init_db.py - creates all tables in the foreground and reports
  which database file is really in use, whether an account exists, and
  whether stored secrets still decrypt with the current pepper and salt.
  users.totp_secret is written under the same pepper as the password
  hash, so a failed decrypt proves the hash is dead without needing the
  password. Read-only apart from CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS.
- upgrade/reset_admin_password.py - local password reset. The in-app
  flow needs SMTP or an enrolled TOTP device and a fresh install has
  neither, which left no way back in. Detects pepper drift first and
  says plainly what the reset cannot recover.

Also removes emoji from env_check print statements. Printing them raises
UnicodeEncodeError on a cp1252 Windows console, killing startup inside
check_env_version_compatibility before any guidance can appear, and the
project style bans icons.

fix(sandbox): defer MARKET fills on stale quotes (#1638)

A MARKET order for a symbol without a fresh tick could fill at the
broker's last_price even when that price was days or weeks old --
the reported case filled at 1047.60 against a same-payload day range
of [1262, 1345], recording a fake +22 percent P&L.

Root cause differs from the issue's theory: there is no cached tick in
OpenAlgo -- the quote is a live REST response, but the broker's
last_price field itself is the previous trade, however old, and the
engine trusted it with no cross-check.

New quote_looks_stale() defers any fill whose LTP falls outside the
quote's own [low, high] day range. Wired into both fill paths:
_process_order (immediate MARKET execution and the polling loop) and
the order_manager marketable LIMIT/SL branch that calls _execute_order
directly. A deferred order stays open and fills via the WebSocket
engine on the next live tick.

Deliberately conservative: quotes with no OHLC (symbol untraded this
session, or tick-built WebSocket quotes) pass through -- there is
nothing to cross-check, and tick-built quotes are live by construction.
Catching a stale price on a truly untraded symbol needs quote
timestamps, which the 34-broker quote contract does not carry today.

Verified by reproduction: the reporter's exact payload now defers where
it previously filled at 1047.60; a coherent quote fills normally.

fix(sandbox): auto-cancel open orders on expired F&O contracts

Expired positions were settled and open MIS orders were cancelled at
square-off, but an unfilled LIMIT/SL order on an expired contract had
no reaper: it stayed "open" forever, kept its margin blocked, and --
once the daily master contract refresh purged the symbol -- made the
WebSocket engine log broker token-lookup errors on every boot
("No brsymbol found in database").

New _cancel_expired_contract_orders() runs as step 1b of the square-off
check cycle (every minute via the backup job), mirroring the expired-
position settlement: get_contract_expiry() for detection, cancellation
via OrderManager.cancel_order so blocked margin is released. Equity
orders, which have no parseable expiry, are never touched.

The WebSocket order-index rebuild additionally skips expired-contract
orders so a boot never subscribes a dead symbol before the reaper's
first cycle. Skip-only by design: cancelling inside the rebuild would
deadlock, since cancel_order re-enters the engine via
notify_order_completed on the same lock.

Verified live: a 2-day-expired NIFTY option order that had been
error-spamming every boot was skipped at startup and auto-cancelled 60
seconds later by the backup cycle, with margin released.

perf(flattrade): burst-friendly dual-window rate limiter (#1663)

Parallel history fetches were serialized: the data-API rate limiter
enforced a fixed 0.55s gap between every pair of requests, process-wide.
45 symbols took 45 x 0.55 = ~25s regardless of worker count -- matching
the reported 24-36s -- while the same client code on Shoonya (which has
no such limiter) finished in ~2s.

The fixed gap was the most pessimistic reading of Flattrade's limits.
The official caps are 40 req/sec AND 200 req/min; 0.55s spacing ran at
~1.8/sec and ~109/min with no bursting at all.

Replace it with a dual sliding-window limiter: a deque of reserved call
timestamps; a call proceeds immediately unless a rolling window is

fix(ws): per-mode subscription tracking and Depth-only trading terminal (#1664)

The /trading chart froze for NFO/BFO/MCX derivatives on some brokers
while the WebSocket stayed healthy and depth messages kept arriving.

Root cause (as diagnosed in the issue, verified in code): the terminal
subscribed the same symbol in two modes -- LTP for the chart, Depth for
the buy/sell buttons -- and the Zerodha adapter tracked subscriptions in
a dict keyed by symbol only. The Depth subscribe overwrote the LTP
entry, the "if 1 in subscribed_modes" gate went false, and the LTP topic
was never published again. The chart's callback starved while depth kept
flowing. The WebSocket protocol subscribes and unsubscribes per
(symbol, mode), so holding both modes at once is legitimate client
behaviour and symbol-only tracking is out of spec.

Frontend (all brokers): the terminal now holds ONE subscription per
symbol -- Depth for tradeable instruments (every mode-3 payload carries
ltp as a first-class protocol field, so the chart ticks off depth.ltp),
LTP for quote-only indices which have no order book. The dual-subscribe
that triggered the bug no longer exists, and total message traffic drops.

Zerodha adapter: subscriptions keyed per symbol:mode; the kite stream is
requested at the highest subscribed mode (so a later LTP subscribe can
never downgrade an active depth stream); mode-aware unsubscribe keeps
the token until the last mode releases it; quote-mode ticks additionally
fan out the LTP topic when mode 1 is subscribed (same starvation class
for modes 1+2).

IIFL Capital adapter: same per-mode tracking via a modes set; the broker
feed subscribes at the highest mode; the tick handler publishes every
subscribed mode's topic from the full packet instead of only the last
subscriber's; mode-aware unsubscribe.

Nubra adapter: the orderbook channel -- the only feed for non-index
instruments -- returned early unless mode 3 was subscribed, so LTP and
Quote subscribers on stocks received nothing at all. It now fans out
LTP and QUOTE topics from orderbook data alongside DEPTH.

Cross-page impact: the adapter fixes also stop /scalping (Quote) and
/positions (LTP) from freezing when /trading holds Depth on the same
symbol in another tab -- server-side subscription state is global, so
the overwrite could starve pages that never misbehaved themselves.

Verified: live regression on Fyers (chart ticks via depth.ltp, buttons
update, index instruments unaffected); adapters compile with ruff at
baseline; frontend tsc + vite build clean. Fyers depth payloads carry
ltp on both HSM and TBT paths. Zerodha/IIFL/Nubra fixes need live
verification by users on those brokers.

feat(sandbox): event-driven MTM via position feed subscriptions

Open positions were valued by a REST poll: every mtm_update_interval
(default 5s) the loop fetched multiquotes for any position symbol the
WebSocket cache did not cover -- and the cache only covered symbols some
browser tab or strategy happened to be watching. Unwatched positions
meant a REST call drumbeat all session (observed: "Multiquotes fetched
2/2 symbols" every cycle for two idle positions).

Open ORDERS already did this right: the WS execution engine subscribes
their symbols and acts on ticks. Positions now get the same treatment:

- The engine holds one feed ref per (user, symbol) with open quantity,
  sharing the existing refcount infrastructure with orders -- a symbol
  an open order already subscribed just gains a count, the pool never
  sees a duplicate subscription.
- After every fill, the execution engine notifies opened (subscribe) or
  flat (release). Flat means no product (MIS/NRML/CNC) still holds
  quantity -- an MIS close while an NRML position remains keeps the
  feed. On any doubt the subscription is kept: a stray subscription
  costs a few ticks, a dropped one costs live MTM.
- Boot rebuild subscribes all open-position symbols (skipping contracts
  already past expiry, which await settlement and may be gone from the
  master contract).
- Expired-contract settlement releases the feed on both the on-view and
  cleanup paths.

The proxy already feeds every tick into MarketDataService, and the MTM
loop already reads that cache first -- so with positions subscribed, the
loop finds tick-fresh prices and the REST multiquotes call degrades to
what it should have been: a fallback that fires only when a symbol's
feed has been silent past the staleness threshold (illiquid contract,
market closed, feed hiccup). DB write cadence is unchanged (the 5s loop
still owns persistence), so tick volume never amplifies writes.

Verified live: boot logs "Position feed: 2 open-position symbols added
to index", the per-cycle multiquotes lines stopped, and positionbook
LTPs track ticks between polls. Behavioural tests cover idempotent
opens, order/position refcount sharing, non-flat close retention
(against a real multi-product DB state), last-ref release, and
stopped-engine no-ops.

Fix HDFC Sky historical data against the live chart API

Historical data could not work at all before this: every intraday request
failed with 400 and every daily request failed while building the DataFrame.
All of the following were found by exercising the endpoint with live
credentials.

chartType must be MINUTE, singular. The documented query-param table says
MINUTES, which the server rejects with 400 Client error, please check params.
The docs' own curl sample uses the singular.

The live response carries eight columns, not the seven in the documented
sample: a trailing cumulative-volume figure for the current trading day, zero
on every earlier day. Constructing the DataFrame raised ValueError on the
width mismatch, so only the leading seven columns are kept now.

Indices were addressed by the master-contract name, which the chart service
answers with an empty result set rather than an error, so they silently
returned nothing. The chart service keeps its own symbol vocabulary and it is
not internally consistent: headline indices want the compact form (NIFTY,
while Nifty 50 yields nothing) and the long tail wants the uppercased broker
name (NIFTY AUTO and INDIA VIX, while NIFTYAUTO yields nothing). Both forms
are now tried and the one that returns candles is cached per instrument.

The API key was being written to the logs in clear text. raise_for_status
builds its message from the request URL and HDFC Sky passes api_key as a
query parameter, so every chart or LTP failure leaked the key into the error
log. Both call sites now inspect the status code directly and report the
server's own message.

The chart service rate-limits per API key with 429 merchantKeyRateLimit,
which was treated as a fatal error and would break any multi-chunk download.
It is now retried with exponential backoff.

Chunking follows the Angel handler: the requested window is normalized (start
at 00:00, an end date of today clamped to now), and each chunk gets four
attempts that retry the same window rather than advancing past it, since
skipping would punch a silent gap into a long one-minute series. A chunk that
legitimately holds no candles is skipped quietly; one that fails every attempt
logs POSSIBLE GAP. Unlike the Angel handler, a run where every chunk failed
raises instead of returning an empty frame, so a hard API error stays
distinguishable from an illiquid contract.

The per-request range caps were measured rather than guessed: DAY accepts
2000 days and MINUTE 31, beyond which the server returns 400 Allowed Date
range exceeded. Every intraday timeframe is resampled from MINUTE and so
shares the 31-day cap.

Verified live across all ten timeframes for NSE and BSE cash (including
BAJAJ-AUTO and M&M), NSE and BSE indices, and NFO and BFO futures and options
with open interest populated, plus a three-month one-minute download spanning
three chunks. The retry, gap-warning and total-failure paths were exercised
with injected faults.

MCX returns 200 with no rows and CDS returns 400 for every symbol, series and
expiry tried, which points to segment entitlement on the account rather than
a mapping error.

fix(workspace): ship a readme per folder so the tree survives a clone

Git does not track empty directories, so `workspace/*` with a single
root readme meant every subfolder vanished on clone. Users would land on
a bare workspace/ with no indication of the intended layout, and the
skills' `mkdir -p` would silently invent folders nobody had seen
described.

Give each folder a tracked readme.md and widen the ignore pattern to
keep them:

    workspace/**
    !workspace/**/
    !workspace/readme.md
    !workspace/**/readme.md

The `!workspace/**/` line matters. Git cannot re-include a file whose
parent directory is excluded, so the directories have to be un-excluded
before a readme inside them can be.

what belongs in each folder, the naming convention, the run command, and
the one caveat that matters per area -- seed a scanner with a known
positive before trusting an empty result, match a dashboard's refresh
interval to the broker's quote cap, aggregate ticks into bars before
computing indicators, check openalgo.ta before writing a custom one, and
watch for lookahead bias in backtests. notes/ says plainly that it is

fix(iifl): refresh the XTS feed token on multiquotes and history

Fixes #1669 -- /positions returned 500 with "Error fetching multiquotes:
Error from IIFL API: Invalid Token".

IIFL is XTS, so market data is served from a session separate from the
interactive one and its feed token expires on its own schedule. When it
lapses the API answers HTTP 200 with
`{"type": "error", "description": "Invalid Token"}`.

Only the single-quote path handled that. `_fetch_market_data` refreshed
the feed token and retried once, while `_process_multiquotes_batch` and
both `get_history` call sites raised straight through -- so an expired
token surfaced to the user as a 500 from /positions even though the
plugin already knew how to recover.

The report singles out MCX, but MCX is a correlation rather than the
cause: it trades until 23:30 IST, hours after the feed token issued for
the equity session has aged out, so MCX users hit the unrecovered path
far more often. The "MCX": 51 segment mapping is correct and unchanged.

Add `_market_data_request()`, which wraps the market-data call and
refreshes the token once on "Invalid Token", and route multiquotes and
both history calls through it. `_fetch_market_data` keeps its existing
retry -- it already works, and leaving it untouched keeps this change
minimal.

Also fix a latent UnboundLocalError in `get_api_response`: FEED_TOKEN was
assigned only inside `if feed_token:`, so any caller relying on the
auth-token path would have crashed before issuing the request.

Verified with mocked responses: an expired token refreshes and retries
exactly once and then succeeds; a failed refresh surfaces the original
error without looping; a valid token makes a single call with no
needless refresh.

feat(kotak): live order-update WebSocket feed

Adds a dedicated order-update adapter on Kotak Neo's Order & Position
streaming socket (wss://<baseUrl>/realtime) and registers it in
_BROKER_FACTORIES, so Kotak sessions push order events instead of relying
on orderbook polling. Verified live: the full lifecycle arrives (open x3 ->
rejected) with the rejection reason carried through.

Doc 13 insists the connect frame is a raw non-JSON string while Kotak's own
vendored HSI client json.dumps() the same dict, so the adapter sends JSON
first and alternates on any attempt that opens without a cn ack. A rejected
handshake does not always announce itself -- Kotak may hold the socket open
and never authenticate it, which is indistinguishable from a quiet market --
so an ack watchdog closes any attempt that goes 10s without an ack and lets
the reconnect flip the encoding.

Fixes SL-M, which Kotak rejects outright from API sessions with 'Market
order with Algo Id not allowed': SEBI bars market orders for retail algos and
Kotak's APIs auto-append an exchange-compliant Algo ID. Plain MKT survives
because Kotak substitutes a protection limit server-side, but a stop-market
has no LTP to protect at placement. SL-M is now sent as pt=SL with a limit
offset one MPP band beyond the trigger (BUY above, SELL below), snapped to
the instrument tick away from the trigger and forced at least one tick past
it, mirroring the Dhan SL-M path from #1647. Kotak's options grid is kept
broker-local: it adds 1-5 -> 10%, 5-10 -> 5% and an absolute Rs 0.10 floor
below Rs 1, which utils/mpp_slab.py's percentage-only table cannot express.

Also fixes tradebook symbols. Kotak sends tok as an empty string on
tradebook rows, so the token-only lookup leaked the raw broker symbol
(YESBANK-EQ) into the UI and every downstream lookup that expects an
OpenAlgo symbol failed -- visible as 'No token found for YESBANK-EQ on NSE'
from the market-data adapter. Lookup now falls back to get_oa_symbol on
trdSym, which was already imported for this purpose and never used.

Payload construction in place_order_api/modify_order ran outside the try,
so a rejected trigger or unresolvable tick size would have escaped as an

perf(kotak): batch WebSocket unsubscribes and order them with subscribes

Subscribes were already debounced and batched, but unsubscribe_quote and
unsubscribe_depth still sent one HSI frame per symbol, so tearing down a
200-symbol option chain fired 200 frames. Both now go through the same queue,
routed off sub_type (mws/mwu for quote, dps/dpu for depth), and dispatch to
the unsubscribe_batch that already existed in kotak_websocket.py and had
never been called.

Sharing one debounce window between subscribes and unsubscribes makes frame
order matter: emitting both applies them in group order rather than call
order, so 'sub, unsub, sub' on one scrip inside a single window would have
left it unsubscribed. The batcher now keeps only the last operation per scrip
per feed family. Families stay independent, so a scrip can hold quote and
depth subscriptions at once and a depth unsubscribe cannot cancel a quote
subscribe.

This also closes an ordering hazard that predates the change: unsubscribes
were sent immediately while subscribes waited out the 50ms debounce, so an
unsubscribe could overtake a pending subscribe for the same scrip.

fix(kotak): close orphanable WebSocket clients on re-init and double-connect

Two latent descriptor leaks found by a file-descriptor audit of the Kotak
streaming module. Neither is reachable through today's call paths, but both
depend entirely on a caller contract that is written down nowhere.

initialize() rebound _ws_client without closing an existing one, so a second
call on a live adapter would orphan the previous WebSocketApp with its socket
and run thread still alive, and nothing would ever close them. It now closes
the predecessor first, outside the adapter lock -- close() joins the run
thread whose callbacks take that same lock, the ordering _attempt_reconnection
already uses. A close() that raises is logged and swallowed so a broken old
client cannot block re-initialisation.

KotakWebSocket.connect() guarded only against connect-after-close. Callers
cannot cover the rest themselves: is_connected() stays False for the whole
handshake window, so a second connect() during it would start a second run
thread and orphan the first WebSocketApp. The check now lives with the thread
slot it protects, and is atomic with claiming it -- the previous code took the
lock twice, so two concurrent callers could both pass a pre-check and both
write _thread.

Adds six Flow node types so strategies can be built on real technical
analysis and historical price data, not just live quotes:

  closes the gap flagged in flow-import-format.md 8.5.

  existing order.update EventBus topic, instead of polling getOrderStatus.

fix(flow): address Codex/cubic review findings on new nodes

P0 - order-update triggers could never execute:
- execute_workflow's trigger_types omitted orderUpdateTrigger, so every
  matching order event died on "No trigger node found" before reaching any
  downstream node. Earlier testing only covered activate/deactivate
  registration, never a firing event, which is how this slipped through.
- Scope watches to their owning account. Order adapters and the sandbox
  engine identify the owner in event.request_data["user_id"]; a symbol-only
  watch previously matched any account's fill and then executed with the
  watch owner's API key. Enforced only when the event carries an identity,
  since some sandbox paths omit it and failing closed there would silently
  stop analyze-mode triggers.

P1/P2 correctness:
- Restore watches at startup from active workflows. They lived only in
  memory while is_active is persisted, so after a restart such workflows
  stayed "active" while firing nothing, and re-activation was rejected as
  already_active.
- Claim a "once" watch inside _watches_lock; the bus dispatches on a pool,
  so concurrent events could both pass the check and fire duplicate orders.
- Normalize order_status: Zerodha's order adapter emits "trigger pending"
  while other paths use "trigger_pending", making that filter never match.
- An explicit exchange filter no longer passes when the event's exchange is
  missing.
- prior_period_ohlc raises instead of falling back to the current,
  still-forming candle as previous_hour/previous_day.
- _parse_timestamp converts aware ISO timestamps to naive local time;
  subtracting an aware value from datetime.now() raised TypeError.
- Add quarterly/yearly rates to _BARS_PER_DAY - Historify's Q/Y intervals
  fell back to the intraday rate, yielding one bar and all-null indicators.
- varCondition no longer coerces unresolvable operands to 0.0, and an
  errored condition now takes NEITHER branch. Returning False routed the
  else-path, so on "RSI < 70 -> BUY else SELL" a typo'd variable fired the
  SELL. Pass-through edges still run so the failure stays visible.
- Non-numeric sourceSeries values fail the node instead of aborting the run.
- Reject {{variable}} Order IDs and unknown statuses with 400 instead of
  500; a trigger has no upstream node to resolve a reference against.
- Delete now tears down price alerts and order-update watches, not just the
  scheduler job, so a deleted workflow leaves no stale registration.
- get_history rejects source="db" without both dates rather than letting
  strptime(None) surface as an opaque 500.
- orderUpdateTrigger defaults exchange to "" (UI: "Any exchange"); an NSE
  default silently excluded NFO/MCX fills from an order-ID-only watch.
- VarConditionNode truncates via CSS with a title tooltip instead of
  slice(14), which rendered distinct operands sharing a prefix identically.

Rate limiting:
Broker data APIs are far tighter than the node graph suggests (Dhan 5 req/s

fix(flow): logic gates must wait for all inputs before evaluating

AND/OR/NOT gates read each incoming edge's stored condition result and
silently skipped any that were still unresolved, then evaluated anyway.
Because the graph walk is depth-first, the first input to finish reached
the gate while the others were unevaluated, so a two-input AND gate both:

  - fired on partial inputs ("A AND B" evaluating true on A alone), and
  - fired again for each remaining input.

With an order node downstream that is two orders from one signal, the first
placed before the second condition was even checked. Reproduced on an EMA
crossover: "AND Gate: [True] -> True" followed by a second "AND Gate:
[True, True] -> True", logging the entry twice.

Gates now skip evaluation until every wired input has a result. That is
safe because the remaining input's own traversal reaches the gate again
once all sources have stored results, so it evaluates exactly once with
the complete set.

Note this is why gate inputs should be wired as pass-through edges
(targetHandle only) rather than via sourceHandle "true": a true-handle edge
is not followed when its condition is false, so the gate is never reached
and its false branch cannot fire.

Pre-existing on main; surfaced while validating crossover examples.

fix(flow): share the outcome of an in-flight history fetch with waiters

The previous single-flight used a per-key lock and had waiters retry after
acquiring it. Because error responses are deliberately not cached, every
waiter then found a cold cache and issued its own broker call - a full
fan-out that happened precisely when the broker was already failing or rate
limiting. Reproduced: 12 concurrent requests against a failing broker
produced 12 calls.

Replaces the lock with a small flight object carrying an Event plus the
leader's result or exception. The leader fetches once and publishes the
outcome; waiters block on the event and return that same outcome rather than
re-fetching. The flight is retired in a finally block after the event is
set, so a later call still starts a fresh attempt and failures stay
retryable.

Verified: 12 concurrent requests produce exactly 1 broker call for a success,
an error response, and a raised exception alike; all waiters observe the same
outcome; a subsequent call after a failed flight does retry; the in-flight
map drains in every case. A bounded wait guards against a leader thread dying
outright.

feat(flow): per-strategy position book and P&L

A Flow workflow could only exit on account-wide or per-symbol P&L, because
nothing in OpenAlgo attributes a position to the strategy that opened it. The
broker nets positions per (symbol, exchange, product) and has never heard of
the strategy tag, so two strategies trading the same contract are
indistinguishable downstream.

Adds a parallel book keyed by strategy, plus a Flow node that reads it, so a
workflow can exit on its own performance:

    {{spnl.total}} >= 5000  ->  closePositions

Position book (database/strategy_book_db.py)
Fed entirely from the event bus, so the order execution path is untouched:
order.placed carries the strategy tag and supplies the orderid -> strategy
mapping (the only moment that tag is known, since it never round-trips
through the broker), and order.update supplies fills. This also means orders
placed through /api/v1 are tracked exactly like Flow-placed ones, and both
live and analyze modes work, without changes to either.

Booking is idempotent: applied quantity is tracked per order and only the
unseen delta is booked, so a broker feed and a postback reporting the same
fill cannot double-count. Partial fills fall out of the same mechanism.
Accounting is weighted-average cost; a position flipping through zero
realizes the closed leg and reopens the remainder at the fill price.
today_realized resets on the first fill of a new trading date, keeping it
aligned with the ~3 AM IST rollover without a scheduler.

Unrealized P&L is deliberately not stored - it is a function of a price that
changes continuously, so it is computed at read time from one position-book
call.

Strategy tagging (services/flow_executor_service.py)
Every Flow order previously went out tagged "flow_workflow", so all
workflows shared one identity and per-strategy P&L would have been
meaningless. Orders are now tagged with the workflow's own name, overridable
per node via strategyTag. The field is deliberately not called "strategy":
optionsMultiOrder already uses that for the structure type (straddle /
iron_condor / custom).

Flow node
strategyPnl exposes {{name.realized}}, {{name.unrealized}}, {{name.total}},
{{name.today_realized}}, {{name.today_total}}, {{name.open_quantity}} and a
per-leg breakdown. Its strategy field defaults to the workflow's own name, so
the common case needs no configuration.

Verified against the event path: a buy 100@100 followed by a sell 40@120 with
LTP 130 books realized 800, unrealized 1800, total 2600, open 60; replaying
both fill events changes nothing; a partial fill reporting cumulative 30 then
100 books 100, not 130; two strategies on the same contract stay separate;
and a fill for an untagged order is ignored. The accounting core is
separately unit-tested over 16 cases including short round-trips,
weighted-average scale-ins and flips through zero.

docs(flow): document that a second trigger node is silently ignored

The executor selects the first trigger node it finds and walks the graph from
there, so any additional trigger - and everything downstream of it - never
executes, and nothing reports this. Verified with a workflow containing two
start nodes feeding separate branches: only the first branch ran.

This is easy to hit when a strategy needs two schedules, e.g. entries every
minute plus a square-off at a fixed time, which reads naturally as two
triggers in one graph.

branch on the same trigger, or a second workflow) and notes the cost of
splitting: branches sharing a trigger also share their data nodes, while
separate workflows each re-fetch, and quotes and the order book are not
de-duplicated by the history cache. Measured on the same strategy, one
workflow issued 4 data-node calls per tick against 13 for the six-workflow

  first is safe in the other direction because apply_fill is idempotent

  traded between midnight and the 03:00 IST rollover and is not IST at

  permanently.

Review round on #1697. All five findings were reachable in the code.

Queued alert runs could fire after deactivation. The pool queue is
unbounded, so an every_time alert whose workflow runs slower than the
poll interval stacked a task per tick, and nothing cancelled those
closures when the alert was removed or the workflow deactivated -

monitoring loop set a shared event and skipped the join; a new alert
arriving before that loop noticed cleared the same event and left two
loops polling, duplicating quotes and every_time submissions. Each
generation now owns its event and the loop watches the one it was
started with, so a restart cannot un-stop it.

evaluate. The requirement table is keyed on the monitor's canonical
names and the configured value is normalized through its own alias
table, so `price_above` and `cross_above` need a target price exactly as

feat(flow): calendar node for new day, week, month and quarter detection

Flow had no way to ask "has a new day, week, month or quarter started".
That looks like it needs memory of the previous run, which Flow does not
have - but it does not: "a new month started" is the same statement as
"today is the first trading day of this month", and the exchange calendar
answers that on its own.

Answering it from the calendar is also more correct than the tests a user
would otherwise write. `day == 1` misses a 1st that falls on a weekend or
a holiday; `weekday == Monday` misses a week whose Monday is a holiday.
Both cases are covered by tests.

New `calendar` node, output shape:

- is_new_day / is_new_week / is_new_month / is_new_quarter / is_new_year
- is_last_day_of_week / _month / _quarter / _year, for square-off logic
- is_trading_day, is_trading_holiday, is_weekend - a holiday is
  distinguished from a weekend
- weekday, weekday_num, day, month, quarter, year, week_of_year,
  day_of_year
- prev_trading_day, next_trading_day, and the first and last trading day
  of the week, month and quarter

Deliberately not exchange-aware: a date is a trading holiday if the
exchange calendar lists one. MCX differs from NSE on a few days a year,
and modelling that would put an exchange selector on every calendar
question for a difference almost no strategy depends on.

New built-in variables, so a condition can compare them directly:
`weekday_num` (1 = Monday, because `weekday` is a name like "Thursday"
that no numeric comparison can use), `quarter`, `week_of_year`,
`day_of_year`, and `session_date` - the trading session date, which
differs from `date` between midnight and the 03:00 IST rollover.

Also fixes a gap in the create route from the previous PR: a truthy
non-object payload (a JSON array or string) skipped the "was a graph
sent?" check and reached .get() as a 500 instead of a 400.

degrades to weekends-only rather than failing, which errs toward treating

feat(portfolio): detect unadjusted corporate actions instead of assuming

Broker feeds arrive adjusted for splits and bonuses, so the engine does not
adjust anything. What it must not do is stay silent when a series clearly was
not adjusted: Historify holds whatever was ingested, so a split that happened
after ingestion leaves a step in the stored history that is indistinguishable
downstream from a real -50% session. Backtesting through one produces a
confident, wrong answer.

split_artifacts() reports such sessions and load_prices() attaches them to the
PriceMatrix and logs them, so a run can surface "this symbol looks unadjusted
on this date" rather than quietly folding it into the return.

The threshold has to sit below the smallest common split ratio, not at it: a
1:2 split is exactly -50%, so the obvious 0.5 misses the very case the check
exists for. 0.35 clears the 20% circuit that caps a real session with room to
spare while still catching 1:2 -- a boundary the tests pin.

Note this covers price adjustment only. Broker history is price-return, not
total-return, so dividends are still absent from every backtest; that is a
separate decision, not something this guard hides.

correct it in the form rather than wait for a release.

feat(portfolio): wire walk-forward and Monte Carlo into the report

Both modules existed and nothing referenced them, so neither reached a user.
They now run with the same policy and cost schedule as the headline backtest --
comparing a walk-forward run charged differently from the run it validates
would be measuring two strategies.

Walk-forward re-runs the allocation over rolling one-year windows stepped six
months apart. The spread is the point, not the average: a strategy whose whole
result came from one exceptional stretch looks very different here from one
that worked repeatedly, and CAGR cannot tell them apart. This portfolio was
positive in 18 of 18 windows, median 14.2%, spanning 2.0% to 48.5%.

Monte Carlo block-bootstraps the return series. Drawing single days
independently would destroy volatility clustering and make drawdowns look far
milder than markets actually produce -- the statistic an investor least wants
flattered. Blocks of roughly a month keep that structure. The seed is fixed so
a risk number does not change each time it is looked at, which would invite
re-rolling until it flatters.

Together they add about 91ms: walk-forward 38ms for 18 windows, Monte Carlo
53ms for 1,000 paths. An earlier 1.8s measurement was the cold openstatz import
in a fresh process, not these.

feat(portfolio): portfolio structure by co-movement, not invented sectors

The plan was a sector and market-cap breakdown, on the assumption that the
symbol master carried that data. It does not: symtoken holds symbol, brsymbol,
name, exchange, token, expiry, strike, lotsize, instrumenttype, tick_size and
contract_value, and nothing else. Historify's symbol_metadata has no sector
column either and is empty. Nowhere in the codebase holds one.

Nor does instrumenttype help -- it carries exchange series codes (A, B, BE,
EQ), and NIFTYBEES and RELIANCE are both 'EQ', so it does not even separate a
fund from a single stock.

So rather than invent labels or ship a stale mapping, this measures grouping
from data that exists, and answers a better question while doing it: which
holdings actually move together. A sector label is a proxy for co-movement;
correlation is the thing itself. Two banks filed under different sectors that
trade as one position are one bet, and a sector chart would show them as two.

Single-linkage clustering, because if A moves with B and B with C then a shock
to B hits all three whatever A and C do between them.

The threshold is 0.6, calibrated against real daily NSE data rather than
picked: over 2016-2026 the highest pair among NIFTYBEES, GOLDBEES, RELIANCE,
INFY, ICICIBANK and SBIN is 0.69, two large private banks sit at 0.64, and gold
is flat against everything. The instinctive 0.7 can never fire on daily Indian
equity returns, which would make the clustering look reassuring precisely when
it should not.

On a six-holding portfolio it reports three effective bets: NIFTYBEES,
RELIANCE, ICICIBANK and SBIN move as one 65% position.

Instrument class is inferred from the listing name and labelled as a heuristic,
because that is all the field supports. The absence of a sector chart is stated
in the response rather than left silent, so it does not read as an oversight.

feat(portfolio): compare every rebalancing rule side by side

The question an investor faces is rarely "how did this do" but "which of these
should I hold". Every variant runs over the same prices and the same cost
schedule, because two results computed over different periods or charged
differently are not a comparison, and the price cache makes the extra runs
nearly free -- the history is read once.

The default sweep is the decision worth making by default: never, yearly,
quarterly, monthly, and a 5% drift band. On ten years of NIFTYBEES/GOLDBEES it
produces the result the calendar-only products cannot show:

  Never      284.72%  Sharpe 1.25  drag 0.000%    0 rebalances
  Yearly     299.78%  Sharpe 1.28  drag 0.333%   11
  Quarterly  309.39%  Sharpe 1.31  drag 0.770%   42
  Monthly    303.28%  Sharpe 1.30  drag 1.214%  122
  Drift 5%   306.02%  Sharpe 1.31  drag 0.509%   11

Monthly trades three times as often as quarterly and ends up behind it. The
drift band matches quarterly's risk-adjusted return on a quarter of the trades.
Neither fact is visible without modelling costs, which is why a frictionless
backtester would recommend the wrong rule here.

Ranked on Sharpe rather than raw return, and both winners are reported,
because the highest-returning rule is frequently not the one worth holding --
here they are different rules.

feat(portfolio): performance attribution -- selection against allocation

The textbook method here is Brinson-Fachler, and it is not computable: it needs
the benchmark's constituent weights and per-segment returns, and openalgo has
neither. The benchmark is a single index price series and nothing in the
codebase holds index membership -- the store has exactly one index symbol.
Running Brinson anyway would mean inventing the numbers the method exists to
compare against.

So this decomposes what the data supports, and it answers the two questions an
investor actually asks:

  selection  -- were these the right things to own? An equal-weighted basket of
                the same holdings against the benchmark, which isolates the
                picks from the sizing.
  allocation -- did the weighting help? The actual portfolio against that
                equal-weighted basket.

They sum exactly to the excess return, which is the property that makes it an
attribution rather than two loosely related numbers, and the tests pin it.
Equal weights produce an allocation effect of exactly zero; overweighting the
better holding produces a positive one.

Weighted by the average weight actually held rather than the target, because a
portfolio that drifted was not the one the targets describe.

On a four-holding portfolio against NIFTY over ten years: excess 127.08% splits
into 115.31% selection and 11.77% allocation -- the picks did the work, the
sizing added a little, and INFY cost 19.47 points on its own.

Endpoint wss://go.mynt.in/NorenWSAPI/ and the connect frame are taken from the
live market-data client, broker/zebu/streaming/zebu_websocket.py, which calls
itself the "OAuth WebSocket API" and sends t="a" with accesstoken/source=API,
acked t="ak". That matches Zebu's OAuth login (api/auth_api.py exchanges the
code at GenAcsTok for an access_token).

Zebu's published WebSocket doc describes the older classic-Noren handshake
instead - t="c" with susertoken, acked t="ck" - which pairs with the classic
login that issues a susertoken. The OAuth variant is used here on the grounds
that it matches this broker's actual login flow and its in-production
market-data client, but the two have not been distinguished against a live
session; if Zebu closes the socket without an ack, the connect frame is the
first thing to try flipping.

The same doc does confirm everything downstream of the connect: subscribe
{"t":"o","actid":...} acked t="ok", feed t="om", unsubscribe t="uo" acked
"uok", and an om field list carrying norenordno / status / reporttype /
trantype / prctyp / fillshares / avgprc / rejreason / trgprc, with the product
in "prd" - the key this adapter reads first.

order_status maps TRIGGER_PENDING to "trigger pending" here, deliberately
unlike broker/zebu/mapping/order_data.py, which folds it to "open" because the
React order book gates Modify/Cancel on order_status === 'open'. This path feeds
the push stream, whose consumers expect the distinct value.

Verified offline only: handshake frames, ack-gated subscribe, heartbeat,
non-om frames ignored, and om frames for a resting SL, partial fill, rejection,
reporttype fallback and the norenoordno spelling. Not yet confirmed against a
live Zebu session - the one attempt was inconclusive because both test orders
were rejected (which may not emit an om frame at all) and the client subscribed
28s after they were placed, and order updates are not replayed.

feat(tradesmart): live order updates over the Noren v2 WebSocket

TradeSmart streams order updates on the same NorenWSAPI socket as market data
(broker-api-docs/tradesmart-api-docs.md, "WebSocket streaming"), but no adapter
existed: services/order_update_service.py had no tradesmart entry and tradesmart
is not in _POLLING_BROKERS either, so TradeSmart sessions got no order updates
at all - not even polled ones.

Unlike every sibling Noren adapter here, TradeSmart uses NO order-update
subscribe frame. Its task table lists order updates as "automatic" with no
request t, where Shoonya/Flattrade/Zebu/Definedge all require
{"t":"o","actid":...} after the connect ack. Nothing is sent beyond the
connect. If a live session delivers no om frames, sending the siblings' t="o"
on ack is the first thing to try.

Second TradeSmart-specific trap: the stored auth token is a composite
"<uid>:::<bearer>" and the socket wants the bearer half only, so it goes
through baseurl.parse_auth() instead of being passed through raw the way the
other Noren adapters pass their token. Passing it raw would put the whole
"<uid>:::<bearer>" string in accesstoken and fail the connect. uid/actid
resolution mirrors tradesmart_adapter.py (token uid -> resolve_uid -> user_id).

Values taken as documented rather than inferred: order statuses PENDING /
CANCELED / OPEN / REJECTED / COMPLETE / TRIGGER_PENDING (note the single-L
CANCELED and the underscored TRIGGER_PENDING), price types LMT / MKT / SL-LMT /
SL-MKT, and product codes C/M/I plus F=MTF, H=Cover, B=Bracket. OpenAlgo has no
constant for the last three, so they pass through as the raw code rather than
being mislabelled as one of CNC/NRML/MIS. The other unsolicited feeds on this
socket - am (alerts/GTT), rm (admin), ms (market status) - are ignored.

order_status maps TRIGGER_PENDING to "trigger pending" here, deliberately
unlike broker/tradesmart/mapping/order_data.py, which folds it to "open"
because the React order book gates Modify/Cancel on order_status === 'open'.
This path feeds the push stream, whose consumers expect the distinct value.

Verified offline: connect frame carrying the bearer half only (asserted no
':::' leak), heartbeat, ack sending no subscribe frame, hk/am/rm/ms/tf/pm and
malformed frames ignored, and om frames for a resting SL, partial fill,
rejection, CANCELED and an MTF passthrough. Not live-verified; the
automatic-vs-t=o question would surface first.

fix(portfolio): analyse holdings that carry no average price

The analyzer refused every account whose broker returns holdings without an
average price -- "no holdings with a usable quantity and price" -- on a payload
that was perfectly analysable. Upstox is one such broker: its holdings arrive
with an LTP for every row and no average at all.

The gate was on the wrong field. Every weight is quantity times the *current*
price; cost basis is needed only for invested value and return percentages, and
neither is required to measure exposure, concentration, co-movement, risk or
health. A row now needs a quantity and a current price, nothing more. The
current price is still recovered from average plus P&L per share when the feed
omits LTP but supplies both, and a row with neither is still dropped -- a
position with no price cannot be weighted, and inventing one would put a
fabricated number into every downstream metric.

Where cost is genuinely absent, invested and percentages come back null rather
than zero: a zero reads as "invested nothing" where null reads as "not
reported", and the P&L shown falls back to the broker's own figure. The page
says so in a banner instead of showing blanks that look like a fault.

Verified against the payload behind the reported failure: 8 of 8 holdings
parsed, 3,579.41 current value and -203.87 P&L, matching the broker's own
holdings page exactly.

fix(noren): SL-M never falls through as SL-MKT; drop un-acked order sockets

Addresses the cubic review of the Noren order-update work.

P1 - Shoonya/Flattrade SL-M reached the OMS as SL-MKT whenever MPP could not
run (no auth token, LTP 0, or a quote exception). SL-MKT is the exact price
type these brokers reject for API orders, so the order was dead on arrival.
Unlike MARKET, an SL-M always carries a trigger price, so the fallback now
derives the protective limit from the trigger and still sends SL-LMT - the
same shape broker/tradesmart/mapping/transform_data.py::_apply_mpp already
used. MARKET's fallback is unchanged: without a quote there is no reference
price to protect off.

P2 - A refused Noren auth ack left the adapter reporting connected but
subscribed to nothing, silent forever, because the broker can hold an
unauthenticated socket open and run_forever never returns. All four adapters
now close the socket on a non-OK ak so BaseOrderUpdateAdapter's backoff loop
retries, mirroring kotak_order_adapter's connect-ack watchdog. Flattrade and
TradeSmart get the same treatment as the two flagged - identical code shape.
It matters most for Zebu, whose connect variant is still unverified: a wrong
guess must surface as a retry loop rather than as silence.

P3 - 11 fixtures in test/test_order_update_adapters.py cover the four
adapters that had none, pinning what a doc-less protocol makes fragile:
connect frame (accesstoken not usertoken, no ::: composite-token leak),
subscribe-on-ack vs TradeSmart's automatic feed, close-on-failed-ack,
TRIGGER_PENDING staying distinct on the push path, CANCELED -> cancelled,
partial fill staying open, reporttype fallback, the norenoordno typo, the
prd/pcode split, and TradeSmart's F/H/B product passthrough.

Not taken: hoisting normalize_order_status into a shared Noren utility. The
REST and push status maps diverge on purpose (trigger pending), and every
broker module here is deliberately self-contained.

fix(noren): keep the SL-M fallback limit on the tick grid

Follow-up to d5d1d0b3f, from the cubic review of it.

The SL-M fallback called calculate_protected_price without a tick size,

never leaving as SL-MKT, and the fallback limit landing on the tick grid at

get_holdings() returns a tuple (holdings, status) and holdings_service
passes that value straight into calculate_portfolio_statistics(). The

while showing 0.00 for Total Holding Value, Total Investment Value,

this look like a display bug rather than a data one.

and re-check for emptiness afterwards so an error tuple of
(None, {"status": "error"}) still yields zeros instead of raising.

1,127,529.00 in investment value previously reported 0.00 and now
report correctly. dict, list, {"payload": {...}}, {"data": {...}},
pre-computed {"data": {"statistics": ...}}, empty and None inputs are
all unchanged.

fix(search): rank /trading symbol search by relevance, add an Index chip

The Symbol Search dialog's backend (BrokerSymbolCache.search_symbols)
returned the first 500 AND-matches in raw cache-iteration order and
stopped. For a query like "NIFTY" that meant option contracts (NFO has
~4,749 NIFTY-prefixed rows on this instance) crowded out index rows
(134 NSE_INDEX rows) almost entirely before the scan ever reached them
-- only one index made it into the capped batch. No exchange was
excluded from the search; the data was always there, it just never
got a chance to be returned.

Fix is a generic relevance fix, not an index-specific one: score every
match by exact/prefix/substring text relevance (then symbol length as
a tiebreaker) before taking the top `limit`, instead of stopping at
the first N found. Verified against the live cache (92k symbols):
searching NIFTY now surfaces 130 distinct indices instead of 1, with
the exact match ranking first, in ~26ms.

Also gives the dialog a dedicated Index chip (any _INDEX exchange) --
previously NSE_INDEX/BSE_INDEX/GLOBAL_INDEX were folded into the Cash
chip alongside plain equities with no way to filter to just indices --
and reorders the ALL-view category priority so Index ranks above Cash,
matching what someone charting an index by name is almost always
looking for.
