fix(db): stop the Telegram startup write from failing with "database is locked"

Reported in #1713: every boot logged a "database is locked" traceback from
telegram_db.update_bot_config. Three things combined to produce it.

The telegram tables are not in their own file. telegram_db.py defaults to
DATABASE_URL, so bot_config lives in openalgo.db alongside auth, symtoken,
apilog, settings and strategies, and it competes with the whole boot sequence
(the 15-way parallel create_all, the schedulers, the symbol-cache restore over
an 82 MB symtoken table) plus the out-of-process websocket proxy.

Nothing set busy_timeout, so the effective wait was Python sqlite3's 5 second
default, per connection, with NullPool opening a fresh connection per
operation. Set it to 15s in the process-wide connect listener so every module
and both processes get it.

The write itself was redundant. app.py reads the bot config, then the
auto-start path passes the same token straight back to update_bot_config, so
the UPDATE that was losing the race had nothing to change. update_bot_config
now compares each supplied field against what is stored and returns without
committing when they all match, comparing the token as decrypted plaintext
because Fernet ciphertext is non-deterministic. Same gate CLAUDE.md already
mandates for upsert_auth.

initialize_bot/initialize_bot_sync no longer write is_active. That flag is
owned by start_bot/stop_bot; writing False during initialization made the
auto-start replay a real change (True -> False) purely so start_bot could set
it back, and a crash in that window left the bot disabled on the next boot.

busy_timeout does not help with a WAL snapshot conflict, which reports the
same "database is locked" but returns immediately. Not addressed here — the
redundant write was the one hitting it.

fix(docker): openalgo-backup archived an empty volume and reported success

The generated /usr/local/bin/openalgo-backup helper passed the volume names as
declared in docker-compose.yaml:

    docker run --rm -v openalgo_db:/data ... tar -czf /backup/db.tar.gz -C /data .

Compose prefixes named volumes with the project name, taken from the directory,
so the real volume in /opt/openalgo is openalgo_openalgo_db. `docker run` with an
unknown named volume does not fail - it CREATES an empty one. The tar then
succeeded with nothing in it, and 2>/dev/null hid any complaint, so users got a
backup archive that looked fine and would restore nothing.

Measured on a real Docker host:

    old (hardcoded name):  4.0K archive,  1 entry   (empty)
    new (resolved name):    15M archive,  9 entries (logs.db, latency.db, ...)

Resolves the volume by asking the container what it is actually mounting at
/app/db, not by matching names. Name matching is unsafe here specifically
because the old command left a stray empty "openalgo_db" volume behind on every
run - a name pattern would match that debris and silently archive nothing again.
This was not theoretical: it happened while testing the first version of this
fix, which is how it was caught.

Also:
- Removes 2>/dev/null from the archive steps so failures surface.
- Verifies the database archive is non-empty before writing the final backup,
  rather than producing a misleading file.
- Resolves volumes BEFORE `docker compose stop`, and installs an EXIT trap that
  restarts the stack. Previously an early failure would have left the platform
  stopped; a failed backup must never take the instance down.
- Treats the strategies volume as optional and warns instead of failing.

install-docker-multi-custom-ssl.sh has no equivalent backup helper, so it is
unaffected.

feat(sip): SIP backtester for NSE and BSE with XIRR and statutory charges

Adds /sip-backtester alongside the portfolio backtester, sharing its data
layer, charge model, chart components and page theme.

Why XIRR rather than CAGR: a SIP pays in on many dates, so CAGR would credit
an installment made in month 60 with five years of compounding it never had.
XIRR is the only return figure that respects when each rupee arrived. The
solver is anchored to the documented Excel XIRR example, because that is what
users will check it against, and it raises rather than inventing a number when
XIRR is genuinely undefined (all flows one sign, one date, fewer than two).

The same reasoning rules metrics out. Sharpe, Sortino and volatility on a SIP
value curve describe the deposit schedule as much as the investment -- the
curve rises partly because money was added -- so they are deliberately absent
rather than reported and misread. What replaces them is measured from the cash
flows or from quantities an investor can check against a statement.

Metrics:

- XIRR, absolute return, multiple, units, average cost
- Rupee-cost averaging quantified: cost per unit against the average price over
  the same dates. Asserted as a mathematical property, not a market claim --
  buying fixed rupee amounts gives a harmonic-style mean that cannot exceed the
  arithmetic mean of the same prices.
- Time below invested: how long the holding was worth less than the money paid
  in, and the longest such stretch. The number that makes people abandon a SIP,
  and one almost nobody reports.
- Rolling XIRR over every 1/3/5/7/10-year window, so a single headline is seen
  as one draw from a distribution.
- Drawdown with recovery time, yearly table, monthly grid of market movement
  with the installment subtracted.

Four heatmaps, the important one being start month x holding period, which
shows whether entry timing mattered and how fast that fades with horizon. Also
a day-of-month sweep, which usually shows the choice barely matters -- worth
demonstrating rather than leaving to guesswork.

Comparisons: lumpsum of the same total on day one (shown even when it wins,
which in a rising market it usually does), frequency comparison with amounts
scaled to the same yearly outlay so weekly does not "win" by investing four
times as much, and a benchmark run as the identical schedule into an index so
it is SIP against SIP rather than SIP against an index CAGR.

Charges use portfolio.costs unchanged -- STT, exchange transaction fee, SEBI,
stamp duty and GST -- levied per installment, since that is how they are
actually charged. Measured: Rs 11.87 on a Rs 10,000 NSE installment, 0.119%
drag over 58 installments. They reduce units bought rather than appearing as a
deduction, which is why a higher-frequency SIP costs more for the same yearly
outlay. The lumpsum comparison uses the same model, or it would be rigged.

Both price sources work because portfolio.data.load_prices is reused rather
than reimplemented: Historify and the broker API behave identically to the
portfolio backtester instead of drifting apart.

Security matches the portfolio backtester exactly: the API key is verified on
every request including source='db' (local history is still the user's data),
a broker session is additionally required for source='api', every field is
marshmallow-validated before reaching the service, both endpoints are rate
limited, and internal failures return a generic message with the detail going
to errors.jsonl.

Tests: 72. Twenty-three are security, driven through a real Flask test client
rather than the schema -- including a structural assertion that verify_api_key
runs before the source branch, so a source='db' request can never skip
authentication, and a test proving the service is never reached with an invalid
key.

fix(sip): close-to-close monthly returns, no FutureWarning, clearer figures

Fixes a FutureWarning seen on a live ICICIBANK run:

    sip/analytics.py:356: FutureWarning: Downcasting object dtype arrays on
    .fillna is deprecated

Cause: `.replace(0, pd.NA)` promotes a float Series to OBJECT dtype, because
pd.NA is not a float. Every arithmetic result downstream was then object, and
.fillna() on object dtype is the deprecated downcast. `.where(x != 0)`
expresses the same "treat zero as missing" intent and stays float64. Three
sites had it: underwater, drawdown and the monthly grid.

The zero was real, not hypothetical: it appears whenever a whole month ends
before the first installment, which happens when the SIP starts after the 1st
with day_of_month=1.

Monthly returns are now explicitly CLOSE TO CLOSE. Each cell compares this
month's closing value with the previous month's closing value, month-end to
month-end, so no gap is skipped and no intramonth open is used as a base. An
open-to-close return would discard the overnight and weekend moves between
months. The basis is stated in the payload so the UI never has to guess and a
future change has to update it.

The first month is now None rather than 0. With no prior close there is no
close-to-close return to report, and printing 0% would claim a flat month that
was never measured. A zero prior close likewise yields a gap, not an infinity.

UI:
- "Units" renamed "Shares held" -- units is mutual-fund language; for cash
  equity these are shares.
- Absolute return promoted from an unlabelled hint under Gain to its own
  figure, labelled "on total capital invested". Showing "+41.26%" beneath a
  rupee gain left the reader to guess what it was a percentage of.
- The headline sentence now states both returns and names each: what the
  capital returned in total, and what that means per year as XIRR.
- The Run button moves into Period and options.

Tests: 87 (up from 72). Includes a fixture that reproduces the zero-prior-close
case, and a close-to-close check that recomputes the grid independently, so a
switch to an intramonth base would fail.

Honest note on the warning guard: the no_warnings() helper clears
__warningregistry__ because catch_warnings does not, and without that a warning
already emitted elsewhere stays silent. Even so, the specific mutation used to
test it no longer reproduces the bug -- the close-to-close rewrite removed the
.fillna the warning depended on. The fix is verified directly instead: object
dtype plus .fillna warns, the current code contains no fillna, and a live-shape
run with a zero prior close raises nothing under -W error.

feat(sip): crisis-period analysis, and match the portfolio backtester layout

Replaces the abstract "Does timing matter?" framing with the question a SIP
investor actually asks: was starting into a crash a mistake?

For a lumpsum the answer is obvious -- buying before a crash is worse than
buying after. For a SIP it frequently inverts, because a SIP started into a
falling market spends the whole decline accumulating cheap units, while one
started after the recovery pays post-rebound prices from its first installment.
That inversion is counterintuitive enough to measure rather than assert, and it
is the most useful thing this page can tell someone afraid to begin.

Each crisis is therefore run two ways from the same history to the same end
date, differing only in when the first installment lands:

  - started into it   -- first installment on the crisis start
  - waited for the end -- first installment on the crisis end

Same money per month, same finish, only the beginning moved. The market's own
move and trough across the window sit alongside for context.

Reuses portfolio.crisis.INDIA_CRISES unchanged, so both tools name the same 32
events rather than maintaining two lists that drift.

Windows the price history does not fully cover are dropped, not clipped: a SIP
that existed for three days of the COVID crash did not live through it, and
saying otherwise is worse than saying nothing. Windows with less than 120 days
of runway after them are dropped too -- a two-week crash leaves one installment,
and one installment is a lumpsum, not a plan.

The summary counts how often starting early won rather than claiming it wins.
It is a tendency in the data, not a law, and the reader should see the score.

Layout now matches the portfolio backtester: three cards across the top
(Benchmark, SIP Schedule, Analysis Period), then a wide setup card with the
data-source dropdown and action button on its bottom border, and the full
charge panel as a right-hand sidebar. Same grid classes, same ChargeControls
component, so the two tools read as one product.

Tests: 96 (up from 87). Nine cover the crisis mechanics -- both variants ending
on the same date, the cheaper average cost that drives the effect, dropped
windows, ordering, and JSON safety. They test the mechanism, not the direction
of the result, which is a property of whatever data the user loaded.

fix(sip): India has no fractional shares — buy whole shares, carry the rest

The engine bought `deployed / price` units, so a Rs 10,000 installment into a
Rs 1,500 share bought 6.67 shares. Indian cash equity and ETFs trade in whole
units only. Pretending otherwise overstates the shares held and every return
derived from them, and the error compounds with every installment.

Now: each installment buys the largest whole number of shares it can afford,
and the remainder carries forward and joins the next one. Nothing is discarded.
Over six months at Rs 10,000 into a Rs 1,500 share that is 40 shares, not 36 —
the carried remainder buys a seventh share in some months, which a per-month
floor would have thrown away.

Charges are now levied on the value actually TRADED rather than on the
installment. Brokerage on money that never traded is not a charge anyone pays.
This moves the numbers slightly: 1% of a Rs 10,000 installment was Rs 100, and
is now Rs 99 on the Rs 9,900 actually bought. Sizing is iterative, because the
charge depends on the trade and the trade depends on the charge: size, charge,
step down a share if it no longer fits.

Uninvested cash is counted in the value and reported. The investor paid it in
and still holds it; excluding it would make the SIP look worse than it was. The
invariant is now explicit and tested: shares x price + cash + charges equals
everything paid in. No money is created or lost.

run_lumpsum buys whole shares too. Leaving it fractional would have handed the
lumpsum comparison an advantage the SIP is not allowed.

A SIP whose installments can never afford one share now raises rather than
silently reporting a plan that never traded. A single installment being too
small is NOT an error — the cash accumulates and buys later, which is what
actually happens.

On the portfolio backtester: it is deliberately NOT changed. It is a
weight-based drift-and-reset simulation and holds no share counts at all — its
state is weights and an equity curve, which is the standard abstraction for a
weight-target portfolio. Adding integer share counts there means per-symbol
share tracking, a cash residual and a rebalance that can no longer hit its
target weights exactly. That is a different simulation, not a bug fix, and it
would change every number the tool has ever produced. Worth doing deliberately
if wanted; not worth doing as a side effect of this.

Tests: 103 (up from 96). Seven cover whole shares, including the conservation
invariant and that the carried remainder really does buy an extra share. The
statutory-charge expectations are now derived from the traded value rather than
hardcoded, so they cannot silently re-encode the fractional assumption.

fix(security): build outbound URLs from HOST_SERVER, hash reset tokens

The password reset link and the RMoney OAuth callback were built with
url_for(_external=True), which derives scheme and host from the request's
Host header. An unauthenticated caller could poison that header so the
reset email pointed at an attacker-controlled origin, handing over the
reset token when the account owner clicked it (GHSA-pmxj-9wx6-hjmf).

Both now use utils.config.build_external_url(), which roots the URL at
the configured HOST_SERVER. HOST_SERVER is set by every official install
script and is not influenced by the request, so it cannot be poisoned.
SERVER_NAME was avoided deliberately: it also changes Flask routing and
breaks subdomain handling.

Separately, the raw reset token was stored in the Flask session, which is
a signed but unencrypted cookie. Whoever triggered the reset could read
the token back out of their own cookie by base64-decoding it, with no
Host header trick and no victim interaction required, needing only the
target's email address. The session now holds a SHA-256 hash only, and
both verification points compare with secrets.compare_digest(). A missing
session entry no longer counts as a match.

Adds regression tests covering URL construction, the cookie-decode
attack, and a guard against url_for(_external=True) returning to either
file.

Reported by tonghuaroot.

fix(order-updates): do not connect or retry on a dead broker token

Restarting between the ~03:00 IST token rollover and the first browser
request left the order-update adapter in a permanent 401 reconnect loop,
emitting a WARNING plus a library-level ERROR every backoff interval for
the life of the worker.

Two independent causes.

The boot scan selected sessions on is_revoked alone. That flag is only
flipped by the auto-expiry sweep, which runs from a before_request hook
and therefore needs a browser request to fire, so between the rollover
and the first request the row still looked live and the adapter
connected with a token the broker had already killed. The scan now also
requires a login in the current trading session, via a new
has_login_this_trading_session() that reads the database only and so is
safe on the boot thread, unlike is_session_valid(). Adapters still start
on login through upsert_auth, which is unchanged.

The reconnect loop treated a rejected handshake like a network blip. A
401/403 says the credential is dead, not that the link flapped, so every
retry was another rejected handshake. BaseOrderUpdateAdapter now stands
down on those two statuses and waits for the next login, while other
failures keep their existing backoff. IIFL Capital already did the
equivalent for MQTT CONNACK 4/5; Groww polls REST and logs at debug.

Net effect is fewer resources, not more: the loop no longer builds a
WebSocketApp and a TLS handshake every 60 seconds forever, and the
adapter thread now exits instead of spinning.

Fix SQLite startup lock by serializing init and cleaning sessions

Merge pull request #1734 from vishalrateria/fix-sqlite-lock-v2

Serialize startup database initialization to remove SQLite write-lock contention.

14 of the 20 startup init functions target the same file (openalgo.db), and
SQLite permits one writer per file, so running them 15-at-a-time made them
contend for the write lock rather than progress in parallel.

Validated by reproducing the contention against the real init functions: with
busy_timeout forced low so contention surfaces instead of being waited out,
max_workers=15 produced lock errors on both the cold and warm paths while
max_workers=1 produced none in any configuration. The existing
busy_timeout=15000 was masking the collision by waiting on it, and does not
cover SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT, which create_all's read-then-write pattern can hit.

Costs nothing: warm restart (what every existing install does) measures faster
serialized, 99ms vs 138ms, because the parallelism was never real - SQLite
serialized those writes anyway and the threads only added contention. Cold
first-run costs about 13ms, once.

docs(startup): correct the stale wording left by the DB-init serialization

Follow-up to #1734, which changed the startup DB init from 15 workers to 1 but
left the surrounding text describing the old behaviour.

- The completion log still said "initialized in parallel", which is now false.
- The strategy-book retry comment still justified itself with "the DB file
  briefly unavailable during a parallel init". The retry is still worth having,
  but for the real reason: openalgo.db is shared with the out-of-process
  websocket proxy, so a write can briefly find the lock held.
- logger.error(f"...{e}") swallowed the traceback. CLAUDE.md requires
  logger.exception() so the failure reaches errors.jsonl with its stack; a
  database that fails to initialise is exactly the case you want the traceback
  for.

Also recorded why max_workers=1 is deliberate, so it does not read as a leftover
and get "optimised" back to a thread pool: 14 of the 20 functions target the
same SQLite file, which permits one writer, so the parallelism was never real.
Noted why the executor is kept rather than replaced by a plain loop - each
function stays its own future, so one database failing cannot abort the rest.

No behaviour change.

fix(flow): persist the node trace so a run that did nothing can be explained

Every flow execution recorded logs=[]. The executor built the trace in memory
and returned it in the HTTP response, but update_execution_status() had no way
to store it, so only a manual "Run Now" ever showed its reasoning - and that
output vanished with the page. A scheduled workflow that fired every minute and
quietly placed no orders left no record of which condition stopped it, which is
precisely when the trace is wanted. add_execution_log() existed for this and was
imported by the executor but never called.

update_execution_status() now takes an optional logs list and writes it once at
the end of the run rather than appending per node: a 48-node workflow costs one
write instead of about fifty. None leaves any existing value alone; an empty
list is still written, because "ran and logged nothing" is itself a fact worth
recording.

Verified against workflow 107: runs before the change persisted 0 entries, the
run after persisted 62, including the AND-gate inputs and the time-window
evaluation that were deciding the outcome invisibly.

feat(flow): add a diagnostic that explains why a workflow places no orders

A flow that silently does nothing gives no clue which of its several gates is
shut, and they are checked in different places: activation state and the
schedule job live on the workflow row, analyzer mode is a global setting,
graph completeness is a strict validator pass, and the time windows are
evaluated against the server's local clock. Answering "why no orders" meant
opening all four by hand.

This checks them in the order an order has to pass them and prints the ones
that are closed, with the fix for each.

The timezone check is there because the two clocks disagree by design: the
scheduler's market-hours gate is IST-aware via pytz, but timeWindow nodes call
datetime.now() and get the server's local time. On a host that is not on IST
those windows are compared against the wrong clock, and the workflow looks
active and healthy while never entering. The official Docker image sets
TZ=Asia/Kolkata, so this bites bare-metal and custom-run installs.

Does not import app.py: that starts the WebSocket proxy and the schedulers on
import, which on a live machine either fights the running instance for port
8765 or brings up a second copy of the trading stack. A read-only diagnostic
must not do that, so it loads .env and talks to the database layer directly.

feat(flow): take the market-hours window from the calendar, overridable per flow

The "market hours only" gate was a hardcoded 09:15-15:30 weekday check applied
to every workflow whatever it traded. Two things were wrong with that.

It was incorrect for anything that is not NSE equity. MCX runs to 23:55 and
CRYPTO never closes, so any such workflow with the switch on could not fire
after 15:30 - the gate silently suppressed it and the flow looked healthy while
never entering. It also skipped only weekends, so a workflow traded straight
through Diwali.

And it was not adjustable. A strategy wanting a few minutes past the close to
square off had nowhere to ask for them.

The window now resolves through get_effective_session_window, the same calendar
the rest of the platform uses, so per-exchange hours, trading holidays and
special sessions are inherited rather than restated - no trading time is written
down here. A workflow can narrow or widen the clock from its own trigger node
with marketHoursStart / marketHoursEnd, and pick the calendar with
marketHoursExchange.

An override moves the clock only. It cannot reopen a day the exchange is shut,
so a workflow cannot configure its way into trading on a holiday.

Read from the graph on every run rather than baked into the scheduler job, so
editing the times applies from the next run, the same way node edits already do.
Jobs created before this change keep working: their stored market_hours_only
flag is honoured when the graph sets nothing itself.

fix(nubra): correct position fields, F&O exchange mapping and history window

Audited the Nubra plugin against the REST API V3 documentation and against
OpenAlgo's broker-module contract, verifying each finding against the live
account rather than the docs alone. Four groups of fixes.

Position field names. The live /sentinel/portfolio/positions payload does not
use the documented names: it returns netQty/buyQty/sellQty/ltp where the docs
promise netQuantity/buyQuantity/sellQuantity/lastTradedPrice. Reading the
documented names yielded 0 everywhere, so the position book showed zero
quantity and zero LTP, get_open_position always reported flat (mis-sizing
every smart order), and close_all_positions skipped every row while still
returning "All Open Positions SquaredOff". Read the observed name first with
the documented one as fallback, and make square-off report what actually
happened instead of asserting success.

F&O exchange vocabulary. Nubra has no NFO or BFO - an NSE option is reported
as exchange "NSE" with derivativeType "OPT", while the master contract stores
it as exchange NFO, brexchange NSE. Nothing folded it back, so every
token-keyed lookup missed and orders, trades and positions fell through to
Nubra's display name under the wrong exchange. New mapping/exchange.py does
not assert the fold: the Nubra exchange plus derivativeType only decides which
OpenAlgo exchanges are worth probing, and the answer returned is the one the
master contract matched. Unresolved instruments are logged by refId rather
than silently wearing a plausible label. The order-update adapter was also
passing RefData field 4 (the exchange token) where field 1 (ref_id, which is
what symtoken.token holds) was needed.

Error surfacing and session expiry. V3 reports failures in "error" while the
service layer reads "message", so every rejection surfaced as the generic
"Failed to place order" and margin errors as "Unknown error from Nubra".
HTTP 440 had no handling at all, so an expired session rendered as an empty
order book. Both are now classified and surfaced.

History window. Chunks were clipped to 03:45-10:00 UTC, the NSE cash session,
truncating every exchange that trades outside it - MCX lost its 09:00 open and
its entire evening session, more than half its candles. Request the whole UTC
day instead and let Nubra return what exists; there is no session table to
keep in sync with exchange circulars. Also replaces a "local time minus 5:30"
clock that only produced UTC on an IST-configured server.

Structure. Adds api/baseurl.py for the hosts, device id, auth headers and
session-expiry contract, replacing four copies of get_base_url and six literal
device-id strings; data.py and master_contract_db.py hardcoded the production
host, so NUBRA_USE_UAT sent orders to UAT while market data and the symbol
master stayed on PROD. Master contract now uses the shared pooled HTTP client
with explicit timeouts instead of requests. Also stops reading open/high/low/
oi from /orderbooks, which does not return them.

Verified live: orderbook, tradebook, positions, holdings, funds and history;
F&O resolution across NFO, BFO and MCX against real master-contract rows; MCX
5m history recovering 67 of 123 GOLD candles the old window discarded.

feat(tradesmart): pace quotes at the new 100/sec cap, separately from history

TradeSmart raised /GetQuotes to 100 requests per second. The other data
endpoints stayed on the older per-user allowance of 120 per minute, so the two
can no longer share one gate: paced for the minute budget, quotes ran at under
1% of what the broker now allows, and paced for the second budget, history
would run 60x over its ceiling.

Split into broker/tradesmart/api/rate_limiter.py, modelled on the Fyers one and
module level for the same reason - services build a fresh BrokerData per
request, so pacing state kept on self is discarded every call and paces nothing
against concurrent requests. Each budget gets its own lock and clock, so a
history call no longer delays a quote.

/GetQuotes is paced at ~90/sec, keeping roughly the 20% headroom Fyers uses.
get_depth rides the same gate because TradeSmart has no separate depth endpoint
and bills it as a quote. History (/EODChartData, /TPSeries) keeps 0.55s. An
unclassified endpoint, including None, falls to the slower gate rather than
being handed the per-second allowance by default.

The effect is on option chains and the OI tracker, which fan out one call per
strike: 90 symbols cost 49.5s of pure pacing before and 1.0s after, at which
point the ten-thread pool and network latency become the limit rather than us.

Rate-limit detection now matches the phrase rather than the number, so a future
change to the ceiling is still recognised as a limit hit rather than surfacing
as an unexplained Not_Ok.

feat(sandbox): implement GTT orders in analyzer mode (issue #1740)

Analyzer mode answered every GTT call with 501, so a GTT strategy could not be
tested before going live - the one thing sandbox exists for. The tables and
config were already in place from Phase 1 of the GTT plan; this is Phase 3,
the engine that uses them.

Adds sandbox/gtt_manager.py: place, modify, cancel and list, plus the trigger
machinery. Margin is reserved at placement so a GTT cannot promise an order the
account cannot fund when it fires. For OCO only one leg can ever execute, so
the default 'max' mode blocks the larger leg rather than both - blocking both
would double-count and reject GTTs the account can afford.

Firing has to happen exactly once. Three evaluators can see the same crossed
trigger within milliseconds of each other, so every one of them goes through
try_claim_trigger(): a single conditional UPDATE from 'pending' to 'triggering'
that lets the database pick the winner. Losers see rowcount 0 and stop. A
process that dies between claiming and firing would otherwise strand the leg
where nothing can ever pick it up again, so reclaim_stranded_legs() reverts
claims older than gtt_claim_timeout_sec; the timeout is part of the predicate,
so a merely slow worker is not yanked out from under itself. Any failure while
firing reverts the claim rather than losing the leg.

The polling engine now evaluates GTTs on every tick, whether or not there are
regular orders pending - a GTT is typically the only thing resting in the book.

Also fixes the sandbox test suite, which was uncollectable and had never run:
test/sandbox/__init__.py made the directory a package named 'sandbox' that
shadowed the real one, so every import in it failed. Removing it lets the real
package win. Behind that were two more reasons those tests could not pass: no
symtoken table to price orders against (now seeded for the two instruments they
trade) and MARKET orders needing a live quote (those four are now skipped with
a reason instead of failing). 37 pre-existing tests run for the first time.

Not yet wired, and tracked in the plan: the WebSocket evaluator, boot-time
catch-up, the hourly expiry job, and teaching reconcile_margin about GTT
reservations. Polling covers triggering in the meantime.

refactor(nubra): move exchange mapping into transform_data per OpenAlgo layout

The previous commit put the Nubra-to-OpenAlgo exchange fold in a new
mapping/exchange.py. That is not where OpenAlgo keeps it. Angel -- the family
template for Nubra -- has only margin_data, order_data and transform_data, and
every broker whose exchange vocabulary differs from OpenAlgo's keeps the map in
transform_data.py as map_exchange(), including dhan, definedge, fivepaisa,
groww, iifl and compositedge. Only arrow has a separate mapping/exchange.py, so
following it made Nubra the second outlier rather than conforming.

Moves the pure mapping into mapping/transform_data.py and renames to the house
convention: to_openalgo_exchange -> map_exchange(brexchange, derivative_type),
nubra_exchange_of -> brexchange_of. Nubra needs the extra derivative_type
argument because one broker exchange ("NSE") covers both the cash and the
derivatives segment, unlike dhan's one-to-one segment codes.

resolve_instrument() moves to mapping/order_data.py instead, since it resolves
against the master contract rather than translating an enum, and order_data.py
is the broker-JSON-to-normalized-rows module that already imports token_db.

No behaviour change: the 12 F&O resolution checks across NFO, BFO and MCX still
pass, and orderbook, tradebook, positions, holdings, funds and history are
unchanged against the live account.

feat(sandbox): complete GTT parity - websocket, catch-up, expiry, reconciliation

Finishes the four integration points the previous commit left open, so a
sandbox GTT now behaves like a live one on every path rather than only under
the polling engine.

WebSocket evaluator. Legs are indexed by symbol and evaluated on the tick that
crosses them, instead of waiting up to a poll interval. Indexed per leg rather
than per GTT because the claim is per leg and one tick can cross both sides of
an OCO. The tick handler no longer returns early when a symbol has no pending
orders: a GTT is usually the only thing resting for that symbol, so the early
return would have skipped every one of them.

Catch-up on boot. Fires GTTs whose trigger was crossed while the app was down.
Stranded claims are reverted first - a leg left in 'triggering' by the crash
that took the app down is invisible to the pending scan, so without that step
the very restart meant to recover it would skip it. Not gated by market hours,
because an off-hours restart is exactly the case it exists for.

Maintenance thread. Reclaims stranded claims every minute and expires due GTTs
hourly. It runs in both engine modes deliberately: the polling engine reclaims
on every tick, but in WebSocket mode - the default - that loop never starts, so
a leg stranded by a killed worker would have sat unclaimable until the next
restart and an expired GTT would have held its margin indefinitely. One
module-level daemon thread doing two indexed queries, not a scheduler.

Margin reconciliation. reconcile_margin counted only open positions, so a
resting GTT looked exactly like leaked margin - and with auto_fix on it would
have released the reservation the GTT needs to place its order when it fires.
Active GTT margin is now part of the expected total, and a failure to read it
skips reconciliation rather than risking that release.

Also fixes a leak in the new tests' own fixture: deleting a GTT row does not
release its margin, so the reservation from one test leaked into the next and
every reconciliation assertion saw a phantom discrepancy.

fix(sandbox): six release blockers in GTT - direction, OCO, cancel, margin, ticks, shape

QA was right on every count. Validated each against the code and the documented
contract before changing anything.

Trigger direction was derived from BUY/SELL. The contract derives it from the
trigger's role: triggerprice_sl sits below the LTP and fires on a fall,
triggerprice_tg sits above and fires on a rise
(docs/api/order-management/placegttorder.md). Action-based logic inverts two of
the four documented cases - BUY-on-dip and SELL-at-target - which fire
immediately on the first tick instead of waiting. Direction is now a stored
column, set from the role at placement, with a migration for existing installs
because create_all never adds columns to a table that already exists.

OCO could execute both orders. Claims were per leg with no parent-level
exclusivity, so two evaluators could each win a different sibling and both
place. The claim predicate now also requires that no sibling is already
triggering or triggered, and that the parent is still active - one UPDATE, so
the database still decides.

A cancelled GTT could still fire. Cancel left legs in 'triggering' untouched
and fire_leg never revalidated. Cancel now cancels claimed legs too, and
fire_leg re-checks both leg and parent state before it touches money.

Margin had three holes. A MARKET leg has no limit price, so it was sized at
zero and reserved nothing; it is now sized off the trigger price. A failed
insert left the reservation orphaned, since block_margin had already committed;
it is now released explicitly. And a failed re-block after a failed fire was
recorded as though it had succeeded, claiming margin the account did not hold.

GTTs placed after WebSocket startup never received ticks: notify_gtt_placed
existed but was never called, created no subscription and no refcount. It is
now called from placement, subscribes, and decrements on resolve so a symbol
nobody watches is unsubscribed.

The sandbox orderbook broke the frontend contract - no trigger_prices (required
by GttOrder and rendered directly by GttTab), a different leg shape, and
cancelled entries by default. It now matches what the broker mappers produce.

Also: `from events import bus` raised, so trigger events silently never
published; expiry published nothing; and a supplied expires_at was overwritten
with 365 days.

Tests: the direction cases encoded the old action-based behaviour and are
rewritten against the four documented scenarios; added OCO sibling contention,
cancel-during-claim, MARKET margin, orderbook shape and expiry regressions.

fix(gtt): close the cancel/fire race, wire logs and alerts, honour immutability

Second QA round. Validated each finding before changing anything; all four
blockers were real.

Cancel could still race a fire. The state check in fire_leg was check-then-act:
a cancel landing between the check and place_order returned success while the
order still went in, and both paths released the same margin, driving used
margin negative. The parent transition is now an atomic CAS - active ->
triggered in one conditional UPDATE - so whoever wins that row owns the
outcome, and cancel, which only matches active, can no longer succeed. A fire
that fails afterwards hands the parent back. The previous regression cancelled
before fire_leg started, which the fix was never in danger of failing; the new
one cancels from inside place_order, and fails against the old code.

A failed WebSocket trigger was never retried. The engine dropped the leg from
its index whatever fire_leg returned, so a leg that correctly reverted to
pending was left live in the database but inert - unsubscribed and unwatched
until a restart. It is now dropped only when the fire actually succeeded. This
also means the earlier live validation, where a CNC sell was rejected and the
margin restored, was only half the story: the recovery worked, the retry did
not.

The trigger_direction migration set every existing leg to 'below'. A target leg
would then fire on the wrong side. It now backfills from the data - a trigger
above the price recorded at placement is a rise trigger.

The sandbox orderbook still exposed cancelled GTTs: the manager defaults to
active-only, but the service passed status_filter through explicitly and
defaulted it to None, overriding that.

Logs and alerts were not captured at all. No gtt.* topic had a subscriber, so
placements, modifies, cancels and triggers produced no log row, no UI refresh
and no alert - in live as well as analyze. Only failures were recorded, and
only because they route through analyzer.error. All eight topics are now wired
to the log, socketio and telegram subscribers, and the triggered/expired events
carry the payload those subscribers read. Verified against a running instance:
placegttorder and gtttriggered rows now appear in analyzer_logs.

Also: modify silently accepted action, symbol, exchange and trigger_type
changes that modifygttorder documents as immutable; and a timezone-aware
expires_at was stored as naive wall-clock, making 13:00Z and 13:00+05:30 the
same instant when they are five and a half hours apart.

fix(latency): keep GTT latency instead of purging it after a week

GTT endpoints were already being timed - an unmapped namespace falls back to
its uppercased name, so placements were landing as PLACE_GTT_ORDER. But that
name is not in ORDER_TYPES, which is the set the purge keeps forever, so GTT
latency was being deleted after 7 days as though it were a quote lookup.

That is the wrong way round for a GTT in particular: it can rest for a year
before firing, so the placement record would be gone long before the order it
describes exists.

Named GTT_PLACE / GTT_MODIFY / GTT_CANCEL to match the PLACE / MODIFY / CANCEL
convention, and added to both copies of ORDER_TYPES - utils.latency_monitor and
database.latency_db each carry their own, and a type present in one but missing
from the other is silently purged.

fix(shoonya): skip incomplete master contract rows instead of aborting the exchange

Shoonya's symbol files ship placeholder rows that carry a Token but blank Symbol/TradingSymbol/Expiry columns (NFO_symbols.txt currently has ~18 at the top of the file). These reached the bulk insert as NaN and tripped the NOT NULL constraint on symtoken.brsymbol. Because the insert runs as one transaction per exchange, a single bad row rolled back that entire exchange. BFO failed earlier still: extract_name and extract_instrument_type raise TypeError on a NaN, aborting the whole master contract download.

Adds drop_incomplete_rows(), called in the NSE, NFO, CDS, MCX, BSE and BFO processors right after the column rename and before any string transform. BFO passes required=('brsymbol',) only, since it re-derives name from the trading symbol. copy_from_dataframe() keeps a final dropna on symbol and brsymbol as a last-resort guard.

fix(sandbox): make the GTT transition atomic, recoverable and always funded

Third QA round. All three findings were real, and they share a root cause: a
GTT transition was several separately committed operations, so anything landing
between them saw a half-applied state.

Cancel could clobber a fire. fire_leg claims the parent atomically, but cancel
read an active GTT and then wrote 'cancelled' onto that stale object. A fire
claiming the parent in between was overwritten: cancel reported success, the
child order was still placed, and the same margin was released twice. Cancel is
now a conditional UPDATE with a rowcount check - only the caller whose UPDATE
matched may cancel the legs or release the funds. Tested with two threads,
cancel held between its read and its write while the fire claims the parent.

A crash mid-fire stranded the GTT permanently. The parent flips to 'triggered'
before the child order exists, so that a cancel cannot slip in; if the worker
died there, the leg reaper reset the leg but nothing reset the parent, leaving
'triggered' over a 'pending' leg - invisible to every evaluator, unable to fire,
cancel or expire. Recovery now reads the only durable evidence of how far the
fire got, the child order itself: no triggered_order_id on any leg means the
order was never placed, so the GTT returns to active with its reservation
restored; a triggered_order_id means the order is real and the GTT is finalised
rather than undone, because undoing it would place a second order for one
trigger. Runs from the same reaper the engines and catch-up already call.

An exception lost the reservation. Margin is released before place_order so the
child order can be funded. A rejection restored it; a raised exception did not,
leaving the GTT back on 'active' holding nothing - it would fire again on the
next tick and be rejected for want of funds. Both paths now go through one
compensation function. If the funds cannot be restored the GTT is marked
'rejected' rather than returned to 'active': visibly dead beats silently armed
and unfunded. The same rule applies to crash recovery.

Each regression was mutation-checked against the old behaviour.

Also registers the WhatsApp GTT handlers, which were the only alert channel
left out - a WhatsApp user would have missed a firing a Telegram user saw.

Sandbox suite: 84 passed, 4 skipped. Ruff unchanged at its 165 baseline.

fix(sandbox): durable GTT-order correlation, no double-block, honest cancel

Fourth QA round. All three financial findings were real, and the test-harness
criticism was the most important of the four - my own tests had been running
against the user's real db/sandbox.db.

Crash could duplicate a child order. The order is committed before the leg
records triggered_order_id, so a crash between those two commits left a real
order with no marker; recovery trusted the marker, re-armed the GTT, and it
could place a second order for one trigger. SandboxOrders now carries
gtt_leg_id, written in the same INSERT as the order and covered by a unique
index, so recovery asks the order table rather than the marker: a correlated
row means the GTT has already fired, whatever the leg says, and the marker is
repaired from it. The unique index also means a replayed claim cannot insert a
second order.

Recovery could double-block margin. It read margin_blocked and re-blocked
whatever it found, so a crash before the release - where the reservation was
still intact - reserved the same money twice, taking used margin from 950 to
1900. It now re-blocks only when the reservation was actually released, and
leaves an intact one alone.

Cancel could report success without freeing funds. release_margin's result was
discarded, so a failure left the GTT cancelled and the money blocked with
nothing to point at. Cancel now checks it, records the amount still owed on the
row, and returns 500 rather than claiming success.

Test isolation. test/conftest set only DATABASE_URL, so the sandbox suite ran
against db/sandbox.db - the real analyzer database - mutating live state and
producing results that depended on whatever it held. All four database URLs are
now pinned to test files, the scoped session is cleared around every test
(which is why several passed alone and failed in a full run), and the fixture
purges orders as well: SQLite reuses a deleted row's autoincrement id, so a
leftover correlated order made the next test's leg collide.

The new tests place a real child order and rewind exactly the state a crash
between the two commits leaves, rather than writing the marker by hand. Each of
the three fixes was mutation-checked.

db/sandbox.db verified byte-identical afterwards. Ruff at its 164 baseline.

fix(sandbox): no GTT state change is published unless the funds actually moved

Fifth QA round. All four findings were real, and three share one shape: the
result of release_margin was discarded, so the row said the money had moved
when it had not.

Rejected orders poisoned the correlation. The CNC-sell rejection path also
carried gtt_leg_id, which is unique and which recovery reads as proof the GTT
fired. A refused attempt therefore marked the GTT triggered and, because the
correlation was already taken, stopped that leg ever ordering again. Only an
accepted order owns the correlation now, and recovery ignores rejected rows
even if one somehow exists - a broker refusing an order is not evidence it was
placed.

Fire continued when the release failed. It released the GTT's reservation and
placed regardless of the outcome, so a failed release meant a second
reservation blocked on top of one never returned - the account charged twice
for one trigger. It now stands down and lets the next tick retry, and the
compensation path restores only what was genuinely released rather than
assuming.

Modify reported success after a failed release, recording a smaller
reservation than the ledger held, so every later reconciliation blamed the gap
on something else. Expiry committed 'expired' with margin_blocked=0 before
checking, leaving funds held against a GTT that no longer existed to point at
them. Both now free the funds first and only publish the transition if that
worked; expiry leaves the GTT active to retry.

All four release paths go through one helper, so no caller can forget to look
at the result, and a raised exception reads the same as a refusal.

Two test-harness fixes. The unique-correlation test always skipped - the
fixture purges orders before each test, so the order it looked for never
existed - and it now creates its own. And test/conftest used setdefault, so an
exported production DATABASE_URL would have won and run the suite against the
real databases; the URLs are now assigned unconditionally, verified by running
with the production values exported.

Each of the four fixes was mutation-checked. Sandbox suite: 97 passed, 4
skipped, clean isolated database, db/sandbox.db byte-identical afterwards.
Ruff at its 194 baseline.

docs(readme): replace em dashes with plain punctuation

Colons where the dash introduced a definition or a list, commas where it was a
parenthetical aside, so each sentence still reads the way it did.

fix(sandbox): move GTT funds and state in one transaction, claim conditionally

Sixth QA round, and the architectural diagnosis was right: FundManager committed
independently of the GTT state update, so a helper that checked the result could
never make the two atomic. Fixed at that level rather than around it.

FundManager gains stage_margin_delta, which applies a margin change WITHOUT
committing. Funds and the GTT share one scoped session, so a caller can now
stage the fund move alongside its own row changes and commit once - either both
land or neither does.

Modify used two commits. A failure between them left the ledger and the row
describing different amounts of the same money, in whichever direction the
margin moved. It is now a single transaction, and its parent update is
conditional on 'active': the read it works from can be stale, and a plain
assignment reported a successful modify against a GTT that had already fired.

Expiry had both faults. It released the funds and then committed, so a failed
commit returned the money while the GTT stayed active - and the next sweep
released the same reservation again. It also assigned 'expired' over whatever
it found, so a GTT that fired between the sweep's query and its update was
overwritten and its child order's margin released underneath it. Expiry now
claims the parent conditionally and stages the release in the same transaction.

Two of the new tests were vacuous when first written and are rewritten:

* the commit-failure tests broke only the first commit, which under a two-commit
  implementation is the funds commit - nothing moved, nothing split, and the
  test passed against the bug it existed to catch. They now break each commit
  boundary in turn and assert the invariant that matters, that the row and the
  ledger agree, rather than asserting nothing changed - an unbroken iteration
  legitimately completes;
* the expiry-race test could not reach the conditional claim at all, because a
  fired GTT is no longer 'active' and the sweep's own pre-filter excluded it. It
  now injects the fire between the query and the update, which is the real race.

Every fix is mutation-checked against a faithful reproduction of the previous
ordering, not a convenient one: the first mutation I tried passed, because a

fix(sandbox): every GTT transition now moves funds and state in one commit

Seventh QA round. Modify and expiry were converted last time; fire and cancel
were not, and both were still multi-commit.

Fire released the reservation through a committing call and recorded
margin_blocked=0 in a separate one. A crash between them returned the money
while the row still claimed it, and recovery reads margin_blocked > 0 as proof
the funds were never released - so it re-armed the GTT without restoring
anything, leaving it active with nothing behind it. The release is now staged
alongside margin_blocked=0 and committed once, which is also what makes that
recovery assumption true rather than merely plausible.

Cancel committed the parent, then the legs, then released the funds. A failure
after the first commit left a terminally cancelled GTT with the money still
blocked - and no retry could claim it, because the row was no longer active.
Parent claim, leg cancellation and the staged release are now one transaction,
so a failure leaves the GTT untouched and cancellable again.

Placement was the same shape and had not been reported yet: it blocked the
margin, then persisted the rows, relying on a compensating release that could
itself fail. Converted too.

Four of the new tests were written wrong first and are fixed here. Breaking only
the first commit lets a two-commit implementation fail at the funds step, so
nothing moves and nothing splits - the test passes against the bug it exists to
catch. Each now breaks every commit boundary in turn and asserts the invariant
that matters, that the row and the ledger describe the same money, rather than
asserting nothing changed: an unbroken iteration legitimately completes.

Every transition is mutation-checked against the previous ordering.

fix(sandbox): compute staged margin in SQL, not Python, to stop a lost update

Two GTT placements racing each reserved 950 while the ledger moved only once.
stage_margin_delta read the funds row, adjusted it in memory and left the commit
to its caller, so both threads read the same starting balance, each wrote its
own total, and the second commit erased the first. Firing or cancelling both
GTTs afterwards would drive used_margin negative and conjure available funds.

The class lock could not help. It is released the moment staging returns, long
before the caller commits, so it never covered the window that matters - and a
lock cannot span processes in any case.

The change is now a single UPDATE that computes the new balance in SQL
(available_balance - :delta, used_margin + :delta), with the sufficiency check
in the WHERE clause rather than in Python, and rowcount deciding whether it
applied. It stays inside the caller's transaction, so funds and GTT state still
commit together.

block_margin and release_margin have the same read-modify-write shape but hold
the class lock across their own commit, so the window does not exist there;
they are left alone rather than churned.

Added the deterministic two-thread placement test, which holds both threads at
the staging step until neither has committed, and asserts the invariant across
mixed activity: the sum of active GTT reservations equals used_margin. Verified
by reverting to the ORM read-modify-write, which fails it.

fix(nubra): surface session expiry, fix error gates, margin triggers and OTP hint

Addresses the cubic review of the previous Nubra commits. Eight of the ten
visible findings were reproduced and fixed; two were checked against the
codebase and rejected, with the reasoning recorded below.

Session expiry (HTTP 440) reached callers as a successful-looking empty result
on every market-data path. The quote fallback re-raised only exceptions whose
text contained "Authentication failed", and the history chunk loop swallowed
everything, so an expired session became zeroed quotes or an empty DataFrame.
Adds a typed NubraSessionExpired so those deliberate per-symbol and per-chunk
catches can let it through while still absorbing genuine partial failures.
funds.py returned {} on 440, which funds_service reports as HTTP 200 with no
data; it now raises so the service answers 500 with the reason.

Error gates missed the standardized shape introduced when get_api_response
began returning {"status": "error", "message": ...}. A 440 carries no "error"
key, so close_all_positions fell through to "No Open Positions Found" and
cancel_all_orders_api cancelled nothing silently. Adds is_error_response()
covering both shapes and applies it at all three gates.

Margin estimation dropped stop triggers: SL and SL-M were mapped to their price
types but the entryConfig was never emitted, so funds_required priced an
untriggered order. The V3 margin request reuses the placement payload verbatim,
and MarginCalculatorSchema already resolves trigger_price for this purpose.

get_ws_urls could abort order-stream startup instead of falling back, because a
transport failure in /userinfo propagated out of a lookup whose own docstring
promises (None, None) on failure. Guarded at the source so both callers benefit.

The OTP hint told users to reload the page to resend, but only the login GET
dispatches an OTP - reloading the React page just re-renders it. Corrects the
hint and the two code comments that repeated the same false claim, and drops
the inaccurate "server-side session" description of the Flask cookie.

Rejected, with evidence:

- "Non-TOTP accounts never receive an OTP; call /sendphoneotp twice for both
  VERIFY_MOBILE and VERIFY_TOTP." The official Nubra SDK's __send_otp returns
  the temp_token immediately on VERIFY_MOBILE and only makes the second call on
  VERIFY_TOTP, which is exactly what this code does. Making the second call
  unconditionally is what previously replaced a token bound to a live OTP
  challenge with one that was not, and /verifyphoneotp rejected it as
  "unauthorized".

- "Successful logins leak session_token into debug logs." utils/logging's
  SensitiveDataFilter already redacts session_token in Python dict-repr form,
  verified by running the live patterns against the exact log line.

Verified against a genuinely expired Nubra session: orderbook, tradebook,
positionbook, holdings and funds all now return HTTP 500 carrying "log in
again" where they previously returned HTTP 200 with empty results.

fix(sandbox): refuse to release more margin than is reserved

Releasing more than is held drove used_margin negative and credited the
difference as available cash. From a standing start, stage_margin_delta(-1) left
used_margin at -1 and available_balance one rupee higher than the account ever
had; release_margin(1) did the same. Money out of nothing, and every figure
derived from the balance wrong from then on.

No valid GTT transition reaches it - the conditional claims already prevent a
double release - but the primitive allowed it, so any future caller or recovery
defect supplying an excessive amount would have created cash silently.

The staged path guards the negative delta in the same UPDATE as the positive
one, so the check cannot be raced past. The committing path checks under the
lock it already holds. Both refuse without changing anything.

Failing closed is the right way round here. An over-release invents money and
corrupts everything downstream; a refused release leaves margin blocked, which
reconcile_margin(auto_fix=True) already exists to correct.

Verified that the legitimate cycle is untouched: block 500, release 500, back to
zero; releasing 500.01 against 500 is refused and leaves the row exactly as it
was. Both guards mutation-checked.

docs(claude): record the migration convention

CLAUDE.md said nothing about migrations, so the natural assumption is that a
change applied from init_db() reaches everyone on restart. It does not: seeding
functions generally only run against an empty table, so an existing install
keeps the old schema indefinitely and the change never lands on the deployments
that already exist. I made exactly that mistake this week and told the user no
migration was needed.

Records what is not visible from the code: that users upgrade with
`cd upgrade && uv run migrate_all.py`, that every schema change ships as a
registered script there, and the properties those scripts are expected to have -
idempotent, --status supported, guarded so a customised value is not clobbered,
and backfilled from the data rather than a uniform default.

Also notes the SQLite constraints that shape the approach (no in-place CHECK
alter, no UNIQUE column by ALTER) with the existing table-rebuild script as the
reference, and that a migration should be tested against a copy of a real
database forced back to the old schema - working on an empty one and failing on
a populated one is the usual way this goes wrong.

already the convention in 9 scripts, the rebuild example is real, and the
empty-table seeding guard is the one in market_calendar_db.

deliberately stopped doing that, and says so in place: a CNC sell leaves a

fix(flattrade): key market data routing on exchange and token, not token alone

The WebSocket adapter discarded the 'e' (exchange) field that Flattrade sends on every tk/tf/dk/df packet and keyed all routing on the bare token. Noren tokens are unique only within an exchange: the current master carries 2259 tokens duplicated across exchanges (CDS/NSE x2256, BSE/MCX x2, BSE_INDEX/NSE x1). Worse than the Shoonya case, _find_matching_subscriptions() fanned out by token while _get_symbol_info() returned the single overwritten mapping, so a collision published both copies to one symbol's topic and left the other subscription completely silent. Rekeys token_to_symbol to scrip_to_symbol and the MarketDataCache to the full scrip ('NFO|65872'), which _create_subscription already builds. Adds _resolve_scrip(), which routes on the packet's 'e' field and falls back to a token index only when it resolves to exactly one subscribed scrip; an ambiguous exchange-less tick is logged and dropped rather than routed to the wrong symbol. Subscription fan-out and both cleanup paths now match on scrip. _create_subscription raises on an unmapped exchange instead of silently building a 'None|token' scrip that no feed message can match.

fix(trading): MCX, NCO and CDS offered CNC instead of NRML on the chart terminal

The charting terminal decided a symbol's product list from its lot size:

    const lots = DERIVATIVE_EXCHANGES.has(exchange) && lotsize > 1
    const productOptions = lots ? ['MIS', 'NRML'] : ['MIS', 'CNC']

Every MCX, NCO and CDS contract carries lotsize 1 in the master contract, so
the second half of that test was always false and the whole commodity and
currency segment was treated as cash equity. The terminal offered CNC, which
those segments do not accept, and the broker rejected the order. In a current
master this is 15772 of 15772 MCX rows, 27335 of 27335 NCO rows and 7691 of
7691 CDS rows - the entire segment, not an edge case. NFO and BFO were never
affected because their lot sizes are 20, 25, 30, 50, 65 and so on.

The segment decides the product, never the lot size, so the lot-size term is
gone rather than special-cased. Order quantity is unchanged: orderQty() is
lots x lotsize, and multiplying by a lot size of 1 sends the same number to
the broker. Only the product list and the quantity label change.

Both decisions are now exported as productOptionsFor() and usesLots() so they
are testable on their own; a mutation back to the old behaviour fails 10 of
the 23 new cases, while the NFO, BFO, NSE and BSE cases stay green.

PlaceOrderDialog already derived its product list from isFnOExchange() rather
than the lot size and was never affected; its own lotsize > 1 test drives the
quantity display mode and is left alone.

fix(upgrade): create the APScheduler job store tables in the migrations

migrate_flow.py documented three tables but created two. flow_apscheduler_jobs
appeared exactly once in the file, in the docstring, and no migration anywhere
in upgrade/ created it - yet the script still reported success, so it read as
covered when it was not. historify_apscheduler_jobs had no migration at all;
migrate_historify_scheduler.py creates the DuckDB schedule tables but the job
store lives in the main SQLite database, and that half was simply missing.

Both were left to APScheduler, whose SQLAlchemyJobStore.start() issues the
CREATE TABLE itself. At startup that DDL lands in the middle of the boot write
burst needing an exclusive write lock on openalgo.db. An install that loses
that race logs "database is locked", and because init_flow_scheduler runs from
exactly one place at boot with no retry, the scheduler stays uninitialized for
the life of the process - which in production is a single Gunicorn worker that
never restarts. Scheduled workflows and downloads then silently never run, and
the failure is swallowed by a bare logger.error with nothing surfaced in the UI.

Creating the tables in the migration removes that DDL from startup entirely,
so the race cannot happen regardless of which writer holds the lock. Verified:
a scheduler started against a migrated database issues zero DDL statements and
round-trips a persisted job.

Both tables are built from APScheduler's own Table metadata rather than
hand-written SQL, so the schema cannot drift from what APScheduler expects and
ix_<tablename>_next_run_time is created with the table. The index is then
checked separately, because Table.create(checkfirst=True) tests only for the
table - a job store table created without its index would be silently accepted
and left permanently unindexed while every due-job poll scans.

Two related fixes fell out of testing:

migrate_flow.py resolved DATABASE_URL relative to the current directory. Its
own documented invocation is `cd upgrade && uv run migrate_flow.py`, so the
default "sqlite:///db/openalgo.db" pointed at upgrade/db/openalgo.db, which
SQLAlchemy creates empty on connect - the migration would report success having
built its tables in a database the app never opens. Relative sqlite paths now
resolve against the project root. migrate_all.py was unaffected because it runs
each script with cwd set there.

migrate_flow.py also gained --status, which CLAUDE.md requires of every
migration and this one lacked.

Tested against a copy of a real 41-table database forced back to the old schema
as well as a fresh one: applies, is idempotent across repeat runs, repairs a
table missing its index, and reports both states correctly through --status.
Full migrate_all.py run passes 23 of 23.

fix(historify): release scoped sessions when a scheduled download finishes

execute_schedule is registered with APScheduler and runs on its worker
threads, which have no Flask app context, so the teardown_appcontext handler
in app.py never fires for them. The function had a try/except but no finally,
so every scoped session it touched stayed bound to the worker thread after the
run ended: auth_db for the API key lookup, plus whatever create_and_start_job
reaches. A SQLAlchemy Session holds its connection from the first query until
commit, rollback or close, so each one left behind keeps an open SQLite read
transaction rather than merely an idle handle.

That is the damage. The count is bounded - APScheduler's default executor is a
10-thread pool and threads are reused, so this is not unbounded growth toward
the descriptor limit - but a read transaction held open across runs blocks WAL
checkpointing and is exactly the kind of thing that surfaces later as
"database is locked" from an unrelated writer.

A finally rather than a line at the end of the function, because the four
early returns are the common paths: a missing schedule, one that is disabled
or paused, no API key configured, or an empty watchlist all return from the
middle of the try and would skip a trailing statement entirely.

This was the one background entry point missing the cleanup.
flow_scheduler_service, flow_price_monitor_service and
flow_order_update_monitor_service already call remove_all_scoped_sessions in a
finally; this matches them. The remaining background services in services/
run a single long-lived thread that binds once, which is bounded and a
different shape of problem.

Covered by test/test_scheduler_session_cleanup.py, which binds a session on a
real worker thread and asserts none survives the job across all four early
returns and the except branch. Removing the finally fails all four. The suite
includes a guard asserting the probe still reports a genuine leak, so the
cases cannot pass by failing to observe anything.

fix(scheduler): create APScheduler job store tables during db init

On a fresh install the Flow and Historify schedulers both failed with
"database is locked" while creating their job store tables, and stayed
dead for the life of the process - so scheduled workflows and scheduled
downloads silently never ran. Reported on a 2-core 1.35 GHz / 4 GB box
where the boot write burst outlasts the 15s busy_timeout.

APScheduler's SQLAlchemyJobStore issues its own CREATE TABLE from
scheduler.start(), which runs after db_ready.set() releases the rest of
the boot, so the DDL has to take the openalgo.db write lock mid-burst.
Scheduler init is one-shot, so a single lost race disables the scheduler
permanently. #1750 fixed this for upgraders via the migration scripts;
fresh installs run no migrations and were never covered.

Create both tables in the serialized (max_workers=1) database-init phase
instead, where nothing else is writing, leaving start()'s checkfirst
create a read-only no-op. The scheduler services call the same helper as
a retrying safety net for callers outside app boot.

Also switches the job stores from url= to engine=create_db_engine(...)
so they follow the project NullPool policy rather than SQLAlchemy's
default QueuePool, and moves flow_scheduler_service off logging.getLogger
onto utils.logging.get_logger.

No new schema: upgrade/migrate_flow.py and
upgrade/migrate_historify_scheduler.py already cover existing installs,
and produce a schema identical to the runtime path.

Closes #1759

fix(indmoney): pace REST calls against one shared per-category clock

Rate limiting was reactive only: a 429 retry helper duplicated verbatim in
four modules (data/funds/margin_api/order_api - byte-identical), plus two
local loop delays. Those delays pace within a single call and do nothing
across threads, and services build a fresh BrokerData(auth_token) per
request, so nothing coordinated concurrent callers. An option-chain load, a
position-book LTP refresh and an order placement could each look
well-behaved while collectively breaching 5/s - which is what produced the
observed 429s on /market/historical/1day, each costing a second of backoff
plus a wasted request against the daily quota.

Adds broker/indmoney/api/rate_limiter.py following the established pattern in
broker/definedge and broker/fyers: module-level lock and per-bucket clock so
every importer paces together, with the documented per-category ceilings
(docs 03-conventions):

    order        10/s   POST /order, /order/{modify,cancel}, /smart/order*
    data          5/s   /market/historical, /market/instruments, /margin
    quote         5/s   /market/quotes/*
    non_trading  15/s   profile, funds, order & trade book, GET /order*

Paced at 80% of each ceiling, as fyers does, since the broker measures its
window from its own clock. Buckets are independent, so a slow quote stream
never throttles order placement. Method matters in classification: POST
/order places (10/s) while GET /order reads back (15/s).

Daily usage against the documented 100,000/day cap is counted per IST day
and warned at 80% and at the cap - previously untracked, so exhaustion would
have surfaced only as failures.

POST /generate/token is deliberately NOT routed through the limiter: it allows
one request per 60s and 5 wrong TOTP codes trigger a 15-minute lockout, so
the correct response to a throttle there is to fail loudly, not sleep and
retry.

Net -152 lines. Verified: 33 checks covering classification, ceilings, 429
retry/Retry-After, and 20 concurrent calls across 5 threads holding 4.20/s
against the 5/s ceiling with a 0.250s minimum gap. Live smoke test of
quotes, depth, funds, order book and a 10-way concurrent burst: no errors.

fix(indmoney): address code review findings across order, auth and streaming paths

Validated each reported issue against the code and, where possible, against a
live IndMoney session. Nine were real and are fixed; one is correct in the
narrow sense but is a deliberate trade, now documented.

Order safety:
- Never auto-retry an order-write 429. Placement/modify/cancel are not
  idempotent and INDstocks offers no idempotency key, so retrying a throttle
  the broker had already accepted would place a SECOND live order. Order
  writes now fail loudly and tell the operator to reconcile against the order
  book; reads still retry.
- _is_smart_order() only matched TRIGGER/OCO, but the order book reports a
  standalone trigger order back as GTT_LIMIT (confirmed live). Stop cancels and
  modifies were therefore routed to the regular endpoints. The vocabulary now
  lives in one place, SMART_ORDER_TYPES, shared with the order-book mapping.

Streaming:
- Group subscribe frames by segment inside _send_subscribe_chunks rather than
  in the adapter. The adapter grouped correctly, but IndWebSocket.resubscribe()
  iterates input_request_dict by mode alone and rebuilt the mixed frames on
  every reconnect - and a mixed frame delivers ticks only for its first
  segment. Both paths now share the one chokepoint.
- Resolve the order-update stream's bare numeric order_id to the canonical
  EQ-/DRV- id before publishing, so an update can be matched to the order that
  was placed. TTL-bounded cache, refresh throttled to one order-book fetch per
  5s, falls back to the raw id rather than dropping the update.

Funds and auth:
- _available_cash() no longer falls back to max() over the balance breakdown.
  That could return option_buy (4449.65 vs a 2980.40 cash limit in the docs'
  own sample), reporting premium buying power as stock cash and overstating
  order size. Unrecognised shapes now fall through to withdrawal_balance.
- validate_access_token() returns a tri-state: True accepted, False REJECTED,
  None unverifiable. A 429/5xx/network failure is not evidence against the
  token, so a transient outage no longer locks a working installation out of
  its own broker session. It also routes through the shared rate limiter
  instead of bypassing the non-trading clock.

Housekeeping:
- get_intervals docstring no longer advertises the removed sub-minute intervals.
- Removed get_order_trades: it had no caller. Groww needs a per-order fetch
  because it has no bulk endpoint; IndMoney has /trade-book, which get_trade_book
  already uses.

Not changed - pacing gap jitter. Reserved slots are ordered but each caller
sleeps independently, so gaps dip to ~0.21s against a 0.25s target. Measured:
the RATE holds at 4.2/s against the 5/s ceiling on every trial, and 0.21s is
4.8/s instantaneous - inside the ceiling, which is what the 20% headroom is
for. Enforcing an exact gap needs a lock held across the sleep, serialising the
bucket so one slow request stalls every other caller. The broker meters a rate,
not gaps. apply_rate_limit() now states the guarantee, and the over-strict
assertion in the test was corrected. definedge, dhan and fyers behave the same.

fix(indmoney): scope order-id cache per user, harden token rejection, add rate-limiter tests

Second round of review findings. All five were real.

Token validation (most serious): a 401/403 whose body parsed to a non-object
- a JSON list, string or null - raised AttributeError on body.get(), escaped
to the outer handler and was reported as 'unverifiable', so
authenticate_broker proceeded with a credential the broker had explicitly
REJECTED. The verdict is now decided from the status code alone before the
body is touched; parsing can only enrich the message, never flip the outcome.

Order-id resolution:
- Key the cache by (user_id, order_id). The order book it is built from is
  per-user, so two accounts holding the same numeric id would have one user's
  canonical id published on the other's stream.
- Throttle refreshes per (user, order id) rather than globally. A global clock
  meant a genuinely new order kept publishing a bare id for the whole window,
  so one order appeared under two different ids across its own lifecycle and
  broke dedup.
- Fetch the order book OUTSIDE the cache mutex. Holding a lock across a network
  round trip stalled normalization for every other order-update stream while
  one user's book was slow or rate-limited.

Smart-order vocabulary: the comment claimed a single source of truth that did
not exist - transform_order_data still duplicated the GTT types inline. Both
now derive from BROKER_ORDER_TYPE_MAP, so adding a GTT type updates the price
mapping and the cancel/modify routing together.

safety-critical policy that an order write is never retried on a 429 - a retry
of a request the broker had already accepted places a second live order - plus

Always clear the Flask session on /auth/logout, not only when logged_in is true.

The password step sets session["user"]; only the broker OAuth callback sets

permanent if OAuth is abandoned - and is also the normal path every morning after
the ~3:00 AM IST broker token expiry. session.clear() sat inside the logged_in
guard, so logout was a no-op in that state and /auth/login bounced the user
straight back to /broker with no in-app escape.

The session is now cleared before the teardown, so a failure in revocation or
notification cannot leave the user stuck. The heavy side effects (cache cleanup,
token revocation, clearing user sessions, SocketIO notifications) stay gated on a
fully active session - running them for a half-logged-in session would publish
CACHE_INVALIDATE_ALL and tear down the shared broker feed for the user's other
logged-in devices (issue #1591).

Also closes an incomplete-logout weakness: the residual session["user"] was
enough to complete broker OAuth via the CSRF-exempt brlogin.broker_callback,
which gates only on "user" in session.

Adds regression coverage for the half-logged-in and fully logged-in paths.

fix(auth): protect /auth/logout against forced logout from other origins

Logout was reachable cross-site. It is CSRF-exempt, accepts GET, and
SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE="Lax" attaches the session cookie to top-level
cross-site navigations, so a link on any page the user visited was enough
to trigger it.

That matters because logout here is not "destroy a cookie". It revokes the
broker token, publishes CACHE_INVALIDATE_ALL so the out-of-process proxy
disconnects the adapter and drains the pool, clears every device's session
and flushes the symbol cache. A forced logout is an availability attack on
a live trading session: running strategies lose their broker session and
recovery needs the full daily OAuth flow.

The endpoint was POST-only after 43e8a1b5b, which added test_logout_csrf.py
for exactly this. 74c25ef26 restored GET for backward compatibility and the
test was not updated, so it has asserted the opposite ever since.

Two layers now:

- Drop the CSRF exemption, so POST is token-checked. SameSite=Lax is not
  enough on its own - ports are not part of the same-site check, so another
  service on the same host is same-site and its POST carries the cookie,
  which is the normal situation on a self-hosted box. Setup.tsx was the only
  caller not already sending a token; the axios client adds it via an
  interceptor and ServerError.tsx sends it explicitly.
- Check fetch metadata for GET, which Flask-WTF never validates. Only
  same-origin (our own pages and redirects) and none (typed URL, bookmark)
