fix(sandbox): stop execution cycles scaling with resting-order count

check_and_execute_pending_orders slept batch_delay (1s) after every
ORDER_RATE_LIMIT (10) pending orders, so a cycle cost ceil(N/10)-1 seconds
purely as a function of queue depth - 9.1s at 100 resting orders, 14.1s at
150 - and paid it even when nothing was fillable.

The sleep protected nothing. Every quote the cycle needs is fetched up front
in one _fetch_quotes_batch call; inside the loop each order is a dict lookup,
local DB writes and an async EventBus publish, with no broker call left to
throttle. ORDER_RATE_LIMIT is the inbound-API limit, reused here to rate-limit
local work.

It compounded: a slower cycle stranded more orders, which slowed the next one.
Measured on the old code, one order's time-to-fill went 4.6s with no backlog to
34.8s behind 150 resting orders - 7.6x on queue depth alone.

Replaced with a periodic time.sleep(0). Under Docker this loop shares a green
thread with request handling (gunicorn --worker-class eventlet --workers 1), so
a long backlog must still yield to the hub; it just no longer costs wall clock.
A 150-order cycle goes from 14.06s to ~0s.

Scope, from live MCX testing against a running instance with real quotes:
MARKET orders that get a quote fill synchronously inside place_order and never
reach this loop - measured 0.08-0.32s, unchanged behind a 100-order backlog. So
this is the recovery path for orders that go through the engine (resting
LIMIT/SL becoming fillable, or a MARKET order that missed immediate execution),
not the immediate path. Relevant to #1768 as the amplifier, not the trigger.

Test added to the CI allowlist, since backend-test runs an explicit file list.

Refs #1768

* fix(fivepaisa): send SL-M as a protective stop-limit, not at market

5Paisa rejects every order it reads as at-market when it comes from an API
key: OrderStatus "Rejected By 5P", Reason "Market order with Algo Id not
allowed" (verified live 2026-08-07 on NSE cash; the same string Kotak
returns). It has no order-type field - Price=0 IS the market flag, and the
order book echoes it back as AtMarket="Y".

The live order book makes the rule unambiguous:

  AtMarket=N            -> Fully Executed
  AtMarket=Y  WithSL=N  -> Rejected By 5P
  AtMarket=Y  WithSL=Y  -> Rejected By 5P  (both SL-M attempts)

Plain MARKET orders already dodged this - transform_data converts them to an
MPP-protected LIMIT off the LTP - but SL-M skipped that branch entirely and
went out as Price=0 + StopLossPrice.

Give SL-M the same treatment, anchored on the TRIGGER rather than the LTP (the
LTP is irrelevant to an order that rests until triggered): offset MPP percent
beyond the trigger in the fill direction, SELL below and BUY above, so the stop
still fills once it trips. NSE wants that direction anyway - an SL SELL limit
must sit at or below its trigger. Same shape as the Dhan #1647 fix.

The limit is snapped to the instrument tick away from the trigger and forced at
least one tick past it, so rounding can never land it back on the trigger or
collapse it to zero on a low-priced scrip. Fails closed when the tick size
cannot be resolved rather than falling back to Price=0, which RMS would reject
anyway - the caller gets the reason instead of a bare rejection.

  YESBANK SELL trigger 22.60 -> Price 22.14  (2 percent below, floored to 0.01)
  YESBANK BUY  trigger 22.60 -> Price 23.06  (2 percent above, ceiled)

SL, LIMIT and MARKET are untouched.

* fix(fivepaisa): subscribe MarketFeedV3 alongside depth so LTP is not zero

The option chain rendered LTP 0.00 on every strike while bid, ask, quantities,
volume and OI were all live.

The REST service was right all along - it returns ltp=201.5, bid=0, ask=0 - so
the WebSocket was overwriting the correct LTP with zero (the frontend merges
live ticks over the REST snapshot field by field, which is also why bid/ask,
zero in REST, showed real values).

5Paisa's MarketDepthService frame carries no traded price at all. Per the
sample frame in the docs it is Exch, ExchType, Token, TBidQ, TOffQ, Details and
Time - the order book and nothing else. LastRate lives only on MarketFeedV3.
Since get_method_for_mode(3) returned MarketDepthService alone, no LastRate
frame ever arrived for a depth-only scrip, _apply_snapshot had nothing to carry
forward, and every depth tick published ltp=0.

Depth mode now subscribes both methods. _on_data already fans every frame out
to all subscriptions for a token, so LastRate is recorded and carried onto the
depth frames that lack it:

  feed frame   -> ltp 136.6
  depth frame  -> ltp 136.6   (was 0), order book still intact

Three supporting changes so this does not trade one bug for another:

- unsubscribe is reference-counted per token, so dropping a depth stream no
  longer tears down MarketFeedV3 while another mode - or another client's depth
  stream - on the same scrip still needs it.
- the reconnect path resubscribes every method of each subscription, not just
  the first, or LTP would silently return to zero after any disconnect.
- the batch drain now gathers same-method scrips from anywhere in the queue
  instead of only a front run. Depth enqueues two methods per symbol, so a
  front-run-only scan alternates every item and emits one-scrip frames - 50 of
  them for a 25-strike chain, exactly the flood the batching exists to prevent,
  and against 5Paisa's preference for fewer larger frames. Three depth symbols
  now produce 2 frames instead of 6.

* feat(fivepaisa): order updates via REST polling; keep the WS adapter unwired

5Paisa had no order-update adapter, so /websocket/order showed nothing.

It does document an OrderTradeConfirmations WebSocket, and this adds a full
adapter for it - but that adapter is deliberately NOT registered. 5Paisa allows
only ONE feed connection per {access_token, client_code}: a second connection
silently evicts the first with a normal close (opcode 8, code 1000). A
dedicated order socket therefore fights the market-data adapter, which uses the
same host and token:

  market-data socket killed          14:41:20,715
  order-update socket connects       14:41:20,824   (~100ms later)
  market-data reconnects (attempt 2) 14:41:30,806
  order-update socket killed         14:41:30,947   (~140ms later)

Both feeds then flap forever and no order update ever lands. Verified live
2026-08-07; 5Paisa documents no connection limit, so the log is the only
evidence and it is recorded in the adapter's header.

Multiplexing order updates onto the market-data socket is not an alternative:
that adapter runs in the websocket_proxy subprocess under gunicorn+eventlet and
Docker, so an OrderUpdateEvent published there lands on the wrong process's
event bus and never reaches subscribers/wsproxy_subscriber.py. It would look
correct in dev and be silently dead in production.

5Paisa therefore joins _POLLING_BROKERS and uses the framework's REST-orderbook
diff (ORDER_POLL_INTERVAL, default 5s), which opens no socket and behaves the
same in every process topology.

The module is kept, unwired, because its normalization is the only written-down
record of the OrderTradeConfirmations payload shapes, and those are not obvious:
ReqType decides which fields exist, and the Trade and SL-trigger frames - the
two that matter most - carry no BrokerOrderID, only ExchOrderID. Since OpenAlgo
keys 5Paisa orders on BrokerOrderId, the adapter learns the pairing from the
Place/Modify/Cancel frames and resolves the rest through it. Field names also
drift from the docs (the table says ExchangeOrderID, every sample sends
ExchOrderID), so a multi-key reader is used throughout.

Also lifts the feed URL table and the RedirectServer JWT decode to module level
in fivepaisa_websocket.py so both adapters share one source of truth for the
host sharding.

Tests cover the five documented ReqType samples verbatim, the ExchOrderID ->
BrokerOrderID resolution, array frames, ack filtering, the full status map and
the host sharding.

* perf(fivepaisa): open a collect window before the first subscribe frame

Mirrors the fixed batch window Zerodha's adapter opens on its batch timer
(zerodha_adapter.py::_start_batch_timer, started when the queue goes 0 -> 1).

5Paisa already coalesced up to 50 scrips per frame, but the batching almost
never engaged. Callers subscribe one symbol at a time - an option chain fires
~50 separate subscribe() calls - and the drain thread sent the very first scrip
the instant it was queued, found the queue momentarily empty (the next caller
was a couple of ms behind), skipped the SUBSCRIPTION_DELAY throttle, hit the
empty-queue check and exited. The next enqueue then started a fresh thread that
again sent a single scrip. The throttle could never engage because the queue was
always briefly empty right after a send.

Waiting once, before the first frame, lets the burst accumulate. Measured on a
25-strike option chain (50 symbols, 2ms apart):

  quote mode   50 frames of 1 scrip  ->  1 frame  of 50
  depth mode    3 frames (1/50/49)   ->  2 frames of 50 (one per method)
  reconnect, 30 depth subs           ->  2 frames of 30

Over-cap and slow-arrival behaviour is unchanged: 120 symbols still split 50 /
50 / 20 with the throttle between frames, and arrivals spaced wider than the
window simply send as they come. The wait is interruptible, so disconnect()
during the window wakes it immediately and the thread clears its handle and
exits without sending.

The cost is 500ms of added latency before a single-symbol subscribe leaves -
the same tradeoff Zerodha's timer already makes, and the same 500ms used for
Paytm, whose server likewise prefers fewer, larger frames.

fix(events): bound EventBus dispatch and stop Flow lock registry growing

Two unbounded structures, reported in #1739.

EventBus dispatched through a ThreadPoolExecutor, whose work queue is an
unbounded queue.SimpleQueue. A publisher outrunning its subscribers grew that
queue until the process was OOM-killed, and production is a single gunicorn
worker that never restarts, so nothing reclaims it.

publish() now reserves one of max_pending (1000) in-flight slots and drops the
callback when saturated, rather than queueing without limit. Shedding is the
right trade: subscribers are best-effort side effects - logging, Socket.IO
refreshes, alert delivery - so losing some beats losing the process, and
blocking instead would push the stall back into the order path that published
the event. Drops are counted and logged sparsely (first, then every 100th) so a
saturated bus does not turn one incident into a second one in the log file.
stats() exposes depth and lifetime drops.

The slot is released in a finally on both sides: any failure to hand work to
the executor returns it, and _safe_call returns it even when a subscriber
raises. A slot leaked there would be permanent and enough of them would wedge
the bus shut for the life of the worker.

The reporter also proposed capping _workflow_locks at 1000 entries with
eviction. That is not safe. execute_workflow guards on lock.locked(); evicting
a lock a thread is currently holding hands the next caller a fresh lock, the
guard passes, and the same workflow runs twice - placing every order in it
twice. Traded a bounded non-leak for duplicate order placement.

Used a weakref.WeakValueDictionary instead. An entry disappears once no caller
holds the lock, so the registry tracks workflows executing right now rather than
every workflow ever executed, and a held lock cannot be evicted because the
holder's strong reference keeps it alive. Note the reported trigger is also
wrong: market ticks travel over ZMQ and never touch the bus. Order, GTT, fill
and order-update events do burst, which is the real exposure.

fd-audit, measured not just read: 20,000 publishes and 50,000 workflow ids each
leave descriptor count unchanged and the registry empty; pending returns to
zero; a saturated bus drains and accepts work again; a held lock survives an
aggressive gc.collect() and is still shared. Verified threading.Lock is
weak-referenceable, which the registry fix depends on.

Closes #1739

Two independent owners were reconnecting the same socket:

  _connection_loop  - retries each URL with exponential backoff, capped at
                      MAX_RECONNECT_ATTEMPTS
  on_close          - separately spawned delayed_reconnect -> connect()

which fired on_close again. Live symptoms, every few hundred milliseconds:

fix(aliceblue): keep the market-data WebSocket alive for a full session

Two defects that only show up over hours, not in a smoke test.

No heartbeat. AliceBlue closes a socket that neither sends nor receives for a
while; the docs are explicit ("Send heartbeat once in every 50 seconds", and
"if user has subscribed for some illiquid stocks which are not traded
frequently ... This may lead to connection closure from server side"). Nothing
in this client ever sent one, so a book of illiquid symbols was dropped
server-side after a quiet stretch - the classic worked-all-morning,
died-after-lunch failure. Now sends {"k": "", "t": "h"} every 50s on a single

disconnect() so repeated reconnects over a session do not leak threads.

so one transient blip mid-session left market data dead until someone
restarted the process - worse for a trading day than the storm it replaced.
The cap is gone; backoff still ramps 2^n but holds at
MAX_RECONNECT_BACKOFF_SECONDS and retries for as long as the outage lasts.
Backoff sleeps in 1s slices so disconnect() is not blocked for 30s, and the
warning is throttled after the first five so an hour-long broker outage does
not bury the log.

batches every instrument into one frame, "#"-joined, with "t":"d" for depth and
"t":"t" for ticks - so LTP, quote and depth all batch. Live logs confirm 19

fix(aliceblue): reuse the market-data WebSocket instead of rebuilding per call

Every quotes and multiquotes call invalidated, recreated, reconnected and
re-authenticated the whole WebSocket session. Measured live: 692ms of that
churn wrapped around 64ms of actual data.

The cache was there, it just could never hit. get_websocket() stored the
connection on self._websocket, but services/quotes_service.py constructs a
fresh BrokerData for every request, so the attribute was always absent and the
"reuse" branch was dead code. CLAUDE.md already says this class of thing
belongs in a module-level singleton.

Beyond latency it was spending quota. Each rebuild costs two REST calls
(invalidateWsSess + createWsSess), and AliceBlue allows 1800 requests / 15
minutes for everything except orders - 2/sec sustained. An option chain
polling every 5s burned roughly a fifth of the budget on session churn that
produced no data, and two tools polling together doubled that.

The connection now lives in _WS_REGISTRY at module scope, keyed by session_id
so a re-login gets a fresh socket rather than reusing one authenticated with a
dead token.

Bounded deliberately, since this is a long-lived single worker. A new
session_id supersedes and disconnects the previous socket: OpenAlgo is
single-user/single-broker, so a second session means the ~3am token rollover
happened, and keeping the old entry would strand a socket plus its reader and
heartbeat threads every single day. Verified bounded at one entry across 500
simulated rollovers and 200 reuses. close_all_websockets() is available for
shutdown and logout, where the session behind these connections is revoked.

Also tightened the connect wait from a 500ms poll to 50ms - the handshake
completes in ~250ms live, so the coarse tick was rounding every connect up to
half a second - and a failed connect now disconnects the half-built socket
instead of dropping it on the floor.

fix(aliceblue): bound the symbol-lock registry and prune quotes on unsubscribe

Two structures grew without limit in a worker that never restarts.

_symbol_locks was a plain dict keyed symbol:exchange:product - an unbounded key
space - holding one threading.Lock per symbol ever smart-ordered, for the life
of the process. Now a weakref.WeakValueDictionary, so an entry disappears once
no caller holds the lock and the registry tracks symbols being ordered right
now rather than every symbol ever ordered. The single call site already binds
the lock for its whole critical section, which is what keeps the entry alive.

Deliberately NOT a size-capped dict: evicting a lock a thread is holding hands
the next caller a fresh one, both run the same symbol's smart order
concurrently against a stale position book, and the position gets sized twice.
Same reasoning as _workflow_locks in #1739. A test pins that two callers get
the same object so nobody reintroduces the capped version.

last_quotes and last_depth were never pruned. They are keyed "exchange:token"
while unsubscribe only cleared self.subscriptions, keyed "exchange|token" - the
mismatched separator is why it looked handled. Every option-chain sweep left
~80 quote entries behind permanently, and since the connection is now pooled
and long-lived (e47c5fdb2) those accumulated for the whole session instead of
dying with the socket. unsubscribe now drops both caches for each instrument,
and only for the instruments being dropped.

Measured after the change: 20,000 distinct smart-order symbols leave the
registry empty with no descriptor growth, and 200 option-chain sweeps leave
last_quotes empty. 7 tests, 4 of which fail against the previous code.

feat(aliceblue): enforce the documented 1800 requests / 15 minutes

AliceBlue publishes a concrete limit (17-rate-limits.md) that nothing in the
plugin honoured: orders are explicitly NOT limited, everything else is capped
at 1800 requests per 15 minutes.

Implemented as a sliding window, not the fixed MIN_INTERVAL pacer other broker
limiters use. 1800/900s averages 2 req/sec, but the broker's limit is a quota
over a window - a burst of 80 quotes for an option chain is perfectly legal so
long as the trailing 15 minutes stays under budget. Pacing everything 0.5s
apart would have made option chains slow for a reason AliceBlue never asked
for, right after e47c5fdb2 made them fast.

Orders bypass it entirely. The broker does not limit them, and delaying an exit
to protect a read quota would be the wrong trade. That falls out cleanly from
where the hook sits: placeorder, modify and cancel build their own URLs, while
get_api_response carries exactly the limited set - orderbook, tradebook,
holdings, positions, funds. Historical data in data.py is hooked too, since it
is also a non-order request.

State is module-level, like the definedge and fyers limiters, because services
build a fresh BrokerData per request so anything on `self` paces nothing. That
is the same defect that had the market-data WebSocket rebuilding on every call
until e47c5fdb2.

A 50-request safety margin is left unspent: our window boundary will not line
up exactly with the broker's, and being throttled mid-session is worse than
being marginally slower. remaining_quota() exposes the headroom.

7 tests cover the shape that matters: orders never blocked even with a full
window, a 200-call burst not paced, slots freed as they age out, the wait
correctly computed on a full window without sleeping 15 minutes for real, and
8 concurrent threads consuming exactly 800 slots rather than oversubscribing.

fix(aliceblue): daily history needs a day boundary, not a wall-clock "to"

Daily history came back empty for every cash symbol. The published root cause
for issue #1775 bug A - that AliceBlue refuses daily data for the current
calendar year - is not what is happening.

Isolated against a live account. Identical request, only the "to" timestamp
differs:

    to = midnight           -> 246 rows
    to = now (intraday ms)  -> 0 rows, {"emsg": "No data available"}

Identical for BHEL and RELIANCE, so it is not symbol-specific, and nothing to
do with which year the range covers. AliceBlue's daily endpoint simply wants a
day boundary.

Our own code produced the bad timestamp: when the end date is in the future it
caps "to" to int(time.time() * 1000), which for any range ending today is an
intraday instant. Virtually every real request ends today, so daily was empty
essentially always. Past-year ranges worked only because their end date was
already a past midnight - which is exactly what made this look like a
current-calendar-year restriction.

Daily requests now round "to" up to the following midnight so today's session
stays inside the window. Intraday is untouched; it wants the wall clock.

feat(optionchain): stream live Greeks and add a Price/Greeks view mode

The option chain advertised "live Greeks" in the tools registry but rendered
none. Greeks now ride the existing tick stream rather than a separate fetch:
every input is already on the client, so a full 80-leg chain recomputes in
well under a millisecond with no extra network traffic and no additional
broker calls.

Frontend:
- lib/optionGreeks.ts implements Black-76 with a Hart normal CDF and a Newton
  implied-volatility solver that falls back to bisection where vega is too
  small for Newton to be reliable. Conventions match opengreeks exactly (vega
  per 1% vol, theta per calendar day); 101 tests pin the output to the Rust
  library to roughly 10 significant figures across ATM/ITM/OTM, 4 hours to
  180 days, with and without a rate, at NFO, BFO, MCX and CDS price scales.
- useOptionChainLive recomputes the whole ladder on every tick batch. The
  forward comes from the ATM legs via put-call parity instead of spot, so the
  futures premium is not baked into every delta as bias.
- Implied volatility is solved from the mid when the book is two-sided and
  falls back to LTP, since a stale last trade makes IV jump around on
  illiquid strikes.
- A Price/Greeks toggle (shortcut G) selects between two column presets drawn
  from the same 27-column pool, each keeping its own visibility and ordering.
  Switching costs nothing because Greeks are computed for every leg either
  way. Existing flat preferences migrate into Price mode.

Backend:
- calculate_chain_greeks solves an entire ladder through the vectorized
  black76 *_array batch functions, which the repo had never used.
- The chain response carries expiry_ts and server_ts so a client can compute
  time to expiry without trusting its own clock, which would otherwise bias
  every Greek on the page.
- POST /api/v1/optionchain accepts with_greeks and interest_rate, computed
  from the quotes it has already fetched.
- The exchange expiry cut-off policy moves into a shared helper so the chain
  and the Greeks service cannot disagree on time to expiry.

Greeks that are not computable stay absent and render as a dash rather than
zero, which a trader would read as a real value. An out-of-the-money leg
whose IV will not converge gets delta 0, not the +/-1 that keying the
fallback off the option type alone would produce.

* fix(samco): restart streaming worker threads after a reconnect

Found by an FD/resource audit of the streaming changes.

_start_subscription_flusher() and _start_heartbeat() both returned early when the
previous worker was still alive. On a reconnect the sequence is stop-then-start,
so the outgoing worker is often still winding down at that moment: the guard
bailed, left the stop flag set, and started no replacement. The old worker then
exited, leaving no thread at all.

For the heartbeat that costs stale-connection detection. For the subscription
flusher it is worse: subscribe() only marks the symbol set dirty and relies on the
worker to send it, so the feed goes silent after a reconnect with no error - on
exactly the path that matters most, broker rollover and outage recovery.

Both now distinguish a healthy worker (return early, as before) from a stopping
one (join it, then start a replacement). Verified: after a tight stop/start the
flusher and heartbeat are both running, stop flags are clear, and the next
subscribe emits its two frames again. A 200-cycle reconnect soak returns to
baseline thread count with no leaked threads, and 20 consecutive starts against a
healthy worker still yield exactly one thread each.

Also name the heartbeat thread, which was anonymous and so invisible to this kind
of audit.

No descriptor or memory leak found elsewhere in the streaming change: sockets
close on every path via the finally in _run_websocket, the 5xx retry reuses the
shared httpx client, and _tick_state is bounded by the subscription set and drains
to zero on both unsubscribe and connection cleanup.

fix(flow): resolve option lot size without trusting SymToken.name

The Options Order node and the /flow index lot-size endpoint both resolved an
underlying with `SymToken.name == "NIFTY"`. `name` carries the underlying root
only where the broker's master contract put it there - Fyers ships the contract
description in every column that could hold one ("NIFTY 11 Aug 26 24450 CE"),
so on Fyers the lookup matched nothing: every options order failed with "NIFTY
has no contract on NFO in the master contract", and the endpoint returned an
empty list, leaving the node with no underlyings to choose from.

Correcting this in each of 35+ broker plugins does not scale, so fix it at the
consumer. Keep the `name` match as the fast path - it is the indexed column and
is right on most brokers - and fall back to the OpenAlgo symbol, which OpenAlgo
normalizes itself and therefore reads the same everywhere. This is the same
column expiry_service and option_symbol_service already key off, which is why
expiry and strike resolution were unaffected.

A prefix match alone is not enough: symbols starting "NIFTY" also include
NIFTYNXT50 at a different lot size (25 vs 65), so each candidate is confirmed
with extract_underlying_from_symbol - the same extractor that builds the
underlying dropdown, so the value offered and the value resolved come from one
function. The prefix predicate is a half-open range rather than LIKE, because
SQLite's LIKE is case-insensitive and cannot seek the index (750ms vs 12ms on a
cold cache).

Verified against a live Fyers master contract, where `name` is wrong for all
84,424 derivative rows: NIFTY 65, BANKNIFTY 30, FINNIFTY 60, MIDCPNIFTY 120,
NIFTYNXT50 25, SENSEX 20, BANKEX 30. SENSEX50 still reports no contract, which
is correct - BSE currently lists no SENSEX50 derivatives.

fix(symbols): normalize the derivative underlying once, for every broker

For a FUT/CE/PE row `name` is meant to hold the underlying root ("NIFTY"), and
every lookup that resolves an underlying depends on it: the Options Order lot
size, the scalping terminal's MCX/CDS chain, expiry lists via
get_distinct_expiries, fno_search_symbols_db, and the options tools' underlying
dropdown via get_distinct_underlyings. Whether it holds that is up to each
broker's master contract, and they disagree - Fyers ships the contract
description ("NIFTY 11 Aug 26 24450 CE") in every column that could carry one.
On Fyers none of those lookups matched: options orders failed outright, the
MCX/CDS chain found no futures to price the ATM from, and the dropdown was
offered 76,981 descriptions in place of ~190 underlyings.

852439446 fixed this at one consumer. Correcting it in each of 35+ broker
plugins does not scale and leaves the next broker to repeat it, so settle it
once on the single path every broker's download already runs through, before
anything reads the table. The root is derived from the OpenAlgo symbol -
normalized by OpenAlgo itself, so it reads the same everywhere - with the same
extractor that builds the dropdown, which is what makes the value offered and

next master contract download, which Indian brokers do at each day's first
login. The fallback in 852439446 covers installs between upgrading and that

* fix(hdfcsecurities): make unsubscribe survive a failed frame

A transient failure sending the unSubscribe frame left state split: `desired`
had already dropped the scrip while `subscribed` still held it, because the
pop ran only after the send. Reconnect replay worked off `subscribed`, so the
instrument came back at the broker after OpenAlgo had released it.

All local state is now retracted in one locked step before the frame goes out,
and reconnect replay follows `desired` -- the wanted set -- rather than what
was last successfully sent. That also replays a subscribe whose frame never got
out, which the old path silently lost. A send failure here means the socket is
going down anyway, and the broker drops the whole subscription set with it.

fix(tradejini): align integration with refreshed CubePlus v2 API docs (#1787)

* fix(samco): always replace a stalled streaming worker on reconnect

Both review findings are the same defect, and the previous reasoning was wrong.

_start_subscription_flusher() and _start_heartbeat() refused to start a
replacement when the outgoing worker missed its 5s join, on the assumption that
the stalled worker would exit on its own. A worker wedged in ws.send() on a dead
socket can stay stuck far longer than that, and because _sub_flush_thread still
referenced the corpse, every later reconnect re-joined it and returned again.

Reproduced: with a worker blocked in ws.send(), three consecutive reconnects
each left zero flusher threads running, and a subscribe afterwards emitted no
frames at all - the quote feed silently dead for the life of the process. The
heartbeat variant leaves the connection with no stale-connection monitor.

Replacing is safe. Each worker owns a private stop event, already set by the
stop call, so once the predecessor's in-flight send returns it re-checks that
event and exits without another send - verified by reading the loop and by test.
Worst case is one duplicate full-set subscribe frame, which is idempotent under
Samco's replace semantics.

Verified after the change: with the predecessor still wedged, a replacement
starts (2 threads), and once the dead socket unblocks the predecessor exits and
the replacement sends normally - recovered instead of permanently dead. The
earlier guarantees still hold: the tight reconnect race stays fixed, 20 starts
against a healthy worker still yield exactly one thread, a 200-cycle reconnect
soak returns to baseline with no leaked threads, and unsubscribe is still not
undone by a coalesced snapshot.

Residual, documented rather than worked around: while the predecessor is wedged
it holds _sub_send_lock, so the replacement cannot send until the dead socket
errors or is closed. That self-heals on the reconnect path, which tears the old
socket down.

* fix(tradejini): stop websocket reconnect leaks in quotes and streaming

A file-descriptor audit of the Tradejini websocket paths found two leaks,
both reproduced with a stubbed socket and re-measured after the fix.

Quote/depth sockets resurrected themselves. TradejiniWebSocket._on_connection
reconnected on any close whose reason was not "Unauthorized Access", and the
SDK reports an intentional disconnect the same way as a dropped connection.
Every get_quotes/get_multiquotes/get_depth call closes its socket in a finally
block, so each request spawned a replacement socket five seconds later that
nothing owned or closed - one descriptor and one OS thread leaked per request,
with the option chain and OI tracker polling those paths. Measured one
connect/close cycle: 2 sockets created, 1 still live, 1 thread alive. Now
close() sets a _closing flag before disconnect(), and the callback skips the
reconnect - rechecking after its sleep in case close() lands during the wait.
Genuine drops still reconnect. Measured after: 1 created, 0 live, 0 threads.

Streaming adapter reconnected in a tight loop. NxtradStream.connect() returns
as soon as it starts its reader thread, so failures never raised into
_connect_with_retry - the loop always broke on the first pass with
reconnect_attempts stuck at 0, and every close event spawned another thread.
A server that hangs up immediately, which is what a 4001 after the 3 AM token
rollover looks like, produced 55 connection attempts in 3 seconds, each with a
TLS handshake and a token lookup, with the backoff and the 10-attempt cap dead
code. Retries now run from the close callback via _schedule_reconnect(), one
attempt in flight at a time, resetting the counter on a successful connect.
Measured after: 1 attempt in 3 seconds, backoff doubling to the ceiling, and
the cap terminating with no stray threads.

The vendored SDK is left untouched: its reader threads are non-daemon and
__tryConnect replaces self.ws without closing the previous socket. Both belong
upstream.

* fix(deltaexchange): add weighted rate limiting across every REST call

Delta does not throttle requests-per-second like Fyers or Dhan. Each endpoint
carries a weight deducted from 10000 units per fixed 5-minute window, split
across two buckets: unauthenticated calls are throttled by IP, authenticated
calls by user id (delta-api-docs/04-rate-limits.md).

Three gaps this closes:

- The 429 retry waited on Retry-After, which Delta never sends. It reports the
  wait in X-RATE-LIMIT-RESET (milliseconds until the window resets), so every
  rate-limited call fell through to a blind 1/2/4s ladder against a window that
  can be minutes from resetting.

- The public market-data path had no 429 handling at all. A rate-limited ticker
  surfaced as a bare "HTTP 429" exception per symbol, which the option chain
  swallows into a blank row.

- Nothing accounted for the quota, so a runaway poller could spend the budget
  that order placement depends on.

broker/deltaexchange/api/rate_limiter.py now holds the weight table, both
buckets and the 429 delay, and is wired into all nine REST call sites. Keeping
the buckets separate matters: market data goes out unauthenticated, so a hot
option chain draws on the IP allowance and cannot starve order placement.

Exhaustion fails fast rather than hanging - past 30 seconds from a reset,
consume() raises DeltaRateLimitError so the caller returns a clean error
instead of parking a web request for minutes. Before parking anyone on the
public bucket it spends 3 units on GET /v2/rate_limits/quota, since Delta's
window is fixed and the local one floats.

Verified live against that meter: 15 tickers through the real BrokerData path
counted 45 units both locally and at the exchange, and the docs' own worked
example (100 open-order + 50 balance + 200 place + 20 batch) totals 1950 units
as documented.

* fix(deltaexchange): address code review findings in rate limiting and streaming

Nine issues from the cubic review of f055f4017 and aa4442d2.

Signature expiry (the serious one). A Delta signature is valid for 5 seconds
(SignatureExpired), and consume() can block up to 30 waiting for the quota
window. order_api, margin_api, funds and auth_api all signed the request
before calling consume(), so every rate-limited authenticated call would have
been signed, parked, then rejected as stale. consume() now runs before
get_auth_headers() everywhere, and the 429 retry re-signs on each pass.

Partial margin. DeltaRateLimitError raised mid-basket fell into the
per-product 'except Exception' and was recorded as one failed leg, so a quota
failure after the first product returned HTTP 200 with an understated total
margin. It now aborts the whole request with 429.

Rate limiter:
- consume() is a loop that re-checks and reserves inside one locked section;
  concurrent callers could each pass the budget check, sleep, then all add
  their weight to a budget with room for one.
- A 429 whose reset is beyond the wait ceiling no longer sleeps first: the
  next consume() would refuse the call anyway, so the 429 is returned.
- The quota probe follows DELTA_BASE_URL instead of hardcoding production.

Streaming:
- Registry mutation and its send now share one locked section, so an
  overlapping subscribe and unsubscribe cannot reach Delta in the opposite
  order from the registry.
- disconnect() clears the replay registry. It survives a dropped connection on
  purpose, but an explicit teardown discards queued unsubscribes, so replaying
  it on a later connect() would resubscribe symbols with no subscriber left.
- The cache merge no longer drops zero-valued fields, which kept a stale bid
  size on screen after a side emptied. Delta puts null inside a present quote
  array when a side empties, so a present array is authoritative (null element
  publishes 0) while a missing array leaves previous values standing - that
  distinction is what stops a frame without a mark price from blanking the LTP.

Not changed: the ticker channel carries no traded volume and it is not
derivable from the feed. volume is optional in the documented quote contract
and consumers merge it with '??', so emitting 0 would destroy the value a REST

stays absent, and the normaliser says why.

retry_delay_from_headers capped the X-RATE-LIMIT-RESET branch at

Retry-After today, but a CDN or proxy in front of the API can, and a

* fix(definedge): stop losing a full trading day at each history chunk boundary

get_history splits long ranges into chunks (30 days for 1m). The chunk end was computed as current_start + timedelta(days=chunk_days-1), and timedelta carries the start time-of-day forward. Since intraday windows began at 09:15, every chunk also ENDED at 09:15, so the last day of each chunk was requested for a single minute:

  06072026 0915 -> 04082026 0915

This stayed hidden while /sds/history ignored the 'to' parameter and returned every candle up to the latest available, which made chunks overlap and cover the hole. Definedge now honors 'to' (verified live: .../minute/070820261500/070820261600 returns only 15:00-15:29), so the gap became real - one whole trading day lost per chunk. Snap intraday chunk ends to end-of-day and advance the next chunk to the following day at 00:00. Correct under either upstream behaviour, since overlapping chunks dedupe.

Also fixes three related sources of silently missing candles:

- Intraday windows were pinned to NSE hours (start 09:15, past end-dates 15:30). MCX runs 09:00-23:30 and CDS/BCD to 17:00, so the whole evening session on the last requested day was dropped, plus 09:00-09:14 on the first. Both bounds are now full-calendar-day, still clipped to IST 'now' when end_date is today.

- A chunk that failed on a timeout or 5xx was skipped with a debug-level note, punching a silent 30-day hole. Now retried three times with backoff; 4xx stays terminal since an expired session will not recover. The failure is logged as a named gap.

- Rows whose timestamps fail to parse are counted in a warning instead of vanishing. That is how the int64 leading-zero bug in #1475 stayed hidden for months.

Adds debug logging of the symbol-to-token resolution, the exact upstream URL, and the raw row count straight off the wire, so an observed gap can be replayed verbatim and attributed to either side. The instrument id is logged as 'instrument=' rather than 'token=' because the log sanitizer redacts any *token= value as a credential.

Verified live: a 06-Jul to 12-Aug 1m request crosses the old boundary at 04-Aug, which previously returned about one candle and now returns every candle Definedge holds; all July sessions return the full 375.

Refs #1753

terminalBreakpoints returns two vertices per forward-priced leg: the
underlying at which the scenario forward crosses zero, and the underlying
at which that forward reaches the strike. Commit c1644369f routed the
plotted domain through it, so the first vertex began framing the chart.

fix(strategy-builder): let the forward converge to spot at expiry

The chain reports a spot and a parity-implied forward that sits above it,
around 79 points on a two-week NIFTY chain. Valuation treated that gap as
a constant, shifting the forward by the same amount at every horizon
including expiry. But a forward pulls to spot as its life runs out, and
an index option settles against the index, so at expiry the two are the
same number.

Every expiry-derived figure was therefore one basis off. A long 24000PE
bought at 34.15 reported a breakeven of 23,886.58 instead of 23,965.85
and a max profit of 15,52,627.38 instead of 15,57,780.25, which also fed
the risk-reward ratio and shifted the probability of profit. Max loss was
right, being just the premium.

The snapshot pins one point on the decay - forward over spot at the leg's
current remaining life - which is enough to recover the implied carry
rate and re-apply it at any horizon. At the snapshot horizon this returns
the forward exactly, so the live mark still reconciles to the traded
price within a tick; at expiry it returns spot.

With the forward converging, a terminal option kink lands on its own
strike again, so the scenario-coordinate breakpoint helpers collapse back
into responsiveStrikes.

Two existing tests encoded the constant basis: a long call over a
10-point basis now breaks even at 105 rather than 95, and a day of decay
now costs a leg its carry as well as its time value, both hand-checked
against an independent Black-76. A third built a flat tail out of a
calendar, which only looked flat because the basis was held constant;
it now uses a vertical, whose legs share one carry curve and whose deep
in-the-money slopes genuinely cancel.

fix(strategy-builder): one carry curve per strategy, and futures converge too

An adversarial review of the forward-convergence change confirmed both
fixes in it and found two more defects, one of which that change created.

Legs inferred a carry rate each. The forward is a parity synthetic built
from two live quotes and the reference is a separately streamed last
price, so the ratio is noisy and a short-dated leg divides that noise by a
very small number. Legs also disagree outright: a chain fetched without

keeps a stale snapshot while its siblings refresh on every tick. Two legs
on ONE expiry that disagree stop cancelling, so a defined-risk iron
condor with one unrefreshed wing reported an unlimited loss - a wrong
category, not just a wrong magnitude. The strategy now resolves a single
rate, the median of what its legs imply, so legs sharing an expiry always
share a factor.

Futures still carried their basis to infinity. A future converges on its
own expiry for the same reason an option does, and leaving only the
option converging made a covered call worse than before: max profit was
overstated by exactly the basis times the quantity, 24,000 against a true

The non-terminal root scan also reported its own outermost grid point as
a breakeven whenever the payoff was flat on zero through that edge. The
value tracked the requested window - widen the request and the number
moved with it - and the chart planted a marker on the frame edge. Only
interior roots count now, at either end.

The futures valuation test carried no expiry timestamp and no fixed
clock, so it read the real system date against an expiry string of
14AUG26 and changed meaning depending on the day it ran. It is pinned
now, and covers convergence at expiry as well as the basis before it.

fix(deltaexchange): keep the pooled feed alive after the last unsubscribe (#1799)

Subscribing to an option chain stopped delivering ticks: the subscription
was accepted and logged, but no data ever arrived and the proxy reported
"Stale feed ... connected but no ticks".

The adapter tore down its own transport in unsubscribe() once its symbol
count reached zero, while the connection pool kept holding and reusing the
same instance. disconnect() sets _stop_flag, so the DeltaWebSocket retry
loop exits permanently, and _get_adapter_with_capacity() reuses the dead
adapter with no health check. Every later subscribe was then queued and
silently buffered by _send_all_locked with no socket to carry it and no
path back to connected. Option chains hit this because switching expiry or
strikes unsubscribes the whole set before subscribing the new one; a
watchlist rarely drops to zero.

Drop the self-teardown and let the pool own the adapter lifecycle. Explicit
teardown still runs through pool.disconnect() and initialize(force=True),
both of which call adapter.disconnect(). Queued unsubscribe frames now also
reach Delta instead of being discarded with the cancelled batch timer.

Also reset the WebSocket retry budget after a healthy connection. The
counter was cumulative for the life of the process, so a long-lived feed
that reconnects occasionally exhausted max_retry_attempt and never came
back.

Verified live against Delta with BTC options: LTP, quote, and depth modes
stream, a full unsubscribe stops the stream at the exchange, and a
resubscribe on the same pooled adapter resumes ticks.

* fix: correct TradeSmart rate limits to the enforced 10/sec and 120/min

The limiter was built on the premise that TradeSmart had raised /GetQuotes to
100 requests per second and exempted quotes from the per-minute allowance. Both
halves were wrong. A single option-chain request (82 symbols) produced:

    Order Recieved 11 in a current second exceeds Limit 10 for user
    Order Recieved 121 in a current minute exceeds Limit 120 for user

both on /GetQuotes, so the real ceilings are 10/sec and 120/min, quotes are not
exempt from the minute window, and the counters are per user rather than per
endpoint.

Pacing quotes at ~90/sec into a 10/sec ceiling meant every call past the tenth
was rejected, each retried at 2s/4s/8s, the retries re-flooded the second
window, and the storm then blew the minute counter as well. The chain failed
after roughly 23 seconds of warnings.

Replace the two fixed-interval gates with a single shared budget over two
rolling windows, modelled on broker.flattrade.api.data: reserve the earliest
slot satisfying both windows rather than spacing every call by a fixed
interval, so a batch inside the allowance goes out at once and only the
overflow waits. The slot is reserved under the lock and slept for outside it,
so waiters do not serialise behind the sleeper.

Run at 8/sec and 110/min for headroom against clock skew and against
order/fund/margin calls sharing the same per-user quota. Tie the multiquote
thread pool to the per-second cap instead of a hardcoded 10.

An 82-symbol chain now paces to about 10 seconds and succeeds instead of
failing. Note that this does not make the option chain fast: at a 30 second
refresh, 82 quotes per cycle is 164/min against a 110/min budget, so requests
still queue and compound. Serving those strikes from the WebSocket feed rather
than per-strike REST is tracked separately.

Rewrite the tests around the corrected model, including coverage for the
per-second rejection message that was previously unrepresented.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(tradesmart): serve bulk quotes from the WebSocket feed instead of REST

TradeSmart caps REST at 10 requests/sec and 120/min per user, and Noren has no
batch-quote endpoint -- /GetQuotes takes exactly one token. A 41-strike option
chain is 82 legs, so the REST path cost 82 calls: about 10 seconds against the
per-second gate, and 164 calls/minute once the UI refreshes every 30 seconds.
That does not fit a 120/minute ceiling at any pacing, so requests queued and
compounded; a single underlying LTP call was observed waiting 9 seconds behind
a saturated minute window.

The other Noren brokers are not doing anything smarter, they are simply capped
higher: Flattrade runs 38/sec and 190/min, Shoonya and Definedge batch 20 at a
time. /GetOptionChain does not help either -- it returns the strike structure,
which the service already builds from the local master contract, not quotes.

The streaming API has no such limit. One subscribe message carries every token,
{"t":"d","k":"NFO|54321#NFO|54322#..."}, and the broker answers with a dk
acknowledgement per token holding the full snapshot: ltp, OHLC, volume, OI and
five depth levels. That is the whole chain in one round trip, off the REST
budget entirely. Depth rather than touchline because the chain needs bid/ask
and quantities.

Add a pooled Noren socket plus its snapshot cache, following the
broker.aliceblue.api.data precedent: module level rather than on the instance,
because the services build a fresh BrokerData per request and instance state is
empty on arrival. Keyed by bearer token, so a re-login replaces and closes the
previous socket and the registry stays at one live connection without needing a
logout hook. Subscriptions are left open so the 30s refresh is served from the
warm cache, bounded at 500 scrips with LRU eviction. Feed updates are merged,
not replaced -- the docs note messages after the first acknowledgement carry
only changed fields, so a delta with just lp must not erase OI and depth.

get_multiquotes now tries the feed first and falls back to the REST fan-out for
anything it cannot supply (no socket, a rejected subscribe, acknowledgements
that did not arrive in time), so this degrades to the previous behaviour rather
than returning holes.

Opening a second Noren session is safe: TradeSmart already runs two
concurrently, the market-data adapter and the order-update adapter, which
documents the choice.

Also fix _quote_dict, which serves both REST and feed records since they share
Noren's field names. It now populates bid_qty/ask_qty, which the option chain
reads and which were always 0, and coerces values defensively because the feed
sends numbers as strings and blanks fields on illiquid strikes.

The websocket client is imported lazily. broker.tradesmart.streaming imports the
market-data adapter, which imports websocket_proxy, which imports that adapter
back, so entering the streaming package first raises ImportError on the
half-built module. Deferring it also keeps the proxy stack out of the import
path of every quote request.

Per the fd-audit skill: snapshots are recorded only for scrips currently held
subscribed. Eviction walks the subscription set, so anything cached outside it
could never be reclaimed -- a rejected unsubscribe or ticks in flight for a
released scrip would have grown that dict for the life of the worker, which a
single never-restarting Gunicorn worker cannot absorb.

fix(tradesmart): bring the WebSocket lifecycle in line with its Noren siblings and fix(latency): record order latency for routes outside the RESTX API  (#1805)

* fix(tradesmart): bring the WebSocket lifecycle in line with its Noren siblings

The TradeSmart plugin had drifted from the patterns Shoonya, Flattrade, Zebu
and Definedge already use, which made an unrelated broker-side problem far
noisier and left two real leaks behind.

Clean closes reported as errors. websocket-client >= 1.9 hands a received
CLOSE frame to on_error as though it were an exception (_app.py: "if op_code
== ABNF.OPCODE_CLOSE: return closed(frame)"), then tears down without passing
the frame on, so every polite server hangup logged an ERROR and the close
callback reported "None - None". close_frame_status() now tells a close frame
from a fault and logs it at INFO with the status code the frame carried.

Heartbeat that could not be stopped. The worker slept with time.sleep(30),
which cannot be interrupted, so _stop_heartbeat always burned the full join
timeout and warned. Every disconnect paid 3 seconds for that. It now waits on
a shutdown event, the way flattrade_websocket.py and shoonya_websocket.py do,
plus a self-join guard and a snapshot of self.ws in _send_heartbeat to close a
race with _close_websocket nulling it.

Reconnects scheduled twice. Both _on_error and _on_close called
_schedule_reconnection, and websocket-client fires both for one disconnect, so
the backoff ran twice per drop and the second call cancelled and re-armed the
timer, pushing the retry out by another full delay. The close callback now
owns scheduling behind a _reconnecting guard, matching
shoonya_adapter.py::_on_error. A rejected connect ack stops the loop instead
of retrying a token that will not come back.

Reader threads left parked. run_forever leaves the socket fully blocking
(settimeout(getdefaulttimeout()), None unless a global default was set), so
the reader parks in recv() with no deadline. Closing from another thread does
not reliably wake it on Windows; only shutdown() does. stop() waited out
THREAD_JOIN_TIMEOUT, warned, and abandoned the thread -- one per disconnect in
a worker that never restarts. _close_websocket now shuts the socket down
before closing, and shutdown must come first because close() closes the raw
socket itself.

Sockets stranded by a failed reconnect. _attempt_reconnection now does its
network I/O outside self.lock, since connect() blocks up to 15s and holding
the lock stalled subscribe, unsubscribe and feed routing for that whole time.
The client is published before connecting and released in a finally: a client
reachable only through a local is unstoppable if connect() raises rather than
returning False, and under eventlet it can, because Timeout and GreenletExit
are BaseException and slip past its own handler. Retries are unbounded across
a broker outage, so that stranded one socket per attempt.

Unsubscribing over a dead socket. _websocket_unsubscribe guarded on the client
existing rather than being connected, so tearing down a pool of 83 scrips
logged 83 "Cannot send depth unsubscription: not connected" warnings. The
broker drops every subscription with the session, so there is nothing to send.
Reference counts still update either way.

None of this addresses the underlying problem, which is broker-side: TradeSmart
permits one WebSocket session per uid where every sibling permits two, so the
market-data, order-update and quote-stream sockets evict each other
continuously. This removes the noise and the amplifiers so that eviction is
visible on its own.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(latency): record order latency for routes outside the RESTX API

init_latency_monitoring only wraps restx_api namespaces, so any order placed
through a Flask blueprint left no latency record at all. The scalping terminal
places, closes and cancels entirely through blueprint routes, so none of its
orders ever reached the latency monitor -- its data calls appeared only because
the React page fetches those through /api/v1. The two Positions close buttons
had the same blind spot.

Six routes are now instrumented, placed innermost so they measure the handler
rather than the session and rate-limit decorators, matching how RESTX resources
are wrapped:

    /scalping/api/order        PLACE
    /scalping/api/close_leg    CLOSE
    /scalping/api/close_all    CLOSE
    /scalping/api/cancel_all   CANCEL_ALL
    /close_position            CLOSE
    /close_all_positions       CLOSE

Two things had to be fixed first, or the new records would have been empty.

The decorator only understood a response that was either a single Response or a
(dict, code) tuple. Blueprints return "jsonify(d), code", which is a
(Response, int) tuple and fell through to {}, so every record would have logged
an order id of "unknown". _response_payload() now handles all four shapes a
Flask view may return, and a file download still degrades to {} because its
.json property resolves to None rather than raising.

The broker was resolved purely from the request body's apikey. These routes
authenticate by session cookie and send none, so records would have landed with
an empty broker and never grouped under the broker they were sent to.
_session_broker() reads it on the request thread, since the executor thread that
writes the record has no session, and only when no API key was supplied -- an
/api/v1 caller still resolves its own broker rather than being relabelled by
whoever happens to be logged into the browser.

Also promotes the keep-forever order types to a module-level KEEP_FOREVER_TYPES.
The copy inside init_latency_monitoring was dead code that ruff already flagged
as unused; the set that actually governs purging lives in
database.latency_db.purge_old_data_logs, and the two must stay in step or a type
present in one and missing from the other is purged after a week despite being
an order. PLACE, CLOSE and CANCEL_ALL are all in that set, so the new records
are kept.

fix(frontend,nginx): stop the endless "Loading new version" reload loop (#1807)

Three independent defects, each verified. Together they explain a route that
flashes "Loading new version…" forever and intermittently 503s, on one browser
but not another.

1. The reload guard could never hold. main.tsx called clearChunkReloadFlag() at
   module scope, two lines before createRoot().render() — so it ran on every
   page load, including the one the reload itself produced. The app shell always
   mounts; only the lazy route chunk fails, so the loop was
   reload -> mount -> clear flag -> route chunk fails -> reload, without end.
   Replaced the one-shot flag with a 30s cooldown that is never cleared: a
   second failure inside the window shows the real error instead of reloading,
   and the auto-recovery re-arms afterwards so a later deploy still self-heals.

2. /assets/<file> served three representations of one URL unsafely. Measured on
   a running instance: brotli 33108 bytes, gzip 41166, identity 154440 — and the
   identity fallback carried no Vary header while every response is cached
   immutable for a year. A stored response without Vary matches any later
   request for that URI (RFC 9111), so a cache could hand the raw copy to a
   client that negotiated brotli. Ranges made it worse: Accept-Ranges: bytes was
   advertised on the compressed variants and a Range was served from whichever
   representation the current request negotiated, so a resume or revalidate
   across representations spliced mismatched bytes and the module failed to
   parse — surfacing as exactly the chunk-load error patterns above. Vary is now
   set on every branch, the compressed branches send Accept-Ranges: none with
   conditional=False, and Accept-Encoding is parsed properly so "br;q=0" is
   honoured instead of matching as a substring.

3. nginx forced a WebSocket upgrade on ordinary traffic. All four install
   scripts set "Connection: upgrade" inside `location / {`, which carries plain
   HTTP — /ws, /ws/ and /socket.io/ have their own blocks — with no
   map $http_upgrade. Every normal request reached gunicorn claiming an upgrade
   with an empty Upgrade:, breaking HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and producing
   intermittent truncated responses and 5xx. Those two lines are replaced by
   proxy_set_header Connection "" in the main block only; the WebSocket blocks
   are untouched.

update.sh reports affected configs and prints the exact edit rather than
rewriting them. With ~420k deployments in the field, an automated in-place edit
of a live reverse proxy that cannot be validated here is not worth the blast
radius, and admins customise these files.

Known remaining: /socket.io/ still forces the header, so Socket.IO long-polling
requests carry it. Lower impact and it needs a map + real nginx testing.

fix(upgrade): give migrations the same 15s lock timeout as the app (#1726)

database/__init__.py registers a global SQLAlchemy connect listener that sets
PRAGMA busy_timeout=15000, which is why the running application waits 15
seconds for a SQLite write lock. Migrations never got it: migrate_all.py runs
each script with subprocess.run, so every migration is a separate process that
imports sqlalchemy directly and never imports the database package. Those
engines fell back to the sqlite3 default of 5 seconds.

Measured before the change, from a migration-style engine:

    create_engine(...) with no database import -> busy_timeout = 5000
    after importing the database package       -> busy_timeout = 15000

So a migration gave up three times sooner than the rest of OpenAlgo under
identical contention, and an install failed with "database is locked" in cases
where waiting a moment longer would have succeeded.

Adds upgrade/_pragmas.py, which registers the same listener, and imports it
from the 21 migration scripts that build their own engine. It deliberately does
not import the database package to reuse that listener: a migration has to keep
working when the application package cannot be imported, which is exactly the
state a half-finished install is in.

Not touched, because they are already covered or out of scope: init_db.py,
migrate_historify.py and migrate_market_holidays.py import database.* and so
pick the listener up already; init_db.py and reset_admin_password.py open
read-only connections that take no write lock; rotate_pepper.py is an
intentionally manual tool excluded from migrate_all.

This widens the window a migration waits for a lock. It does not create or
release one, so a lock held by a running instance, or a db/ folder on OneDrive
or a network share where WAL cannot work, still needs fixing at the source.

Verified: busy_timeout now reports 15000 from upgrade/, and migrate_sandbox,
migrate_gtt, migrate_leverage and migrate_order_mode all run clean with
--status. Ruff on upgrade/ is back to its 4 pre-existing errors.

fix(flow): resolve tracked QA discrepancies and repair node component behaviour across triggers, orders, conditions and data nodes (#1815)

* fix(flow): evaluate the Price Alert node's own condition vocabulary

The Price Alert node is a trigger: the price monitor watches the symbol and
fires the workflow, then the graph walk evaluates the node itself to decide
which branch to follow. That evaluation compared the stored condition against
the monitor's canonical names only, while the editor writes its own
("above", "below", "crosses_above", "crosses_below"). An unmapped name matched
no branch, so condition_met stayed False and the run took No:

    Price alert: RELIANCE LTP=1304.8 above 1304.0 = False

The order wired to Yes was skipped and the run still reported completed with
no errors, which is indistinguishable from the level never being reached.

Normalize through FlowPriceMonitor.normalize_condition, the alias table the
monitor and the workflow validator already share; only the executor was out
of sync with it.

Two related corrections in the same path:

- A monitor-fired run no longer re-fetches a quote. The monitor has already
  matched the level against the tick that fired it, so re-checking races that
  tick - a price that retreats before the graph walk would route to No - and a
  stateless re-check can never confirm a crossing at all. The trigger price is
  carried through instead.

- An unrecognized condition, and the conditions that need the previous tick
  (moving_up, moving_down, and their percent forms), now return status error
  rather than False. An error takes neither branch, so a misconfigured node is
  visible instead of reading as an unmet level.

* feat(flow): batch the Margin Calculator lot-size lookups into one request

Replace GET /api/symbol-lotsize with POST /api/symbol-lotsizes, which
resolves a set of exact (symbol, exchange) pairs in a single grouped query.

The set is capped at MAX_LOT_SIZE_LOOKUP (50) to match the basket limit

or a non-array now raises with the reason named, rather than falling back to
the single position - a fallback that priced a different estimate from

* perf(flow): stop the margin editor re-rendering and refetching needlessly

The lot-size debounce was handed the refs array. Its effect depends on
that value and the array was rebuilt every render, so each render cleared

only for the remainder: adding a leg to a 50-leg basket costs 1 contract
instead of 50. The comment claiming this already worked is corrected.

Individual React Query entries were tried first and discarded - written
with setQueryData they have no observer and are evicted on the cache's own

* fix(flow): deliver condition results into logic gates, restore time-condition role in logs

A wire into an AND/OR/NOT gate carries the source condition's *value*, but
execute_node_chain treated it as control flow and filtered it by the branch
taken. A False input therefore never travelled its `true` edge to the gate, so
the gate stayed parked on "waiting for N more input(s)" and never evaluated:

  - OR fired only when every input was True, i.e. it behaved like AND
  - NOT could never fire at all, since NOT's useful case is a False input
  - no gate could ever drive its False branch
  - the outcome depended on which input the depth-first walk evaluated last,
    so the same graph and the same market data gave different results

Exempt gate-targeted edges from branch filtering. The gate reads each source's
stored boolean and already ignores the handle a wire left from, and its own
once-per-run guard is what prevents double firing, so always delivering these
edges does not reintroduce the duplicate orders the pending-wait was added to
stop. Errored conditions are still withheld from gates: an unevaluated
condition must not reach a gate as a bogus False and place a phantom order.

Verified over the full truth table x both traversal orders: 16/16 OR cases and
16/16 AND cases now correct (previously the two mixed True/False cases failed
whenever the False input was evaluated last), and NOT(False) fires.

Also restore conditionType (entry/exit/custom) to the Time Condition node's log
line and result payload. It is a role tag that never affects the comparison,
but without it a graph with several time gates logs identical lines and you
cannot tell which gate fired - or, as when an exit-tagged gate was wired to a
BUY order, misfired.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(flow): make varCondition defend itself, and surface server errors in the UI

varCondition already refused an operand that failed to resolve, on the grounds
that routing a real trading branch on a value the author never configured is
worse than not branching at all. Two paths still did exactly that:

  - an *empty* operand. get_str substitutes its default for a falsy field, so a
    blank Left Value became "0" and compared as `0 > 30 = False` with a success
    status, quietly taking the else-path on nothing at all.
  - an operator _compare does not recognise. ops.get(operator, False) fell
    through to False, indistinguishable from a condition that genuinely did not
    hold, so the flow took the else-path forever.

The editor's validator rejects empty operands, but that guard lives outside the
node and does not cover imported JSON or a hand-edited flow, so both are now
errors that take NEITHER branch. Operand parsing moves into a _operand helper
that also stops treating a literal 0 as absent - it is falsy, so routing it
through get_str's default substitution made it indistinguishable from an empty
field. A missing or blank operator still takes the documented '>' default;
only a value the author actually typed and _compare cannot honour is an error.

Verified 32 cases: the full operator table (symbols and legacy word forms),
interpolation on both operands, indicator paths including a negative MACD
histogram, every empty/whitespace/None/missing spelling of an absent operand,
literal and negative zero operands, and unknown operators.

Also surface the server's own error text in the web client. Flask returns the
useful reason in the response body, but the axios interceptor left it there and
every caller reads error.message, so a blocked workflow showed the editor
"Request failed with status code 400" while the actual cause ("A varCondition
node needs leftValue") reached only the server log.

* fix(flow): close 16 validated QA findings across triggers, execution and node contracts

Independently verified each finding in the 2026-08-21 production QA audit
against current source before fixing; several were overstated, one was
materially worse than reported, and six further defects surfaced.

Triggers
- Price alerts: a one-shot alert was removed on the monitor thread right
  after submitting its worker, so the worker found it gone and dropped the
  run. Measured 40/40 dropped once the pool is warm - only the first alert
  in a process survived, because Thread.start() happens to yield the GIL.
  The run now owns de-registration and claims the alert by identity.
- A consumed one-shot trigger now clears is_active. Without that, restoring
  alerts at startup would re-arm a spent alert and re-fire its order.
- Added restore_price_alerts(), mirroring restore_order_update_watches:
  an active price-alert workflow no longer goes silently dead on restart
  while the activate endpoint refuses it as already_active.
- Order-update watches: queued runs now re-check that the workflow is still
  active and that the watch is the same generation, so a deactivate or a
  deactivate/reactivate cycle cannot execute or clobber the new watch.
- Price monitor registry, running flag, stop event and thread now transition
  under one lock, and the poll loop releases its scoped sessions.

Scheduler lifecycle
- Activation persists is_active before registering, checks every result, and
  rolls back on failure. It previously registered first and discarded what
  the database returned, so a failed write reported success while a live
  persistent job traded against a row marked inactive - unstoppable, since
  deactivate short-circuits and delete only removes the job when active.
- Deactivation removes the job by workflow id with strict=True, so a jobstore
  failure aborts instead of marking the workflow inactive with its job armed.
- Scheduled callbacks now require the workflow to still exist and be active.
- The API key is no longer pickled into flow_apscheduler_jobs.job_state,
  where it sat in cleartext in the same database that Fernet-encrypts it.
  It is resolved per run, so regenerating the key no longer breaks schedules.
- Turning market-hours gating off in the editor now takes effect.

Execution reporting
- Replaced the check-then-acquire duplicate-run guard with an atomic
  try-acquire; two simultaneous triggers ran the whole workflow twice.
- A node returning status error now stops its branch and marks the run
  failed. A rejected entry leg used to let the hedge leg place and the alert
  fire, then record the run completed and answer HTTP 200 success.
- Execute and webhook responses map already_running to 409 and failure to
  5xx, and the webhook returns the run's own message instead of always
  "triggered".

Node contracts
- Modify Order reads the live order and changes only what was supplied. It
  had been sending hardcoded action BUY, product MIS, price type LIMIT and
  quantity 1 for fields the editor never collects - flipping a live SELL to
  BUY on brokers that carry action, NRML to MIS on those that carry product,
  and silently resizing a 500-lot order to 1.
- Close Positions honours its advertised symbol/exchange/product filter
  instead of always calling the unconditional square-off.
- HTTP Request: headers parse from the JSON string the editor writes (they
  were silently dropped), PATCH works, timeout is read as milliseconds and
  capped at 60s, and the node uses its own client rather than the shared
  broker pool.
- HTTP Request rejects non-http(s) schemes and loopback, private, link-local
  and reserved destinations, and logs a redacted URL. The URL interpolates
  from webhook-supplied context, so its caller could steer the request.
- Fund Check and Position Check fail closed instead of guarding against zero
  or an empty symbol, which made them always true; the validator now
  requires the fields they read.
- Delay is capped at 300s; it sleeps inside the workflow lock and the
  triggering request.

Other
- Webhook lookups cache the workflow id, not the ORM instance. The cached
  instance was detached after the first run committed, so the next webhook
  within the 5 minute TTL raised DetachedInstanceError on an uncaught line.
- Regenerating a webhook secret evicts the cache and its failure is checked;
  rotation previously left the old secret working for 5 minutes while
  rejecting the new one.
- Workflow PUT accepts only name, description, nodes and edges, and reports
  needs_reactivate when a live trigger's configuration changed.
- Execution history limit is clamped; limit=-1 meant unlimited in SQLite.
- Unknown /api and asset paths return real 404s instead of a 200 React
  shell. Extensionless React routes still fall through to the SPA.
- Cleared the Ruff findings in the files touched.

Frontend half of the 2026-08-21 QA audit remediation. Two of these are
data-loss bugs that outrank the audit's own Critical list.

Losing work
- A failed workflow GET left isLoading false and the data undefined, so the
  editor rendered a blank canvas indistinguishable from a new workflow.
  Adding two nodes and saving PUT those two over the real graph and reset
  the name to the store default. Retries are capped at 1, so one dropped
  session reached it. There is now an explicit error state with Retry, and
  the canvas is never rendered without its data.
- Activate and Deactivate invalidate the workflow query, and the refetch
  returned a new object identity that re-ran the hydration effect and called
  setWorkflow - replacing the canvas with the last saved graph and clearing
  isModified. Unsaved edits vanished a moment after clicking Activate, with
  no warning and no undo. The canvas now hydrates once per workflow, and
  is_active updates on its own.
- The workflow list had the same shape: a failed fetch rendered "No
  workflows yet", telling the user their workflows were gone.

Running what is on screen
- Run Now, Activate and Deactivate save first when the canvas is dirty.
  They send only the workflow id, so the backend acted on the last saved
  graph: changing a quantity and hitting Run Now showed a successful run of
  the previous graph with nothing to indicate it. Awaiting the save also
  closes the race between a pending Ctrl+S and the execute request.
- Saving an active workflow whose trigger configuration changed now warns
  that it must be reactivated, using the needs_reactivate flag the server
  returns.

Output variables
- Nine node types rendered an output-variable name as their input's fallback
  while saving an empty string, so the box looked filled, the executor
  stored nothing, and every downstream reference resolved to its own literal
  text. The names are now persisted. The indicator node had the same effect
  through a placeholder rather than a fallback; it gets a real default too.
- Workflows already saved with a blank name are repaired on load, so what
  the panel shows is what the next save will store.

Node contracts
- Basket Order counted `orders` as an array while the editor writes
  newline-delimited text, so every basket read "Orders: 0"; the subtitle
  read `strategy`, which nothing writes, instead of basketName.
- Margin counted `positions` while the editor writes positionsJson, so every
  margin node read "Positions: 0". It now uses the tested parseLegs helper.
- Close Positions keyed its filter badge on exchange and product, which ship

* fix(flow): close the remaining discrepancies from the QA validation

Condition nodes now fail rather than answer from a substituted value. `false`
is a real answer that routes the graph down the false branch, so a check that
could not run must not produce one -- an exit gate reading a silent `false`
would simply not fire.

- priceCondition validated an operator against nothing, so an unrecognised one
  fell through the comparison to `false`. An unknown `field` read 0.0 out of
  the quote dict and compared that. A non-numeric threshold became 0.0. All
  three now return an error and take neither branch. `value` is interpolated,
  which it was not before.
- positionCheck logged "unknown condition - returning False", which is
  indistinguishable downstream from a condition that genuinely did not hold.
- timeCondition rejects an operator it cannot evaluate, and keeps the seconds
  it parses. Dropping them made "after 15:29:59" fire a minute early, while
  waitUntil honoured the very same string -- two nodes disagreeing on one time.

Other contract gaps
- cancelAllOrders stores its result like every other action node; an
  outputVariable set on it used to stay undefined, so the downstream reference
  resolved to its own literal text.
- Editing the trigger of an active workflow now re-arms it during the save
  instead of only reporting needs_reactivate. The registration is a snapshot
  taken at activation, so a new schedule time or alert symbol saved cleanly
  while the scheduler kept running the old one. If re-arming fails the
  workflow is deactivated rather than left on a stale registration, and
  needs_reactivate says so. Activation, save and replace share one
  _register_trigger, so they cannot drift again.

Lifecycle
- Both monitors' shutdown is registered with atexit, following the scalping
  risk monitor's precedent. Neither had a caller anywhere, so the poll thread,
  the bus subscription and both worker pools survived until the process was
  killed. The price monitor never released its pool at all.
- Both are idempotent, and the order monitor clears _initialized so a later
  get() re-subscribes. __init__ returns early on that flag, so the singleton
  was previously unrecoverable after a shutdown.

Editor
- A batch of ReactFlow changes only marks the canvas modified when it contains
  a real edit. `dimensions` changes fire on first measurement and `select` on
  a click, so a freshly opened graph read as dirty before the user touched
  anything -- which matters now that Run Now and Activate save first, since it
  turned a read-only glance into a write.

Cleared the last of the flow-scope Ruff findings.
