* fix(flow): close the Critical and High residuals from the third audit

FLOW-004 (Critical) - the save race the auditor reproduced with a Zustand probe
- A save PUTs the graph as it stood when the request was issued. Edits made
  while it was in flight were not in that payload, but markSaved() cleared the
  dirty flag anyway: the canvas showed B, the server held A, and the editor
  reported nothing unsaved -- so Run Now and Activate then executed A.
- markSaved now takes the revision that was actually sent and only clears the
  flag when the graph still matches it, and saveIfDirty loops (bounded) until a
  save completes with the canvas unchanged. If it cannot converge it throws
  rather than executing a revision the user is no longer looking at.

FLOW-003 (Critical) - startup reconciliation
- Activation writes a row flag and a scheduler job, and a crash or a failed
  write leaves those disagreeing. Neither state self-corrects: deactivate
  short-circuits on already_inactive and activate refuses already_active. The
  jobstore is persistent, so a stale job was restored at every boot and kept
  trading a workflow the user believed was off.
- reconcile_scheduler_jobs() removes jobs whose workflow is inactive or gone,
  restores a missing job for an active scheduled workflow, and runs at startup
  beside the other Flow restorations.

FLOW-031 (Critical) - the residual half
- A price alert re-derives its condition from the next poll, so clearing the
  latch is enough there. An order update arrives from the bus once and is never
  replayed, so a refused submit dropped that fill entirely. It now runs inline
  on the dispatch thread as a last resort, and logs the event identity if even
  that fails.

FLOW-016 (High) - value checks were gated on strict, and the editor saves
non-strict, so a save stored exactly the node the importer would refuse. They
now run at both levels while presence checks stay strict-only, so a half-built
graph is still savable. A non-string constant is rejected as the wrong type
rather than skipped, and a LIMIT or SL order without a positive price - or an
SL/SL-M without a trigger price - is refused. MARKET still allows price 0.

FLOW-013 (High) - method is validated against what the executor implements, so
TRACE is refused instead of failing at run time, and timeout has a lower bound:
1 ms is not a fast request, it is one that can only ever fail.

FLOW-015 (High) - object-form indicator params are refused at import, and the
executor normalises them instead of failing, so graphs already stored keep
running while new ones are corrected.

feat(trading): market replay on the charting terminal

Upgrades openalgo-charts to 1.3.0 and wires up its replay controller, so a
session can be walked forward a bar at a time on /trading.

The controller is headless by design: it feeds the series a prefix of the loaded
bars, which is what makes every indicator redraw as it stood at that moment
rather than needing replay-aware code of its own. The transport bar, the scrub
and the clock are ours to draw, and they render only while replay owns the data.

Both the price and the volume series are driven. The chart merges every series
onto one time axis, so a volume histogram left at full length would drag future
timestamps back onto it and undo the illusion.

Replay is torn down whenever the bars underneath it change: on a symbol load, on
an interval change, and on destroy. The controller snapshots the bars it started
on and stop() puts that snapshot back, so carrying it across a symbol change
would restore the previous instrument's data onto the new one.

Replay opens a quarter of the way into the session rather than at bar 0, so
there is history to read on the left and session left to walk on the right. An
empty chart reads as broken.

scales, chart-level timezone support with IST unchanged as the default, price

fix(trading): white scrollbars, wasted toolbar row, and the drifting watermark

Three things found by measuring the live /trading page rather than reading it.

WHITE SCROLLBARS. The global scrollbar rule was already there and looked right,
but `scrollbar-color` computed to `auto` everywhere, so the browser painted its
light default on a dark panel. The cause is that index.css carries two
incompatible token systems: the base :root and .dark define channels
("240 3.8% 46.1%") for hsl(var(--x)), while .analyzer and the accent themes
define complete oklch() colours. Under those, hsl(var(--muted-foreground) / .35)
expands to hsl(oklch(...) / .35), which is invalid, and an invalid
scrollbar-color falls back to auto. scrollbar-width in the same rule is valid,
which is why one applied and the other did not.

Fixed two ways. The scrollbar colours are now literals that no token system can
invalidate, and color-scheme is declared per theme, which is the broader fix: it
makes every native control follow the palette, not just scrollbars. Note
.analyzer is a dark theme applied INSTEAD of .dark rather than alongside it, so
it declares dark itself; .sandbox is the light one.

There are 30 further hsl(var(--x)) declarations in index.css that are dead under
the oklch themes. Not touched here, since each needs its own decision.

A ROW THAT WAS 91 PER CENT EMPTY. The layout picker owned a full-width bar
carrying 134px of content across 1536px and costing 45px of chart height plus a
border. It is a page-level control, so it now renders through a `leading` slot
at the head of the first pane's toolbar, and only the first: repeating it per
pane would imply the layout is per-pane. Chrome above the chart drops from 155px
to 110px, and the chart goes from 77.6 to 83.8 per cent of the viewport.

THE WATERMARK LEFT THE CORNER. A primitive belongs to a pane, and the mark was
pinned to pane 0. Add an oscillator that wants its own pane and "bottom of pane
0" becomes the middle of the chart, which is where it ended up. It now follows
whichever pane is last. The engine emits no event when a pane is created, only
paneRemoved, so this is driven from the indicator funnel, which is the only
thing that creates one here. Raised upstream as openalgo-charts#1.

Pin the chart engine to ^1.4.0 and pick up three things the terminal wants.

Corner session clock and bar countdown. Both ship off in the engine for good
reason: a countdown repaints every second, and a chart opened on a historical
range would count down against a bar that closed months ago. A live terminal is
exactly the case they were built for, so this host opts in. The clock reads the
exchange's wall time through the chart's configured timezone and shows the
offset, so what a trader sees is the market's clock rather than the machine's.

Chart settings moves from the toolbar gear into the right-click menu. That is
where a terminal user reaches for it, and the toolbar row is the most contended
strip on the page.

Fix the settings dialog clipping the descenders of its Appearance and Trading
tab labels. The fields panel is `flex-1`, i.e. `flex: 1 1 0%`, and a flex item
with a zero basis has a scaled shrink factor of zero: it absorbs none of the
overflow when the dialog hits `max-h`. The browser took the excess out of the
only children with a real basis instead, squeezing the tab strip from 28px to
16.6px, and `overflow-x-auto` (which also computes `overflow-y` to `auto`)
clipped rather than spilled the difference. It landed on precisely the descender
band, so the `p` in Appearance and the `g` in Trading lost their tails while
Price, Readout and Axes looked untouched -- and it only reproduced on those two
because their panels are the tall ones that push the dialog to its max height in
the first place. Pin the title, tab strip and footer with `shrink-0` so the
scroll panel is the only thing that gives.

feat(trading): reset to defaults, one checkbox, toolbar undo and redo

Reset to defaults, bottom left of the chart settings dialog. It resets EVERY
tab, not the visible one, and it resets to THIS TERMINAL's baseline rather than
the engine's per-control defaults. That distinction is the whole feature: the
host turns the corner session clock and the bar countdown on at construction,
both off in the engine, so a reset driven from the schema would have switched
off chrome nobody touched. The baseline is captured once per chart build, on
the line before stored preferences are replayed, and re-taken on every build so
it follows a theme switch instead of freezing one theme's palette.

Persisted settings are now pruned to the keys that genuinely differ from that
baseline. Without it a reset stores the entire default set and the next boot
replays it, nailing the chart to whichever theme was on at reset time. With it,
an untouched control keeps following the theme, which is what "default" has to
mean for the reset to be worth having. The control disables itself when nothing
deviates, so its state answers "am I already at defaults" without hunting five
tabs for a changed swatch.

Grid visibility had two owners writing the same two booleans: the context menu
through its own storage key, and the settings dialog straight through to the
engine. A settings patch now mirrors into the field the menu reads, so the tick
matches the chart and a rebuild re-applies whichever control the user last used.

One checkbox everywhere: TickBox. There were three -- two hand-rolled copies of
a masked-tick control and two fallbacks to accent-color on a native box -- and
none of them ever drew a tick. Two independent faults: the tick was painted
bg-[hsl(var(--primary-foreground))], and this app defines that token twice, as

perf: generate frontend asset compression at startup, not in git (#1896)

* perf: generate frontend asset compression at startup, not in git

The Vite build emitted .br and .gz next to each hashed asset and CI
force-committed them with frontend/dist/ on every rebuild. Compressed
output can be neither deflated nor delta-compressed by git, and Vite's
content-hashed filenames mean every rebuild produces brand new blobs that
never go away, so these variants had grown into 165 MB of the 248 MB that
frontend/dist occupies in history. Repository history tripled in 60 days
(81 MB to 248 MB) and clone times with it, all to carry bytes that are
reproducible in 30 ms from the raw assets sitting next to them.

Generate them at startup instead. utils/precompress_assets.py walks the
built tree, gzips what is worth gzipping, and skips everything already
current. Idempotent, atomic (these assets are cached immutable for a year,
so a torn write could not be corrected by a later rebuild), and it sweeps
orphaned variants so the directory cannot grow without bound across
upgrades. Failures are isolated per file and never propagate: asset
negotiation already falls back to the raw file.

Only gzip is produced. Brotli would save a further ~15% but needs a
third-party extension, and the deployments that benefit are a thin slice:
OpenAlgo recommends Cloudflare, which re-compresses at the edge regardless
of what the origin sends, the Docker install's nginx sets gzip on for
proxied responses, and laptop installs serve over loopback. That leaves a
direct install with no CDN paying ~260 KB extra on a first visit against
year-cached assets. react_app.py still negotiates .br if an operator
supplies it.

Runs synchronously in setup_environment, ahead of the background DB
thread. Under eventlet a threading.Thread is a green thread, so running
~3 s of gzip there would stall the whole worker mid-request; at boot,
before the first request, it costs nothing observable. Later boots find
every variant current and finish in ~30 ms.

Tracked frontend/dist files drop from 586 to 270. History growth drops
from roughly 83 MB/month to 28 MB/month. Note this does not shrink an
existing clone: the 250 MB already in history stays until someone decides
a rewrite is worth breaking every fork.

Verified: generation reproduces the previous build's variant set exactly
(158 files, byte-identical coverage, all decompressing to their sources);
0 descriptor growth and +0.2 MB RSS over 200 iterations; 69 CI-safe tests
pass including 9 new ones.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: drop the gzip variant when it stops matching its asset

Codex review on #1896 caught a correctness bug, and there was a second
instance of the same class next to it.

serve_assets prefers any <asset>.gz sibling for a client advertising gzip,
and serves it with Cache-Control: immutable for a year. So a variant left
next to an asset it no longer encodes is not merely wasteful, it is served
*instead of* that asset, and the wrong bytes are then cached for a year.

Two paths left one behind when an asset was rewritten in place:

- compression stopped helping, so _write_variant returned early without
  touching the variant already there (the case Codex reported)
- the asset dropped below the 1 KB threshold, so _is_compressible skipped
  it before any variant handling ran at all

Reproduced both: a gzip client was served the previous build's bytes.
_remove_orphans did not catch either, because it only looks for variants
whose source is gone, and in both cases the source is still present.

The fix makes one invariant hold rather than patching the two paths:
<asset>.gz exists only while it holds a smaller, current encoding of
<asset>. The loop now visits every file and converges it to that state,
removing the variant when the asset stops qualifying, and _write_variant
removes it when compression does not shrink the file.

Content-hashed filenames make this unlikely on a normal Vite build, since
new content means a new name. It is reachable for any asset served out of
dist/assets whose name is stable across builds, and the consequence is a
year of cached wrong bytes, so it is worth closing rather than reasoning
about reachability.

Three regression tests added, each verified to fail without this change.

perf: partial-clone the repo in the install scripts (#1897)

All four install scripts cloned the full history. That is ~280 MB, nearly
all of it superseded frontend/dist bundles that a server never reads.
install-multi.sh clones inside the per-instance loop, so a five-instance
install downloaded ~1.4 GB.

--filter=blob:none makes it a partial clone: the server sends every commit
and tree but no file contents, and git then fetches only the blobs the
checkout needs. Measured against GitHub, that is 20 MB rather than 276 MB,
holding 2,776 blobs instead of 71,197 while keeping all 4,824 commits,
18,909 trees, 62 tags and every branch. Blobs outside the current checkout
arrive on demand.

Chosen over --depth 20, which is the same size but truncates rather than
lazy-loads. A shallow clone fetches no tags and a single branch, so
checking out a release tag or a feature branch needs three extra commands,
and rolling back further than the clone depth is impossible. Fetching all
branches shallowly is not an alternative: at 107 branches each dragging in
its own dist bundles, --depth 20 --no-single-branch measures 234 MB.

The one thing given up is that history access needs the network at that
moment, so a rollback during a GitHub outage would fail where a shallow
clone's would not. Against that, update.sh upgrades via git pull, so a host
that cannot reach the remote could not have reached the broken state
either. A host whose git server does not support filtering simply
full-clones with a warning and exit 0, which is exactly today's behaviour,
so this is never worse than cloning with no flag.

Verified against a real partial clone: git pull fast-forwards and stays
20 MB; git log, git log --stat and git tag all resolve with no network;
checking out HEAD~50 and a release tag both work, lazily fetching blobs;
and the diagnostics page's git rev-parse --abbrev-ref/--short HEAD
(issue #1388) still resolves. Nothing in the codebase uses git describe or
git rev-list --count. All four scripts pass bash -n.

Per install: 276 MB down to 20 MB.

feat(flow): support MCX commodity options in the options nodes ,ffeat(flow): build multi-leg option baskets leg by leg and Fix :(shoonya): never return a quote for a different instrument (#1904)

* feat(flow): support MCX commodity options in the options nodes

The Options Order and Multi-Leg nodes could only resolve NSE and BSE index
underlyings. Naming an MCX product asked the quote service for a spot symbol
that does not exist on MCX, and the order failed with "Could not determine
LTP".

MCX differs from the equity segments in two ways this handles:

- There is no separate derivatives exchange. The future, the option and the
  quote all live on MCX, so there is no NFO/BFO equivalent to map to.
- There is no spot instrument. CRUDEOIL on its own is not tradable, so the ATM
  reference is priced off the nearest unexpired future, which is what the
  option chain, IV surface and straddle charts already do. With no unexpired
  future the node fails with a 404 rather than guessing a reference price.

The declared exchange stays a fallback rather than an override: a named
underlying always decides its own exchange, so a workflow whose exchange field
still holds the node default cannot misroute a SENSEX or CRUDEOIL order. The
fallback is what reaches a stock option or an unlisted commodity.

/flow/api/index-symbols now answers for the MCX underlyings alongside the
index ones. An underlying with no usable lot size is omitted rather than
returned as null, so the dropdown never offers something the executor would
refuse to size.

test/test_flow_mcx_options.py pins the editor's list to the executor's, so the
two cannot drift.

* feat(flow): build multi-leg option baskets leg by leg

The Multi-Leg node offered five readymade strategies and, for anything else,
the message "Configure custom legs via API". Every basket whose legs do not
share one expiry or sit at an offset from the money - a calendar spread, a
diagonal, a ratio, a basket pinned to chosen strikes - was reachable only by
hand-writing the workflow JSON.

The panel now builds those legs. Each names its own side, strike, expiry,
quantity and pricing, and a readymade strategy can be loaded as a starting
point to edit. Strike and expiry are picked from the contracts the exchange
lists: strikes carry their moneyness and the symbol they resolve to, expiry is
the listed dates. Every field can still be typed, which is how a {{variable}}
is entered and the fallback whenever the contract lookup is unavailable.

Fix the validator, which required `offset` on every leg. A leg naming an
absolute strike was refused before it could be saved, so the strike path the
executor implements was unreachable even from hand-written JSON. A malformed
`expiry` and a non-positive `strike` also passed and failed mid-basket, which
matters because a basket fills leg by leg: by the time leg three is rejected,
legs one and two are already on and the position is not the one anybody chose.

Move the expiry selection rule into flow_node_contracts.select_expiry so the
panel and the executor resolve a relative expiry identically. The panel shows
which contract a leg will trade; a second copy of the rule would let that go
stale.

Inherited fields show the value they resolve to rather than naming the
inheritance, and write nothing until changed, so a leg left alone keeps
following the node and a scheduled basket still rolls to the next expiry.

Add jsdom pointer-capture and scrollIntoView stubs to the test setup: without
them any test that opens a Radix Select dies before its assertion, which is
why this panel had no component coverage.

* fix(shoonya): never return a quote for a different instrument

Shoonya GetQuotes intermittently answers a valid request with a complete,
stat=Ok snapshot of another instrument on the same login. Measured against the
live API on 25-Aug-2026, two NFO options polled round-robin at 2 req/sec for 13
minutes: 119 of 1318 replies came back wrong (9.03%), every one of them the NSE
index, in a run that never requested the index at all.

Nothing about the price reveals it. A leaked index quote is internally
consistent and its LTP sits inside its own OHLC, so the stale-quote check in
sandbox/execution_engine.py cannot catch it. The only signal is the echoed
exch/token. Unchecked it reaches order fills: a sandbox MARKET buy on
NIFTY18AUG2624600CE filled at 24391.25, the NIFTY spot, against an LTP of 39.85.

quote_matches_request() compares the echoed exch/token against the request on
all five GetQuotes paths - get_quotes, get_depth, the get_history today-candle
patch, and both multiquotes fetchers, the last two of which bypassed
get_api_response and had no check at all. A mismatch is retried up to
SHOONYA_QUOTE_ATTEMPTS times (default 3) and then refused rather than returned.
Single-quote paths raise; multiquotes rows carry an error instead of a price, so
one bad symbol does not fail a batch of twenty.

Three attempts because the failures are near-independent: for a given scrip
P(wrong) was 8.19% and 9.86% while P(wrong given the previous reply for it was
wrong) was 5.66% and 9.38%. Verified live over 300 quotes - 36 caught on the
first attempt, 3 on the second, 1 exhausted and raised, none returned a wrong
price.

The reporting in log_wrong_instrument_response is commented out: at a 9-12% leak
rate the full-payload line floods log/errors.jsonl. Detection and discarding are
unaffected.

The same session's WebSocket touchline feed carried 1719 ticks with zero wrong
instruments, so this is specific to the REST endpoint. Preferring the feed
remains the better fix where one is available; this guards the paths that have
none.

test/shoonya_getquotes_soak.py measures the raw broker behaviour on both
transports without going through the guard, discovering the nearest-expiry ATM
contracts rather than carrying hardcoded symbols that expire.

fix(auth): add a sign-out control to the broker login pages

The broker-auth pages render outside Layout, so they have no Navbar and
therefore no logout control. Combined with POST /auth/login redirecting
back to /broker whenever a `user` is already in the session
(blueprints/auth.py:310), a user who completed the OpenAlgo password
login but not the broker login had no UI path out: revisiting /login
bounced them straight back. The only escapes were typing /auth/logout by
hand or clearing cookies.

Adds BrokerAuthSignOut, wired into BrokerSelect and BrokerTOTP. No
backend change is needed: logout() already clears the session
unconditionally, and _is_foreign_initiated() already permits same-origin
requests.

Reuses the navbar's LogoutConfirmDialog unconditionally rather than
signing out on the first click. OpenAlgo allows up to
MAX_SESSIONS_PER_USER concurrent devices sharing one broker feed, and a
session that still carries `logged_in` reaches these pages too: the
broker-token-expired reconnect flow (issue #1400) is deliberately
admitted by broker_login(). For that session logout() takes the full
teardown path, revoking the broker token, running clear_user_sessions()
across every device and broadcasting force_logout. Confirming every time
means a click here can never silently tear down another device's live
trading session, and the warning stays identical to the one users
already know from the navbar.

When the XHR logout fails the fallback is a top-level GET /auth/logout
rather than a client-side route change. client.ts deliberately sends the
POST without a CSRF token if fetchCSRFToken() throws, Flask-WTF then
rejects it, and routing to /login would claim a sign-out that never
happened while the session cookie stayed valid. The GET path is not
CSRF-validated and is accepted as same-origin, so it actually completes.

fix(auth): start a clean session on successful password login

Clear the session before writing any authenticated value, so leftovers
from an abandoned earlier flow cannot survive into the authenticated
session: a password-reset token, a stale broker key, or a half-finished
TOTP park being layered under the new values instead of replaced.

This is state hygiene, not a session-fixation fix. Flask signs the whole
session into the cookie (SecureCookieSessionInterface), so there is no
server-side session id an attacker could pre-plant and later reuse, and
login already yields a brand new signed cookie value. A scanner finding
that reported this as a MEDIUM session-fixation issue was a false
positive; the small genuine improvement underneath it is this one.

Placement matters: the clear runs after the password check but before
session["user"] is written, and "logged_in" is not set until
handle_auth_success() completes broker auth, so nothing authenticated is
discarded. The two-stage login is unaffected, since stage 2 reads only
session["user"], and session.permanent is re-set in
handle_auth_success().

Safe for CSRF: POST /auth/login is exempt (no session exists yet) and
the SPA re-fetches a token from /auth/csrf-token before each mutating
request, so there is no cached token to invalidate.

test(strategy-builder): stop the in-flight-margin test racing its own refetch

`frontend-test` failed on `npm run test:coverage` with the identity-reset
margin test finding "Margin Req." present when it asserted absence. It
passes on a plain run and fails only under coverage, the same split
5462a4fc saw, but a slow timeout does not fix this one.

The test resolved its post-reset /margin request immediately with 20,000.
That is a legitimate response: it sets marginSupported(true) and renders
the tile on its own once the effect's 400ms debounce fires. So the
assertion was racing the component's own refetch, and v8 instrumentation
under coverage lets the debounce land first. The test was asserting a
transient state, not an invariant.

Defer the second response instead of resolving it. With the post-reset
request still in flight nothing legitimate can populate the tile, so its
presence can only mean the stale response repopulated state after the
reset - which is exactly what the test is for. The original assertion is
kept verbatim and is now deterministic rather than timing-dependent.

Then resolve the fresh request and assert the tile shows 20,000 and never
10,000, so the absence check above cannot pass vacuously.

Verified by disabling the post-await isCurrent() guard in the margin
effect: the test fails on the absence assertion, so it still catches the
regression it was written for. Full suite green under both `test:run` and
`test:coverage` (56 files, 1086 tests).

* Pool the Motilal market-data WebSocket per session

services/quotes_service.py and services/depth_service.py build a fresh
BrokerData for every request, so caching the socket on self._websocket could
never hit: every depth and multiquote call opened a brand new WebSocket, and
nothing ever closed it. The request handlers only unregister their scrips,
which does not close the connection.

The abandoned clients did not even become garbage - connect() starts a reader
thread bound to the instance - and their on_close handler kept scheduling
reconnects, so file descriptors and threads grew with request volume rather
than with users.

Move the connection into a module-level registry keyed by the auth token,
mirroring broker/aliceblue/api/data.py:

- reuse the pooled socket when it is connected;
- disconnect and evict the stale entry before replacing it;
- close a socket that fails to connect instead of leaving it half-open, and
  return None (both call sites already treat None as "no socket");
- evict and close a superseded session, so the daily 6 AM token rollover does
  not strand a socket plus its reader thread;
- close_all_websockets() for logout and shutdown.

Five requests on one session now open one socket instead of five. The connect
wait also polls at 50ms instead of 500ms, which stops rounding every handshake
up to half a second.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Close three more Motilal WebSocket leaks found by re-auditing

Follow-up to the per-session pooling: auditing the pooled implementation, and
then the layers around it, turned up three leaks the first pass missed. Two of
them only became reachable once the socket started outliving a request.

data.py - registration race. The socket has to be built outside the registry
lock (connecting takes ~250ms and holding it would serialise every caller), so
two requests that miss the cache together - the normal cold start, e.g. an
option-chain and a depth call arriving at once - each built one, and the second
registry write overwrote the first without closing it. Measured 4 concurrent
cold-start requests: 4 sockets created, 0 closed, 3 leaked. The incumbent now
wins (other requests may already be registering scrips on it), the late socket
is closed, and a dead incumbent being replaced is closed too. Same run now
leaks nothing.

motilal_adapter.py - duplicate poll threads. _start_data_polling() had no
liveness guard, and connect()'s guard only covers the connect thread, which has
normally already exited by then. Several proxy recovery paths call connect() on
a live adapter (websocket_proxy/connection_manager.py:495,550 and
server.py:982,1031), so each one started another poller, and the old one never
stopped: it loops on _stop_poll/running, which a reconnect does not touch.
Three connects meant three threads republishing every subscription to ZMQ every
500ms - duplicate ticks downstream, not just wasted CPU. Now one per adapter.

motilal_websocket.py - two fixes:
- Reconnect bursts. Every on_close scheduled a delayed_reconnect thread, and
  pruning only dropped dead refs, so 20 drops left 20 threads each sleeping up
  to 30s to accomplish one reconnect (connect() collapses them into a single
  attempt anyway). One pending reconnect is now kept.
- Tick caches were never purged. last_quotes/last_depth/last_oi are written on
  every inbound packet and unregister_scrip cleaned the subscription maps but
  not these. That was survivable while each request abandoned its own
  short-lived client; with the socket pooled per session they live as long as
  the login and accumulate one entry per distinct scrip ever quoted - an
  option-chain sweep touches hundreds of strikes per refresh. A 300-strike
  sweep now leaves zero residue.

Sockets and threads are constant with traffic again: one pooled market-data
socket, one feed socket, one order socket per user, one thread each.

fix(brokers): route broker loggers through get_logger so tokens are redacted

utils/logging.get_logger attaches SensitiveDataFilter, which redacts broker
credentials from log records. A bare logging.getLogger() bypasses it, so
anything those loggers emitted went to the log files and to log/errors.jsonl
unredacted.

This was not only a missing filter. websocket_proxy/base_adapter.py:119
already sets self.logger = get_logger("broker_adapter"), so every
BaseBrokerWebSocketAdapter subclass that reassigned
self.logger = logging.getLogger(...) in its own __init__ was actively
replacing a redacting logger with a non-redacting one. Roughly twenty
adapters did exactly that.

Converts 73 call sites across 60 files in 30 broker plugins. Logger name
strings are preserved verbatim, so nothing changes in the log output except
that secrets are now filtered. import logging is dropped only where no other
logging.* reference remains.

Deliberately unchanged:
- broker/pocketful/api/data.py:506-507, which call
  logging.getLogger("other.module").setLevel(...) to quiet third-party
  loggers rather than to create their own.
- broker/angel/streaming/smartWebSocketV2.py, a vendored Angel SDK file.
- 26 root-logger calls (logging.warning(...) with no logger object) in the
  XTS-family mapping modules. They bypass the filter too, but only ever log
  exchange codes, so they are a latent risk rather than a live leak.

Verified: zero logging.getLogger left under broker/ outside the setLevel
calls above; every touched file imports get_logger and compiles; no file
lost import logging while still needing it; the diff contains nothing but
the import swap and the call-site rename; ruff reports 721 findings before
and after, all pre-existing. Note F401 is in the project ruff ignore list,
so unused imports were checked by grep rather than by the linter.

fix(brokers): stop logging broker credentials in cleartext

Removes credential values from log messages across 12 broker plugins. The
values are gone entirely rather than truncated: a 10-character API key
prefix is still key material, and fivepaisa logged the first 50 AND last 50
characters of its access token on adjacent lines, which together expose far
more of a JWT than either alone.

Sites where the value reached the log unredacted:
- dhan/api/auth_api.py:118      "Access Token obtained: {access_token}"
- dhan/api/auth_api.py:41       "Using API Key: {BROKER_API_KEY[:8]}"
- flattrade/api/auth_api.py:24  "Full API Key: {full_api_key}"
- flattrade/api/auth_api.py:30  "Using API Key: {BROKER_API_KEY}"
- mstock/api/auth_api.py:116    "Feed token received: {auth_token}"
- mstock/api/auth_api.py:262    refresh token prefix plus the full OTP
- mstock/api/funds.py:24        "Auth token (first 30 chars): ..."
- fivepaisa/api/auth_api.py:66  "The Request Token is :{request_token}"
- fivepaisa/api/auth_api.py:80  json.dumps of the access-token request body
- fivepaisa/streaming/fivepaisa_websocket.py:166-167  token prefix + suffix
- seven XTS adapters            "Using API Key: {api_key[:10]}..."

SensitiveDataFilter only rewrites key-value shapes, so a message reads as a
leak or not depending on its wording. "Feed Token: {t}" is redacted because
the bare `token` alternative matches "Token:", but "Access Token obtained:
{t}", "Full API Key: {k}" and "Token prefix: {t}" are not, because a word
sits between the keyword and the colon. The "Feed Token:" family was
therefore already redacted; those lines are cleaned here anyway, since
relying on message wording to keep a secret out of a log is not a control.

Three call sites are deliberately left interpolating a token because their
wording does match the filter and is verified redacted: groww/api/funds.py:16
and kotak's two "Using access_token: {...}" lines.

Verified by running the real SENSITIVE_PATTERNS from utils/logging over each
message shape before and after. No credential interpolation remains outside
the three verified-redacted lines above. All touched files compile, and ruff
reports 721 findings across broker/ both before and after, all pre-existing.

fix(security): close three credential-exposure gaps found while auditing

1. Bearer redaction missed composite credentials

The rule was (Bearer\s+)[\w\-\.]+, which stops at the first separator. Two
brokers send a two-part credential in that header: tradejini uses
"Bearer <api_key>:<access_token>" and aliceblue uses
"Bearer <user_id> <session_id>". In both cases the filter redacted the
harmless first half and left the actual secret in the log. Found
independently in two brokers, so it is the pattern that is wrong, not the
call sites.

The value class now continues across ':' and single spaces between word
characters. It still stops at a quote, comma or brace, so it cannot run past
the closing quote and swallow neighbouring fields of a headers dict, which is
pinned by a test.

Also adds `cookie` to the key alternation. A cookie value is a credential,
and set-cookie was previously untouched by any pattern.

utils/logging.py had no tests at all despite being the last thing between a
broker token and log/errors.jsonl, so test/test_logging_redaction.py pins the
shapes that matter. Reverting the Bearer rule fails exactly the two composite
cases.

2. Frontend sent mutating requests with no CSRF token

client.ts caught a failed fetchCSRFToken() and continued, so the request went
out unauthenticated. Flask-WTF then rejected it and the caller saw an opaque
CSRF error instead of the real cause. It also meant a failed logout still
cleared local state and routed to /login while the server session was very
much alive. The interceptor now fails the request with a message naming the
method and URL.

3. tradejini logged full response headers

auth_api.py:118 did this at INFO on the OAuth token endpoint, where a
Set-Cookie would have carried a session. order_api.py:115 and :949 did the
same on order endpoints. All three now log the header field names only. The
`cookie` pattern above is the defence in depth behind them.

fix(options): validate strike interval and option type at the resolver boundary

The legacy option-symbol resolver trusted two inputs it should not have.

The strike interval was used as a divisor with no guard. `get_atm_strike()`
computes `round(ltp / strike_int) * strike_int`, so a `strike_int` of 0 raised
ZeroDivisionError, and a negative, NaN or infinite interval produced a strike
that formats into a symbol no exchange lists. Both surfaced as HTTP 500 with a
traceback rather than a client error.

An unrecognised option type was silently priced as a put. Every offset
calculation branches on CE and takes the else branch for everything else, in
both legacy paths, so "CALL", "C" or None resolved to the put strike:

    CE ITM2    -> 23500
    PE ITM2    -> 23700
    CALL ITM2  -> 23700   <- the put strike, no error, logged as correct

The path fails closed, because the bogus suffix flows into the symbol and
find_option_in_database() returns 404. The cost is the diagnosis: the caller is
told the symbol was "not found in NFO" when the fault was the option type, and
a broker quote call is spent before saying so.

The same shape affected a non-finite LTP in find_atm_strike_from_actual(): NaN
compares false against every strike, so min() returned the lowest strike in the
chain and reported it as ATM.

Validation goes at the resolver rather than in a fourth schema because the one
genuine in-process bypass is services/flow_openalgo_client.py:397, whose caller
services/flow_executor_service.py:2086 reads optionType through get_str() with
no enum check, unlike the options-order nodes in the same file. Guarding the
boundary covers that path and every future caller in one place.

Guards run at Step 0, before the quote request and the database lookup, so a
rejected request never reaches the broker. Range validation alone would not be
enough: strike_int is fields.Int with Range(min=1), which accepts a 401-digit
integer that raises OverflowError on math.isfinite(), so that and
Decimal("sNaN") are refused explicitly. validate_strike_interval() returns a
float so the next line is guaranteed to be able to divide by it.

Contract change: find_atm_strike_from_actual() now returns None for a
non-numeric LTP where it previously raised TypeError. All six call sites
already branch on None, so a bad underlying LTP degrades to a clean "no data"
answer instead of a 500.

Valid input is untouched: calls and puts, lowercase ce/pe, fractional intervals
such as 2.5, the ATM/ITM/OTM maths and the existing error contracts. A float
strike does not leak into symbol text, since construct_option_symbol()
normalises 23500.0 to 23500.

test/test_option_symbol_service_validation.py adds 145 cases. Neutering the two
validators while leaving their names in place fails 91 of them; the 54 that
still pass are exactly the positive-contract tests.

* feat(gtt): add GTT order support for Angel One, Fyers and Upstox

Extends GTT beyond zerodha/dhan to three more brokers. The service layer
resolves broker.<name>.api.gtt_api dynamically and the compatibility matrix
is derived by parsing for it, so each broker registers itself by shipping
api/gtt_api.py plus mapping/gtt_data.py -- nothing outside those was needed.

Angel One has no OCO rule type, so an OpenAlgo OCO becomes two rules
returned as a composite "<sl_id>-<tg_id>" trigger id that modify and cancel
decode; a failed second leg rolls the first back. Its GTT rule carries no
ordertype, so MARKET is MPP-converted as zerodha does. cancelRule needs
symboltoken and exchange, which the cancel contract lacks, so each rule is
read back through ruleDetails first.

Fyers signals OCO by the presence of orderInfo.leg2 rather than a type flag.
leg1 must sit above the LTP and leg2 below, so the target leg maps to leg1
and the stoploss leg to leg2. A leg carries no order-type field, hence MPP
again. All calls share the existing process-wide rate limiter.

Upstox has no OCO at all: every GTT needs an ENTRY rule (UDAPI1141) and a
MULTIPLE needs 2-3 rules (UDAPI1137), making its multi-leg form a bracket,
not an exit-only pair. An OpenAlgo OCO therefore opens the entry position
before arming the legs -- logged loudly at place time and documented in
placegttorder.md, since the resulting EDIS rejection names demat
authorisation rather than the entry leg. Its GTT payload has no limit-price
field, so MARKET becomes Upstox's own market_protection band instead of an
MPP limit, and created_at/expires_at arrive as epoch microseconds and are
normalised to ISO 8601 (they rendered as the year 58623 otherwise).

Book mappers are active-only per the gttorderbook contract, and normalise
trigger_type to the "single"/"two-leg" vocabulary the GTT tab keys OCO off.

signatures and error contracts across brokers, and the 113 sandbox GTT
tests pass. Live-verified so far: fyers SINGLE place and upstox SINGLE
place plus book.

fix(trading): validate indicators in the browser, drop the npm install

Two things contradicted the premise that custom indicators need no build.

The pre-flight validator required frontend/node_modules, so a trader's first
indicator triggered a 560 MB, 521-package install to reach the 368 KB of
openalgo-charts it actually uses. It now resolves in three steps: the dev copy
if a React developer already has it, then a small skill-local cache, then it
fetches that one package at the version pinned in frontend/package.json.
openalgo-charts declares zero dependencies, so that is a single download,
about a second, 2.2 MB cached. npm is a .cmd on Windows and Node 24 will not
spawn one without a shell, hence the quoted args.

More importantly, Node was a hard requirement for getting any feedback at all,
which it should never have been: the chart already has the real library loaded.
The loader now validates there. It intercepts registerIndicator to check the
descriptor before it reaches the catalogue, and wraps calc so its first result
is measured against the bars. Both silent killers are caught and reported as a
toast naming the file: a column that is not bars.length long, and a plot key
calc never filled. Neither raises anything at runtime otherwise, which is what
made a broken indicator look like one that simply does not work.

Also: no page reload to pick up a new file. The built-in tier is still imported
once, but the custom index is re-read whenever the catalogue is requested, so a
file added while the chart is open appears on the next picker open, and an

fix(trading): take the forming bar's volume from history

The live candle reported volume 0 on a symbol visibly trading, and every
volume-derived study read 0 with it: the volume histogram's last bar, OBV,
VWAP, and any custom indicator asking bars[last].volume.

The cause is a subscription the terminal cannot change. Anything tradeable
holds exactly one subscription and it is Depth, because the old dual LTP+Depth
subscribe froze the chart on brokers whose adapters track a single mode per
symbol (issue #1664). A depth payload carries ltp but no last-traded quantity,
so the builder's 'ltq-sum' mode has nothing to accumulate. Seeding hides it
until the bar rolls: the new bucket opens at 0 and stays there for its whole
life.

The periodic history reconcile already fetches this data every 30 seconds or
so, and already skips the forming bar. It now takes one field from it. Only
volume: OHLC stays with the ticks, which are fresher than a poll and must not
jump backwards to it. The higher of the two readings wins, since volume within
a bar only grows, which also keeps the histogram monotonic if a poll lands
mid-print.

It re-seeds the builder rather than patching rawBars, because the builder folds
the next tick into its own copy of the bar and would write the stale 0 straight
back over it. Tests pin that, and pin that the correction does not carry into
the next bucket.

A broker whose history omits the in-progress candle simply has nothing to
match, and the bar behaves as before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(flow): stop nodes acting on data they do not have

An audit of all 61 node types, then each finding reproduced before it was
touched. What follows is grouped by what goes wrong, not by file.

**Conditions answered on failed reads.** priceCondition, positionCheck and
fundCheck read the broker response without checking its status, so a 401 gave
ltp 0.0 and `status: success`: "if LTP < 100 then BUY" fired on an expired
session, and "if no position then BUY" doubled an open one. priceAlert has
always checked this; these now do too.

**An errored condition settled a gate.** Its placeholder False was stored, so
an AND gate saw it as evaluated rather than staying pending, computed
[False, True] and drove its FALSE branch to a real order. The run was marked
failed afterwards, by which point the order had been sent.

**A condition reachable by two paths ran twice** and followed its branch each
time, placing two orders from one trigger. Gates already carried a
once-per-run guard; conditions are combinational in exactly the same way.

**Gates ignored inputCount.** Configured for three inputs and wired for two,
they evaluated on two, so a deleted edge silently downgraded
"A AND B AND in-window" while still drawing three slots.

**timeWindow could not cross midnight.** `start <= now <= end` makes
22:00-02:00 unsatisfiable: always False, and always True once inverted, which
turns the "trigger outside window" toggle into an always-on gate.

**Subscriptions were never given back.** The websocket client is a
process-wide singleton, so one left behind is held for the life of the worker
and counts against the ceiling /trading and the sandbox engine share. They are
now tracked per workflow and released when it is deactivated or deleted.

**unsubscribe reached unsubscribe_all by accident.** A specific mode with no
symbol fell through to it, clearing every subscription on the instance -
including the ones the sandbox engine uses to trigger pending SL and LIMIT
orders. Only an explicit "all" gets there now. A rejected unsubscribe was also
computed and never read, so a failed teardown reported success.

**waitUntil had no bound.** It sleeps inside the workflow lock and the
triggering request, so a target six hours out pinned a worker and answered
"already running" to everything in between. Over 30 minutes it now points at a
schedule trigger instead.

**Two injection paths in httpRequest.** The URL was interpolated twice, so a
payload could substitute its own {{...}} and have it expanded on the second
pass - demonstrated pulling a workflow variable into an outbound request. And
the header JSON was interpolated before json.loads, so a value carrying a
quote became structure and added a header the author never wrote. Both are now
resolved once, and after parsing.

**Every broker rejection said "node failed".** The client reports the reason
under "error" and the dispatch read "message", so insufficient funds, an RMS
block or a closed market all surfaced as that literal string in the run record
and the webhook reply.

Also: multiQuotes.symbols was the only data-node field never interpolated;
optionsOrder and optionsMultiOrder now take an explicit expiry date as well as
a relative type; and order-path symbols are upper-cased, because the lookup is
exact and an alert does not control its own casing.

The webhook body is parsed as JSON whatever the sender declared, falling back
to form fields and then to raw text, because the platforms that post here are
the ones least able to set a Content-Type - a TradingView alert on its default
plain-text message was refused 415 before the handler ran. A secret carried in
the payload still requires JSON.

Two test stubs are corrected rather than the guards loosened: they returned a
position without the `status` the real client puts on every return path.

Adds the flow-builder skill. Its validator calls the importer's own
validate_workflow so it cannot disagree with the server, then adds the check
the importer skips: a data key nothing reads. That one matters because Flow
ignores unknown keys, so `strikeOffset` where the field is `offset` imports
cleanly, runs successfully and silently uses ATM. The node reference is
generated from the validator and the executor, and coverage.py fails if a node
type is undocumented.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(websocket): a lock shared with the loop thread must be real

The websocket client runs its asyncio loop on a real OS thread, because
asyncio cannot run on a green one, and it invokes every registered
market-data, auth and error callback from that thread. Under eventlet
threading.Lock is a green semaphore owned by the hub, so those callbacks
and the request path were contending on a primitive that can only be
handed between greenlets.

Contended, the hub tries to resume a waiter belonging to another thread,
raises "greenlet.error: Cannot switch to a different thread" inside
fire_timers, and leaves the loop thread blocked on that lock forever. The
feed then stops answering pings and stops resolving subscribe acks, so
every later subscribe waits out its full 12 second timeout. What the user
sees is the first order going through and the next one hanging the app
for over a minute, with the order itself having taken 62 milliseconds.

Four crossings existed: WebSocketClient.lock, the sandbox engine's _lock
(_on_market_data), the scalping risk monitor's _lock (_on_tick, _on_auth)
and the Flow executor's tick data_event. They now take their primitives
from utils/real_threading, which resolves to the unpatched originals
under eventlet and to the stdlib otherwise.

The Event needed more than a swap. A green Event never wakes on a set()
from a real thread, so the waiter sits out its whole timeout; a real
Event.wait() wakes but blocks the hub, freezing every other request for
the duration. real_threading.wait_for polls the flag and yields between
checks, which is the only form that does both.

Separately, the proxy's error replies carried no request_id, so a client
awaiting a subscribe ack had nothing to match them against and waited out
its own timeout for a reply that had already arrived. send_error now
echoes it and the client settles the pending future, which turns a 12
second stall on "Broker adapter not found" into an immediate error.

None of this reproduces locally: uv run app.py never patches anything, so
every case behaves correctly on the dev server whatever the primitive is
made of. test/test_eventlet_cross_thread_locks.py proves each direction
under a real hub, in a subprocess because monkey_patch cannot be undone,
and its first case asserts the defect itself so the file cannot pass
vacuously.

fix(database): wait for the SQLite write lock in Python, not inside SQLite

PRAGMA busy_timeout is served by C code that sleeps without handing control
back to eventlet. Under gunicorn+eventlet a greenlet waiting that way freezes
the entire worker for the whole timeout, and that is not merely slow: the
greenlet holding the write lock cannot be scheduled to commit while the waiter
is blocking the hub, so the wait can only ever end in "database is locked".
Measured, a holder that needed the lock for 0.5s produced a 16.46s failure with
the hub stopped throughout. Waiting the same 0.5s in Python succeeds in 0.47s
with the hub running.

This is what was left of the Flow webhook hang after the green-lock fix. The
sandbox order itself completes in 93 milliseconds, REST quote fallback and all;
the remaining minute was three of these stalls in the bookkeeping that follows
the fill, each ending in a logged failure:

    16:19:55.843  order executed, trade written
    16:20:10.862  strategy_book_db: database is locked   (15.019s, exactly the
                                                          old busy_timeout)

So the in-SQLite wait drops to 100ms, which bounds how long one attempt can
freeze the hub, and the real waiting moves into a Python retry loop whose sleep
eventlet turns into a yield. The total budget stays 15 seconds, so a write that
legitimately has to queue still gets what it always had. Retrying a statement
is what busy_timeout does internally anyway, so this changes when the app waits
rather than what it waits for; a non-lock error is re-raised untouched and
still fails fast.

Applied by defaulting the sqlite3 connection factory process-wide rather than
per engine, for the same reason the pragma listener lives here: several modules
build their engine with create_engine directly instead of going through
database.engine_factory, and a connection that missed this is exactly the one
that would freeze the worker.

fix(eventlet): stop real OS threads touching the hub's primitives

Two crossings remained after the lock fix, both reported from production and
both ending in the same traceback: greenlet.error: Cannot switch to a different
thread, raised inside fire_timers, leaving the offending thread blocked for
good. Issues #1402, #1473 and #1569.

Logging. logging.Handler serialises emit() with a lock built in __init__, and
under gunicorn+eventlet the app is imported after monkey-patching, so that lock
is green. Every real OS thread in this project logs: the websocket client's
asyncio loop, the Telegram bot thread and its Kaleido renderer, the broker
snapshot feed threads. Measured, a real thread logging while a greenlet holds
the handler lock deadlocks permanently and raises exactly the production
traceback. #1569 reports the give-away that precedes it, "AttributeError:
'StreamHandler' object has no attribute 'lock'" on unrelated requests.
Handler.createLock is patched on the class, so third-party handlers get a real
lock too, and handlers built before this module was imported are re-locked.

Callback dispatch. _handle_message runs on the asyncio loop's real OS thread
and called every registered subscriber inline. Those subscribers reach SocketIO,
the event bus and the sandbox engine, all of which use eventlet primitives, so
the crossing was reached on any tick that opened a position. #1473 names this
exact path. The loop thread now only enqueues onto a real queue and a green
thread does the calling, so everything downstream runs in the world those
primitives belong to. The queue is bounded and sheds the newest payload with a
counted warning, because the producer is a feed that never blocks.

Cooperative joins. Thread.join() on a real OS thread blocks, and a greenlet
blocking stops every other request on the worker. Reached from the /telegram
stop route (10s) and from websocket client teardown (5s).

Audited the whole tree rather than these call sites: /python, /trading,
/whatsapp, /flow and /scalping are green-to-green and cooperative already, and
every broker/*/streaming adapter is exempt because app.py starts the proxy as a
child process under eventlet. hdfcsecurities and hdfcsky already guard their
feed-thread state with a real lock. The one place still joining a real thread
from a real thread, telegram's Kaleido render, is correct as written.

None of this reproduces on the dev server, where nothing is patched.
test/test_eventlet_cross_thread_locks.py proves each direction under a real
hub, in a subprocess because monkey_patch cannot be undone.

fix(websocket): wake the caller when the loop thread returns a result

asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe hands back a concurrent.futures.Future whose
result() waits on a threading.Condition. Under eventlet that condition is green
while the loop thread resolving it is a real OS thread, and the two cannot pass
a waiter between them, so the waiting greenlet is never notified. The future
resolves correctly and the caller sleeps on regardless, reading the value only
when its own timeout expires.

Measured, an ack that arrived in 0.3s cost the caller the full 10s. That is why
subscribe() took its whole 12 seconds whenever it had to wait at all, which is
most of what was left of the Flow webhook stall, and it is the same waiter the
hub raises greenlet.error trying to switch into.

Nothing crosses the boundary now except one plain boolean: a real Event the
loop thread sets, polled here with a sleep eventlet turns into a yield.
call_soon_threadsafe replaces run_coroutine_threadsafe so no concurrent Future
is built at all. The timeout stays real and coroutine exceptions still
propagate to the caller.

docs(sandbox): state that short options are not SPAN margined

Every sandbox margin is traded value over leverage, and for an option the
traded value is premium times quantity. That is right for buying one and wrong
for selling one, where a broker blocks SPAN plus exposure on the underlying
notional and the premium received barely enters into it.

Measured on a live instance, one NIFTY lot: selling at a premium of 100 blocks
6,500 against roughly 1.2 to 1.5 lakh live, and selling at a premium of 2
blocks 130 against the same real requirement. The gap widens as the strike goes
further out of the money, because the sandbox number shrinks with the premium
while the real one does not move.

No configuration closes it. option_sell_leverage divides, so its lowest
supported value already blocks the most it can, and since SPAN is roughly
constant per lot while premium is not, no single multiplier can track it.

The margin PRD had no mention of this, which is why it keeps being reported as
a bug. See issue #1795.

fix(sandbox): serialize concurrent position updates with a lock (#1808)

Two same-symbol fills arriving together each read the same quantity, add their own delta and write, so the second silently overwrote the first. Both orders still showed complete, so the orderbook and the positionbook disagreed with nothing logged.

A class-level lock serializes the read-modify-write. It has to be class-level because OrderManager.place_order builds a fresh ExecutionEngine per request, so an instance lock would give every request its own mutex.

The regression test fires several concurrent pairs rather than one: a single pair only interleaves about two thirds of the time, so it would have signed off on a reintroduced race one run in three.

Closes #1808.

test: stop .env from overriding the suite's database isolation

conftest assigns DATABASE_URL and friends to db/*-test.db so a run cannot touch
the operator's data. utils/config.py then calls load_dotenv(override=True) at
import, which re-reads .env and puts the real paths back. Whether that happened
depended entirely on which module a given test imported first, so the suite
wrote to the isolated databases on some runs and to the real ones on others.

The visible result was seven Flow workflows from test/test_flow_qa_regressions.py
appearing in the operator's Flow Editor, named "retention test", "age test",
"mine", "theirs" and so on, removable only by hand. Verified before and after:
a full run put seven workflows in db/openalgo.db before this change and none
after, with the same seven landing in db/openalgo-test.db where they belong.

Disabling the loader is confined to the test harness, so nothing about how the
application reads .env changes.

Two consequences worth knowing. Tests that were quietly passing off the
operator's live broker session now skip instead, which is the isolation working
rather than a regression: test/sandbox/test_margin_scenarios.py and
test_cnc_sell_validation.py skip identically when run on their own. And
test_mcx_underlying_resolution.py now has to seed its own symbols instead of

fix(sandbox): resolve the position-book session boundary in the DB clock (#1789)

sandbox_positions.updated_at is written by func.now(), which on SQLite is CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, i.e. UTC. get_open_positions compared it against a boundary built from naive local wall time, so on any non-UTC host the two clocks were mixed. Measured on an IST host the boundary landed 5:30:00 late, dropping open positions last updated between 03:00 and 08:30 IST from the position book, which is what a polling strategy reads to decide whether it is flat.

The boundary is now resolved through sandbox/session_boundary.last_session_expiry_utc, the helper the T+1 cutoff and the MIS square-off already use, anchored to IST like every other caller. On a UTC host the resolved value is identical to the old naive one, so only non-UTC hosts change behaviour.

Closes #1789.

fix(dhan): stop symbol mapping from routing orders to the wrong instrument (#1929, #1930) and fix(dhan): correct master contract mapping and symbol construction (#1929, #1930) (#1932)

* fix(dhan): gate master contract mapping on SEM_SEGMENT to stop token collisions

Dhan scopes SEM_SMST_SECURITY_ID per segment, not per exchange. assign_values
matched on SEM_INSTRUMENT_NAME alone, so NSE segment D (equity F&O) and NSE
segment M (NSE commodity, all OPTFUT) both mapped to NFO. That gave 8,642
security ids two contracts each - token 153964 was both a TCS option and a
SILVERM option - and get_symbol() returns the first match, so a live equity
option position could resolve to a commodity symbol. The position book lookup
then missed it and a strategy would conclude it was flat and skip the exit,
leaving the position open at the broker. The same lookup backs the squareoff
path in order_api.py.

- assign_values dispatches on SEM_SEGMENT, with per-segment instrument sets
- NSE segment M maps to NCO (NSE Commodity) instead of being folded into NFO;
  its security id space (121601-171512) is disjoint from MCX (471725-584158)
  and overlaps NSE segment D, which is what caused the collision

  were stranded as Unknown
- _get_instrument_type returns OPTIDX/FUTIDX for MCX index derivatives and
  handles NCO, so the history API sends the right instrument type
- map NCO orders to NRML in map_order_data
- log any duplicate (exchange, token) at load time rather than failing the
  download, so a future regression is visible instead of silent
- drop columns with errors="ignore"

17,284 -> 0, NFO 99,722 -> 74,322, MCX 15,576 -> 16,298, NCO 0 -> 25,400.

commodity value, and guessing one risks placing a real order on the wrong

folded into NFO, but left it unmapped; this maps it to OpenAlgo's existing

an empty result there means nothing. Only the option chain serves this
segment. The websocket does not feed it either - subscribing to NSE_COMM
yields no packets while an MCX control on the same socket streams normally.

- map_exchange_type / map_exchange handle NCO both ways, so orders no longer
  go out with a null exchangeSegment (DH-905)
- _get_exchange_segment and _get_instrument_type cover NCO
- streaming EXCHANGE_MAP gains NCO; SEGMENT_TO_EXCHANGE gains 6, which is
  INFERRED from the annexure gap and could not be observed because Dhan does
  not stream the segment - flagged as such in the code

fix(flow): rate limit the webhook and answer 429 as JSON

The Flow webhook was the one unauthenticated, CSRF-exempt, order-placing
entry point in the product with no rate limit on it. /chartink has always had
one, and the legacy /strategy webhook had one too, so this closes a gap rather
than adding a new policy: it reads the same WEBHOOK_RATE_LIMIT variable and
default, so an operator who has already tuned that budget gets it applied here
without touching anything.

Two limits at the same budget, because neither subsumes the other. The
caller-address limit is the only key that can stop someone walking the token
space, since every guess carries a different token and would score against an
empty bucket, while each miss still costs a database lookup. The token limit
bounds what a single leaked token can do to the broker account however many
addresses replay it, which is the limit that actually caps order flow given
the payload secret is optional. Both are shared scopes, so the two spellings
of the route draw on one budget instead of granting double the configured rate
to a workflow that alternates between them.

The 429 handler matters more than the limit. app.py returns JSON only for
paths under /api/ and redirects everything else to the React /rate-limited
page. A browser reads that page; TradingView does not. A throttled alert would
follow the redirect, receive 200 and HTML, and be recorded as delivered, so a
workflow silently dropping orders looked exactly like a healthy one. A
blueprint errorhandler is consulted before the application one, which corrects
the answer for Flow without changing behaviour anywhere else.

feat(strategy): add the strategy-module schema and store

First phase of the new /strategy module: multi-leg options strategies with
end-to-end risk management, replacing the legacy webhook module retired in
58dc8adb. Schema and persistence only; no routes, no engine, nothing reachable
from the UI yet.

Six tables, all sm_ prefixed. The prefix earns its place: this codebase already
has strategy_portfolio, strategy_book, strategy_order_tags,
strategy_pending_fills and the /python strategy host, none of which are
related to each other or to this.

  sm_strategy            config: legs, risk parameters, scheduler, token hash
  sm_strategy_run        one activation, start to stop
  sm_strategy_order      every order the engine places, audit grade
  sm_strategy_checkpoint periodic runtime snapshot, for crash recovery
  sm_webhook_event       every inbound webhook, accepted or rejected
  sm_strategy_event      risk-event audit trail

Adapted from the Postgres original rather than transcribed. JSONB becomes JSON,
INET becomes String(45), and the two circular foreign keys become plain
integers because SQLite cannot ALTER TABLE to add a constraint and so has no
equivalent of use_alter. Timestamps are stored naive UTC and rendered with an
explicit offset at the boundary: SQLite does not preserve a timezone on a
DateTime column whatever you pass it, so storing aware values would hand back
naive ones on the next read.

Three things this fixes rather than inherits:

Deleting a strategy removes its children explicitly instead of trusting
ondelete="CASCADE". Those clauses are decorative here, because SQLite enforces
a foreign key only under PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON and this project never sets it.
That is not merely untidy: SQLite reuses rowids after a delete, so an orphaned
audit trail silently re-attaches itself to whichever strategy is created next
and inherits the id. The test that pins this fails without the explicit
delete, having first been found by exactly that symptom.

Checkpoints can be pruned. The original writes one row per open run every few
seconds for the length of a session and never removes any, which in a single
worker that never restarts is unbounded growth. Recovery only ever reads the
newest row.

A PATCH is confined to an allowlist. Without it a caller could set its own
webhook_token_hash and mint a working token; the test drives exactly that
payload.

The webhook token is 32 bytes of entropy behind an oaws_ prefix, stored as a
SHA-256 digest and shown once. SHA-256 rather than a slow KDF on purpose: the
input has no dictionary to defend against, and an unsalted deterministic digest
is what makes dispatch an indexed lookup instead of a table scan.

Migration drives its DDL from the ORM metadata rather than restating it. Six
tables and eighteen indexes is a lot of surface for a transcription error, and
one that drifts produces the worst kind of bug: the app starts, the query
compiles, and a column quietly holds the wrong thing.

Verified against a copy of the live database: 6 tables and 18 indexes created,
--status accurate before and after, idempotent on re-run, and all 45
pre-existing tables identical in row count afterwards. 25 tests.
