Four defects from the original are fixed here and pinned by tests that say so:

A leg with no usable side is refused, not defaulted to "B". The original never
writes a side on signal-mode legs and its evaluator treats anything but "B" as
a short, so those legs were evaluated with an inverted sign: P&L, stop and
target all pointed the wrong way and the stop fired on a favourable move.

Run P&L is marked from each leg's own entry, quantity and last price, not
summed from a per-leg mtm field written on an earlier pass. A stale field can
no longer poison the total every strategy-level rule is judged against.

Peak and trough are written on every evaluation, not only on one stop path. The
original recorded both as zero for any run closed by an overall stop, a target,
a lock-profit floor, the scheduler or the kill switch.

A trail step configured in plain lock mode is ignored rather than quietly
turning a static floor into a rising one, which is a different product than the
user asked for.

Two defects were introduced and caught by the tests rather than shipped. The
side guard was defeated by a `or "B"` in the same function it was guarding.
Reading a finished run's state registered a lock for its id and never removed
it, so any caller probing arbitrary run ids grew the registry without bound in
a worker that never restarts; locks are now created only for writers.

A continuous trail passes its trigger as the gap. The core requires a positive
trail_step before it will move a stop at all, so the natural reading of an
X-only configuration would have disabled trailing outright.

Locks hold in-memory bookkeeping only, per CLAUDE.md: a greenlet waiting on one
cannot yield, so callers read what they need, release, then do the slow work.

23 tests here, 206 with the risk core.

feat(strategy): add per-run order dispatch for the strategy module

One place where a strategy run turns a decision into an order. Entries,
rule-driven exits, manual closes and square-offs all go through it, so the live
and sandbox paths cannot drift and the engine never has to know which it is on.

Three deliberate departures from how the rest of the product places orders,
each of which would be a defect if inherited unchanged:

Mode is per run, not global. OpenAlgo's analyzer setting is one platform-wide
switch and place_order() consults it, but a strategy picks live or sandbox when
its run starts and two runs may disagree. This module branches on the run's own
mode and calls each pipe directly. It neither reads nor writes the global
toggle, so no change to the shared service was needed.

Action Center is bypassed. place_order() routes API-key orders into the
semi-automatic approval queue when that is on. Correct for a signal arriving
from outside, wrong here: a stop-loss exit that waits for a human to approve it
is not a stop loss. Dispatch calls place_order_with_auth, the same path without
the queue, and a test asserts the queue is never consulted.

Broker authorisation is resolved per order and never cached in run state.
Indian broker tokens expire daily around 3 AM IST and a run can be open across
that boundary, so a refreshed token is picked up transparently. When
authorisation cannot be resolved the order is refused and reported rather than
attempted: leaving a position open and saying so is recoverable, silently
failing to exit is not.

Also fixes the exit-side defect from the original, which derives an exit action
from the leg's CONFIGURED side. That defaults to "B" for every leg including
short ones, so a rule-driven exit on a short placed another SELL and doubled
the position instead of covering it. Here the action comes from the side the
leg actually holds, and an unusable value raises rather than guessing.

Failures are values, not exceptions: the engine places orders in a loop across
legs, and one raising placement must not abort the others or unwind the run. A
rejection keeps any broker reference it came with, because the audit row is
more useful with it.

11 tests. Note for future readers: importing services.place_order_service as
the first import of its cycle fails with a partially initialised module
(it imports restx_api, which imports options_multiorder, which imports it
back). The app never hits this because restx_api always loads first. Dispatch
imports lazily inside the call for the same reason.

feat(strategy): add the symbol resolver and the CRUD API

Two independent pieces of the /strategy module, plus the wiring that makes the
API reachable. Still no engine: nothing here places an order.

Symbol resolver. Turns a configured leg into a concrete tradable contract:
expiry rank to a real date, ATM offset or an outright strike to a symbol, and
lot count to a quantity read from SymToken rather than assumed. It delegates
every piece of market knowledge it can to services/option_symbol_service.py,
including the rule that an MCX commodity option has no spot to measure against
and takes its nearest futures contract as the underlying instead.

Three things it refuses to guess. A lot size of zero or less is a hard failure,
never a silent 1, because a wrong quantity is a wrong order. A strike stays a
float throughout: VEDL25APR24292.5CE is a real contract and int() would round
it into a different one. The monthly expiry rank is read off the data as the
last expiry within its calendar month, not off a weekday, because NFO moved
monthlies from Thursday to Tuesday and MCX never had a weekday rule at all.
Failures are values carrying a machine-readable code, not exceptions, so the
engine can report which leg failed and why.

CRUD API. Fourteen session-authenticated routes under /strategy/api, sharing
the STRATEGY_RATE_LIMIT budget the platform already defines. The substance is
the validator: the store deliberately does no validation, so this is where a
bad payload is refused with a message that says what is wrong instead of
becoming a 500 or, worse, a silently mis-parsed leg.

Two properties worth naming. A strategy that is not yours answers 404, never
403, because 403 confirms the id exists; a mutation test that removed the
ownership filter fails seven cases. And PATCH re-validates the whole merged
configuration rather than the changed fields alone, so a two-field invariant
cannot be broken one request at a time: PATCH of an entry time later than the
stored exit time is refused. The create and update paths share the store's own
UPDATABLE_FIELDS allowlist rather than keeping a second, looser copy.

Also closes two gaps in the store that building the API exposed. The kill
switch had no audit vocabulary, so engaging or releasing it was the only state
change that left no row; webhook_locked and webhook_unlocked now exist.
list_checkpoints was the one read helper keyed on run id alone, so it would
answer for any run at all and left ownership to caller convention; it now takes
an optional strategy_id and the route passes it, making neither layer alone
load bearing.

Neither file opens an engine, session, thread, socket or subprocess, so the
resource surface of this change is nil.

497 tests across the module and the shared risk core.

feat(strategy): add the run lifecycle and tick decision engine

Four entry points: start_run, stop_run, close_leg, process_tick. The rules stay
in services/risk/ behind risk_adapter, so this module never decides whether a
stop was hit, only what to do about the answer.

Two orderings here are load bearing.

Locks are released before orders are placed. A run's lock guards in-memory
bookkeeping only; placing an order reaches the broker over the network, and a
greenlet holding a lock cannot yield, so dispatching inside the critical
section would stall the single worker for the length of an HTTP call. The tick
path evaluates under the lock, collects what it decided, releases, then
dispatches.

Entries go BUY before SELL. A spread whose short leg is placed first can be
refused for margin the account would have had once the long leg existed.

Starting is guarded by one conditional UPDATE rather than a read then a write.
The UI, the scheduler and an inbound webhook can fire at the same instant, and
a check-then-set would let two of them both see "stopped" and both place a full
set of entries. The original uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which SQLite parses
and does not honour, so that guard would have been silently absent here;
putting the condition in the UPDATE puts the check and the write in one
statement SQLite does serialise.

Resolution happens before anything is claimed. A leg that cannot be resolved
leaves no run row, no claimed strategy and no orders, which matters because
resolution is the step most likely to fail: a rolled expiry, a strike outside
the chain, a master contract that was never downloaded.

An exit uses the symbol the run actually holds, read from its own state, never
a re-resolved one. An ATM offset resolved again hours later names a different
strike, and exiting that would open a new position rather than close one.

Two things the tests found rather than confirmed. A leg is closed by its fill
arriving, not by its exit being placed, so nothing was finalising a run after
its last exit filled and a flat strategy would have sat in "running" until
somebody stopped it by hand; apply_fill now finalises a run that has gone flat,
after releasing the lock. And a rejected exit clears its own marker, so a
failed attempt is not mistaken for a duplicate and the position stranded.

Peak and trough are read out of live state and written on every stop path, not
just one. Trail-to-entry fires only on a stop-driven exit, never on a manual
close: that rule answers the market moving against the book, and an operator
closing a leg by hand is an override, not a signal.

Also adds get_strategy_unscoped to the store, named so it is obvious when it is
legitimate: the engine reaches a strategy through a run it is already
executing, where there is no user in scope to filter by.

22 engine tests, 519 across the module and the shared risk core.

feat(strategy): add the risk tick feed with websocket primary and REST fallback

Gives the engine one call, get_ltp(symbol, exchange), and hides where the price
came from. Subscriptions are refcounted per run, so two strategies holding the
same contract share one subscription and it is released when the last one lets
go.

Per symbol it runs a small state machine: WS_LIVE until no tick arrives for the
stale threshold, then POLLING over batched multi-quotes, back to WS_LIVE on the
first websocket tick, and STALE only when both sources have failed long enough
that the engine should stop trusting the price at all. A 429 backs off 2, 5, 10,
30 seconds and marks the feed degraded rather than giving up.

The threading boundary is the whole reason this module exists separately.
The producer is treated as a real OS thread: it does one frozenset membership
test and a put_nowait on a real queue from utils.real_threading, and takes no
lock. A green lock touched from a real thread raises inside the hub and wedges
that thread permanently. The set is rebuilt rather than mutated, so the producer
never reads a structure being changed under it, and a tick for a symbol nobody
holds costs exactly one dict lookup.

The consumers are green threads and never block on that real queue: they drain
with get_nowait and sleep, because a greenlet blocking on a real primitive
stalls the single worker. The state lock holds in-memory bookkeeping only; the
subscribe call, the REST fetch, the notify callback and even the transition log
lines happen after it is released.

One real defect found and fixed during the work rather than shipped: the poll
cycle broke out of the batch loop on any failure, so with a book larger than one
batch a single failing batch starved every batch behind it and those symbols
aged to STALE on a feed that was working. Now only a rate limit or a missing
API key stops the cycle; a per-batch error continues.

Two threads and one queue for the whole process, both shared singletons started
on first use and joined on stop. It borrows the shared websocket client rather
than opening a socket, unregisters its own callbacks on teardown, and never
calls unsubscribe_all, which is global to a client that /scalping and Flow also
use. Every registry has a matching removal and a cap.

Worth recording for whoever reads services/scalping_risk_monitor_service.py
next: its comment at :122 says its callbacks run on the websocket client's
asyncio loop thread. That stopped being true when the client gained its dispatch
queue, which hands callbacks to a green thread. Its real lock is still correct,
just no longer for the stated reason. Left alone here.

35 tests, each verified non-vacuous by mutation.

feat(strategy): add the lifecycle routes and make the kill switch flatten

Four routes that move money: start, stop, close_all, and closing one leg. They
sit on the engine committed in 5fceb878 and add only the things a route layer
owes: refusing what should not reach the engine, and saying so with a status
code the UI can act on.

Mode is required on start and never defaulted. A caller that forgot the field
would otherwise place real orders on a strategy the operator believed was on
paper. A start refused because something else got there first answers 409 while
a bad configuration answers 400, because the UI tells those apart.

close_all is its own route rather than an alias for stop. The effect is the
same; the audit trail is not. "The operator closed everything" reads
differently from "the run stopped" when reconstructing a session afterwards, so
it records close_all_manual before stopping.

The kill switch now flattens. Locking the webhook alone stopped new signals and
left whatever was already open still exposed, which is not a kill switch. It
locks first, so a signal arriving mid-flatten cannot re-enter behind it, then
stops any active run. If the broker is unreachable the lock still stands and
the failure is logged at error level: the position stays open, but nothing new
can be added on top of it.

The engine is imported inside each handler rather than at module scope. It
pulls in the order path, which imports restx_api, which imports back into the
order path, so making this blueprint the entry point of that cycle fails with a
partially initialised module. app.py never hits it because restx_api loads
first.

18 tests, including that every lifecycle route answers 404 rather than 403 for
a strategy that is not yours.

feat(strategy): add the webhook receiver and the scheduler

Two independent triggers for a strategy run, plus the bridge that lets the
webhook drive the engine.

Webhook. A public, unauthenticated, CSRF-exempt path that can start and stop
real trading, so it is almost entirely refusal logic: token, kill switch, IP
allowlist, payload shape and size, action, mode, the live opt-in, idempotency
and cooling off, in that order. Every outcome writes one audit row with a
result label from the store's own vocabulary, including the rejections, because
an alert that silently stopped working is exactly what that table is for.

An unknown token answers 404 from the view rather than by falling through to the
app's handler. Unauthenticated 404s feed Error404Tracker and count toward an IP
ban, so a scanner walking the token space could otherwise get the owner's own
address banned. A malformed token is refused on shape before any lookup, and is
indistinguishable from an unregistered one in body, status and timing.

The dedupe and cooling-off windows are bounded TTLCaches rather than dicts,
since the process never restarts. Dedupe collapses TradingView's retries;
cooling off is what stops a misconfigured alert oscillating start, stop, start.

The engine arms that cooling-off window on every stop, not just the ones a
webhook asked for. Without it a strategy stopped by its own risk rules, by the
scheduler or by the kill switch would accept a stale alert a second later and
re-enter the position it had just closed.

webhook_bridge exists because the two modules were built to different
signatures deliberately: the handler holds a strategy row, which is what its
token lookup produces and what every validation stage needs, while the engine
takes ids because the UI and the scheduler drive it too. One file knows both
shapes. It also decides that a webhook stop applies to the strategy's current
run, and that stopping an already-flat strategy is a success rather than an
error worth retrying.

Scheduler. APScheduler on Asia/Kolkata, avoiding four traps present in the
existing schedulers rather than copying them: the timezone is passed on every
trigger as well as the scheduler, because Flow's and Historify's cron jobs
carry none and therefore run in server-local time; job defaults are set,
because APScheduler's default misfire grace is one second and python_strategy
inherits it, so a 09:15 job that slips silently vanishes; jobs use a module
level callable with args rather than a lambda; and every job function ends in
a finally that releases scoped sessions, because a scheduler worker has no
Flask app context and teardown never fires.

It also closes a real hole in the original: there, the square-off job comes
only from scheduler.auto_stop_time, so an intraday strategy with exit_time set
and auto_stop_time blank was never squared off at all and simply held its
position past the intended exit. The exit_time now installs that job when no
auto_stop_time is given.

Neither module starts anything at import. Two existing modules do, which means
any tool that merely imports the app spins up live schedulers.

Also fixes test hygiene: the module's suites share one scoped_session, and a
sibling that deleted rows underneath it left stale objects in the identity map
that surfaced as ObjectDeletedError in files that never touched them. Each
suite now starts from a clean session.

103 webhook tests, 30 scheduler tests, 705 across the module.

feat(strategy): add crash recovery and periodic checkpointing

If the process dies, the next boot reconstructs every run that was still open
without anyone intervening. Live run state is in-process, so this is what makes
that safe.

The checkpoint writer is one shared green thread, started by an explicit
start() and never at import, writing a snapshot per live run every few seconds.
It prunes on a slow cycle, which the original never does: it writes a row per
run per interval for a whole session and removes none, which in a worker that
never restarts is unbounded growth. Recovery only ever reads the newest row, so
pruning costs nothing. The run lock is held just long enough to build the
snapshot and released before the database write.

Recovery merges two sources with a deliberate precedence, and the split is the
substance of it. Identity and disposition come from the order rows, which are
authoritative about what was actually placed and filled. Volatile risk state -
last price, effective stop and target, trail flags, the favourable extremes -
comes from the checkpoint, because no order row carries it. A leg's side is
derived from its entry order's action rather than from configuration, so a
recovered leg can never come back with a side it did not trade.

Two asymmetries matter. A dead order is never upgraded by a checkpoint: a
rejection is a fact and nothing may talk it back into a fill. A working order
may be upgraded, because the checkpoint is written from the same fill the
engine applies and the row can lag it. And a dead exit leaves the exit markers
clear so the engine's duplicate-exit guard will retry rather than treating the
leg as already on its way out.

Order status is normalised in exactly one place. The original has two functions
that disagree about submitted, trigger_pending and modified; here an
unrecognised status is treated as working, because reading an unknown exit as
dead would let a second exit be placed, and a second exit opens the opposite
position rather than closing twice.

A run that comes back holding nothing is finished rather than resumed, since no
tick would ever arrive to close it. Recovery is idempotent and will not
overwrite live state. A run that cannot be recovered is finalised as
recovery_failed so one bad run cannot wedge every future boot.

21 tests, mutation-checked: inverting the position precedence, letting a
checkpoint upgrade a rejected entry, removing the prune, and removing the
per-run guard each fail the test that covers them.

Known gap this makes visible, fixed next: nothing yet writes fills back to
sm_strategy_order, so rows sit at "open" with no fill price. That is why a
checkpoint is currently allowed to upgrade a working order at all.

feat(strategy): apply broker order updates to strategy state, event driven

Closes the gap recovery made visible: nothing was writing fills back to
sm_strategy_order, so rows sat at "open" with no fill price and the engine's
apply_fill was never called by anything. A leg cannot be evaluated without its
entry price, because that is what every stop, target and trail is measured
from.

No polling. The platform already publishes an OrderUpdateEvent on the
in-process bus for every asynchronous status change, live or sandbox, before
relaying it to the account-level websocket stream. This subscribes once and
applies what it hears, following the shape of
services/flow_order_update_monitor_service.py: one singleton, one subscription,
and a shared bounded pool rather than a thread per event, because a basket
fills leg by leg and updates arrive in bursts.

Two properties it owes the rest of the engine.

Cheap for other people's orders. Most updates on that bus belong to another
surface, and deciding so costs one indexed lookup on broker_order_id.

A fill is applied exactly once. The same fill can arrive from a broker postback
and from the order-update stream, and applying it twice would add the leg's
realized profit to the run a second time, leaving the strategy judged against a
total it never made. The order row's own status is the guard, so a fill only
lands on the transition into a terminal state. A rejection is equally final: a
late, out-of-order "complete" for the same reference cannot resurrect it into a
position the account never held.

A fill reporting no average price is recorded but deliberately not applied.
Seeding a leg from zero would give it a stop derived from nothing.

The callback itself does no work: the bus dispatches every subscriber in turn,
so anything slow inline would delay the others, and this one runs for every
order the platform places. Pool workers get no Flask app context, so each task
releases its scoped sessions in a finally (issue #1738).

12 tests. The idempotency guard is mutation-checked: removing it fails two of
them.

feat(strategy): drive risk from the tick feed and start the module at boot

Three wires that were missing, and the single entry point that turns them on.

The tick feed had no per-price hook. It kept a last price and reported source
transitions, but nothing called the engine, so no stop, target or trailing stop
would ever have fired. set_on_price now delivers every usable price, and both
the websocket and the REST fallback go through it: a leg that has fallen back
to polling has to be evaluated on polled prices too, or the fallback would keep
the price fresh on screen while protecting nothing. The hook is invoked outside
the feed's lock, because it evaluates risk and can place an order, and a
greenlet cannot yield while holding a lock.

A run did not subscribe its own instruments. start_run now asks for prices
before the entry orders go out, since a fill can be reported within
milliseconds and a leg with no price has no stop. _finalise releases them.
Subscriptions are refcounted per run, so two strategies holding the same
contract share one. A subscription failure is logged rather than raised: by
that point the run holds real positions, and refusing to start it because a
price feed is unavailable would leave them unmanaged rather than merely
unpriced.

runtime.start_strategy_module is the one call app.py makes, and the ordering in
it is the substance. Order updates subscribe first, so a fill arriving while
recovery reconciles order rows is applied rather than falling between the two.
Recovery runs before any price arrives. The risk hook is registered before any
symbol is subscribed, so there is no window where prices arrive and nothing
judges them. Checkpointing starts once there is state worth snapshotting. The
scheduler goes last, because it can start new runs and must not do that until
recovery has decided what is already running.

Every step is guarded independently. A platform that will not boot because its
strategy scheduler failed to start is worse than one that boots without it.

Nothing starts at import. Two existing modules in this codebase start
schedulers at import time, which means any tool that merely imports the app
spins up live jobs.

6 runtime tests asserting the ordering itself, 5 more on the price hook,
including that a hook calling back into the feed does not deadlock.

fix(strategy): sync cron jobs on every write, release run state unconditionally

Two findings from the fd-audit the project requires after a change touching
threads, sessions and registries.

The scheduler was only ever built at boot. Nothing called sync_strategy_jobs or
remove_strategy_jobs from the CRUD routes, so the in-memory job store reflected
the configuration as it stood at startup and nothing else. A schedule saved
today would not fire until the next restart, an edited start time would keep
firing at the old one, and a deleted strategy would leave its jobs behind. That
is the quiet kind of failure: the operator sets 09:15, the UI confirms it, and
nothing happens. The job store is in memory precisely so the database stays the
single source of truth, which only holds if every write syncs.

The sync is never allowed to fail the request. The configuration is saved
either way and the next boot re-derives every job from it, so losing the save
because a background scheduler was down would be the worse outcome.

_finalise now releases the run's state and its lock in a finally. Everything it
calls catches internally today, so this is insurance rather than a live leak,
but if any of it ever threw, the state and the lock would stay in their
registries for the life of a worker that never restarts, and the strategy would
read as running with nothing managing it.

Also fixes a test fixture that wrote a configuration the validator would
refuse. It went unnoticed because no earlier test issued a PATCH, and PATCH
re-validates the whole merged configuration rather than the changed fields.

Audit result for the rest: engines only through engine_factory, no StaticPool;
the scoped_session registered for teardown; four thread sites, all module-level
singletons behind a lifecycle lock with idempotent stops; no HTTP client,
socket, ZeroMQ context or subprocess opened directly; every cache bounded
(TTLCache or an explicit cap); and every registry with a matching removal.

fix(auth): stop a cache miss reporting itself as an expired broker session

auth_cache and feed_token_cache are TTLCaches with a maxsize, and every read
was shaped as a membership test followed by a subscript:

    if cache_key in auth_cache:
        cached_result = auth_cache[cache_key]

The entry can go between those two lines. The TTL can lapse, an LRU eviction
can drop it (two different key schemes share auth_cache, auth-{name} and
{sha256}_{bool}), or another path can delete it. A database query sits in the
middle of that window in get_auth_token_broker, which widens it considerably.

The recovery path then made it worse. Its except handler ran

    del auth_cache[cache_key]

on the entry that had just vanished, raising a second KeyError that nothing
caught. So the code written to recover from a failure was itself the failure:
the error escaped get_auth_token_broker into /quotes and /multiquotes, and the
user was told "Broker Session Expired" on a session that was perfectly valid.

In this installation's log it appears 43 times as

    auth_db: Error checking revocation status: 'bcb4ec41..._True'
    quotes:  Unexpected error in quotes endpoint: 'bcb4ec41..._True'

where the "error" being logged is the cache key itself, and the stored token
had is_revoked=0 throughout.

Six sites fixed across get_auth_token, get_feed_token and
get_auth_token_broker. Reads become one get, so there is no window between
asking and receiving; removals become pop(key, None), so removing something
already gone is not an error. Behaviour when the key is present is unchanged,
and a normal cached read still comes from the cache rather than the database.

Seven regression tests, driving the race directly with a cache that claims a
key and then does not have it, rather than waiting on a real TTL. Six of the
seven fail against the original code.

Four things about those two endpoints are worth writing down, because each
would be easy to get wrong twice:

They key on different exchanges, and both are right. /expiry wants the
derivative exchange, because NIFTY options live in NFO; /optionchain wants the
underlying's own, NSE_INDEX. One helper now holds that.

They disagree on expiry format, and the mismatch fails silently.
services/option_chain_service.py:159 builds its lookup key by slicing

being rejected, and the chain comes back empty with no error. Feeding one

is worth knowing about.

weeklies and monthlies, so rank-to-date is derived client-side from the dates
themselves rather than by position, which is why the same rule also resolves a
monthly-only futures list.

results are folded onto the base name and ordered exact, then prefix, then

feat(strategy): add signal-mode strategies

The second strategy kind. Batch enters every leg on start and exits them on
stop, which suits a multi-leg options spread. Signal mode is the other shape:
one TradingView alert moves one leg, a strategy may hold several unrelated
symbols, and quantity is raw shares rather than lots.

    {"action": "long_entry", "leg_id": 1}
    {"action": "short_exit", "symbol": "RELIANCE", "exchange": "NSE"}

Same tables and the same machinery for state, orders, risk and recovery. What
differs is the protocol, the leg shape, and the run lifecycle: a signal
strategy has one run per trading day, opened lazily by its first signal, rather
than one per start and stop.

The distinction between a no-op and a refusal is the design. An exit for a
position that is not held, an entry on a side already held, and any signal
outside the trading window are all answered 200 with a note, because an alert
engine repeats itself and answering a repeat as a failure invites a retry -
and a retry on an order path is how one alert becomes two positions. A signal
blocked by the strategy's direction or by the leg's own side is a
configuration mismatch the operator should see, so that refuses.

The side a leg is held on comes from the signal that opened it, never from
configuration. A leg's configured side says which signals it ACCEPTS, which is
not the same thing; the original conflates them and records no side at all, so
the risk core evaluated every signal leg as a short and its stop fired on a
favourable move. Four tests fail if that is reverted. For the same reason a
signal leg does not exist in run state until a signal opens it, rather than
being seeded with a placeholder side at run start.

An opposite entry squares the existing position before opening the new one.
Reversing without closing leaves both on the book.

One fix this made necessary elsewhere: a signal leg returns to "configured"
after an exit so the same symbol can be signalled again the same day, and
run_pnl keyed realized P&L on status == "closed". That dropped the leg's
realized profit out of the run total entirely, leaving every strategy-level
rule judged against a number the run never made. Realized now comes from any
leg that has it; unrealized only from open ones.

feat(strategy): route signal actions through the webhook and accept signal legs

Completes signal mode: the engine landed in ca7c0755, this is the configuration
and the routing.

The webhook router is shared between the two kinds, so which actions are valid
now depends on the strategy rather than being global. A batch strategy takes
start and stop; a signal strategy takes the four directional actions. Sending
one kind's vocabulary to the other is a configuration mistake, not a
half-understood request, so it is refused and the message names what this
strategy actually accepts.

Signal actions branch out before the batch-only stages, and skip the dedupe and
cooling-off windows deliberately. Those exist because a repeated start would
open a second position, whereas signal mode is already idempotent by meaning: a
second long_entry on a leg already long is a no-op, and an exit for a position
that is not held is a no-op. A sixty second window would do harm rather than
good here, because a genuine long, short, long sequence inside a minute is a
real thing a strategy does, and suppressing the third leaves the position
backwards.

A no-op is reported as a success with its reason in the message. Reporting it
as a failure would invite the retry that turns one alert into two positions. A
signal refused by the strategy's direction or the leg's own side is a
configuration mismatch and does report as a refusal.

A signal leg is a different shape from a batch leg rather than a superset. It
names its own symbol, exchange, side and absolute quantity, and it carries no
option fields at all, because multi-leg option spreads stay in batch mode.
Sending position, lots or any option field to a signal leg is refused rather
than accepted and ignored, which is how a strategy ends up looking like it does
something it does not. Per-leg stop, target and trail use the same helpers as a
batch leg, so both kinds are evaluated by exactly the same rules.

Quantity is raw shares with its own bound, not lots.

feat(strategy): serve the strategy books from the broker rather than stored rows

The Detail page's Orders, Trades and Positions tabs now read what the broker
actually holds, filtered to this strategy, instead of being derived from the
stored sm_strategy_order rows. Those rows record what was placed; the broker
knows what happened to it, and for money that difference is the whole point.

Each view calls the platform's own global service and filters its response, so
the envelope, field names and formatting are byte-identical to /orderbook,
/tradebook and /positions and the existing tables render them unchanged. The
statistics block is recounted over the filtered rows, because a global
statistic on a filtered list is simply wrong.

A sandbox run reads the sandbox books. Live reads the broker with
original_data=None, the internal-call form, so the platform-wide analyzer
toggle cannot divert a live run into the sandbox or a sandbox run into the real
broker. A mode outside the known set is refused rather than defaulted, and a
strategy that has never run answers an empty success without calling a broker
at all.

Positions carry a weaker guarantee than the orderbook, and the module says so
rather than pretending otherwise. A position row is per contract, so if the
same contract is also held from a manual order, another strategy or a webhook,
the row is shared and its quantity and P&L cannot be divided. A strategy's
reported P&L therefore comes from its own fills, never from these rows.

A broker refusal is passed through as 502 with the broker's own message, which
is more useful than anything this layer could invent, and one failing tab
cannot take out the page.

Three asymmetries in the existing services worth knowing: only the orderbook
carries a statistics block; the sandbox position book carries four extra
top-level totals the live one does not; and the sandbox envelopes carry a mode
field. The recount takes its key set from whatever the service returned and
reports zero rather than an account-wide value for anything it cannot derive.

No new engine, session, thread, executor, client or cache: it composes existing
services.

fix(strategy): route the public webhook, and correct the order vocabulary

Writing the API reference found three things wrong, one of them significant.

The public webhook had no Flask route at all. The whole validation pipeline
existed and was tested to 103 cases, the frontend built and displayed the URL,
and the module docstring described it, but nothing was ever registered to serve
it. Every inbound TradingView alert would have hit the app's 404 handler.

It is now POST /strategy/webhook/<token>, CSRF exempt and unauthenticated by
design, because the URL token is the credential and TradingView cannot carry a
CSRF token. Exempted in app.py beside the /chartink and /flow webhooks.

Two limits at one budget, reading the same WEBHOOK_RATE_LIMIT the other two
webhooks use. By caller address, because that is the only key that can stop
someone walking the token space: every guess carries a different token, so a
token-keyed limit would score each against an empty bucket and never fire. By
token, because that bounds what a single leaked token can do to the broker
account however many addresses replay it.

A throttled caller gets 429 as JSON rather than the app-wide redirect to the
React page. A browser reads that page; TradingView does not, and would record
the redirect as a delivered alert, so a strategy silently dropping signals would
look exactly like a healthy one.

An unknown token is answered by the view rather than by aborting. An
unauthenticated 404 feeds Error404Tracker and counts toward an IP ban, so a
scanner walking the token space could otherwise get the owner's own address
banned.

exit_signal was missing from ORDER_KINDS. Signal-mode exits are recorded with
that kind, so the published vocabulary was incomplete and a caller filtering on
it would have missed every signal-driven exit.

And a comment claiming sandbox orders carry a synthetic SANDBOX-<n> id was
simply wrong: the sandbox engine returns a date-prefixed numeric id like any
other. Corrected rather than left to mislead.

The module docstring said lifecycle and the webhook "are not routed here yet,
so nothing in this file can reach a broker". Both are now routed and it does.

help text: it is which signals a leg accepts, not the side it is held. Whichever
signal opens the leg decides that, and it lives in run state. Conflating the two
is the defect the engine already refuses.

Kind switching reshapes the legs rather than throwing them away. openbull
reseeds one fresh leg; discarding a four-leg basket's risk settings to change a
radio button is worse, and the property that actually matters, that no option

fix(strategy): refuse a leg the direction can never trade, and enforce whole lots

Two configurations that looked complete and could not work.

A leg whose side the strategy's direction can never act on is now refused. A
long_only strategy discards every short signal before it reaches a leg, so a leg
declared short never opens and nothing anywhere complains: the direction gate
refuses the signal, the leg stays flat, and the operator watches a strategy do
nothing for a reason the form never mentioned. The message names both values and
says which to change. Batch legs are unaffected, since they carry a B/S position
rather than a side and enter as a basket regardless of direction.

Quantity on a derivative leg must now be a whole number of lots. The lot size is
read from the master contract rather than assumed, matching SymToken.name first
and falling back to the normalised symbol prefix for the brokers whose master
contract puts a description in name instead. Cash exchanges have no constraint.

Checked in two places, deliberately. The form catches it while the user can
still act on it, and the engine checks again at entry, because a strategy saved
before the master contract was downloaded, or edited directly, reaches the
engine unchecked. Refusing an alert costs one alert; letting it through costs a
broker rejection on a position the operator believes is open.

A lot size that cannot be determined is not treated as a failure at either
layer. The master contract may not be downloaded yet, and refusing a
configuration for a reason the user cannot fix from that screen is worse than
letting the engine check again when the real contract is known. A None answer
means "cannot say", never "any quantity is fine", and both call sites treat it

feat(strategy): count a signal leg in lots or in units

A signal leg on a derivative is now configured the way it is actually traded:
five lots of NIFTY, not 325 units. The lot size comes from the master contract,
so the same configuration reads 325 today and whatever five lots is worth after
the next revision.

That is the real reason for the mode, not convenience. Exchanges revise lot
sizes - NIFTY moved from 75 to 65 - and a leg stored as 325 units silently
becomes five lots under one size and 4.33 under the next, which is not a
quantity any broker accepts. A leg stored as five lots is still five lots.

qty_mode is "lots" or "units", and defaults to whichever the venue implies:
lots on a derivative exchange, units on cash. An explicit value always wins, so
a caller that wants absolute units on a futures leg can say so. Lots on a cash
leg is refused rather than silently treated as units, because cash has no lot
size to multiply by.

The conversion happens in one place, resolve_quantity, which is also where the
refusals live. An unknown lot size in lots mode is an error rather than a guess:
the quantity would be fabricated, and fabricating the size of a real order is
the one thing this must not do. Units on a derivative still have to land on a
lot boundary, checked here as well as in the form, because a strategy saved
before the master contract was downloaded or edited directly arrives unchecked
and the broker would refuse rather than round.

The lot count is kept on the leg alongside the resolved quantity, so the audit
trail and the UI can show what was configured rather than only what was sent.

Both surfaces get this, since they share the validator.

Verified against the live master contract: 5 lots of NIFTY is 325 at a lot size
of 65, 2 of BANKNIFTY is 60 at 30, 3 of SENSEX is 60 at 20.

feat(strategy): add the lots and units toggle, and stop the drain loop idling hot

Two unrelated pieces that happened to land together.

The wizard can now count a signal leg in lots. A Lots / Units toggle sits with
the quantity label, defaulting to what the venue implies, and the resolved

resolve a strike, and a signal leg is only ever cash or futures, so all three
would have had to be invented to read one number back. No new endpoint, no
master-contract query from the browser.

The toggle keys off the leg's own exchange rather than its segment or its tab,
because that is what the validator checks. Typing a cash exchange onto a leg
already in lots moves it to units rather than leaving it in a state that cannot
be saved.

Switching mode keeps the number and reinterprets it rather than converting it.
Rewriting 5 into 325 silently edits something the user typed, and it only works
in one direction: 325 converts back to 5 lots only when the lot size is known
and divides exactly, so a converting toggle would sometimes convert and
sometimes not. A number that is wrong in the new mode now fails visibly instead
of quietly becoming a different trade, and the round trip is asserted as an
exact equality.

Separately, the tick feed's drain loop no longer wakes two hundred times a
second on an idle worker. Its threads are process-lifetime singletons that are
never stopped when the last run ends, so a worker that had run one strategy in
the morning was still polling an empty queue at midnight. The idle wait now
depends on whether anything could arrive at all rather than on how recently
something did: while any symbol is subscribed it stays at the short interval,
because this is the risk path and a tick waited on is a stop evaluated late;
with nothing subscribed no tick can arrive by definition, so it waits far
longer. No latency is added to any path that can carry a tick.

fix(strategy): make a signal run mean one trading session, not one round trip

Two bugs that only appear after hours, which is exactly where this module has
to hold up.

A signal run was reused for any run that was not stopped, with no check on when
it started. The docstring promised one run per trading day and the code
delivered one run until somebody stopped it, so a strategy whose square-off did
not fire kept accumulating into the first day's run: its P&L, peak, trough and
audit trail merged every following session into one, and a strategy left alone
over a long weekend reported a single run spanning four days.

The boundary is the platform's own session reset, SESSION_EXPIRY_TIME, not
midnight. OpenAlgo revokes broker tokens at 03:00 IST because that is when
Indian broker tokens expire, so a session runs until then: Monday 22:00 and
Tuesday 01:00 are the same session, and Tuesday 03:01 is the next one. Rolling
at midnight would have split a session in half and merged across the real
boundary, which is precisely backwards. Timestamps are stored naive UTC and are
converted to IST before the session is worked out, since comparing a UTC date
against an IST one moves the boundary five and a half hours.

A run from an earlier session is only rolled when nothing is held. An open leg
is a live position, and finalising the run that owns it would leave it with no
run managing it, which is far worse than a merged P&L figure.

The second bug came out of testing the first. apply_fill finalised any run that
went flat. That is right for a batch basket, entered and exited as a unit, and
wrong for a signal run: a leg exiting is an ordinary mid-session event and the
next alert reopens it, so five round trips in a day produced five runs. Only
batch runs now end on going flat.

7 tests, including that Monday 22:00 and Tuesday 01:00 share a session, that a
run still holding a position is never rolled, and that a batch run does still
end when it goes flat.

fix(strategy): record when risk fires with no broker session to act on it

OpenAlgo revokes broker tokens at the session reset, 03:00 IST by default,
because Indian broker tokens expire daily. Until the user logs in again there
is nothing to place an order with, and a positional strategy is still holding.

A stop reached in that window was refused, which is correct: pretending to exit
would be far worse. But the only record was a log line, so the operator saw a
position sitting past its stop with no explanation anywhere they would look.

It now writes a critical row to the audit trail, so it reaches the Events tab
and can drive a banner. Recorded once per run per episode rather than once per
tick, because the tick that fires a stop is followed by every tick after it and
a row each would make the trail unreadable exactly when it is needed most. When
the session returns, that is recorded too, so the trail reads as an episode
with a beginning and an end rather than a single alarming line.

Only risk that actually fired is worth a critical row. A tokenless window on a
strategy with nothing to do is not an incident and records nothing.

The marker set is bounded by the number of concurrent runs and is cleared when
authorisation returns or the run ends, in the same finally that releases the
run's state.

Verified already sound while looking at this: the tick feed re-subscribes after
a websocket reconnect (the client re-authenticates but does not restore
subscriptions, so the feed does), and its cached API key is dropped on a 403 so
the daily token rollover is picked up without a restart. Exits resolve broker
authorisation fresh on every call rather than caching it in run state, so a
token refreshed mid-session is used immediately.

The duplicate-exit guard was claimed with exit_kind under the state lock

fix(strategy): harden the webhook path

Five findings from the security review of the public webhook.

The token was written verbatim into logs.db by the traffic logger, which
keeps 30 days and is readable at /traffic, so anyone who could read the
log could replay the webhook and place orders. The path segment carrying
a credential is now masked for /strategy, /flow and /chartink alike; a
/flow symbol suffix is kept, since that is what makes the log worth
reading.

The caller was identified by request.remote_addr, which behind a reverse
proxy is the proxy: every caller looked like one address, so the IP
allowlist was either useless or blocked everything and the audit trail
named the proxy. get_real_ip now, as the rest of the app uses.

The body was read in full before anything checked its size or the token,
so an unauthenticated caller decided how much the worker read. An
oversized Content-Length is refused with 413 before the read.

The rate limiter was keyed on the raw token. Its in-memory storage
empties the event list for an expired window but never removes the key,
so that was a second copy of the credential in process memory for the
life of the worker, one per token ever presented including every guess.
Keyed on the digest now: same bucket, not replayable.

An audit row for an unrecognised token names no strategy, so nothing
showed it and nothing deleted it: anyone who could reach the URL could
grow the database without limit, invisibly. The rows are worth keeping,
a run of them being the first sign of somebody walking the token space,
so they are capped at the newest 1000 rather than dropped, pruned every
hundredth so the check is not itself the cost of the flood.

fix(strategy): a fill that beats its own order row is no longer dropped

Found on a live sandbox run: both legs of a running strategy sat at
entry_avg 0.0 with the sandbox reporting both orders complete, at 97.2
and 70. No leg_entry_filled event was ever written.

_place_entries dispatches and only then records the order row, and the
sandbox executes a MARKET order synchronously inside the dispatch call.

that broker id yet, _apply_update reads it as another surface's order,
and it is dropped for good. In sandbox this is not a race that sometimes
happens: it happens every time. A live broker whose fill beats the
insert lands in the same place.

The consequence is worse than a missing number. stop_from_points refuses
a non-positive entry, so a leg with entry_avg 0.0 has no stop, no target
and no mark to market, while the page shows it open and the strategy
reports itself running. The risk engine manages nothing.

An update that matches no row is now held in a small bounded TTL cache
and replayed the moment its row is written, which the engine and the
signal path both do straight after recording an order. The replay runs
after the leg's own bookkeeping, never before it, or the entry_status

Fix Fyers HSM WebSocket authentication timeout (#1950)

* Fix Fyers HSM WebSocket authentication timeout

The market-data feed stopped authenticating: the socket connected, the
binary auth frame was sent, and nothing came back until the 15s timeout
fired with "Failed to authenticate with Fyers HSM WebSocket (timeout)".

Cause: Fyers' gateway now silently drops any HSM handshake that carries an
Authorization header. The WebSocket upgrade still succeeds and on_open
fires normally, but the auth frame is never answered - no error frame, no
close frame, no close code - so the failure reads like a bad token.

The HSM feed authenticates purely in-band, via the request-type-1 frame
carrying the JWT's hsm_key, and needs no handshake header at all. Verified
against the live endpoint: a bare JWT, an "<appId>:<token>" pair and even
"Authorization: x" all produce silence, while no header - or any other
header, including User-Agent and an arbitrary X-Custom - returns the
type-1 response. The header's value is irrelevant; its presence alone is
disqualifying. The official fyers-apiv3 SDK passes no headers here either.

The endpoint and frame layout are unchanged: wss://socket.fyers.in/hsm/v1-5/prod
is still the only live version (v1-4 and v1-6..v2-0 all 404), and the auth
frame is byte-for-byte identical between fyers-apiv3 3.1.7 and 3.1.16.

Also verify the auth verdict properly. A type-1 frame only means "this is
an auth response"; the outcome is the status string at offset 7, which is
"K" when accepted. Treating any type-1 frame as success would report a
rejected token as a healthy connection that never delivers a tick.

Note the <appId>:<token> Authorization header is still required by the
order socket and the TBT socket - this applies to the HSM socket only.

Verified live end-to-end: connect() returns True and LTP callbacks stream
for NSE equities.

* Fix Fyers order-update WebSocket delivering no order events

The order socket connected, authenticated and subscribed cleanly, but the
Order Stream showed zero orders no matter what was placed. Every update was
being received and then silently discarded.

Three problems, the first of which alone accounts for the symptom:

1. The "orders" envelope was never unwrapped. Fyers sends
   {"orders": {...}, "s": "ok"}, but normalize() looked for the record flat
   or under "d"/"data" - never "orders" - so every update fell through to
   `return None`.

2. The field names were the SDK's, not the wire's. The code read status,
   side, type, filledQty, limitPrice and productType; the raw socket sends
   org_ord_status, tran_side, ord_type, qty_filled, price_limit and
   product_type. Those camelCase names exist only after the official SDK
   applies its order_mapper, and we connect raw. This would have kept the
   record empty even after fixing (1), and since the old guard required a
   "status" key it would have been dropped a second time. Both shapes are
   now accepted, since only the mapped shape appears in the docs'
   response-attribute tables.

3. The subscribe key was wrong: "action_data" instead of "SLIST". The docs'
   prose names the value "action_data", but that is only the variable name
   in their Python sample.

Note for anyone testing this: Fyers acks *any* subscribe payload with
{"code":1605,"message":"Successfully subscribed"}, including one carrying
the wrong key - verified by probing the wrong key, the right key and a
three-action list. The ack cannot be used to confirm the handshake, so it
is called out in the module docstring.

Status is read from org_ord_status, which carries the documented 1-7 codes.
The raw frame also has a separate, differently-coded ord_status field (55
for Pending Cancel, 91 for cancelled), which is accepted only as a last
resort so an unexpected shape is surfaced rather than dropped; an unmapped
code now logs the record's field names instead of vanishing.

Verified against a live cancel on NSE:YESBANK-EQ: the subscribe ack is
ignored, org_ord_status 6 normalizes to "open" and 1 to "cancelled", with
symbol, exchange, side, LIMIT price and product all correct, and no
unmapped-status warnings.

feat(strategy): measure per-leg stop, target and trail in points or percent

Each leg gains risk_unit, either points or percent, governing sl_pts,
target_pts and both halves of trail together. Points is the default, so
every strategy written before this behaves exactly as it did and nothing
stored has to change: legs are JSON, so there is no migration.

One toggle for all three on purpose. A leg whose stop is a percentage of
entry and whose target is an absolute distance is far more likely to be
a mistake than an intention.

The conversion lives in risk_adapter and nowhere else. services/risk/
speaks points from entry and learns nothing about units, because a
second unit inside the core would mean two ways to express one stop and
two places to get it wrong. That is the rule the module already follows
everywhere else: consumers translate, they do not decide.

A percentage is measured against the leg's own entry, so 2 percent on a
short filled at 2500 stops at 2550 and a 4 percent target is 2400.
Percentages are capped at 100 in the validator, since 150 percent of
entry below a long's entry is a negative price rather than a wider stop.
A percent leg with no confirmed fill gets no levels at all: a percentage
of zero is not a stop at the entry price, it is one that cannot be
computed yet, and deriving it would put the stop on the entry and fire
it on the first tick.

The unit is visible wherever the numbers are. The Risk tab gains a
"Measured in" column and renders every figure with its unit attached, so
"2" is never ambiguous between two points and two percent of a 2500
entry, and the wizard carries a Points / % of entry toggle on both leg
editors with the input labels and the percent ceiling following it.

The field names keep saying pts on the wire and in the database. They
read wrongly for a percent leg and are kept anyway: renaming them would
break every stored strategy and every existing caller for a cosmetic
gain, and the unit is shown beside the number in every place an operator
reads it.

Six tests cover the arithmetic on both sides of the book, the trail, the
untouched legacy leg, and the unfilled percent leg. Two BDD source
anchors were corrected: they are line numbers, and this change moved the
lines they pointed at.

fix(trading): index rows were live all along, the consumer discarded the ticks

Reported as "websockets work for stocks but not for indices" in the watchlist.
The subscription was never the problem.

An index is quoted on its own pseudo-exchange, NSE_INDEX or BSE_INDEX, but it
has no session of its own: NIFTY opens and closes exactly when NSE does. The
timings table stores real exchanges only. Confirmed against the running
instance, /admin/api/timings returns

  BCD, BFO, BSE, CDS, CRYPTO, MCX, NCO, NFO, NSE

with no index entry, so the lookup in isMarketOpen found nothing and took its
conservative "no timing, assume closed" branch, every minute of every day.

That matters because useLivePrice gates a tick on the market being open:

  const hasWsData = exchangeMarketOpen && wsData?.data?.ltp && ...

while the subscription itself is ungated. So indices were subscribed, their
ticks arrived, and the consumer threw every one away and fell back to the REST
multiquotes snapshot. A stock beside them updated live because NSE has a row.

Both lookups, plus getMarketStatus, now resolve the calendar exchange first by
stripping the _INDEX suffix. That is the real relationship rather than a
special case: the index follows its parent exchange's calendar by definition,
holidays and special sessions included.

Not verified end to end in a browser: the running instance serves its own
prebuilt dist and does not see this tree. What is verified is the mechanism in
code and the timings payload above, taken from that instance.

fix(trading): backfill bars the tick stream never built, and do it on reconnect

A hole appeared near the right edge of the chart, with the newest candles
detached from the run, and a reload always fixed it. The reconcile that should
have covered this only ever snapped bars the chart already had:

  for (let i = 0; i < this.rawBars.length; i++) {
    const f = byTime.get(this.rawBars[i].time)
    if (f && ...) this.rawBars[i] = f
  }

It iterates rawBars, so a bucket the client never built is not in the loop at
all. The REST response holds it, and nothing inserts it. That is why only a
reload closed the gap: a fresh load takes the whole series from history.

A bucket goes missing whenever the tick stream is not running for a full
interval. The socket drops, the machine sleeps, or the tab is hidden and the
feed pauses. The candles either side are correct, so the chart shows a clean
hole and the OHLC legend disagrees with the broker for those buckets.

The reconcile now inserts them: any bar in the fetched window that rawBars lacks
and that closed before the live bucket. Merged and re-sorted rather than spliced
at an index, because a history page landing during the await would invalidate
any index computed before it.

Only closed buckets are filled. The forming bar stays with the tick stream,
which is fresher than a poll and must not be dragged backwards to it. That rule
was already there for the snap pass and it applies unchanged here.

It also runs immediately when the socket reports open, instead of waiting out
the rest of the 25 to 35 second cycle staring at the hole. The periodic pass is
deliberately slow and jittered, which is right for steady state and wrong for
the moment a gap appears, so the body is split into runReconcile() and both
paths share it.

The window is unchanged: min(3, lookbackDays(interval)) calendar days, so about
225 bars on a 5m chart and 1125 on a 1m one.

Known and deliberately not addressed here: the snap pass rewrites every closed
bar in that window on every cycle with no equality check, then triggers a full
setPriceData whether or not a number moved. Comparing first would make it a
no-op almost always. That is an optimisation and this is a correctness fix, so
it belongs in its own commit.

fix(kotak): use ranged GET instead of HEAD for scripmaster fallback accessibility check (#1730)

* fix(kotak): use ranged GET instead of HEAD for scripmaster fallback accessibility check

HEAD requests to Kotak's CDN (lapi.kotaksecurities.com) reliably hit an
infinite redirect loop ("Exceeded maximum allowed redirects"), even though
the identical URL returns 200 immediately via GET. Since every fallback
URL failed its accessibility check, accessible_urls stayed empty and
download_csv_kotak_data() raised "Scripmaster API failed" unconditionally
-- even when the CSV data was fully downloadable the whole time.

Verified as not account-specific: reproduced identically from two
unrelated networks/IPs with a valid, active Kotak session on both.

Swap to a ranged GET (bytes=0-0) -- avoids the redirect loop, and is
intended to avoid a full duplicate download of each multi-MB file (once
for the check, once in the real download), though Kotak's CDN currently
ignores the Range header and returns the full body anyway, so today this
is a correctness fix only, not a bandwidth win. Accept both 200 and 206.

Verified end-to-end after the fix: full master contract download
succeeds, 153,899 records loaded across NSE Cash/F&O, BSE Cash/F&O, CDS,
and MCX.

Fixes #1729

  ratchets the local cap down instead of retrying at a rate the account was

* fix(flattrade): act on rate-limit rejections, restore partial-fill updates

Follow-up to 47ec47cc6, addressing review findings. Each was reproduced against
the code before fixing.

Partial fills were invisible on the polling path (regression from 47ec47cc6).
PollingOrderUpdateAdapter detects a change by diffing (order_status,
filled_quantity) per orderid, but Flattrade's transform_order_data never emitted
filled_quantity, so every poll read 0 and a partial fill that left the order
OPEN published no event at all - the fill stayed invisible until the order
reached a terminal state. Moving Flattrade to REST polling therefore lost fill
visibility the WebSocket t="om" feed used to provide. The OrderBook response
does carry it (03-orders.md: "fillshares" = total traded quantity, "avgprc" =
average traded price), so the mapping now emits filled_quantity,
pending_quantity and average_price, coerced totally because Noren sends them as
strings and omits them on an order that has never traded.

Pacing without clamping was half a fix. order_api.py imported
is_rate_limit_error and note_rate_limit_rejection and called neither: it
reserved a slot and then ignored what the broker said, so an account below the
configured cap kept re-offering the rejected rate and every later poll failed
the same way. funds.py and margin_api.py had the same gap, and a rejected funds
call surfaced to the dashboard as empty funds and zero PnL. All four paths now
run responses through clamp_from_response.

Read endpoints clamp and retry with backoff. Order endpoints clamp but
deliberately do NOT retry: this code cannot distinguish "rejected for rate" from
"accepted, response lost", and a duplicate order is far worse than a failed one.

Environment overrides are bounded by the published table (40/200 non-order,
10/40 order). The override exists so a higher-tier account is not pinned to the
conservative default, but nothing legitimate sits above the published figures,
and a stray zero on "38" would silently disable the pacing this module exists
to provide.

Close-frame handling had two holes. A close whose reason names an auth failure
("Invalid Session", 403) returned before _is_fatal_auth_error ran, leaving the
adapter on the generic reconnect loop retrying a token that will never work
instead of its bounded token-refresh path. And branching on the decoded status
code meant a bodiless close - which RFC 6455 permits - fell through to the error
path instead of being reported as a close; _is_close_frame now decides that, so
the status code being unknown no longer changes the routing.

Also fixes a test that asserted on the module-level limiter singletons. Those
bind at import from FLATTRADE_MAX_PER_SECOND / FLATTRADE_MAX_PER_MINUTE, which
this same change tells higher-tier accounts to set - so the test failed on a
correctly-configured machine even though the defaults were right. It now clears
the environment and checks _env_int, with a separate environment-independent
invariant that the live caps never exceed the published ceiling.

* test(flattrade): assert no sleep instead of timing the batch loop

The multiquote-batching guard asserted `elapsed < 0.5` against the wall clock.
That is flaky under CI load, and it fails open in the other direction too: any
sleep short enough to fit under the threshold would pass, so the guard was
weakest against exactly the regression it exists to catch.

no dependence on machine speed, scheduler jitter, BATCH_SIZE, or how many
symbols the test happens to use - and it catches a reintroduced sleep of any
duration, reporting the total and the call count in the failure message.

chunk-count alone: every symbol dispatched exactly once, and no chunk larger
than BATCH_SIZE. A second test covers the <= BATCH_SIZE branch, which returns
before the loop and was previously unexercised.

fails the guard with `assert [1.1, 1.1, 1.1, 1.1] == []`. 87 tests (was 86).

fix(intervals): only advertise intervals the history API will accept

A chart set to 60m failed every history request with a 400 and showed no
symbol and no bars.

Two endpoints disagreed. /api/v1/history validates the interval against a
fixed list. /api/v1/intervals advertised whatever keys the broker's own
timeframe map happened to hold, and a broker map often carries an alias
for a resolution it already has: Zerodha maps both 60m and 1h to Kite's
60minute, 1h having been added later for flux scan and 60m left behind. So
intervals offered 60m, the chart put it in the timeframe dropdown,
pickInterval accepted it as broker-supported, and history rejected it.

The failure outlives the mistake, which is what made it look like a broken
install rather than a bad setting: the choice is remembered, so every
reload asked for the same rejected interval and failed the same way, with
no symbol on screen to change and no obvious way back.

Fixed as a class rather than as the one alias. SUPPORTED_INTERVALS moves
to utils/constants.py, the history schema validates against it instead of
an inline literal, and the intervals service offers only the broker keys
that appear in it, debug-logging whatever it withheld. Any broker carrying
a legacy alias is covered, not just this one.

The alias still works as input to the broker module; it is simply never
advertised. Checked against d:/demo/broker-api-docs/zerodha-api-docs:
the map reaches all eight documented Kite resolutions, so nothing is
missing from it. 60m was an extra, not a gap.

The constant lives in utils/constants.py rather than beside either
endpoint because both import it and neither should import the other: the
service layer reaching into restx_api pulls the whole API package, and its
database engine, in at import time.

PiConnect permits one WebSocket session per {uid, accesstoken}. The dedicated
order-update socket authenticated with the same credentials as the market-data
adapter, so the broker evicted the older connection with a clean close (opcode
8, payload \x03\xe8 = RFC 6455 code 1000, "normal closure"). Each adapter owns
an independent reconnect loop, so they evicted each other indefinitely.

Verified live 2026-09-01: 13 of 13 market-data closes landed 100-190ms after
the order adapter logged its Noren connect, producing 19 order-socket connects
and 26 market-data reconnects in 5m56s, with the depth book resubscribed 12
times. After the fix the same workload showed 0 evictions and 2 reconnects,
both from an ordinary TCP reset rather than a close frame.

create_flattrade_order_adapter() now returns a PollingOrderUpdateAdapter, the
same resolution 5Paisa already uses for an identical single-session
constraint. The decision lives in the broker plugin so the shared registry in
services/order_update_service.py is untouched. Order updates arrive on the
ORDER_POLL_INTERVAL cycle instead of instantly; FLATTRADE_ORDER_WS=TRUE
restores the dedicated socket for whoever implements real multiplexing (send
t="o" on the market-data socket and relay t="om" across the process boundary).

Also in this change:

- Decode peer-initiated close frames. websocket-client routes a server close
  through on_error as a raw ABNF and then calls on_close with (None, None), so
  an orderly hangup was logged as "WebSocket error: fin=1 opcode=8" with the
  status code discarded. The code is now recovered, reported as a close rather
  than a fault, and stashed for on_close so teardown still runs exactly once.

- Share request pacing across every Flattrade HTTP entry point. Only data.py
  was paced; order_api.py, funds.py and margin_api.py issued unpaced calls
  against the same account, and close_all_positions/cancel_all_orders_api
  looped order calls with no pacing at all. The limiter moves to
  broker/flattrade/api/rate_limit.py with a separate, tighter budget for order
  endpoints.

- Learn the account's real ceiling. Flattrade names it in the rejection
  ("... exceeds Limit N for user"); note_rate_limit_rejection() parses that and
  ratchets the local cap down instead of retrying at a rate the account was
  never provisioned for.

- Default to observed enforcement, not the published table. The docs list
  40/sec and 200/min for non-order endpoints, but a live account was rejected
  at 10/sec and 120/min - the figures TradeSmart publishes for the same Noren
  backend. Starting at the published cap meant discovering the truth by being
  rejected, once per process restart (observed twice in one morning). Defaults
  are now 9/110 with margin; FLATTRADE_MAX_PER_SECOND / FLATTRADE_MAX_PER_MINUTE
  raise them for higher-tier accounts, and the clamp still protects a raised cap.

- Drop the fixed 1.1s inter-batch sleep in get_multiquotes. It was
  per-invocation so it could not see concurrent option-chain fetches (three
  42-symbol fetches started at 11:16:41, :44 and :49 before any finished),
  while the limiter's rolling window bounds them together. Definedge already
  reaches the same conclusion in its own multiquote path.

- Fix two protocol mismatches against broker-api-docs/flattrade-api-docs: the
  heartbeat acknowledgement is t="hk", not t="h" (every ack was falling through
  to the market-data tick parser), and the connect ack's "s" was compared
  case-sensitively against "OK" while the docs spell it "Ok".

- Route the sync quote fetcher through the pooled httpx client instead of a
  bare httpx.post, per CLAUDE.md FD hygiene - it runs once per symbol under a
  ThreadPoolExecutor.

* fix(flattrade): act on rate-limit rejections, restore partial-fill updates

Follow-up to 47ec47cc6, addressing review findings. Each was reproduced against
the code before fixing.

Partial fills were invisible on the polling path (regression from 47ec47cc6).
PollingOrderUpdateAdapter detects a change by diffing (order_status,
filled_quantity) per orderid, but Flattrade's transform_order_data never emitted
filled_quantity, so every poll read 0 and a partial fill that left the order
OPEN published no event at all - the fill stayed invisible until the order
reached a terminal state. Moving Flattrade to REST polling therefore lost fill
visibility the WebSocket t="om" feed used to provide. The OrderBook response
does carry it (03-orders.md: "fillshares" = total traded quantity, "avgprc" =
average traded price), so the mapping now emits filled_quantity,
pending_quantity and average_price, coerced totally because Noren sends them as
strings and omits them on an order that has never traded.

Pacing without clamping was half a fix. order_api.py imported
is_rate_limit_error and note_rate_limit_rejection and called neither: it
reserved a slot and then ignored what the broker said, so an account below the
configured cap kept re-offering the rejected rate and every later poll failed
the same way. funds.py and margin_api.py had the same gap, and a rejected funds
call surfaced to the dashboard as empty funds and zero PnL. All four paths now
run responses through clamp_from_response.

Read endpoints clamp and retry with backoff. Order endpoints clamp but
deliberately do NOT retry: this code cannot distinguish "rejected for rate" from
"accepted, response lost", and a duplicate order is far worse than a failed one.

Environment overrides are bounded by the published table (40/200 non-order,
10/40 order). The override exists so a higher-tier account is not pinned to the
conservative default, but nothing legitimate sits above the published figures,
and a stray zero on "38" would silently disable the pacing this module exists
to provide.

Close-frame handling had two holes. A close whose reason names an auth failure
("Invalid Session", 403) returned before _is_fatal_auth_error ran, leaving the
adapter on the generic reconnect loop retrying a token that will never work
instead of its bounded token-refresh path. And branching on the decoded status
code meant a bodiless close - which RFC 6455 permits - fell through to the error
path instead of being reported as a close; _is_close_frame now decides that, so
the status code being unknown no longer changes the routing.

Also fixes a test that asserted on the module-level limiter singletons. Those
bind at import from FLATTRADE_MAX_PER_SECOND / FLATTRADE_MAX_PER_MINUTE, which
this same change tells higher-tier accounts to set - so the test failed on a
correctly-configured machine even though the defaults were right. It now clears
the environment and checks _env_int, with a separate environment-independent
invariant that the live caps never exceed the published ceiling.

* fix(mstock): correct order handling and batch WebSocket subscribes

Audited the integration against the official Type B docs (converted to
markdown in the broker-api-docs repo) and fixed what diverged.

Orders:

- SL orders sent ordertype STOP_LOSS, which mStock does not accept. The
  docs contradict themselves: the Orders glossary lists STOPLOSS_LIMIT /
  STOPLOSS_MARKET while the place- and modify-order field tables list
  STOP_LOSS / STOP_LOSS_MARKET, and the code took one value from each.
  The glossary values match the Angel-style convention this API derives
  from, and OpenAlgo's own Angel adapter uses them, so SL now sends
  STOPLOSS_LIMIT. The reverse direction becomes a named mapper that
  accepts every spelling mStock returns, including the bare "SL" its
  order book echoes.

- A rejected order was reported as a success with a null orderid. mStock
  returns HTTP 200 for business failures (RMS rejection, market closed,
  insufficient funds are all documented as "Failure (HTTP Status 200)")
  and the caller keys off the HTTP status alone. place_order_api now
  reads the payload's status field and surfaces a non-200 so the caller
  takes its error path and shows the broker's own message. cancel_order
  and modify_order had the same shape and are fixed alongside.

- place_smartorder_api referenced an undefined AUTH_TOKEN after the
  order was already placed, so every smart order raised NameError once
  the order had reached the broker and left the position cache stale.

- Order-book logging moved from debug to info for live diagnosis.

Market data:

- Historical chunking issued back-to-back requests against a documented
  1 req/sec Data API limit; it now paces like the batch-quote path.

Streaming:

- A header-prefixed binary frame can carry several packets, but only the
  first was parsed and the rest were silently dropped. parse_binary_message
  splits the frame and tolerates an implausible header.

- Subscribes are coalesced (issue #1352 pattern, as angel/zerodha): a
  500ms window drains into one frame per mode instead of one frame per
  symbol, and the mode-upgrade settle pause is paid once per flush rather
  than once per symbol. mStock's tokenList accepts many tokens per
  exchangeType, so a whole batch fits in one message.

- MCX's exchangeType is not documented by mStock and the mapping was an
  admitted guess; it now warns on use, as does the fallback that quietly
  returned NSE for any unmapped exchange.

order-type mapping both ways, the documented success and HTTP-200
rejection payloads, multi-packet frame splitting, subscribe coalescing,
and exchange mapping. Ruff clean.

* fix(mstock): close the one-off quote socket on every exit path

fetch_quote opens a dedicated WebSocket per call and backs the depth API
(services/depth_service -> BrokerData.get_depth). It closed the socket
only after the success and no-quote returns, both trailing close()
statements, so any exception in between - a send hitting a connection
reset, broken pipe or timeout - jumped to the handler and returned with
the descriptor still open.

Measured before the fix by replacing create_connection with a fake that
records closure: 100 calls down the send-failure path left 100 sockets
open, growing strictly 1:1 (10 -> 10, 200 -> 200), so a leak rather than
a cache filling. Nothing bounds it. Production is a single Gunicorn
worker that never restarts, and the call runs per depth request, so a
broker-side disconnect leaked one descriptor per request until the
process hit "too many open files" - which takes down every socket and DB
connection in the worker, not just mStock. mStock's documented BOD
(07:00-08:30) and EOD (19:00-21:00) windows are when mid-call
disconnects cluster.

The close now runs in a finally, and is itself guarded: closing an
already-broken socket can raise, and an exception in a finally would
replace the value the caller is about to receive.

Also re-check self.running after the reconnect backoff before
reassigning self.ws. The backoff sleep is not interruptible, so a
disconnect_stream() landing during it left the dying thread to overwrite
self.ws on wake; had a connect_stream() followed, that clobbered the
live client's WebSocketApp and orphaned its socket beyond the reach of
the next disconnect_stream().

Verified after the fix: 0 sockets left open across all three fetch_quote
paths at 100 calls each, and flat thread and socket counts over 30
connect/disconnect cycles, 30 subscribe bursts, 30 disconnects with an
armed batch timer, and the reconnect loop. Separately confirmed that
