* fix(strategy-book): commit the startup prune even when it deletes nothing

A DELETE takes SQLite's write transaction the moment it runs, whether or not
it matches a row. Both prunes in the strategy book committed only when the row
count was truthy, so the ordinary case, a prune with nothing old enough to
remove, left that transaction open on the calling thread's session.

They run from `init_strategy_book_db()` during application startup, which has
no Flask app context, so the `teardown_appcontext` handler that would have
released the session never fires. The write lock on openalgo.db was therefore
held for the life of the process. Every other writer backed off for its full
15 second budget and failed with "database is locked": the strategy module's
recovery among them, which is why a run that had already finished stayed open
across every restart, its strategy stuck reading "running" and refusing to
start, edit or delete. Session last_seen updates failed the same way.

Measured on a real instance: the write lock was held 15.5 seconds and counting
from the first statement, `DELETE FROM strategy_order_tags WHERE created_at <
?`, against a table holding one row that was not old enough to prune. After the
fix the same startup reports no lock error at all and recovery finalises the
stranded run on its own.

Committed unconditionally now, and logged conditionally, which is the shape the
two equivalent prunes already use: `strategy_module_db._prune_webhook_events`
and `traffic_db`. The tag prune also removes its session in a `finally`,
because startup owns no app context and nothing else will.

The first two tests assert the defect itself, so the file cannot pass
vacuously: with the fix reverted they fail, and take 32 seconds doing it
because they wait out the lock they are describing.

  anything. This is what the public reference already says

  signals._day_run, which calls store.create_run directly and never this path.

  exists. `dispatch_attempted` is written immediately before each dispatch

fix(python-strategy): stop waiting for a dying process under the global lock (#1979)

* fix(python-strategy): stop waiting for a dying process under the global lock

Stopping a strategy froze the whole app. `stop_strategy_process` held
PROCESS_LOCK across `process.wait(timeout=5)`, and that one line carried two
separate faults.

`Popen.wait(timeout=...)` blocks inside C, `waitpid` on Linux and
`WaitForSingleObject` on Windows. Neither is a yield point, so under
gunicorn-eventlet, where one OS thread runs every greenlet, the call stops the
entire worker for the length of the timeout rather than just the caller. Moving
the wait out of the lock, which is what the report proposed, would not have
fixed this half: the hub is frozen by the C call itself. The psutil branch of
the same function had already been fixed this way and carries a comment saying
so; the subprocess.Popen branch beside it was still calling wait() directly.

The lock is process-wide and every start, stop, restart and status read takes
it, so holding it for the death of a subprocess serialised all of them behind
a wait that lasts as long as the strategy takes to notice its signal.

`wait_for_popen_exit` polls `poll()` against a deadline, mirroring the existing
`wait_for_psutil_process_exit`, and `terminate_popen_safely` escalates exactly
as the inline code did, graceful signal first and a forced kill only if the
process outlives it. The lock is now held to claim the strategy and, afterwards,
to write the bookkeeping back, with the wait in between outside it.

Claiming pops the entry, so a second stop arriving mid-wait is told the strategy
is not running instead of signalling the same PID again. A failed termination
puts the entry back: the process is still alive and something has to still be
tracking it, or it is left running with nothing able to stop it.

Two of the tests assert the defects themselves and fail on the previous code,
one on `Popen.wait` being reached at all and one on the lock being held for the
whole termination, so the file cannot pass vacuously.

Reported as issue #1737.

fix(mstock): recover dropped subscribes, stand down on dead tokens (#1983)

* fix(mstock): address review findings on the batching and order changes

Four issues raised in review of #1974, each verified against the code and
the Type B docs before fixing.

Subscribe coalescing dropped unsubscribes. unsubscribe() cleared local
state but never touched subscription_queue, so a subscribe followed by an
unsubscribe inside the 500ms window still sent the subscribe at the flush:
mStock then streamed a token the adapter no longer tracked, and every tick
took the "data for unsubscribed token" path. unsubscribe() now prunes
pending entries for a token once its last subscription goes, and the flush
revalidates the drained batch against live subscriptions to catch an
unsubscribe landing between the drain and the send.

Header-prefixed LTP and Quote frames were discarded. parse_binary_message
treated "shorter than 383" as "bare packet", but a header-prefixed LTP
frame is 4 + 51 = 55 bytes and a Quote frame 4 + 123 = 127, both below
that threshold, so the whole frame was dropped. It now branches on the
exact bare sizes (51/123/379) and parses the header for everything else.
Two call-site guards in _on_ws_message and fetch_quote tested the same
size set and would have rejected these frames before the parser saw them,
so a fix confined to parse_binary_message would not have worked; both now
delegate. The header fallback also assumed 379 on an implausible

* fix(mstock): make the feed usable without a login ACK, close review findings

The live symptom was /websocket/test showing LTP "---" with the console
reporting a successful subscribe. The log tells the story:

    10:39:13  mstock WebSocket connected
    10:39:18  WARNING: WebSocket not connected; subscription for TCS
              held locally and will be sent on reconnect

is_connected() required _logged_in, which was set only when a *text*
frame arrived. mStock documents no acknowledgement for the LOGIN frame -
the Market Data WebSocket page says only that it must be sent promptly or
the socket is dropped, and that every response is binary - so _logged_in
never became true, every subscribe was held locally and no tick ever
arrived. "mstock login confirmed" never appears in that session's log.

Sending LOGIN is the handshake, so the session is marked ready once the
frame is away, and any inbound frame confirms it. A failed LOGIN send
leaves the session unusable so the reconnect loop retries rather than
subscribing into a socket that is about to close. Marking ready is
idempotent, so the resync fires once per connection.

Also closes the second round of review findings, each reproduced before
being changed:

- "nan" or "inf" in a tuning knob parsed cleanly as a float and then blew
  up the int() cast at module import, taking the whole app down rather
  than degrading one broker. _env_float now rejects non-finite values,
  and the attempt count has a floor of 1.
- A retiring reconnect thread could pass the generation check and then
  overwrite an app a newer connect_stream() had already published. The
  check and the publication now happen under one lock, and the socket
  callbacks are scoped to their generation so a retired connection's
  close or error can no longer clear the live connection's flags.
- An auth stand-down cleared only the client's running flag; the adapter
  still reported connected=True, so the proxy kept serving a cached feed
  that would never produce another tick. The client now calls back into
  the adapter, which marks itself disconnected.
- A refused subscribe_batch left the queue already cleared, so with the
  client still connected no login was coming and nothing would ever send
  those tokens. They are requeued and the timer re-armed.
- The flush revalidated queued entries by token presence, so
  unsubscribing a depth stream while an LTP one remained still sent the
  stale higher mode. It now compares against the highest mode still
  wanted.
- A 4-byte frame made the packet-size fallback zero and divided by it.
- The positions debug dump built its string eagerly even though DEBUG is
  off by default; now lazily formatted.

Tests: the recovery suite waits on the state it is about to assert
instead of fixed sleeps, so it does not flake under scheduler load - the
two timing tests that must measure real elapsed time keep doing so, since
that is the defect they pin. test_close_failure_does_not_mask_the_result
now performs a successful read whose close() then raises, which is the
case its name claims; previously the read was empty, so it only proved an

Follow-up to #1979, from a cubic finding posted three minutes before that merge

a hard restart, and the process it names is long gone. `needs_stop` is true for

introduced, and stale metadata is a common state, not an exotic one.

value. `_strategy_may_still_be_running` reports true only when the strategy is
still tracked, a stop is still in flight, or the recorded PID answers. Checking
state rather than matching on the message string also keeps the guard from
breaking the next time one of those strings is reworded.

The protection itself is unchanged: a process that survives termination, or a
concurrent stop holding the claim, still aborts the delete with a 409.

Three tests: stale metadata does not block, a live PID does, and tracked or
mid-stop both count as running.

position is still open, and Flow's Position Check reads pos.get("pnl", 0)
for its pnl_above/pnl_below guards - so with the key absent those guards
evaluated 0 and could never fire for a Kotak account. The positions CSV
left its P&L column blank for the same rows.

Writes Kotak's documented "Profit N Loss" formula (Positions.md) in full
rather than the realized half alone:

  PnL = (Total Sell Amt - Total Buy Amt)
        + Net Qty * LTP * multiplier * (genNum/genDen) * (prcNum/prcDen)

It collapses to the realized-only form when Net Qty is 0, so closed legs
keep reporting exactly what #1971 gave them - the four SENSEX legs from
the issue still total +988.00. The mark-to-market term needs a price,
which #1973's LTP backfill now puts on the row; that backfill is
best-effort, so an open position with no quote reports 0.0 rather than
its bare cost, which would read as a total loss.

The scaling terms are all "1" on the segments reachable through OpenAlgo
today, but they are what the formula specifies, and a field arriving
absent, unparseable or zero falls back to 1.0 rather than raising.

Confined to broker/kotak/. This adds no field the shared layer did not
already carry: 32 of the other broker adapters emit pnl from
transform_positions_data, and the CSV writer, the positions page and the
Flow client are all written against it. Kotak was the outlier.

* fix(mstock): scope the dead-feed notice, order the connect flag, reset budgets

Three defects from review, each reproduced before being changed, plus the
flaky wait that hid the third.

A retiring worker could kill the stream that replaced it. connect_stream()
resets _feed_dead, so an old generation reaching its terminal path passed
the idempotency guard and cleared running, _connected and _logged_in - and
fired the callback - belonging to the connection that had just come up.
_notify_feed_dead() now takes the generation its caller serves and checks
it against the current one under the state lock, so a retired worker is
ignored while the live generation is still honoured.

connect() advertised a feed that had already died. It started the worker
and then set connected=True, so a connection failing outright reached
_on_feed_dead() first and had its False overwritten, handing the proxy a
cached adapter whose thread had exited - the same "subscribe succeeds, no
tick arrives" symptom as the login gate. The flag is now set before the
thread starts, and re-checked after connect_stream() returns.

An exhausted retry budget outlived its subscription. send_retries was
cleared on success and on resync but not on unsubscribe, so a token that
had spent its budget came back spent: review said it could not be sent at
all, which is not quite right - the budget gates requeues, not the first
attempt, so it got one send and no retries, measured as 1 attempt where a
fresh token gets 4. The dict also grew a permanent entry per token ever
seen. The budget is now dropped with the last desired subscription.

The retry test waited on the queue draining, which the flush clears as its
first act, before subscribe_batch records the attempt. A poll landing in
that gap returned early and the assertion could fail under load. It now
waits on the attempt count, which only reaches its final value at the end
of the exhausting flush.

Verified: a retired generation leaves the live stream running and silent
while the current one still reports; a feed dying during connect leaves
the adapter disconnected; an unsubscribed token gets a full budget again
on re-subscribe; 63 tests pass three times over; and reverting each of ten
fixes in turn still fails the suite.

feat(agent): chat code blocks lose the gutter and the height cap

The chat rendered code in the platform's CodeMirror editor at a fixed 24 rows.
A 37 line script therefore showed a header reading "37 lines" above a body
that stopped at 25, with the rest behind an inner scroll region nobody found:
the code read as truncated rather than scrollable, and a block that cannot be
read whole cannot be trusted whole.

Chat code rendering moves to its own component, modelled on ChatGPT and
informed by ragz. Three decisions:

* No line-number gutter. Numbers earn their place in an editor, where they are
  how a person cites a line to a colleague or reads a traceback. In a chat
  answer nobody cites a line, the block is usually copied whole, and the
  gutter competes with the code for the eye. /python keeps its numbers,
  because that is a real editor and this is not.

* No height cap. Every line renders and the conversation scrolls, which is
  what a reader expects. The only scrolling axis inside the block is
  horizontal, for a long line.

* Not CodeMirror. An editor per block is an editor instance per message, each
  with its own state, extensions and DOM, in a thread that only grows. A
  highlighter renders once to static markup. The chat needs reading, not
  editing, and the cheaper thing is also the better behaved one.

Highlighting is still deferred until a fence closes, so a long answer is not
re-tokenised on every token, and only the languages the agent actually emits
are registered: an unregistered language falls through to plain monospace
rather than being highlighted as something it is not.

react-syntax-highlighter was already a dependency but had no importer, so this
is the first code to pay for it: the chat bundle grows about 64 kB raw, 17 kB
gzipped, for the five registered languages.

The test that pinned the editor mount is rewritten rather than deleted: its
intent, that an open fence is not highlighted, still holds. Two tests are
added for the decisions above, because an absent gutter and an absent height
cap are invisible to every other test in the file.

Generated Python is also crisper. The SDK section never said that history
timestamps are already IST, so scripts imported zoneinfo and converted a
timezone that was already correct, then added an environment guard for
something the strategy host sets before the script runs. Measured on the same
request: 37 lines before, 27 after.

feat(agent): payoff diagrams and combined premium charts

Asking for a payoff now draws one. Two failures the operator hit repeatedly,
both because the tool did not exist: a payoff request came back as a V drawn
out of slashes in a code block, and a combined premium request was refused
outright because "the chart tool only accepts one listed instrument at a
time".

The payoff maths is not reimplemented, and that is the point. strategyMath.ts
computes the curve and PayoffChart draws it, both of which are what
/strategybuilder uses. The tool resolves legs and emits them; the card hands
them to the existing builder and the result to the existing chart. A second
implementation would drift, and the copy living in the chat is the copy nobody
notices is wrong. Same reasoning CLAUDE.md gives for services/risk/.

Every number on the curve is fetched, never supplied by the model: strike, lot
size, tick size and option type from the instrument master, premium from the
live quote or the position's own average, IV from the greeks service, spot from
the underlying quote. A contract absent from the master is refused rather than
guessed, and a missing spot refuses the whole diagram rather than centring a
curve on nothing. Legs come either from contracts the operator named or from
their own open positions, so "what is my payoff" works.

Cash equity is excluded and said so out loud. A StrategyLeg is an option or a
future, so shares held against a short call cannot be modelled; dropping them
quietly would draw a naked short call where a covered call is held, which
understates the risk.

The combined premium series is built from CLOSE per aligned bar, not from
summed OHLC. A straddle's combined high is not the call high plus the put
high: the legs are anti-correlated and their highs fall at different moments
inside one bar, so summing them invents a peak that never traded.

A defect found while testing this end to end: both tools annotated their leg
list as list[str], so agno advertised items as a plain string while the
docstring told the model it could pass an object carrying side and lots. A
short leg has no other expression, so a model following the documentation was
refused by schema validation before the tool ran, and the turn ended with "the
payoff tool rejected the short-leg format". The annotation now matches what
the code has always accepted, and both forms were checked against the
generated schema rather than assumed.

Verified live: a NIFTY 29SEP26 short straddle draws from real premiums of
324.00 and 205.60, giving breakevens at 23,320.40 and 24,379.60, which match
the figures the model had previously worked out by hand. The combined premium
of the 08SEP26 straddle reads 218.95 against legs of 129.15 and 89.80. The
payoff frame is 1,011 bytes and the answer 325 characters, so the series never
enters the conversation.

fix(agent): let LiteLLM decide which models take a reasoning effort

Not every model thinks. GPT-4 and GPT-4o take no reasoning effort, LiteLLM
forwards the parameter unchanged, and OpenAI answers with an error rather than
ignoring it. This is the same shape as the temperature failure earlier in this
project: a parameter the provider would not accept was sent because nothing
checked first.

reasoning, but it read that from an operator checkbox on the model row. One

* fix(shoonya): stop abandoned websocket clients leaking sockets and threads

A connected ShoonyaWebSocket could never be garbage collected, because
every long-lived reference into it was a bound method: the WebSocketApp
callbacks, the run_forever thread target, the heartbeat thread target,
and the adapter callbacks it stored. The object therefore kept itself
alive, __del__ never ran, and a client dropped without stop() stranded
one ESTABLISHED socket plus three threads for the life of the process.
Because the client also held the adapter (on_message = adapter._on_message),
an adapter dropped without disconnect() leaked its ZMQ socket and bound
port the same way.

Route those four edges through weakrefs:

- _WeakCallback stores bound-method callbacks via weakref.WeakMethod, so
  the adapter stays collectable and its cleanup() actually runs. Plain
  functions are still held strongly; they have no owner to leak.
- _weak_dispatch backs the four WebSocketApp callbacks.
- _make_ws_runner replaces _run_websocket as the thread target. A weak
  dispatch is not enough here: it would resolve the weakref and then hold
  the client strongly in its frame for the whole connection. The runner
  keeps only the WebSocketApp alive.
- _make_heartbeat_runner waits on the shutdown event without a strong
  reference, so an abandoned client is reclaimed promptly instead of
  being pinned for a full HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL. _heartbeat_worker becomes
  _heartbeat_beat, one beat with no wait inside it.

_wait_for_thread_completion gains a self-join guard, mirroring the one in
_stop_heartbeat: stop() can now genuinely be reached from __del__ during
GC, and joining the ws thread from itself would block for the full 5s
timeout on every teardown.

Adapter: initialize() now stops any existing ws_client before replacing
it. Every current caller either disconnects first or builds a fresh
adapter, so this was not reachable in production, but overwriting a live
client orphans it with nothing left holding a reference to call stop().

Verified against a local Noren-speaking websocket server, measuring TCP
sockets via psutil and thread counts. Before: abandoning a connected
client leaked 5 sockets / 15 threads over 5 iterations, overwriting a
live client 5 sockets / 10 threads. After: all six lifecycle paths
(connect/stop, server-side drop, connect timeout, abandoned client,
overwritten client, dropped owner) leak zero sockets and zero threads.
Callback delivery, 100-scrip subscription batching, heartbeats and
reconnect-on-the-same-object all still behave as before.

Note for future refactors: the __del__ methods are load-bearing and only
work while all four reference edges stay weak. Reinstating any one as a
bound method makes them dead code again, silently.

Smaller decisions worth stating:

* Truncation is ordered by id, not created_at. Two messages in one turn can
  share a timestamp at the stored resolution, and an ordering that ties is one
  that can drop the wrong row.
* The route checks ownership first. A conversation id is a small integer, so
  without that check an operator could truncate somebody else's thread by
  guessing.
* A row stored before the run entry existed simply has none. Its transcript
  still truncates and its run stays in the session store, ageing out of the
  history window on its own. That is the honest degradation, and it beats
  refusing to truncate at all.
* Sending an unchanged question is refused. It would truncate the answer and
  then reproduce it, charging a turn to arrive back where the operator started.
* The editor opens with the caret at the end rather than the text selected. An
  edit is usually a correction at the tail, and a full selection would make the
  first keystroke destroy the question.
* Copy takes the stored string, not the rendered DOM, so pasting an answer does
  not carry bullet glyphs and table borders into an editor.
* Actions appear on hover AND on focus-within, so they are not mouse-only.

There is no confirmation dialog on edit, deliberately. The answer visibly
disappearing is its own warning, and it is undone by asking again.

fix(agent): editing a message silently did nothing

An edit reverted to the original text and no turn ran. The cause was a guard
of mine that returned silently on an id it could not parse, and it could never
parse any of them: message ids are `stored-153` for a rehydrated row and
`user-3` for a live one, and both give NaN. So editing had never worked once,
on any message, and it failed in the one way that is hardest to report.

Two fixes, and the second is the reason the first is possible.

The client now parses `stored-<row>` rather than coercing the whole id, and an
id it cannot use produces a visible message instead of a silent return. An
edit that quietly reverts is precisely what this looked like.

And a live message now has a row to name at all. The start frame carries the
`ag_message` id the route just stored, so the question being answered is
re-keyed the moment the server reports it. Without that the newest question,
the one an operator is most likely to want to correct, would be the only one
that could never be edited.

The resume path deliberately does not carry the field. It continues a run that
is already open and creates no question, so claiming a message id there would
be inventing one.

freezes the single production worker for a quarter of an hour, orders
included, while behaving perfectly on the dev server. It runs on a real
OS thread, proved in an eventlet subprocess on elapsed time and hub
liveness: an inline poll blocks 1.04s with the hub ticking 0 times, while
start_login returns in 0.001s and the hub ticks 40 times during the poll.

that login internally, and it ran for every row on GET /agent/api/models.

that consumed plan quota, and falling back to the bare name would have

feat(kotak): historical data for NSE, BSE, NFO, BFO and indices

Replaces the get_history placeholder with the Neo market-data historical
endpoint, GET /market-data/1.0/historical/details, keyed by the same
segment|token neosymbol the quotes path already builds.

Intervals: 1m, 3m, 5m, 10m, 15m, 30m, 1h, D, W. Neo's 60min is advertised
as 1h because 60m is not a canonical interval; 60m stays an accepted alias,
following the precedent in intervals_service.

Behaviour measured against the live API rather than taken from the spec:

- Rate limit. Neo publishes none, but the endpoint 429s after roughly five
  requests in a second. Paced at 4/sec with a module-level limiter, because
  history_service builds a fresh BrokerData per request and Historify runs
  concurrent workers that would otherwise burst. 429 retries the same request
  with exponential backoff rather than falling through to another candidate.

- An empty range is a 400, not an empty success. Both "No data found" and
  "Data not available ... Market has not yet opened" are answered with no
  candles, so a pull whose last chunk lands on a weekend or on today before
  the open no longer aborts. "Invalid neosymbol" and "Historical data is not
  supported for this exchange" stay hard errors.

- Chunk caps confirmed exact: each interval accepts its documented span and
  rejects one day more, so chunk_days - 1 uses the full allowance.

- Index names are case sensitive here and disagree with the quotes endpoint:
  INDIAVIX answers to "INDIA VIX", not "India VIX". Index lookup tries the
  master contract token first, then the descriptive name and its upper-case
  form, which is also what makes NIFTYNXT50 resolve.

- Candle rows can arrive with six elements and no OI, so rows are padded to
  the seven-column contract with OI zeroed.

Daily and weekly candles are shifted +5:30 to land on IST midnight; intraday
keeps the true UTC instant.

MCX and CDS are refused before the request is sent. Neo answers every MCX and
CDS contract with "Historical data is not supported for this exchange",
verified across four commodities and three segment spellings. Both remain
fully supported for quotes.

Verified against a live session: a two-year 1-minute pull returns 184,595 rows
over 25 chunks with no duplicates and no gaps at the chunk seams, and every
NSE_INDEX and BSE_INDEX symbol returns intraday and daily data.

fix(installer): never start a container from a failed build (#2005)

* fix(installer): never start a container from a failed build

`docker compose build` ran unchecked and was followed unconditionally by
`docker compose up -d`. The script has no `set -e`, so a failed build fell
straight through: the previous image is still tagged, so the container
restarted on the OLD code, the loop continued, and the script printed
"INSTALLATION COMPLETE" and exited 0.

The result is silent: the container comes up healthy, the git checkout on
disk is at the new commit, and the .env has been rewritten, but the
running code is whatever was last built successfully. The operator has no
indication anything went wrong.

Seen when Debian bullseye's security pool was drained after its
2026-08-31 LTS EOL and every image build began failing on apt 404s. The
instance reported success while running a five-day-old image.

Now: a failed build logs an error naming the domain, skips `up -d` so the
running container is left alone, records the domain, and continues with
the remaining instances rather than aborting them. The closing banner
reports COMPLETED WITH ERRORS and lists what was not updated, and the
script exits 1 so CI and `&&` chains see the failure.

A container that fails to start is tracked the same way.

Verified with a harness faking a build failure for one of three domains:
the other two deploy, the failed one never reaches `up -d`, the banner
names it, exit code is 1.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(installer): restore working routing when a build fails

Addresses review feedback on #2005.

The skip introduced by the previous commit created a worse failure than the
one it fixed. The deploy loop allocates ports, then overwrites both
docker-compose.yaml and the Nginx vhost, and only afterwards builds. A single
Nginx reload at the end of the run activates whatever is on disk.

Previously a failed build still ran `docker compose up -d`, which recreated the
container from the new compose file -- stale image, but on the new ports -- so
the container and Nginx stayed aligned by accident. Skipping that left the
running container on its old ports while Nginx was reloaded onto the new ones,
making a working instance unreachable through its domain.

The two generated files are now snapshotted immediately before they are
regenerated, and restored if the build fails, so the domain keeps pointing at
the ports its container is actually listening on. For a fresh install there is
nothing to restore, so the generated vhost and its symlink are removed rather
than left pointing at a port that will never be served.

No restore after a failed `docker compose up -d`: compose has already acted on
the new file, so a container may exist stopped or partially recreated on the new
ports, and reverting Nginx alone would guarantee a mismatch.

Failure messages no longer claim the previous image is still running. That was
only ever true for a failed update, and the banner now reports which instances
did not deploy without asserting what is running.

Nginx paths move to NGINX_SITES_AVAILABLE / NGINX_SITES_ENABLED, defaulting to
the previous literals, so the failure path is testable without touching the real
Nginx configuration. Sourcing with OPENALGO_INSTALLER_LIB_ONLY=1 returns before
any imperative section, exposing the helpers to tests.

test/test_installer_failure_routing.py covers a failed build alongside a domain
that still deploys successfully, asserting the failed domain's compose ports
match its reloaded upstreams, and that a failed fresh install leaves no dead
vhost. Both tests fail if restore_instance_config is neutered.

The `docker compose up -d --wait` readiness gap raised in review is left as a
follow-up, as agreed -- it predates this PR.

* fix(kotak): decode unavailable HSM fields instead of publishing them as prices

The HSM feed marks a field it has no value for this tick with 0x80000000.
setLongValues was meant to drop those, but buf2long sums shifted bytes with no
sign extension, so the marker arrives as +2147483648 and never once equalled
the signed TRASH_VAL it was compared against. The guard was dead: an absent
price decoded to 21474836.48 and reached the quote path, which reads bp/sp/op/
h/lo/ltp/c with a bare float() and no filter of its own. Four hardcoded
21474836.48 filters downstream are the evidence this was hit in production.

buf2long is deliberately left unsigned - it also reads message lengths, topic
ids, field counts and timestamps, none of which are two's-complement - so the
sentinel is matched against both constants instead.

The scrip decoder also rounded prices to a hardcoded 2 decimals while the depth
and index decoders in the same file already honoured the broker-declared
precision. That truncated CDS and BCD, where USDINR ticks at 0.0025, and made
this feed disagree with its own depth feed on the price of one contract.

Demonstrated against the pre-change file:
  unavailable previous close   21474836.48 -> 21.35
  USDINR at 4dp                      87.23 -> 87.2350

Adds the first test coverage for broker/kotak/streaming/. It loads the decoder
by path because the package __init__ imports the adapter, which imports
websocket_proxy, which imports the adapter back.

* feat(kotak): stream market data over SFeed with per-data-centre routing

Kotak has moved market data off the legacy HSM feed. Checked against the live
prod config on 2026-09-07, all ten data centres select "sh" (SFeed) or "ks"
(cdtstream) and none selects "hs"; the primary data centres no longer carry an
_hs_broadcast_endpoint key at all. Kotak's own SDK removed HSWebSocket and
HSIWebSocket in 2.2.0 with no replacement, keeps no HSM fallback (every failure
path in resolve_dynamic_urls lands on the hardcoded SFeed URL), and never
announced any of it.

mlhsm still completes a WebSocket upgrade and its certificate is renewed to
November 2026, so nothing is broken today - but OpenAlgo reached it only by
hardcoding the host past the config service that no longer points anywhere near
it. That is a feed with no supported path to it, not a supported feed.

SFeed is a different protocol, not a newer HSM: little-endian and packed where
HSM is big-endian, a 9-byte header with a uint16 message code where HSM has a
one-byte type, batched packets where HSM sends one per frame, and prices scaled
by a per-exchange divider delivered once in the auth response rather than by a
precision carried in each tick. So this is a new decoder, not an extension.

Replicated from the wire format rather than depending on neo_api_client: that
package is asyncio-only, and an event loop inside a threaded adapter would have
to be owned, shut down and reconnected by code that has no loop. sfeed_protocol
carries the struct layouts and message codes; sfeed_websocket speaks them over
websocket-client, keeping the concurrency model the adapter already uses.

The new client is a drop-in for KotakWebSocket - same method surface, same
normalized dicts under HSM's field names - so kotak_adapter and everything
downstream are unchanged apart from choosing which client to build.
kotak_feed_config resolves that choice per data centre and falls back to the
default SFeed endpoint on any failure, as the SDK does. HSM is kept for a data
centre that still asks for it.

Getting the data centre out of login means the stored auth token grows a fifth
part. It is appended, never inserted, and every reader now takes the first four
positionally, so tokens issued before this change keep working and no existing
user has to log in again. That change and its readers are in one commit
deliberately: splitting them leaves a commit where a five-part token reaches a
reader expecting four, which is exactly the "too many values to unpack
(expected 4)" that breaks every quotes request.

test_kotak_auth_token_format guards that with an AST scan over broker/kotak
rather than a grep - the reader missed during development was invisible to a
line-oriented search because ruff had wrapped its .split( and its ":::" onto
separate lines.

The order feed is untouched. Both sources resolve it to the same
<baseurl>/realtime host, so the migration is market data only.

fix: Upstox multiquotes never populated prev_close, breaking %-change (#1725)

### Problem
`BrokerData.get_quotes()` (single-symbol) already has a fallback chain for
`prev_close`: it prefers the v2 `/market-quote/quotes` endpoint's
`ohlc.close`, falling back to v3 OHLC's `prev_ohlc.close` only if that's
empty. The batch path used by `/api/v1/multiquotes` — `_process_quotes_batch()`
— never got this fallback: it fetches `v2_quotes` for bid/ask/OI, but reads
`prev_close` ONLY from v3's `prev_ohlc.close`.

On accounts where Upstox's v3 batch OHLC response has an empty `prev_ohlc`
(confirmed live), every symbol in a multiquotes response comes back with
`prev_close: 0`, even though the single-symbol quotes endpoint returns the
correct value for the very same instrument. Any consumer that derives a
day change % from multiquotes (screeners, movers, a market ticker, etc.)
sees every row/tick as "no change" or filters the row out entirely when it
guards against a zero prev_close — even though live prices are flowing
fine.

### Fix
Mirror `get_quotes()`'s fallback in `_process_quotes_batch()`: read
`prev_close` from the already-fetched v2 quote's `ohlc.close` first,
falling back to v3's `prev_ohlc.close` if the v2 value is unavailable.

### Notes
Verified live against a real Upstox session: the same symbol via
`/api/v1/quotes` returned a correct non-zero `prev_close`, while
`/api/v1/multiquotes` returned `prev_close: 0` for it (and every other
requested symbol) before this fix; after the fix both paths agree.

* fix(flattrade): stop a WebSocket close stalling the reconnect (#1965)

A Flattrade market-data close cost seconds of feed downtime that had
nothing to do with the broker.

_stop_heartbeat() joined the heartbeat worker without waking it. The
worker slept on _stop_event, which only stop() ever set, so a close
blocked the websocket-client reader thread for the full 3s
HEARTBEAT_JOIN_TIMEOUT, logged "Heartbeat thread did not terminate within
timeout", and still left the worker running. That stall sat in front of
the on_close callback, i.e. in front of the adapter's reconnect
scheduling. Measured on the unpatched code: 3.02s per close with the
orphan worker still alive; 0.00s and no orphan after.

The worker now sleeps on a per-connection Event that _stop_heartbeat()
sets before joining. A fresh Event per connect means a worker left over
from a previous socket cannot be re-armed by the next one.
_check_connection_health() can route back into _stop_heartbeat() on the
worker's own thread, so a self-join guard replaces the RuntimeError that
path used to raise.

The adapter separately called ws_client.stop() while holding self.lock.
stop() joins the reader thread, and that thread runs the adapter's own
_on_close, which takes the same lock, so disconnect() and
_attempt_reconnection() each waited out a join timeout instead of
proceeding. Both now hold the lock for bookkeeping only and do the
blocking work outside it, publishing the new client before connect()
because _on_open -> _resubscribe_all() sends through self.ws_client on
the reader thread.

The flapping that triggered the report was the dual-socket eviction fixed
in #1961 (order updates poll REST by default), which landed before the
issue was filed. This is the residual cost of any close, from any cause.

The tests fail on the unpatched code with the real symptoms: the 3.01s
stall, the warning quoted in the issue, the self-join RuntimeError, and
"the reader thread could not finish _on_close in 3.00s".

* feat(flattrade): back off and diagnose a repeatedly evicted session (#1965)

Hardening, not a confirmed defect: unlike the two fixes in the previous
commit, this one was reasoned from the code rather than reproduced, so it
is kept separate and is safe to revert on its own.

reconnect_attempts is reset by every successful connect, so it cannot
escalate the delay when the broker keeps evicting a session that did
authenticate: each eviction re-arms a flat 5s retry and OpenAlgo hammers
PiConnect indefinitely. _backoff_level is reset only by a session that
actually stayed up for STABLE_SESSION_SECONDS, so a flap escalates
5 -> 10 -> 20 ... to the existing 60s cap while a genuine network blip
after a healthy session still retries in 5s.

It is deliberately not wired into MAX_RECONNECT_ATTEMPTS. A contended
session must keep retrying slowly rather than give up for good, since
whatever holds the session may go away.

After three consecutive short sessions the log stops reporting an
ordinary reconnect and names the cause: PiConnect allows one WebSocket
session per uid/accesstoken, so a session evicted seconds after
authenticating almost always means another client is using the same
Flattrade credentials - a second OpenAlgo instance, a leftover process,
or a separate script. No code change can fix that, so the log has to say
it.

* feat(upstox): pace every REST entry point against a shared rate limiter

Upstox publishes two independent budgets, each governed by three simultaneous
rolling windows: order APIs at 10/sec, 500/min, 2000/30min, and standard APIs
at 50/sec on the same longer windows. broker/upstox/api/rate_limiter.py holds
one limiter per category, each reserving the earliest slot that satisfies all
three windows, so a burst is permitted while the sustained rate is held down.

State is module level, not on BrokerData: services build a fresh
BrokerData(auth_token) per request, so pacing state kept on an instance is
reset away on every call and paces nothing against concurrent requests.

Replaces the local flat RATE_LIMIT_DELAY = 1.0 between quote batches in
data.py, which throttled batches to a fifth of the documented 50/sec while
doing nothing about the order-book, funds and history calls sharing the same
budget. Adds reactive 429 handling on top of the proactive pacer, since the
pacer is an estimate and Upstox's clock is the truth.

* fix(upstox): close websocket resource leaks in the streaming adapter and client

Six leaks off the steady-state path, each measured with an offline fake-socket
harness before and after.

connect() had no re-entrancy guard. A second call while a loop was already
running built a second WebSocketApp, overwrote the client's ws slot and left
the first socket and thread with nothing holding a handle to either, since
disconnect() also nulled the thread handle. The orphan stayed blocked inside
run_forever() for the life of the process. UpstoxWebSocketClient.connect() now
runs under a connect lock and refuses re-entry while a loop is alive; the
adapter tests ws_client.running too, because self.connected is False for the
whole 2-30s backoff window. The guard cannot touch the internal reconnect:
_run_websocket rebuilds the WebSocketApp inline on the same iteration of the
same thread and never re-enters connect(). Refusing rather than tearing the
first connection down keeps a live feed and its server-side subscriptions, and
is the only safe choice given threads are deliberately not joined here.

initialize() replaced a live ws_client without stopping it, orphaning the same
socket and thread through a different door. It now releases the old client
first and severs its callbacks, which also breaks the adapter-client reference
cycle.

disconnect() called cleanup_zmq(), which is irreversible, so a restarted
adapter reported success, opened a real socket and held an Upstox connection
slot while every tick was dropped into a closed publisher. The release stays
in disconnect() because nothing outside this package ever calls cleanup(), so
leaving it to the destructor would swap a dropped-tick bug for a ZMQ leak.
connect() now re-establishes the publisher instead, with the instance count
restored symmetrically.

cleanup() was reachable only from __del__, which cannot run while the socket
thread is alive because that thread reaches the adapter through the callbacks.
Rather than make the destructor work, disconnect() now releases everything
that costs a descriptor and cleanup() is a strict superset that only drops a
client already holding no socket and no thread. The Upstox __del__ override is
removed; the base destructor still releases ZMQ.

A firing batch Timer cleared self.batch_timer unconditionally, discarding the
handle to whatever was armed in the meantime and leaving it invisible to every
cancel path. The handle is now cleared only on identity with the running
Timer, and a generation stamp bumped by each teardown stops a Timer that
already slipped past its cancel point from acting on a torn-down adapter.

The reconnect backoff slept in one block, so a disconnect landing inside it
still woke the loop into a database read and an outbound HTTPS authorize on
behalf of a torn-down adapter. It now waits in slices and re-tests the running
flag. Total delay while running is unchanged, so the backoff curve and the
50-attempt budget are untouched.

Also drops the dead THREAD_JOIN_TIMEOUT and the unused SSL context.

fix(upstox): stamp the synthetic daily candle in IST, not host local time (#2030)

When a daily history request covers today and the historical endpoint has
not published today's bar yet, the adapter synthesises one from the quotes
API. It built the timestamp by adding 5h30m to a NAIVE datetime and then
calling .timestamp(), which reads the result in whatever zone the host
runs in. That is not a timezone conversion: the value came out 19800s off
on an IST machine and 39600s off in a UTC container, so the same code
produced a different epoch per deployment.

It never surfaced because the interval == "D" branch normalises through
.date() before converting, discarding the error -- so the bar was only
ever accidentally correct, and only for daily.

The synthetic bar also travelled in a different format from every real
one: milliseconds versus Upstox's ISO 8601 string, so safe_to_datetime()
produced a naive value for it and a tz-aware value for the rest, two
conventions reconciled solely by that .date() call.

Now emits IST midnight as ISO 8601 with the offset, byte-identical to a
real Upstox daily candle, so one convention flows through. Verified the
synthetic and real bars yield the same epoch, and that the today_found
check at the top of the branch still parses it (it already accepted
either form).

This does not close #1765. It removes a confirmed timezone defect found
while investigating it; the reported 86400s shift did not reproduce
against a live session, and the historical-vs-synthetic path selection
that likely drives the other symptoms is untouched.

fix: stop background writers on Ctrl+C so the next start is not blocked

Issue #2031: on Windows, stopping `uv run app.py` and restarting immediately
fails with "database is locked" on health.db, and repeated attempts leave
orphaned Python processes behind.

The lock is a symptom. A SQLite lock is an OS file lock and the kernel drops
it when the process dies, so a process that has exited cannot still hold
health.db. The only thing that can be holding it is an old instance that is
still running, and its health collector writes a sample every
HEALTH_SAMPLE_INTERVAL seconds (10 by default) for as long as it lives. Each
orphan is a permanent writer, which is why every successive start failed more
often than the last.

socketio.run() is the last statement in app.py and nothing runs after it, so
there was no point at which the collector was told to stop. utils/shutdown.py
supplies one: stop the collector, then release this thread's scoped sessions,
in that order because collect_metrics releases its own session in a finally and
sweeping first would let one more sample start. Registered only in the process
that serves; under gunicorn the __main__ block never runs.

Not done, deliberately: raising the busy timeout on health.db, as the issue
suggests. database/__init__ already retries a blocked statement for
LOCK_RETRY_BUDGET_S (15s), cooperatively, and installs that for every SQLite
connection in the process by wrapping sqlite3.connect, so health.db has it
today despite building its engine by hand. Setting connect_args timeout would
also be inert, because the connect listener runs PRAGMA busy_timeout=100
afterwards, and were it not inert it would reinstate the eventlet freeze that
test_sqlite_lock_cooperative.py exists to prevent.

health_db.py now builds its engine through engine_factory.create_db_engine like
every other module. The engine is identical, measured: NullPool,
_CooperativeConnection, busy_timeout=100, WAL. Being the one module that did it
by hand is what made health.db look as though it had opted out of the policy.

Verified: 7 new tests, which fail when the teardown order or the run-once guard
is reverted; 254 passing across the CI-safe suite plus the SQLite lock tests;
ruff clean on the new files. An fd-audit found no new descriptor or memory
holder: no engine, session, thread, socket or unbounded collection is created,
and the two module-level flags are bools.

fix(samco): stop reconnecting after a rejected session token (#2035)

A 401/403 from the broker was treated as a network fault. `_on_close`
respawned the retry thread unconditionally and `connect()` returns False
without raising, so `reconnect_attempts` never incremented and
`max_reconnect_attempts` never tripped: a dead token produced an
unbounded reconnect storm that ran until the process restarted, churning
a fresh socket and thread per iteration and risking an IP rate-limit.
Indian broker tokens roll over daily at ~3 AM IST, so this is a
scheduled event rather than an edge case.

The client now judges and latches the failure, since the adapter's
on_close callback only receives `ws` and never sees the close code.
`_on_error` reads `status_code` off the handshake exception, which is
more reliable than the stringified message, and `_on_close` checks the
close reason. `_wait_for_connection` returns as soon as the flag is set
instead of burning the full connection timeout, and
`_initialize_connection` clears it so a retry carrying a freshly re-read
token is not blocked by the previous attempt's verdict.

The adapter passes down `is_auth_error` inherited from
BaseBrokerWebSocketAdapter, so samco shares the fleet's 401/403
vocabulary, and short-circuits in every path that can schedule a
reconnect. Clearing `running` is what breaks the loop: both the retry
loop and `_on_close` test it before starting another attempt.

Part of marketcalls/openalgo#1343. The subscribe batch-queue the same
issue asks for is already in place as the coalescing flusher in
samcoWebSocket.py.

* feat(fivepaisaxts): batch websocket subscriptions into one request per mode

The XTS market-data API takes an `instruments` array per request, but the
adapter sent one request per symbol. That request is a blocking HTTP POST
with a 10s timeout issued inline from subscribe(), so a 1000-symbol
startup was 1000 sequential round-trips and every reconnect replayed the
whole book the same way.

Adds the coalescing queue the sibling 5Paisa adapter already has: a
single processor thread drains (mode, instrument) items into requests of
up to 50 instruments, behind a collect window that lets a burst
accumulate, with a throttle applied only when more batches remain.
Instruments of one mode are gathered from anywhere in the queue rather
than its front, because callers interleave modes and a front-run-only
scan would alternate item by item and emit one-instrument requests, which
is the flood this exists to prevent. Failed batches are re-queued, except
while stopping, where disconnect() has emptied the queue and _on_open
will replay the book anyway. unsubscribe() cancels a still-queued
subscribe, so a quick subscribe/unsubscribe cannot resurrect a stale
server-side subscription.

Two pieces of client bookkeeping had to be corrected for this to be safe,
both silent failures:

unsubscribe() read its xtsMessageCode back from the stored entry for its
own correlation id and fell back to 1501. Batched subscribes are stored
under a batch id, so the lookup would miss and every LTP and depth
unsubscribe would target the quote feed. It now derives the code from the
mode via a shared map, the same way subscribe() does.

`subscriptions` doubles as the tick filter, so a batched entry has to
have individual instruments removed on unsubscribe or they keep being

* feat(fivepaisaxts): batch websocket subscriptions into one request per mode

The XTS market-data API takes an `instruments` array per request, but the
adapter sent one request per symbol. That request is a blocking HTTP POST
with a 10s timeout issued inline from subscribe(), so a 1000-symbol
startup was 1000 sequential round-trips and every reconnect replayed the
whole book the same way.

Adds the coalescing queue the sibling 5Paisa adapter already has: a
single processor thread drains (mode, instrument) items into requests of
up to 50 instruments, behind a collect window that lets a burst
accumulate, with a throttle applied only when more batches remain.

than its front, because callers interleave modes and a front-run-only
scan would alternate item by item and emit one-instrument requests, which
is the flood this exists to prevent. Failed batches are re-queued, except
while stopping, where disconnect() has emptied the queue and _on_open
will replay the book anyway. unsubscribe() cancels a still-queued
subscribe, so a quick subscribe/unsubscribe cannot resurrect a stale
server-side subscription.

Two pieces of client bookkeeping had to be corrected for this to be safe,
both silent failures:

unsubscribe() read its xtsMessageCode back from the stored entry for its
own correlation id and fell back to 1501. Batched subscribes are stored
under a batch id, so the lookup would miss and every LTP and depth
unsubscribe would target the quote feed. It now derives the code from the
mode via a shared map, the same way subscribe() does.

`subscriptions` doubles as the tick filter, so a batched entry has to
have individual instruments removed on unsubscribe or they keep being
accepted. Fixing that surfaced a pre-existing defect in the same filter:
it compared exchangeInstrumentID against an int while the adapter stores
a string, so it matched nothing and dropped every 1105 tick. Both now
compare on a normalised key.

* feat(tradejini): coalesce feed syncs into one request per feed

A subscribe request REPLACES the server-side symbol list for its feed
rather than appending to it - subscribeL1([A]) after subscribeL1([A, B])
silently drops B - so every change has to re-send the complete list. The
proxy calls subscribe() once per symbol, which made that O(N^2) in tokens
sent: 1000 symbols cost 1000 requests carrying ~500k token entries
between them, and the teardown cost the same again.

_request_feed_sync() marks a feed dirty and a single worker sends one
complete list per feed once the burst settles. This is the samco pattern
rather than zerodha's fixed timer, because a debounce suits a protocol
where every frame restates the whole set. Wired into subscribe,
unsubscribe and the reconnect replay - the replay goes through the same
queue, so one landing mid-burst folds into that send instead of racing
it.

cancel_when_empty is OR-ed across requests. An emptied feed has to be
cancelled outright, since an empty list would leave the old server-side
list in place, but a reconnect replay passes False because there is no
list to cancel yet. If both land in one window the cancel wins, which is
both what the unsubscribe asked for and safe.

The worker exits when idle rather than sitting on a 1s wait for the life
of the connection, and decides that under the same lock
_request_feed_sync holds when it adds work and checks liveness - an
unlocked test would strand a feed added in the instant before the return,
because the requester would see the thread alive and start no
replacement. disconnect() drops queued syncs before the client goes, so a
pending flush cannot fire at a socket being torn down.

The other half of the issue, holding the adapter lock across
subscribeL1/subscribeL2, was already fixed: _sync_feed snapshots the
token list under the lock and releases it before calling out.

Part of marketcalls/openalgo#1350.

fix(agent): stop the LiteLLM usage warning printing on every turn

Reported from a Windows install and reproduced here on macOS, so it is neither
platform nor deployment specific: it appears on every instance running a
chatgpt/ plan model, several lines per turn.

    UserWarning: Pydantic serializer warnings:
      PydanticSerializationUnexpectedValue(Expected `ResponseAPIUsage` ...)

The chatgpt/ provider runs through /v1/responses, so LiteLLM serialises the
reply's usage as a ResponseAPIUsage, which wants input_tokens and output_tokens.
What comes back carries the chat-completions shape, completion_tokens, and
pydantic says so. Nothing downstream reads the serialised object, and the counts
are taken from the fields that are present: a real turn reports input 23762,
output 5, total 23767, no cost, billing subscription, which is correct for a
plan.

So it is noise, and noise on every turn is worse than it sounds: a warning
nobody can act on is one everybody learns to scroll past, including the next one
that matters. The filter names this category, this message, from pydantic.main,
so anything else pydantic has to say still gets through. Delete it when LiteLLM
returns the right shape.

The `(?s)` in the pattern is load-bearing and nearly was not there. The warnings
module compiles the message with a bare re.compile and matches from the start,
and the real text carries a newline before the interesting part, so without
DOTALL the leading .* stops at the newline and the filter matches nothing. It
was written that way first, the warning kept printing, and an assertion against
a truncated string reported success.

fix: make Ctrl+C on the dev server actually exit

Ctrl+C printed a traceback every five seconds and then stopped exiting at all,
needing two or three presses to get a prompt back:

    Error submitting job "Strategy pending-stop reconciliation
    (trigger: interval[0:00:05])" to executor "default"
    RuntimeError: cannot schedule new futures after shutdown

Three separate causes, found in that order.

The schedulers were never stopped. The teardown added for issue #2031 stopped
the health collector and released this thread's sessions, and nothing else. Six
APScheduler instances were left running: the strategy module's, Flow's,
Historify's, Chartink's, the Python strategy host's and the sandbox square-off.
Each is on a daemon thread, so the interpreter does not wait for it and it keeps
firing while the process tears down, into the thread pools concurrent.futures
has already closed. The strategy module reconciles pending stops every five
seconds, which is the cadence in the log. stop_strategy_module() had existed
since that module shipped and nothing ever called it.

The websocket proxy thread was the hang. On the dev server the proxy runs on a
real OS thread in this process. It was created non-daemon with its cleanup
registered through atexit, and those two cannot both work: atexit runs only once
every non-daemon thread has been joined, so the cleanup that releases the proxy
thread was queued behind the wait for that same thread. What used to break the
tie was the proxy module's own SIGINT handler, which cleaned up and called
os._exit(0). utils/shutdown.py registers its handler later in app.py and
replaced it, so Ctrl+C stopped reaching that cleanup and the server stopped
exiting. shutdown_runtime now stops the proxy, and the thread is a daemon so a
cleanup that times out cannot wedge the exit anyway.

The health collector slept its whole sampling interval in one call, so it could
not see its stop flag. stop_health_collector joins for five seconds, so with the
default ten second interval that join timed out every time and Ctrl+C paid five
seconds before the rest of the teardown began. It now sleeps in slices, the
pattern services/strategy_module/checkpoint.py already uses.

Order, and why each position is load bearing. The collector stays first, for the
#2031 reason. The five schedulers that stop without waiting come next. The
strategy module follows them, because its teardown joins two threads and
unsubscribes a websocket. The proxy follows that, because its cleanup joins a
thread. The session sweep stays last, because a job that fires after it runs
outside any Flask app context and nothing unbinds what it binds.

Nothing waits on a job in flight. stop_squareoff_scheduler was the one teardown
that did, so it takes a wait parameter now: an operator leaving analyze mode
still waits for a square-off that is closing positions, the signal path does
not. A signal handler that blocks on a broker call leaves the process alive, and
a live process is the only thing that can still be holding a database, which is
the whole of #2031.

Schedulers are found in sys.modules rather than imported. Importing
blueprints.chartink calls scheduler.start() at module scope, so a teardown that
imported it to ask whether it was running would start, on the way out, the very
thing it is there to stop. A test pins that, and fails against an import.

Verified on the real server, not only in tests: started app.py, waited for port
5000 and port 8765 to listen and the Zerodha feed to settle, then sent a console
break, which shares a handler with Ctrl+C on Windows. Before the proxy fix it
never exited. After it, 6.29s. After the collector fix, 1.69s and 1.52s on a
repeat, exit code 149, which is 128 plus the signal and so proves our handler
ran rather than the default kill. The log shows the feed unsubscribing, the
proxy closing and releasing its port, and the shared ZMQ context cleaned up.

Also verified: 8 new tests, each of which fails when the fix is reverted; 15 in
the file and 296 across the CI-safe suite; ruff clean on what this touches,
leaving the pre-existing format drift in app.py, squareoff_thread.py and
health_monitor.py alone. An fd-audit found no new descriptor or memory holder:
the change acquires nothing, and a probe over 25 start/teardown cycles held
handles flat at 196 and threads back at 1.

fix(kotak): value a carried-forward position at its cost, not at Kotak's overnight re-valuation

Kotak's cfBuyAmt/cfSellAmt do not hold what an overnight leg cost. The
back office re-values every carried-forward leg at the previous day's
settlement price and carries it in at that price, which is what makes
Kotak's documented "Profit N Loss" formula produce the day's
mark-to-market rather than the P&L since entry. Dividing those amounts
by the carried quantity therefore returns the settlement price.

Issue #2061 is that arithmetic showing through: five overnight short
option legs each reported a different wrong average, four of them equal
to the LTP to the paisa because an illiquid option's last trade is its
previous close, and a book the broker's own app showed 1.42 lakh down
reported +13,765.50. The ratios between the carried valuation and the
real average were 2.51, 2.31, 3.12, 4.70 and 1.18, so no scaling term
explains it, only a re-valuation does.

Value the carried leg at upldPrc instead, when Kotak sends one. It is
the only per-unit price in the payload not derived from that valuation,
and it is Kotak's spelling of Noren's upldprc, documented there as
"Average price uploaded with holdings". The cfBuyAmt/cfSellAmt path
stays as the fallback, which is what makes this safe without an account
to try it on: if upldPrc carries the settlement price too, cf_qty *
upldPrc * factor is the amount already in use and no number changes.

Also divides the average by Kotak's documented "Total Qty * multiplier *
(genNum/genDen) * (prcNum/prcDen)" rather than by the quantity alone, so
the average and the P&L sit on one basis. Every term is 1 on the
segments reachable today, so this changes no number in practice; without
it a row with a multiplier of 2 reported an average that no longer
reproduced its own P&L.

Tests pin all five legs from the issue to the paisa, against the average
and the P&L the Kotak app showed for each, plus the book total of
-142,761.34. Also pinned: the no-upldPrc fallback still produces exactly
what 2.0.2.3 did, and an upldPrc equal to the carried valuation changes
nothing.

feat(positionbook): say on the row when an average is not an entry price

The raw payload on #2061 settles what d1dda9ca9 could not: upldPrc is
"0.00" on all five carried legs, so the fallback runs and the numbers on
screen are unchanged. cfSellAmt / cfSellQty gives 8.60, 11.90, 130.18,
65.40 and 808.00, exactly the AVG column, against real averages of
7.2969, 4.7480, 43.8816, 20.9912 and 171.9277.

A carried row holds seventeen fields and upldPrc is the only price among
them. Kotak's other endpoints are all current-day: orders, trades, and
order history by order number. So the entry price of an overnight F&O
position is not reachable through this API at all, and no amount of
mapping will produce it.

What is reportable is the carry-forward valuation, which is a true
number: the price the leg was carried into today at. Keep it, and add
average_price_basis to the row to say that is what it is. The key is
absent on every position whose average really is an entry price, so a
caller that does not care is unaffected and one that does can test a
single self-describing field rather than having to know that Kotak
carried legs behave differently.

It qualifies pnl as much as average_price, since both come off the same
amounts, and it is set on a fully-closed carried leg too, where
average_price is 0.00 by Kotak's own definition but the realized P&L is
still only today's slice of a position opened earlier.

Reporting 0.00 as the average instead was considered and rejected: it
would strip the Positions page of its live marking, since
useLivePrice.ts:273 gates on average_price > 0 and recomputes P&L from
it, leaving P&L frozen between REST polls and P&L% at 0.00%, and a zero
average is in any case indistinguishable from a leg that is genuinely
closed, which Kotak also reports as 0.

Also normalizes negative zero in pnl. A leg marked at exactly the price
it was carried at lands on -0.0 through floating point, which serializes
as "-0.0" and formats as "-0.00"; four of the five rows in #2061 are
that case.

chart `NIFTY/RELIANCE`, `2*CE25000 - CE25200`, `1/GOLD`, or any expression over

than `click`, because the field must not lose focus first or the caret being
written to is already gone; the reciprocal wraps the whole box instead, since a
reciprocal of part of an expression is almost never what was meant. When the box
holds arithmetic, Enter charts it rather than the highlighted row: those rows
match the last leg typed, and loading one would silently discard the expression.

`terminal.loadExpression` fetches every leg in parallel with the first failure
winning, because a combination missing a leg is not a chart with a gap, it is no
chart at all. A leg naming its own exchange (`NSE:RELIANCE`) keeps it; a bare
one inherits the pane's, which is what someone typing `NIFTY/RELIANCE` means.

A computed chart is not an instrument and must never look tradeable. It carries
`synthetic`, and the order path refuses it by name with its own message rather
than leaning on the `quoteOnly` alias continuing to mean this. It sets no tick,
no lot size and no product options, opens no live subscription, and disables
history paging, which would otherwise have to page every leg. The dialog says a
computed chart cannot be traded before you load it.

Weighted legs are the point for an options book: a ratio spread, a straddle, or
a spread scaled by lot size are all just coefficients. A sold combination is a
credit, so the series goes negative and that is allowed. A leg that did not
print gaps the whole combination rather than pricing it from an earlier minute,
which for an illiquid strike is the normal case.

fix(deltaexchange): read history dates as IST and stop future candle padding and Add automated broker QA audit suite  (#2074)

* fix(deltaexchange): read history dates as IST and stop future candle padding

Delta's get_history built its request window at UTC midnight, but OpenAlgo
hands every broker plain YYYY-MM-DD strings that mean IST calendar dates:
services/history_service passes them through, and the chart backends that
consume the result (blueprints/scalping.py, blueprints/chart_test.py) build
them from datetime.now(IST).date() and then re-group the returned candles by
IST date. A requested day therefore ran 05:30 IST to 05:29 IST the next
morning instead of covering the day that was asked for.

That also made Delta invent data. Its /v2/history/candles fills whatever
window it is given: past the last trade it emits flat, zero-volume candles at
the previous close right up to `end`. With `end` at 23:59:59 UTC (05:29 IST
tomorrow), asking for today returned hours of synthetic bars, which the
trading terminal plots as real ones because the feed does not trim past the
range it asked for. Measured on BTCUSDFUT at 13:25 IST: 964 of 1440 1-minute
bars were fabricated. On the chart that drew today's candles, crossed
midnight IST, and laid down a fresh day exactly 5h30m long.

- _to_epoch now localises the date to Asia/Kolkata: 00:00:00 to 23:59:59 IST
- each chunk's end is capped at the current time, so Delta is never asked for
  a window it would have to fabricate; a chunk wholly in the future is skipped
- a timestamp <= now filter on the assembled frame as a backstop

Verified against the live Delta India API across all 13 intervals in
TIMEFRAME_MAP. A single requested IST day now stays inside 00:00-23:59 IST on
every interval; today's series ends on the bar actually forming with zero
future bars; and 2026-08-01 to 2026-09-16 comes back gap-free on each one
(1m: 67,235 bars over 46 chunk requests, every diff exactly 60s). Daily and
weekly keep their uniform 86400s / 604800s steps.

Hourly and above open on an IST half-hour because Delta buckets on the UTC
grid; that is genuine for a 24x7 UTC exchange, and the terminal's candle
builder anchors on the last history bar, so live bars stay aligned with it.

returned nothing and TIMESTAMP expanded to the literal text `~0,8...DT:~8,6`.

fix(installer): read docker-run.bat RAM and core counts from PowerShell

WMIC is absent from Windows 11 24H2 and later, so both detection lines printed
"'wmic' is not recognized" straight at the operator and left their variables
empty. `set /a TOTAL_RAM_MB=%TOTAL_RAM_BYTES:~0,-6%` then evaluated the leftover
text as `~0`, which is -1, so every tier test took its lowest branch. Measured
on a 32GB 8-core machine, the container was started with shm=256MB, one compute
thread and a 256MB strategy memory cap, instead of shm=2048MB, four threads and
1024MB. The RAM-scaled limits from issue #822 were therefore inverted on exactly
the machines they exist to size.

Read both values from PowerShell, which returns megabytes directly and keeps the
byte count out of set /a, where anything from 4GB up overflows 32-bit signed
math. Cores are now summed across sockets rather than taking whichever socket
reported last. Each value is rejected unless it is all digits, so a blank or
unexpected reply can no longer reach the arithmetic, and a failed detection says
so in plain language and keeps the cautious limits rather than choosing them
silently.

Note the parentheses and the pipe inside the PowerShell argument must NOT be
caret-escaped: cmd does not treat them as special inside double quotes, so a
caret is passed through to PowerShell and breaks its syntax. Verified both ways.

Verified on Windows 11 26200: detection now reports 31965MB and 8 cores, giving
shm=2048MB, threads=4, strategy_mem=1024MB. With PowerShell unreachable, and
again with it returning non-numeric text, the container still starts on the
cautious limits after an explained note.

fix(agent): close a spoken approval window when its run is decided or abandoned

A run that paused for approval kept its voice window open for the full
`voice_confirm_window_seconds`, default 30, no matter what happened to the run
afterwards. `forget_pause` was called from exactly one place, the success path
inside `judge_approval`, though its docstring claimed "approved, rejected or
abandoned". Nothing called it when the operator decided the run on the card,
when the run was cancelled, or when the trader moved on.

Meanwhile the browser offers every finalised trader line against whichever run
is pending, and `CONFIRMATIONS` accepts `ok`, `sure`, `right`, `correct`,
`please`, `do`, `it`, `go` and `ahead`, which are conversational fillers rather
than answers. So an order read back, then left alone, stayed approvable by a
word said to something else half a minute later.

Three changes:

- `stream_continue` closes the window when a paused run is resumed, whichever
  surface decided it and whichever way. A voice approval has already popped the
  window by then, so that path is unaffected.
- `_on_run_cancelled` closes it too, because an abandoned run is not an order
  anyone is waiting to place.
- `teardown` in the browser controller clears `pendingApproval`. Only a
  successful approval cleared it before, so a hung-up session left the last
  order read back as the target of the next thing said in a new one.

`judge_approval` now consumes the window with its own atomic pop rather than
reading it with `get` and consuming it with `forget_pause` several statements
later. The check and the claim are one step, as CLAUDE.md requires of anything
that can turn into an order: with them apart, two utterances interleaved between
the read and the consume were both told yes.

What is deliberately unchanged: a question asked while an order is read back
still leaves the window open, because the trader is still deciding about that
order. `test_conversation_near_a_pending_order_is_not_an_approval` pins it and
a new test states it in its own right so it is not lost.

Four of the six new tests fail without these changes and pass with them,
verified by reverting the source and keeping the tests. The other two pin
behaviour that already held and now has a name.

feat: store and serve OpenScript studies for the trading chart (#2084)

* feat: store and serve OpenScript studies for the trading chart

Adds strategies/openscript, where a trader's OpenScript studies live,
and the routes /trading will use to list, read, write and delete
them. Nothing is reachable from the interface yet; the editor panel
and the compile-and-plot path follow.

An OpenScript file is not a custom indicator with a different
extension, and the difference is the reason for a second folder
rather than a wider rule on the first. A custom indicator is
JavaScript the page imports and runs, so it has the session, the API
and the origin, which docs/custom-indicators.md says plainly and
correctly. An OpenScript file is text a compiler turns into a list of
instructions an engine walks. A script can only name what the
instruction set gives it, so there is no spelling for a network call
or a reach into the page: nothing was handed over, so there is
nothing to escape from. A study from a stranger can draw a wrong
line. It cannot place an order.

That is also why the read route sets text/plain and never a
JavaScript type. A response the page could import would hand a
trader's file the page's own authority and undo the whole reason for
the format. There is a test for the mimetype, because the obvious
edit is to copy the indicator route beside it.

The security policy needs no change. csp.py allows scripts from this
origin and nothing that builds code out of text, so a language
compiling to JavaScript would need unsafe-eval turned on for every
page in the platform. This one compiles to data and runs under the
policy as it stands. No nginx location, port or directive is added
either: everything is under the path already proxied, so a hosted
install upgrades without a config migration.

The folder sits beside strategies/indicators for the same reasons it
does: gitignored, so an upgrade leaves a trader's work alone, and
inside the Docker named volume, so it survives a rebuild.

A save is atomic and keeps a backup. The browser editor will be the
only copy of a script, so a save interrupted partway leaves the
previous study whole rather than half of the new one, and the write
closes the descriptor mkstemp returns even when the wrapper cannot be

* fix: colour the characters the compiler actually saw

The editor painted one word in three colours. A string title came out
part green, part violet, part grey, and the further down the file the
worse it got.

A token's offset is into the source after the compiler has collapsed
line endings, not into the text handed to it. On a file whose lines
end with a carriage return every offset is therefore short by one per
line seen so far, and the error accumulates. Slicing the raw text by
those offsets returns the wrong characters: the word study arrives
carrying the previous line break and missing its own last letters,
and a comment ends mid-word with the remainder painted as code.

The editor now works in the language's own normal form. A script is
normalised when it is read and a paste is normalised as it lands, so
the characters on screen, the offsets the compiler reports and the
colours behind them all count the same way. The rule is taken from
the compiler rather than written here, because it is the language's
and a second copy of it is a second answer. A source that somehow
still is not in that form is handed back unpainted, since every
colour available to it would be on the wrong characters and no colour
is better than a wrong one.

This shipped because the test that should have caught it asserted the
wrong thing. The spans still reconstruct the source exactly when they
are cut in the wrong places, so the coverage property held and the
line-endings case passed while the colours were nonsense. The kinds
were never asserted on such a source. They are now, and the new case
fails against the code this replaces.

trader can act on, once, and is never retried: a queue growing behind a
fired alert is worth less than the next alert arriving on time.

Permission for notifications, and the audio context a browser only starts
inside a gesture, are both taken from the click that arms the alert. That
is the one moment either request explains itself, and the only moment a
browser allows them.

**A chart with an armed alert keeps fetching while its tab is hidden.**
Hiding stopped the poll and the bar-close repair unconditionally. The
stream runs either way, so an alert still evaluated on whatever ticks
arrived, but the two refreshes that correct a bar were gone, and the
default policy is precisely the one that waits for a bar to close. A
chart with nothing armed still stops, which is the saving a background
tab is for.

**Values in the message, filled from the bar that fired it.** Eleven
placeholders, listed in the form with a click to insert one, so a
notification on a locked phone carries the number instead of sending the
trader back to the chart. A placeholder spelled wrong, or one the chart
has no value for, is left exactly as typed: a sentence with a hole in it
reads as a broken alert, and the text as written reads as the typo it is.
A bar with no volume prints the placeholder rather than claiming zero,
because zero volume is a real reading and this is not it.

**And a symbol whose name contains an operator character.** The search
box splits on operators so a half-typed expression can look up its second
leg, which is why `NIFTY/` searches on the empty leg rather than on
nothing. Splitting on `-` as well made BAJAJ-AUTO unsearchable: the box
split into BAJAJ and AUTO, the caret sat in the second, and typing the
hyphen emptied the list. Both the whole box and the leg are searched now
and the results merged, ranked against the whole box when the whole box
names something. Neither query can be dropped: the leg is the only one
that works mid-expression, and the whole box is the only one that finds a
name with an operator inside it.

The same omission is in the engine's own grammar, where SYM_BODY admits
`&` and not `-`. That is why M&M loads and BAJAJ-AUTO does not, and it is
written up for the library in the handover notes.
