* fix(flattrade): recycle a feed that answers heartbeats but sends no ticks

A Noren session can keep acking heartbeats while delivering no market
data. _on_message stamped _last_message_time for every inbound frame
before classifying it, heartbeat acks included, so _check_connection_health
saw a healthy connection and never recycled the socket. The feed stayed
silently dead for the rest of the session: prices frozen on their last
value, position MTM stale, and everything that runs on ticks - scalping
stop losses, sandbox order and GTT triggers, Flow price conditions -
quietly not firing, with the app still reporting a live connection.

Market-data liveness now has its own clock. Frames that are neither auth
acks nor heartbeat acks stamp _last_data_message_time, and
_check_connection_health gained DATA_SILENCE_TIMEOUT alongside the
existing HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT. It closes through the same _close_websocket()
the old path used, so the adapter's existing reconnect recovers.

The arming rule is the delicate part. Flattrade answers every subscribe
with a snapshot frame, so a session opened outside market hours receives
one per subscribed scrip within a second of connecting. Arming on frame
count would then recycle the socket every DATA_SILENCE_TIMEOUT until the
market opened, and Flattrade meets reconnect churn with a server-side
session cooldown - the reason the adapter keeps a persistent session at
all. Arming instead requires frames in DATA_ARM_BUCKETS distinct buckets
of DATA_ARM_BUCKET seconds within DATA_ARM_WINDOW: a burst lands in one
bucket however large it is, while a live feed clears three in about a
minute. Arming is per connection, so a market that closes while armed
costs exactly one recycle and the replacement starts disarmed.

Reported as issue #2075. The socket-level evidence in that report points
at a different subsystem - the CLOSE-WAIT descriptors are Meta addresses
(RIPE FB-BLOCK), not Flattrade, whose endpoint sits behind Cloudflare -
but the silent freeze it describes is real and is this.

test/test_flattrade_data_silence_watchdog.py covers it: 6 of its 7 tests
fail without the change. Most of them pin the arming rule, since that is
where a wrong guess costs a broker session rather than a stale price.

The same pattern exists in the Shoonya, Tradesmart, Zebu and Definedge
adapters and is not addressed here.

fix(trading): chart a hyphenated symbol, and fire alerts when the price is reached (#2091)

* fix(trading): let a hyphenated symbol be typed, picked and charted

The earlier fix decided "is this an instrument or arithmetic" by
comparing the box to a row's bare symbol. That left two holes, and the
reported failure went through both.

`NSE:BAJAJ-AUTO` is the form this dialog writes back into the box
itself, and it did not equal the bare `BAJAJ-AUTO`, so the click spliced
rather than loaded. Once anything had been spliced on, the box read
`BAJAJ-NSE:BAJAJ-AUTO`, which names nothing, so every later click
spliced again and the search fell back to the leg: the reported screen
offered NIFTYAUTO and BSEAUTO for a box that was trying to say
BAJAJ-AUTO, with no way back to it.

So the question is no longer asked of the string. `BAJAJ-AUTO` is a
subtraction to any parser and an instrument to everybody else, and
`NIFTY-BANKNIFTY` is the same shape and genuinely a spread; no amount of
reading the text separates them. What separates them is whether an
instrument of that name exists, which the search has already answered by
the time anybody can click. A box that names a real instrument is not an
expression, whatever its hyphens look like, and nothing is ever appended
to it.

A hyphenated symbol spliced into a real expression is now quoted.
Unquoted, `NSE:BAJAJ-AUTO` inside an expression parses as `NSE:BAJAJ`
minus `AUTO`, two instruments that do not exist; quoting is the chart
grammar's own escape and keeps the exchange prefix, so
`'NSE:BAJAJ-AUTO'/NIFTY` resolves as written. Verified against the
library's parser rather than assumed. Only hyphenated names are quoted,
so nobody is left wondering what the quotes around RELIANCE mean.

* fix(trading): stop folding a hyphenated instrument into arithmetic

BAJAJ-AUTO still would not chart after the search-box fix, and the
search box was never the last word. Verified against the running
platform: the chart asked the history API for BAJAJ and then for AUTO,
and got "Symbol 'BAJAJ' not found for exchange 'NSE'" both times. The
symbol search resolved the instrument correctly and the terminal passed
it down correctly; it was taken apart one layer below both.

Every history load goes through ExpressionFeed, and it decided what to
fold by reading the name: `isChartExpression('BAJAJ-AUTO')` is true,
because `isPlainSymbol` says no and the grammar parses it as a
subtraction. So the one feed every chart depends on split the instrument

and never can, being several instruments on possibly different venues,
which is why its legs resolve against a default; one instrument always
carries its own. `loadExpression` already sends `exchange: ''`, so the
request has always known the answer. That also makes the `req.exchange`
fallback for legs dead, and it is removed rather than left to imply a
shape that can no longer arrive.

The same rule now guards `loadSymbol`, so a pick that names an exchange
is never re-read as arithmetic on the way in either.

Ranking: an exact match on what was typed now outranks category.
Category is the right tie-break between near matches and the wrong one
between a near match and the answer, so BAJAJ-AUTO sat fourth under
NIFTY EV, NIFTYAUTO and BSEAUTO, and Enter charted an index.

charts, and RELIANCE/BHEL still folds.

* fix(flattrade): recycle a feed that answers heartbeats but sends no ticks

A Noren session can keep acking heartbeats while delivering no market
data. _on_message stamped _last_message_time for every inbound frame
before classifying it, heartbeat acks included, so _check_connection_health
saw a healthy connection and never recycled the socket. The feed stayed
silently dead for the rest of the session: prices frozen on their last
value, position MTM stale, and everything that runs on ticks - scalping
stop losses, sandbox order and GTT triggers, Flow price conditions -
quietly not firing, with the app still reporting a live connection.

Market-data liveness now has its own clock. Frames that are neither auth
acks nor heartbeat acks stamp _last_data_message_time, and
_check_connection_health gained DATA_SILENCE_TIMEOUT alongside the
existing HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT. It closes through the same _close_websocket()
the old path used, so the adapter's existing reconnect recovers.

The arming rule is the delicate part. Flattrade answers every subscribe
with a snapshot frame, so a session opened outside market hours receives
one per subscribed scrip within a second of connecting. Arming on frame
count would then recycle the socket every DATA_SILENCE_TIMEOUT until the
market opened, and Flattrade meets reconnect churn with a server-side
session cooldown - the reason the adapter keeps a persistent session at
all. Arming instead requires frames in DATA_ARM_BUCKETS distinct buckets
of DATA_ARM_BUCKET seconds within DATA_ARM_WINDOW: a burst lands in one
bucket however large it is, while a live feed clears three in about a
minute. Arming is per connection, so a market that closes while armed
costs exactly one recycle and the replacement starts disarmed.

Reported as issue #2075. The socket-level evidence in that report points
at a different subsystem - the CLOSE-WAIT descriptors are Meta addresses
(RIPE FB-BLOCK), not Flattrade, whose endpoint sits behind Cloudflare -
but the silent freeze it describes is real and is this.

test/test_flattrade_data_silence_watchdog.py covers it: 6 of its 7 tests
fail without the change. Most of them pin the arming rule, since that is
where a wrong guess costs a broker session rather than a stale price.

The same pattern exists in the Shoonya, Tradesmart, Zebu and Definedge
adapters and is not addressed here.

check gained a DATA_SILENCE_TIMEOUT beside the existing heartbeat
timeout. Arming follows #2089: frames in three distinct 30-second
buckets within five minutes, so the snapshot burst Noren sends when
scrips are subscribed outside market hours cannot arm it and a session

costs one recycle and the replacement starts quiet.

Noren doc's ack is "hk", so an "hk" ack fell through to the market-data
path. Harmless while nothing read it, but under the watchdog it would
count as a tick and keep a dead feed looking alive. Both now close the
socket outside the heartbeat lock as well, matching Flattrade.

Definedge is shaped differently and the fix lands in different places.
It classifies message types inline in _on_message rather than behind a
helper, so the data clock is stamped in the four market-data branches
(tk/tf/dk/df) - more precise than "everything that is not internal",
since a connect, subscription or unsubscribe ack cannot be mistaken for

and its settings follow that file's lowercase instance-attribute style.

type log and still refreshed the stall clock, which is the same defect
arrived at differently.

Firstock was checked and is not affected: it keeps no application-level
liveness clock, judging the connection by websocket pong alone. That
leaves it with no tick-silence detection rather than a broken one, which
is a separate gap and not addressed here.

docs: write down the words this platform uses, and the ones it does not (#2097)

Two of these had already been fixed once each, which is the argument for
writing them down: release 2.0.1.0 renamed "virtual/paper trading" to
sandbox, and the word "armed" was taken out of /trading earlier today
and then found again on /strategy, in the Python strategy guide, in the
run log and in a scheduled-start toast. A word that comes back costs the
rename a second time.

Sandbox mode and analyzer mode are the platform's words. The schema has
said so since before the rename: sandbox.db, blueprints/sandbox.py,
/api/v1/sandbox/*, and RUN_MODES = ("live", "sandbox"). Three words for
two ideas is how somebody ships a strategy believing it is safe.

Arm, armed and arming appear nowhere a trader reads. An alert is Active
or Stopped, a toggle is on or off, a destination is Live or Sandbox.
Internal identifiers and library state names are not covered, because
nobody trading reads those; the moment one reaches a screen it is.

And the rule underneath both, which is what stops this recurring when
another project is hosted here: a specification's internal vocabulary is
not this platform's vocabulary. OpenScript's own spec says "paper" for
the simulated destination and "arming" for the switch to live, and those
words stay in that spec. On a screen here they are Sandbox and Live.

* wip(openscript): strategy runner, NOT WIRED AND NOT WORKING

Preserved on a branch so the work is not lost. Do not merge this. The routes do
not function and the tests that cover them pass against a stub whose method
names do not match the service, which is why nothing caught it.

What is here and is worth keeping:
- services/openscript_runner_service.py, a process registry and lifecycle modelled
  on blueprints/python_strategy.py: start_run, stop_run, status_of, running_runs,
  reap_finished_runs, stop_every_run, with logs under the platform's own
  log/strategies path.
- strategies/scripts/openscript_runner.py, the child program: loads a stored
  compiled program through the engine host surface, drives execute_bar bar by bar
  with checkpoint and restore across a moving bar, and places orders through the
  platform SDK so they pass place_order_with_auth. It never passes force_live and
  adds no bypass of the analyzer toggle.
- blueprints/openscript.py now stores the compiled program the browser produced
  beside the source, which is the thing that makes a server-side run possible at
  all: the engine has no compiler and the container has no JavaScript runtime.

Confirmed broken, each reproduced:
- The blueprint resolves the service by guessing names from a tuple.
  _STATUS_NAMES holds none of the names the service defines, so status and stop
  answer 503 and a running strategy cannot be stopped over HTTP.
- start calls start_run with the filename alone; start_run takes four arguments.
  Every start raises TypeError. Underneath that is a design hole rather than a
  slip: the start route accepts no body, so it has no way to say which symbol,
  exchange or interval a run is for. How a run learns its instrument is undecided.
- The blueprint is never registered in app.py, so none of the routes exist.
- test_openscript_runner_routes.py stubs a service with start(filename),
  stop(filename) and status(). The real one has different names and arity, so all
  37 route tests pass over the seam that is broken.
- reap_finished_runs has no caller, so a run that ends by itself stays in the
  registry and that script can never be started again for the life of the worker.
- The child passes supplied as the window length while the index grows, so
  bar.isLast is permanently false once the rolling window drops its first day.
- The run's timezone is put in the instrument record as Asia/Kolkata, but the
  engine reads only UTC, so a script that reads the clock is silently answered
  absence on every bar instead of being refused before it starts.
- The child program lives under strategies/, which docker-compose mounts as a
  named volume. Docker seeds a named volume from the image only when it is empty,
  so this file is absent on every existing containerised install after an upgrade.
- _place sends a bar's intents one at a time with no compensation, so a bar whose
  call produced two orders can leave one side sent and the other not. A reversal
  is close plus open, so this is reachable and it is money.

Two decisions were deferred rather than taken, correctly:
- A script using exit() or order.bracket() is refused before it starts, because
  pairing a stop and a target is an OCO and this platform has no single call that
  sends one with the other cancelling on fill.
- A run begins flat after replaying history, so a strategy whose history would
  have left it long starts flat instead.

Nothing here can place a live order: there is no route, field or flag that
switches a strategy to live. Where an order goes is decided by the platform-wide
analyzer setting at the moment it is sent.

* feat(openscript): the three fixes, and a guard in place of force_live

NO force_live, decided. This runner sends through the platform's own order path
and never asks to bypass the analyzer toggle. That decision has a consequence the
platform documents in place_order_service.py: the destination is read per order,
so an operator turning the analyzer on while a strategy holds a position would
send that strategy's exits to the sandbox while the broker still holds what its
entries opened, and both calls report success.

Rather than leave that silent, the run watches for it. The destination of the
first accepted order is remembered, every later order is checked against it, and a
run whose destination changes underneath it stops at once and says so in its log,
naming what is open. It does not try to put the position back: the entry is where
it is, and a run that can no longer reason about what it holds should send nothing
further. Five tests cover it and all four mutations of it go red, including
removing the guard, warning without stopping, and reading the wrong mode marker.
One of them is a check on the source itself: no line of this runner may pass
force_live.

THE THREE FIXES.

Nothing swept finished runs. reap_finished_runs had no caller anywhere in the
application, so on a headless deployment a run that ended by itself stayed in the
registry and that script could never be started again for the life of the worker.
It is now an interval job on the platform's own scheduler.

The first attempt to restore schedules was the only attempt. restore_schedules
set its flag before doing any work, so a worker that imported the module before
the scheduler was running burned it: every schedule failed into the log and
nothing tried again, and a scheduled strategy silently never ran. The flag is set
on success now, and a failure leaves it down for the next call. Registering the
reaper is explicitly not allowed to cost the restoration, because a run left in
the registry is cleared by the next read of it while a schedule that was never
restored is a strategy that never runs.

On Windows a stop killed the run mid-bar. Popen.terminate there is
TerminateProcess, which is the forced step under a gentler name, while the
docstring promised the run finishes the bar it is on. The child is already spawned
into a process group of its own, so the gentle step is now a console break it can
handle, and it handles SIGBREAK beside SIGTERM. Killing is what happens if that is
refused, not what happens first.

Also: the stub scheduler in the route tests was narrower than the real one and
rejected an interval job, which made the module look broken when it was the fake
that was. A stub narrower than the thing it replaces is the same defect class as
the stub that hid the broken seam last week.

200 tests pass.

feat(trading): backtest a strategy from the right rail, beside the editor (#2102)

* feat(trading): backtest a strategy from the right rail, beside the editor

A trader could write an OpenScript strategy, compile it and run it live in
sandbox, and could not ask what it would have done. The engine and every figure
in its report have been finished and specified for some time; what was missing
was somewhere to press the button.

NO SERVER CALL BEYOND FETCHING BARS. The engine that runs a compiled program is
the package this page already imports to compile one, and it is arithmetic over
data with no dependency of its own. The browser holds the program because it
compiled it, and can fetch bars because the chart does it constantly, so a
backtest is a function call rather than a service. Running a strategy LIVE is a
different problem for different reasons, and that half is already server side: a
tab that closes must not stop a position.

ON THE UI THREAD, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. The engine costs about 30ms over
a thousand bars, 68ms over five thousand and 211ms over twenty thousand, which
is under a click's worth of delay. It reaches 1.3 seconds at a hundred thousand,
so a run past MAX_BARS is refused with the count rather than freezing the
workspace. A worker is the way past that ceiling and has to be a served file
rather than a blob, because this application's policy allows scripts from its
own origin and nothing else.

THE CURVE IS DRAWN WITH THIS PLATFORM'S OWN ENGINE, driven the way CandleViz
drives it: createChart on a host div, the app's theme tokens through
buildChartTheme, a dynamic import so a trader who never opens the panel never
pays for the bundle, and one instance created and destroyed per mount. Equity
and drawdown share one time axis as two panes rather than two charts, because
the first thing a reader does is look down from a peak to the trough under it.
Drawdown keeps the sign the record carries, so the worst moment of a run is at
the bottom of its own pane.

The instrument and the interval are the chart's and are read at the moment Run
is pressed, not held as props: a backtest of something other than what the
trader is looking at is the one result they will misread. Only strategies are
listed, because a study places no orders and has no report.

THREE THINGS THAT FAIL WITHOUT THROWING, each caught by a test that was checked
by breaking the code:

The history API counts seconds and the engine counts milliseconds. Unconverted,
every bar lands in 1970, the report window excludes all of them, and the run
answers a summary of nothing while looking fine.

Absence is not zero. Number(null) is 0 and Number.isFinite(0) is true, so
reading a point through a bare coercion placed a timeless bar at the epoch and
drew a missing equity at zero. My first implementation of the chart had exactly
this and the test caught it.

backtest answers a union, not a record: it can refuse a run before its first bar
over a cost model stated twice or a quantity it cannot size. Reading .record off
that refusal is undefined and would have shown a report of nothing. The
typechecker found this one.

Tick and lot size are read from the platform rather than assumed, and when the
instrument has no stored row the panel says which defaults the money rests on.
Every figure in money depends on them, so a guess is wrong by a factor with a
report that reads perfectly.

19 tests. 2691 frontend tests pass, tsc and biome clean.

* fix(zerodha): address review findings on the MCX units conversion

Eleven findings across three review rounds. Grouped by what went wrong.

Sizing an underlying MCX has revised
------------------------------------
MCX halved MCXBULLDEX with the November 2026 contract, so 30 and 15 are
both live at once -- confirmed against Angel One's scrip master, which
carries 30 for 25SEP2026 and 28OCT2026 and 15 for 27NOV2026 and
30DEC2026. A table keyed on the underlying alone cannot express that.

The conversion factor now comes from the master contract row, which is
per contract and therefore already right for every expiry. That is not
merely a better source but the only correct one: OpenAlgo builds an order
as lots * symtoken.lotsize and this adapter divides it back to contracts,
so any other number turns a correct request into a wrong order. The
static table became expiry-aware for master-contract generation, and is
now only the fallback.

Where the fallback cannot answer -- a revised underlying with no master
row -- it no longer guesses. The symbol cannot disambiguate the expiry
either, because Kite writes MCXBULLDEX26NOV30000CE (year, month, strike)
where OpenAlgo writes MCXBULLDEX27NOV2630000CE (day, month, year,
strike), and no pattern separates them. So an outbound conversion refuses
and an inbound one passes the quantity through unscaled.

A stale install degrades safely: before the master contract is rebuilt
lotsize is Kite's 1, so lots * 1 = 1 and dividing by 1 sends one
contract -- exactly the behaviour that predates this work.

Contract size is not a price multiplier
---------------------------------------
Valuation used the physical contract size, which is only the multiplier
where a commodity is quoted in the unit it trades in. GOLDGUINEA is 8
grams quoted per 8 grams and GOLDM is 100 grams quoted per 10 grams, so a
rupee move on one contract was reported as 8 and 100 rupees. GOLDGUINEA
was a regression on behaviour that had been correct.

Funds P&L now uses Kite's own position multiplier, which is authoritative
and arrives with the positionbook. The tradebook has no such field, so it
uses a quotation-multiplier table covering the gold family, the base
metals and three agricultural contracts; everything else quotes in the
unit it trades in and its lot size already is the multiplier. Each entry
is annotated `contract size / quotation unit` and a test re-derives every
value from its own comment, because the first version of that table had a
correct number under a comment describing a different contract.

Errors that did not reach the caller
------------------------------------
A quantity that is not a whole number of contracts was reaching the
service layer as a raised exception, which its blanket handler reported
as "internal error" with a 500 and an order-failed event. Place, modify,
smart order, basket margin and GTT now return 400 naming the reason, each
in the return shape its own service unpacks -- place hands back a
response object, modify hands back a status code, and returning the wrong
arity raises inside the service and produces the same 500 this exists to
avoid.

A bad leg in a margin basket was caught by an existing catch-and-skip
handler, so the remaining legs were priced and returned with a 200 as
though they were the basket asked for. It now refuses the request.

Decisions made on a quantity that could not be sized
----------------------------------------------------
Treating an unresolved size as a factor of 1 is safe when reading an
orderbook for display and dangerous when the number decides whether to
trade. Thirty held contracts read as thirty units against a thirty unit
target matched exactly, and the smart order reported "position already
matched" while 450 units sat open. Reading an open position now refuses
rather than guessing.

Close-all ignored the result of every exit it placed and always reported
"All Open Positions SquaredOff" with a 200. A refused exit leaves the
position open, and saying otherwise stops anyone watching it. It now
collects failures and names the symbols still held. That swallowed error
predates this work; the new sizing rejection is what made it reachable.

Also: CARDAMOM is mapped at 100 from Angel One's master, closing the last
underlying where the same quantity meant different things on the two
brokers; a null `name` no longer aborts the whole master contract refresh
(NaN is truthy, so a falsiness check passed it to .strip(), and Kite
ships thousands of blank names on other segments); and the quotation
lookup resolves the full underlying before matching, so GOLDPETAL is no
longer read as GOLD and valued as a kilo.

Verified against the live Kite dump: MCXBULLDEX 30 for Sep/Oct and 15 for
Nov/Dec, CRUDEOIL 100, CARDAMOM 100, NFO NIFTY unchanged at 65. The
complete table agrees with Angel One's scrip master on all 30 rows.

feat(trading): one strategy deployed on many instruments, with pause, stop and restart (#2103)

A run used to be identified by its script, so a strategy could be deployed
once, a second start was refused as already running, and two runs of one file
shared an order tag: each one's book listed the other's orders. The unit is
now a deployment, which is a script, the instrument it runs on and the bar it
runs on. The id is minted in one place, because the registry key, the log
name and the order tag have to agree, and it is bounded because the column
the tag is stored in is. A name that does not say which deployment is refused
rather than guessed.

Pause and Stop are separate: Pause ends the process and leaves the position,
Stop closes what the run holds and then ends it. The closing is the run's
own, because only it knows its own size, and a close that did not happen
leaves the run registered and still holding.

A bar now closes on the tick stream rather than when history catches up,
which was measured at about thirty five seconds late and came off every fill.
A strategy a trader left running comes back after a restart, adopting a
still-live orphan rather than starting a second beside it. A deployment's
instrument, exchange, interval and product are picked from what the platform
knows rather than typed, and a deployment can be removed, which takes its
schedule with it and is refused while it runs.

Three defects found rather than reported: every deployment showed the
account's profit as its own; switching between live and analyzer silently
killed every idle strategy; and the test suite wrote a trader's own strategy
state, so running it cleared the record of every live strategy.

No schema changes and no migration. The run settings file changed key and is
read forward, verified against a file written in the previous version's
shape: every field preserved and nothing rewritten.

fix: a deployment made where another was removed is not that one (#2106)

The id was worked out from the script, the instrument, the exchange and the
interval alone, so removing a deployment and making another like it produced
the same id again. Every book is a filter on that id, because it is the tag
each order carries, so the new deployment inherited the old one's orders,
fills and position: a strategy deployed a minute ago opened showing a day of
trades it never made, and a position it does not hold.

Those four parts say what a deployment runs. They do not say which
deployment it is. A new one is now minted with a token of its own, kept in
its settings, so two deployments that look alike are still two. Six
hexadecimal characters, which leaves the id readable: it is what a trader
sees in the global orderbook, not an internal key.

Three things fall out of that and all three are the same rule.

A deployment made before tokens existed keeps the id it already has. Its
orders carry that tag and its books are the answer to what it did, so
deriving a fresh one for it would hand its whole history to nobody.

Changing a deployment's instrument or interval makes another rather than
moving that one, which is what the form already promised. Keeping the id
would leave the new instrument showing the old one's orders.

And a run wears its deployment's own id rather than minting one from the
four parts. That was the same defect one layer down: a run tagged with a
derived id would have traded all day into a book nothing was looking at.

Deploying the same script on the same instrument and interval twice is now
refused in words. It was impossible before only because both collapsed onto
one key; two of them are two runs, two positions, and a trader who believes
they have one.

Two defects in the same twenty lines, found while chasing "WhatsApp alert
is not sent" from /trading.

The reason was thrown away. `post` returned a boolean, so every refusal
arrived as one hardcoded sentence: "Check that a device is paired under

server's own sentence is now what the trader reads, and status codes
still never appear.

WhatsApp was started, and whatsapp/notify defaults wait_for_delivery to
true, so an alert asking for both paid the whole Telegram round trip
first. On a price being reached that delay is the thing an alert exists
to beat, and it grows with every channel. Nothing there depends on
anything else there, which is why one refusing never stopped the next,
so they now go together under allSettled.

Both tests fail against the old code, which is the only reason to
believe them: the concurrency one with "expected [telegram] to have a
length of 2", the message one with "expected ... to contain 'Username
not found or not linked to WhatsApp'". The fetch stub could not carry a
reason at all, which is how a whole class of wrong message stayed
invisible; it can now.

This does not make an unlinked account deliver. On the instance this was
reported from, whatsapp_users and telegram_users are both empty, so both
channels answer 404 and both alerts correctly reach nobody. What changes
is that the trader is now told which thing to go and fix.

The previous commit refused a self send when no owner JID had been
captured. That was wrong and it blocked the one path that works.

The comment it was written from describes wars 0.1.3. The library
installed is 0.1.4, whose send documents `wa.send("Hello there")` as
"text to owner" among its calling shapes and raises ValueError when no
owner is configured, so a failure there is loud rather than silent. The
playground has been delivering through exactly that form on this install
the whole time, with own_jid empty.

Refusing it also had no way back. own_jid is captured from the first
is_from_me message, and 0.1.4 exposes no own_jid, self_jid or my_jid to
ask for, which is why the probe at pair time has always come back with
nothing. So an install that had paired and not yet received an inbound
message could never self send at all.

Measured after the revert, through the endpoint, username rajandran,
whatsapp_users still empty and own_jid still empty: HTTP 200, sent
["<self>"], and wars returned message id 3EB00FEBB5131208E46F9B.

What stands from the previous commit is the part that was actually
wrong: the paired owner now resolves as a recipient without a /link, and
a send that reached nobody answers with an error status instead of
success. Both were verified again after this change.

fix: keep notify's HTTP code where callers already expect it, and pin the shape

A send that reached nobody was answering 502. The `status` field being
wrong was the defect worth fixing, and it is fixed; the transport code
was mine to add and should not have been.

This endpoint is public with a large installed base nobody here can
survey. Those callers were mishandling a `status` that lied to them;
they should not also have to start handling a 5xx this path has never
returned, which is a new outage for anything that raises on non-2xx or
retries on 5xx. The request was accepted and processed, which is what
200 says, and what became of it is in the body, which is where this API
puts every other outcome. So the change now reaches a caller through the
field they read.

Unchanged, and now pinned by tests rather than by review:

- a delivered send answers 200, "success", "Delivered to N, failed M"
  and the per-recipient report under data, wording included
- a partly delivered send is still a success; only a report with NO
  deliveries reads as an error
- self, phone, phones and username are all still accepted, the owner
  fallback having been added inside the username branch without
  displacing the other three
- an unknown username is still a 404, so the fallback is additive: it
  only catches what already failed
- wait_for_delivery=false still answers with its own queued shape

Measured against the running instance, all eight refusal paths byte for
byte as before: 401 twice, 400 five times, 404 once, each with status
error and its original sentence.

chore(release): bump platform to 2.0.2.6 and add release notes

48 commits since 2.0.2.5, excluding the automated frontend build commits.

The release is themed on OpenScript and chart alerts. OpenScript arrives on
/trading as a language for studies and strategies: written in a panel on the
chart, compiled on every save, backtested in the browser beside the editor,
and run on the server as one deployment per instrument and interval, with
Pause, Stop and restart. Chart alerts gain per-alert channels, a log that
survives the tab, and firing at the price rather than at bar close. The
charting terminal moves from openalgo-charts 2.2.0 to 2.5.1.

Zerodha MCX quantity is now counted in units like every other broker (#1998),
which API callers trading MCX on Zerodha must act on; the notes and the
changelog say so at the top, along with the master contract re-download.

This release requires a database migration: upgrade/migrate_alert_log.py,
registered in migrate_all.py. The notes also record that the openscript
engine is not yet in requirements-nginx.txt, with the manual install for an
Ubuntu server.
